text: summary A multirotor has no control surfaces: all control is a change in motor RPM. The module explains how four six, eight propellers produce throttle, roll, pitch and yaw, why the props spin in different directions, what a mixer is, and why the thrust-to-weight ratio defines the character of a drone. This is the foundation on which PID, filters and all of tuning stand. theory Thrust and weight A propeller throws air downward and gets thrust upward. To hover, the total thrust of all the motors must equal the weight. Thrust grows roughly as the square of RPM: to double the thrust, RPM has to be raised about 1.4 times. The thrust-to-weight ratio T/W is the maximum thrust of all the motors divided by the takeoff weight: - about 2:1 — the minimum for controlled flight: heavy platforms, cargo octocopters; - 3:1–4:1 — calm long-range 7–10"; - 6:1 and above — freestyle and racing. Whoops, 3–3.5" and cinewhoops have no line of their own here; in the “Bands by class” table below they get estimated rows: whoops, toothpicks and 3–3.5" freestyle — like 5" freestyle, cinewhoop — like long range, 3–4. A wing does not hover, and T/W for it is a different quantity: in level flight it needs a thrust of about the weight divided by the lift-to-drag ratio, i.e. less than the weight; the criterion for a wing is thrust in a climb and at cruise speed aero-wing . The threshold for any class is one and the same: this list; f-motors-esc and f-aero-props take their numbers from here. At T/W 2:1 hover takes half the thrust — that is about 65–71 % throttle subsection below , and there is almost no margin for maneuvering and wind gusts. This is the main argument for why a heavy drone cannot be tuned like a five-inch. Hover throttle: what it depends on and what is normal Mechanism. In hover each motor delivers a fraction of its maximum thrust f = 1 / T/W — this follows exactly from the force balance. The throttle u is then greater than f, because thrust grows faster than throttle: RPM is roughly proportional to throttle the ESC applies an average voltage u·U to the motor, f-esc-firmware , and thrust to the square of RPM. If thrust went strictly as u², the hover throttle would be u = √f. The real curve lies between the straight line and the square. ArduPilot describes it as T = 1 − e ·u + e·u², where e is MOT_THST_EXPO 0.65 for a 10", 0.55–0.6 for a 5", ap-tuning ; hence u = − 1 − e + √ 1 − e ² + 4·e·f / 2·e . The arithmetic for T/W 2.5: f = 1 / 2.5 = 0.40; by the square law u = √0.40 = 0.63; by the 0.65 curve: u = −0.35 + √ 0.35² + 4 · 0.65 · 0.40 / 2 · 0.65 = −0.35 + √1.1625 / 1.3 = −0.35 + 1.078 / 1.3 = 0.56. The hover throttle is 56–63 %, even though only 40 % of the thrust is needed. What number the firmware shows. Betaflight and INAV show the throttle u rcCommand 3 , the average motor . ArduPilot MOT_THST_HOVER , CTUN.ThO and PX4 MPC_THR_HOVER show the thrust fraction f before linearization, i.e. ≈ 1 / T/W ap-setup-scratch , px4-setup-scratch . 0.40 in ArduPilot and 40 % in Betaflight are different quantities. Above that throttle there is no margin. - 60 % is the course's stop criterion for the first hover of a 5–7" bf-setup-scratch , inav-setup-scratch : that is T/W 2.25–2.8, which for such aircraft means an error in the mass or the table. For the cargo class this is what normal looks like; its limit is 65–71 %. - Below 20 % — T/W 10–25: the aircraft is very twitchy, low throttle is hard to modulate. Below 12 % a stop in bf-setup-scratch — T/W 19–69, more than any class in the table: more likely a throttle reading error. - Toward the end of the discharge the throttle grows. The band is compared on a full battery; T/W 2.5 turns into 2.5 × 0.84 = 2.1 toward the end of the discharge. Check. The median hover throttle from the log must lie within the band for its T/W, between the thrust fraction f = 1/ T/W and √f for T/W 4.1 from the worked example below — 24–49 %; the 0.65 curve gives a point inside the band, 40 %, not its lower bound . Above the band — the mass is larger than weighed, or the thrust table was measured at a different voltage. Reaction torque and rotation directions A motor spinning up a prop simultaneously tries to turn the frame in the opposite direction — this is the reaction torque. headings: Forces: Newton's second law for a drone Air drag Moments: why an aircraft is “snappy” or “lazy” Equations as a tool Place in the system Step 1. Data Step 2. Mode table Step 3. Moments of inertia Step 4. Cross-check with the log Lab
text: summary “How a multirotor flies” explained the principle; this module turns it into equations you can calculate with. Hover, climb, bank and turn are four force balances that give you numbers: how much thrust and current each mode needs, with what acceleration the aircraft starts moving at a 30° bank, why a heavy aircraft on long arms is “lazy” moment of inertia and lever arm , and why you have to add throttle in a bank to hold altitude. Everything is worked through for a 1.4 kg 7", which is then checked against the log. theory Forces: Newton's second law for a drone The forces acting on the aircraft are: the weight m·g downward, the total thrust T along the aircraft's axis perpendicular to the prop plane , and air drag D against the velocity. Equation of motion: m·a = T + m·g + D as vectors . Four modes: 1. Hover. a = 0, thrust is vertical: T = m·g . For 1.4 kg: T = 1.4 × 9.81 = 13.7 N = 1400 gf. Per motor — 350 gf. This is the very “hover throttle” you see in the log. 2. Climb. To accelerate upward with acceleration a: T = m· g + a + D. Accelerating to 3 m/s in 1 s → a = 3 m/s² → T = 1.4 × 12.8 = 17.9 N 1830 gf, +30% over hover . A steady 3 m/s climb: a = 0, you only need to compensate drag — at that speed D is small ~20 gf with the same C_d = 1.1 and A = 0.03 m² for a 7" , T ≈ m·g + D ≈ 1410–1420 gf. Conclusion: what costs a lot is acceleration , not climb rate. But a propeller in an ascending flow works worse V₀ in the thrust formula grows , and the real throttle in a climb is higher than this estimate gives. 3. Bank or pitch while holding altitude. The aircraft is tilted by an angle φ, and the thrust tilts with it. The vertical component must equal the weight: T·cos φ = m·g → T = m·g / cos φ . The horizontal component accelerates it: m·a = T·sin φ → a = g·tan φ . - φ = 30°: T = 1.155·m·g +15.5% throttle , a = 5.7 m/s². - φ = 45°: T = 1.41·m·g, a = 9.8 m/s² 1 g . - φ = 60°: T = 2·m·g — a T/W of 2:1 is no longer enough to hold altitude. This is why in Angle mode with a 60° tilt limit a drone with T/W 2:1 sinks in sharp maneuvers, and why Betaflight/INAV/ArduPilot have throttle compensation by tilt angle e.g. thr_corr_value Betaflight , throttle_tilt_comp_str INAV , ATC_ANGLE_BOOST ArduPilot in different forms . Tilt throttle compensation: whether to enable it and how much. It only works in self-leveling modes; in Acro no firmware has it — the pilot adds throttle in a bank. How it works according to the source code: Firmware Parameter, default What it does Starting point --- --- --- --- Betaflight 2025.12.5 thr_corr_value 0 off , range 0–150; thr_corr_angle 800 tenths of a degree, 1–900 only in Angle and Horizon while armed: adds to the throttle command scale 0–1000, 1 = 0.1 % of travel thr_corr_value × the sine of the tilt relative to thr_corr_angle flight/imu.c ; the addition does not depend on throttle, and per the code at thr_corr_angle it is about 0.6 × thr_corr_value the comment in fc/core.c : “40 for FPV” at an angle of 45.0° — clearly too little: at a hover throttle of 40 % a 30° bank needs about +4 % of travel, and 40 gives 1.6 %; closer — about 100 with thr_corr_angle 450 course estimate: 100 × 0.41 ≈ 41 units = 4.1 % INAV 9.1.0 throttle_tilt_comp_str 0 off , 0–100 % in Angle and Horizon the throttle above idle is multiplied by 1 + 1/cos φ − 1 × str/100, cos φ is limited to 0.6 about 53° fc/fc_core.c ; in navigation modes the firmware enables 100 % by itself course estimate: 50 — str 100 multiplies throttle, not thrust, and because thrust is nonlinear it overcompensates: at a hover throttle of 40 % and a 30° bank you need about 44 % throttle curve 0.65, f-physics , str 100 gives 46 %, str 50 — 43 % ArduPilot 4.7 ATC_ANGLE_BOOST 1 on throttle × 1/cos of the current body tilt _thrust_angle_rad from thrust_vector_rotation_angles , AC_AttitudeControl.cpp , cos is limited from below to 0.1; above 60° the addition smoothly decreases to zero at 90° inverted_factor ; in Stabilize and in altitude-holding modes, not in Acro AC_AttitudeControl_Multi.cpp leave the default Course rule: Acro 5" — don't touch it it has no effect ; Angle for a beginner, cinewhoop and filming in Angle — enable it from the starting value; ArduPilot — leave it at 1. Check: in Angle, a 30° bank with the throttle stick held still — the altitude in the log baro or GPS or against an object of known height holds; the aircraft sinks — raise the value in Betaflight the addition is small: 40 at a 30° bank with thr_corr_angle 450 gives about 1.6 % of travel, at 45° and steeper — 2.4 %, while a 30° bank at a 40 % hover throttle needs about +4 %; hence the starting point of about 100 , it climbs — lower it. 4. Turn coordinated turn . The centripetal acceleration v²/r comes from the horizontal component of thrust: m·v²/r = m·g·tan φ → r = v² / g·tan φ . 15 m/s at a 30° bank: r = 225 / 5.66 = 40 m. To make a 20 m radius at the same speed you need a 49° bank and throttle ×1.52. Air drag D = ½·ρ·C_d·A·v² , ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, A — frontal area, C_d ≈ 1.0–1.3 for a “box with arms”. A 7" with a frontal area of 0.03 m² at 20 m/s: D = 0.5 × 1.225 × 1.1 × 0.03 × 400 = 8 N — more than half its weight! That is why the maximum horizontal speed is limited: at a tilt φ the drag is balanced by T·sin φ, and there is no further acceleration. Falling: at D = m·g the aircraft reaches its terminal velocity v_t = √ 2·m·g / ρ·C_d·A ; for our example ≈ 26 m/s — the speed at which it will hit the ground if all motors fail at a great height. Moments: why an aircraft is “snappy” or “lazy” Rotation about an axis is set by the moment M = ΔT·L : the thrust difference between opposite motors ΔT multiplied by the lever arm L the distance from the motor to the axis . Angular acceleration α = M / I , where I is the moment of inertia I = Σ mᵢ·rᵢ² the mass of each part times the square of its distance to the axis . - Mass at the ends of the arms motors, props is expensive: r² grows fast. 4 motors of 35 g on 15 cm arms give I = 4 × 0.035 × 0.15² ≈ 0.0032 kg·m²

text: summary The bridge between “how it flies” and “power circuit design”. Without it, people repeat other people's decisions: they fit a capacitor because “that's how it's done” and don't understand why the BEC is hot. The module gives you the minimum you need to calculate: Ohm's law, power, series and parallel connection, the thrust → power → current → sag chain worked through with formulas, safe multimeter use, and the LiPo handling rules — charging, storage, damage, fire. theory Three quantities and two formulas - Voltage U volts — the “pressure” in the circuit. A 4S battery — 14.8 V nominal, 16.8 V full. - Current I amps — the “flow”. A 5" motor at full throttle — 30–40 A. - Resistance R ohms — what impedes the flow. A motor winding — fractions of an ohm, a wire — milliohms. Ohm's law: U = I·R. If 60 A flows through a resistance of 10 mΩ wire + connector , 0.6 V drops across it. Power P = U·I = I²·R = U²/R watts . The same 60 A through 10 mΩ — 36 W of heat in the wire and connector. That is why current is the main enemy: losses grow with the square of the current. Series and parallel - Series S : voltages add up, the same current flows through all cells. 6 cells of 3.7 V = 22.2 V 6S . Resistances add up too. - Parallel P : the current splits, the voltage is the same, capacities add up. 4 cells of 3 Ah = 12 Ah 4P ; the internal resistance is divided by 4. 18650 cells of 3 Ah and 30 mΩ in a 6S4P pack: 22.2 V, 12 Ah, R_int = 30 × 6 / 4 = 45 mΩ. The chain from thrust to sag 1. The thrust you need is T from mechanics: m·g in hover . 2. From the motor's table: thrust → power P_mech and current I_motor at voltage U. 3. Battery current ≈ ΣI_motors + loads ESCs pass current through, they don't multiply it; but at partial throttle the battery current is lower than the motor phase current — the ESC works as a step-down converter . 4. Sag ΔU = I· R_int_batt + R_wires + R_connectors . Under load U_onboard = U_open − ΔU. 5. The power the battery delivers: P = U_onboard·I; the losses P_loss = I²·R_total — heat up the battery and wires. Example: a 10" cargo craft, 4 × 5 A = 20 A in hover, R_int of a 6S Li-Ion 4P battery 45 mΩ, wires and XT60 15 mΩ → ΔU = 20 × 0.06 = 1.2 V, losses 24 W. At full throttle 100 A → ΔU = 6 V ! and 600 W of losses — Li-Ion is not for racing. Energy and capacity Capacity in Ah or mAh — how much current for how many hours. Energy Wh = Ah × U_nom. 6S 4 Ah = 88.8 Wh. At an average power of 300 W — 0.3 h = 18 min in theory, ~14 taking into account the usable 80%. C rating — the maximum current as a multiple of capacity: 4 Ah × 25C = 100 A. Real values are often lower than the marking; look at the sag under load. How to choose a pack the rule — in f-power , “Capacity and C rating” : capacity — by the average current, Q ≥ I_avg × t / 60 × 0.8 ; label C × Q ≥ I_peak — only a filter; the cell resistance decides: the sag I_peak × R_cell on a fresh pack is no more than 0.5 V, i.e. R_cell ≤ 0.5 / I_peak. Multimeter: what and how - Voltage V⎓ : probes in parallel with what you measure; black in COM, red in V. Almost always safe. Checking a battery: the total and each cell through the balance connector spread thresholds — one line in f-power , “Charging, storage, disposal”: after charging ≤ 0.02 V, after a flight ≤ 0.05 V, after charging and resting more than 0.05 V — retire it . - Continuity • : only on a de-energized circuit. A beep between + and − of the power bus = a short circuit. On a circuit with a capacitor the beep may be short, then the resistance rises — that is normal. - Resistance Ω : de-energized. Motor windings — three identical values 0.05–0.3 Ω; a cheap multimeter will show noise — what matters is that they are the same . A difference — an inter-turn short. - Current A : probes in series , red in the 10 A jack; above 10 A — not allowed the fuse or the meter will burn . The main beginner mistake: leaving the probe in the A jack and measuring voltage — that is a short circuit through the meter. On-board current is measured with the FC's current sensor calibrated or with an inline wattmeter. - Diode test : checks diodes and junctions — will be useful later. LiPo: rules that are not up for discussion - Per-cell voltages: full 4.20 V HV — 4.35 , nominal 3.7, storage about 3.8 3.80–3.90 per the manufacturer's datasheet, f-power , under load warning at 3.5 and critical threshold at 3.3 Betaflight defaults for 4–6S; for 1S and Li-Ion the thresholds differ — table in f-power , below 3.0 — damage. - Charging : only with a balance charger, current ≤ 1C 4 Ah → 4 A unless the manufacturer allows more; in a LiPo bag or on a non-flammable surface; never leave it unattended; do not charge it cold or hot: the limit is per the pack's datasheet Gens Ace allows charging at 10–45 °C, f-power . - Storage : at storage voltage, somewhere cool, not full for longer than a day — it loses capacity and swells. - Damage : swelling, a puncture, a smell — the battery never flies again. Discharge it to 0 through a load a discharger or a resistor; not salt water — procedure in f-power and dispose of it properly. A crashed drone → the battery goes to an open, non-flammable spot for 30 minutes. - Fire : LiPo burns on its own and is hard to extinguish. Plan ahead: a bucket of sand, a place to throw it, don't breathe the smoke. A lot of water cools it and is acceptable for LiPo there is no metallic lithium in it , but the best tool is prevention: correct charging, inspection, a LiPo bag. - Short circuit : the short-circuit current is hundreds of amps, a connector welds in a fraction of a second. Solder the power connector one pin at a time, insulate your tools, don't put an XT60 on metal. {{diagram:thrust-sag-chain The chain from thrust to sag: more thrust — more current, a bigger drop across the internal resistance, lower voltage under load.}} Place in the system - Receives: thrust in hover and in maneuvers f-mechanics ; the motor current at that thrust — from the thrust table f-aero-props . - Provides: batter

text: summary The battery is the heaviest and the most dangerous part of a drone. This module explains how LiPo differs from Li-Ion, what “S”, “mAh” and “C” really mean, why voltage sags under load, how to estimate flight time, and how to burn down neither the battery nor the workshop. At the end — a real log from a heavy 10", where the voltage sag told more than any spec sheet. theory Designations - S — the number of cells in series. 6S = 6 cells, the voltages add up. - mAh — capacity. 1300 mAh = 1.3 Ah. - C — discharge current as a multiple of capacity. 1300 mAh × 100C = 130 A according to the label. Marketing C ratings are almost always inflated; go by internal resistance and real tests. How to choose capacity and C for your current — see the subsection “Capacity and C rating: how to choose” below. - P — parallel cells in packs built from cylindrical cells 6S2P = 12 cells . LiPo vs Li-Ion - LiPo: nominal 3.7 V/cell, full charge 4.2 V LiHV — 4.35 V . Delivers huge currents, but less energy per gram. For freestyle, racing, anything with high currents and short flights. - Li-Ion 18650, 21700 : nominal about 3.6 V, full 4.2 V, deeper discharge — down to 2.8–3.0 V. Noticeably more energy per gram, more modest currents. For long-range 7–10", wings, long hovering at moderate throttle. Selection rule numbers — el-battery-packs : Li-Ion gives more minutes if 1 the average current per cell is no higher than 1.5C — a course guideline for a 21700 without airflow cooling, the cell datasheet has no such number for a 4.2 Ah P42A that is 6.3 A per cell, 25 A for a 4P pack and 2 the peak current per cell is no higher than 0.6 × the rated continuous current P42A: 0.6 × 45 = 27 A, 108 A for a 4P pack . If even one check fails — more P the weight grows, recalculate the time or LiPo; if you need peaks of tens of amps per kilogram of pack — LiPo. Take the average current from a log or from the hover calculation f-components-choice ; the check after the flight — average current from the log / P, and a warm, not hot, pack. Voltage sag Every cell has an internal resistance R. At current I the voltage drops by I × R. On a sharp throttle input the sag is instantaneous, and the flight controller sees not “how much is left” but “how much is left minus the sag”. Hence false low-voltage warnings on punch-outs and real ESC shutdowns on a depleted battery. Flight time Estimate: time, min ≈ usable capacity, Ah / average current, A × 60. Usable capacity is about 80% of the rating: never run the battery down to zero. Take the average current from the log, not from your head. BEC and on-board voltages The flight controller, receiver, camera and VTX run on 5, 9 or 12 V, not on 6S. These voltages come from BECs — regulators on the flight controller or the ESC. Before connecting peripherals, check: which pad powers it, whether the BEC has enough current a VTX at high power can draw more than an amp , and that the VTX is not on 5 V if it needs 9–12 V. Case: voltage sag on a 10" Log of a heavy 10" on 6S battery at 23.8 V at the start of the flight : median current 14–16 A, but p95 on the aggressive profile is 124 A, peak 147 A. On those peaks the voltage dropped to 16.2 V, i.e. 2.7 V per cell. Conclusion: at such currents the battery is working at its limit, and the ESC must be checked for a continuous current of about 125 A. No label would have told you this — the log did. Calculating flight time honestly t ≈ capacity × usable fraction / average current. Fraction: 0.8 for LiPo landing at 3.5 V/cell , 0.85 for Li-Ion down to 3.0 V/cell . Average current — from the log BAT.Curr / amperageLatest , not from hover: 5" freestyle — 25–40 A average with 60–100 A peaks; 7" long range cruise — 8–12 A; X8 15" hover ~30 A. Example: 6S 4000 mAh Li-Ion on a 7" at 10 A: 0.85 × 4 / 10 × 60 ≈ 20 min. Check after the flight: the mAh put back by the charger must match CurrTot /mAh drawn in the log within ±10% — otherwise the current sensor is calibrated wrong BATT_AMP_PERVLT , ibata_scale . Sag and internal resistance in numbers U under load = E − I·R. A “fresh” LiPo 6S 1300 mAh 100C: R ≈ 2 mΩ/cell → 12 mΩ/pack; at 80 A the sag is 1 V 4.0 → 3.84 V/cell . The same pack after 150 cycles — 6 mΩ/cell → 36 mΩ → 2.9 V of sag: this is why “old” packs trigger the OSD warning on the very first punch. Li-Ion 6S4P P42A ≈ 40–50 mΩ/pack: at 60 A — 2.4–3 V, one cell's worth is “lost”; that is why warning thresholds are set by voltage under load or by mAh the rule and numbers — next subsection . Heat: 60 A × 60 A × 0.045 Ω = 160 W in the pack — Li-Ion heats up noticeably; LiPo 100C — 80 × 80 × 0.012 = 77 W. In detail chemistries, packs, BMS — the “Li-Ion packs” module. Voltage thresholds: warning and landing Two different voltages. The rest voltage E is what a cell shows with no current, 1–2 minutes after landing estimate : it tells you the state of charge. The voltage under load U = E − I·R is what the flight controller sees in flight, and alarms trigger on it. The difference is the sag: at the same state of charge it is larger the higher the current and the older the pack above: 2 → 6 mΩ/cell over 150 cycles . Hence two rules: 1. The threshold in the firmware is set under load — so that at a typical cruise current it corresponds to the desired remaining charge. Short punches are filtered out by a delay, not by lowering the threshold. 2. The threshold is verified after landing — by the rest voltage and by how many mAh the charger put back into the battery. Chemistry limits — from the datasheet. - LiPo. Tattu Grepow : “never discharge below 3V per cell under load”, full charge 4.2 V/cell; for its UAV batteries Tattu recommends a cutoff of 3.5 V/cell. Gens Ace: automatic cutoff at 3.0 V/cell. - LiHV. Charge to 4.35 V/cell, only for packs where this is allowed; lower thresholds — as for LiPo Oscar Liang . text: summary A brushless motor doesn't spin by itself: it is driven by an ESC electronic speed controller , which receives commands from the flight controller. The module explains what numbers like “2207 1750KV” mean, what poles are, why everyone moved from analog PWM to digital DShot, and which ESC firmware is current in 2026 after BLHeli_32 was shut down. theory Motor designation - 2207 — stator size: 22 mm diameter, 7 mm height. A bigger stator — more torque. - KV — RPM per volt with no load. 1750KV on 6S 25.2 V — roughly 44,000 rpm without a prop. Less under load. - 12N14P — 12 stator coils, 14 magnets. The number of magnets is motor_poles in the firmware; the RPM filter needs it. Selection rule: a big prop needs a lot of torque and a low KV, a small prop — a high KV. A high-KV motor on a big prop overheats and pulls a huge current. How much exactly: RPM under the prop ≈ k × KV × U, so for a given prop KV × cell count is almost constant — the same 5" on 4S needs a higher KV than on 6S 2300–2700 versus 1700–2100 ; the table by class and the check after assembly — in f-aero-props “KV for the prop and cell count” . What an ESC does A brushless motor is three-phase. The ESC energizes the phases in turn, creating a rotating magnetic field. It determines the rotor position without sensors — from the EMF induced in the unpowered phase sensorless . Hence desync: on a sharp throttle change the ESC can “lose” the rotor, and the motor will twitch or stop. Control protocols - PWM — a 1000–2000 µs pulse at about 50 Hz. Analog, slow, requires range calibration. Still found on servos and heavy-lift ESCs. - OneShot, Multishot — the same pulses, only shorter and more frequent. A historical stage. - DShot150/300/600 — a digital protocol: a 16-bit packet with a checksum, no calibration needed, noise does not shift the throttle. The number is the speed in kilobits. - Bidirectional DShot — the ESC sends back the motor's eRPM. The RPM filter is built on this. {{diagram:dshot-frame A DShot frame: 11 throttle bits, a telemetry request bit and 4 CRC bits.}} RPM is calculated from eRPM like this: RPM = eRPM / number of magnets / 2 . ESC firmware in 2026 - BLHeli_S — old 8-bit ESCs, open source. They are flashed with Bluejay — with bidirectional DShot and the RPM filter. - BLHeli_32 — 32-bit ESCs. The project was shut down in June 2024: the firmware server is offline, there will be no more updates. Existing ESCs keep working and can still be configured. - AM32 — open-source firmware for 32-bit ESCs, the de facto replacement for BLHeli_32. Switching from BLHeli_32 to AM32 is one-way. {{lesson:f-esc-firmware Bluejay and AM32 settings tables from the source code, choosing the PWM frequency for the aircraft, and a “symptom → setting” cheat sheet, including for desync.}} ESC current ESCs are chosen by continuous current with a margin over the real peak current from the log; for a first build, when there is no log yet — by the motor's peak current from the thrust table: ESC continuous current ≥ 1.3 × that current f-components-choice , Step 5a . A 4-in-1 is convenient and light, but overheating one channel often kills the whole board. Motor physics in two formulas A brushless motor is two constants linked to each other: KV rpm per volt and Kt torque per amp . Kt = 60/ 2π·KV N·m/A: a 1750KV motor gives 0.0055 N·m per amp, a 380KV motor — 0.025 N·m/A. So low KV = a lot of torque per amp = a big prop without overheating; high KV = RPM for a small prop. RPM under load: n = KV · U − I·R_winding — the drop from the winding resistance tens of mΩ and from the battery's internal resistance. Heat in the winding P = I²·R: at 30 A and 40 mΩ — 36 W per motor; the only heatsink is the bell itself and the prop airflow. The stator size sets the torque the volume of magnetic material : a 2207 and a 2306 have almost the same volume, and the difference is smaller than between manufacturers. It is usually believed that a wider stator 2306 gives slightly more torque and a sharper response, while a taller one 2207 sheds heat better on long flights — compare by the thrust tables of specific motors, not by the size numbers. The number of pole pairs 14 magnets = 7 pairs sets the eRPM → RPM conversion and the commutation frequency: at 30,000 rpm, 7 pairs = 3500 electrical revolutions/s. What an ESC does every microsecond An ESC is a three-phase inverter on 6 MOSFETs. It commutates the phases according to the rotor position, which it estimates from the back-EMF in the unpowered phase zero-crossing . ESC firmware parameters that matter: - PWM frequency 24/48/96 kHz — the PWM frequency on the switches. Rule: the smaller the motor and the higher its RPM, the higher the frequency needed — whoop and 2–3.5" 48 kHz, 5" 48 freestyle or 24 racing , 7" 24–48, 10" and larger, heavy aircraft and planes 24 kHz; higher — smoother current and quieter, but weaker braking and thrust at low throttle and a hotter ESC. Why, how to choose for any aircraft and what to check after a change — the subsection “PWM frequency: how to choose for the aircraft” in f-esc-firmware . - Timing motor timing; 0–30° in the firmware, default AM32 15°, Bluejay 22.5° — commutation advance: higher — more RPM and current, more heating, but more margin against demagnetization; lower — cooler and more efficient, but heavy props and motors with high inductance desync more often on a sharp throttle input. Start — the firmware default; change it by the procedure in f-esc-firmware . - Demag compensation — protection against desync on sharp throttle changes, especially accelerating from low RPM with a heavy prop the demagnetization current grows with the motor current . The starting point for any class is the ESC firmware default Bluejay — Low, AM32 — demag_comp from the table in f-esc-firmware ; raise it by one step only when there is a sign of desync: in Blackbox, an eRPM dip of one motor on a sharp throttle input, by ear — “sneezing”. Large motors on heavy props — 7" and larger — need this more

text: summary The propeller is the only part that turns electricity into flight, and the only one beginners choose “by the picture”. The module gives you the physics at a level sufficient for an informed choice: where thrust comes from, why a big slow prop is more efficient than a small fast one, what pitch and efficiency are, how to read a manufacturer's thrust tables and how to pick a motor-prop-battery combination for the required T/W and flight time. With calculations on the example of a 7" and an X8. theory The actuator disk: where thrust comes from The simplest model: the prop is a disk of area A that accelerates the air from a speed V₀ the incoming flow to Vₑ behind the disk . Thrust is the change in the air's momentum per second: {{diagram:actuator-disk The actuator disk: thrust is the change in the flow's momentum; power grows faster than thrust.}} F = ½ · ρ · A · Vₑ² − V₀² , where ρ is the air density ≈1.225 kg/m³ at the ground . In hover V₀ = 0, and thrust grows with the square of the speed of the air thrown back. Consequences: - A big disk is more economical. For the same thrust a big prop throws a lot of air slowly, a small one — little air fast. Kinetic energy ~ V², momentum ~ V: at equal thrust the power on the small prop is higher. That is why long-range and cargo aircraft fly on big slow props. - Air density matters. In the mountains and in heat ρ is lower — thrust drops at the same RPM; an aircraft that barely hovered on the plains will not take off in the mountains. - The model is ideal: real losses tip vortices, blade profile drag, flow swirl reduce the efficiency. Pitch, diameter and designation “5×4.3×3” = 5" diameter, 4.3" pitch, 3 blades. Pitch — how far the prop “screws” into the air per revolution without slip. More pitch — more flow speed and thrust per revolution, but more torque and current. More blades — more thrust from the same diameter at the cost of efficiency. How to choose the pitch and the number of blades. There is no rule of the form “pitch X for class Y”: the combination is chosen by comparison, and the procedure is the same for any class. Start — the prop from the thrust table of the chosen motor the manufacturer measures it on recommended props or from the course's examples: 5" freestyle — a 5.1×3 tri-blade f-motors-esc , 7" long range — 7×3.5 practice , 15" cargo — 15×5 MN4006 table . Then compare it with a neighboring option — a pitch one step higher or lower, 2 ↔ 3 blades — on two numbers from the table or the test stand: g/W at hover thrust flight time and the current at full throttle no higher than the ESC and motor ratings . The direction depends on the mission course estimate : freestyle and racing value thrust and response from a small diameter — more blades and pitch; long range and cargo value g/W — two blades and the pitch at which g/W in hover is highest. The lab assignment is the same comparison for your own build: two prop options, the choice by numbers in step 2 of the practice 7×4 is the fallback option to 7×3.5 . The check after choosing — hover current and motor temperature subsection “KV for the prop”, step 4 of the “Procedure” . Dimensionless coefficients Manufacturers and databases UIUC describe a prop by: - Cₜ = T / ρ·n²·D⁴ — the thrust coefficient n — rev/s, D — diameter, m ; - Cₚ = P / ρ·n³·D⁵ — the power coefficient; - J = V / n·D — the advance ratio flight speed relative to prop speed ; - η = J·Cₜ/Cₚ — the efficiency in flight in hover J = 0, and one speaks of the static efficiency in g/W . The practical conclusion from the formulas: thrust ~ n², power ~ n³. To double the thrust you need 1.41 times the RPM and 2.8 times the power. This is exactly why “adding throttle” is so expensive in current. Motor + prop: the operating point The motor sets the RPM through KV and voltage, the prop sets the load. The operating point is where the motor's torque equals the prop's drag torque. Motor manufacturers publish tables: prop, voltage, throttle → thrust g , current A , power W , g/W. This is the main document for selection. The higher the KV with the same prop, the higher the RPM, thrust and current. Overdo it — overheating of the winding and the ESC. Rule: a big prop — low KV, a small one — high; how much exactly — in the next subsection. KV for the prop and cell count Mechanism. KV is RPM per volt with no load; under the prop's load the motor spins slower: RPM ≈ k × KV × U , k ≈ 0.75–0.85 at full throttle des-sizing : an MN4014 330KV at 22.2 V — 7326 rpm with no load and 6000 with a 15×5 prop, k = 0.82 . A prop is designed for certain RPM: thrust ∝ n² , power ∝ n³ and the blade tip speed v = π × D × n / 60 depend on it. So what you choose is not the KV but the RPM under the prop , and the KV follows from it: KV ≈ RPM / k × U . For a given prop KV × cell count is almost constant : the same prop on 4S needs a KV 6/4 = 1.5 times higher than on 6S. An error in this direction is a classic: a motor meant for 4S spins the prop 1.5 times faster on 6S, thrust grows 2.25 times, power and current — about 3.4 times 1.5³ , and that means overheating and a burned ESC; the opposite error — a sluggish aircraft hovering near its limit. Guidelines by class. KV — Oscar Liang's table “Motor & Prop Sizes, KV, Battery Cell Count” updated in July 2025 ; the other columns are the course's calculation with k = 0.8, U = 3.7 V × S and the middle of the KV range, i.e. an estimate. text: summary The flight controller FC is a small computer that reads the sensors, runs the controller and commands the motors thousands of times a second. This module explains what sits on the board, what each sensor is responsible for, how to read a wiring diagram, and why the same wire behaves differently on different pads. After it, the board diagram stops being a puzzle. theory Processor The heart of an FC is a microcontroller. The series determines the capabilities: - F4 — the most common and cheapest; limited in the number of UARTs and cannot invert UARTs in software: SBUS needs an external hardware inverter on the board, and only some ports have one see the module on SBUS . - F7 — faster, more UARTs, software inversion. - H7 — the most powerful, the standard for ArduPilot and PX4 on complex platforms. What matters is not “the best processor” but whether the firmware you need supports the board: each firmware has its own list of targets. Sensors - Gyroscope gyro — angular rate on three axes. The main sensor: stabilization runs on it. It is read thousands of times a second and is sensitive to vibration. - Accelerometer accel — acceleration; at rest it shows the direction of gravity. Needed for self-leveling modes ANGLE and navigation. - Barometer baro — pressure, from which altitude. Sensitive to prop airflow and to light — it is covered with foam. - Magnetometer mag, compass — heading. It is afraid of power wires: it is mounted on a mast together with the GPS, away from the current. - GPS — position and velocity. Needed for position hold, return to home and missions. Combining these sensors is the job of the state estimation filter: in ArduPilot it is the EKF extended Kalman filter: it fuses the gyro, accelerometer, compass, GPS and baro into a single estimate of attitude, velocity and position, module ap-ekf , in Betaflight a simplified scheme without navigation. Buses - UART — a serial port: receiver, GPS, VTX, telemetry, companion. The wires cross over TX → RX . - I2C — a bus for several sensors compass, external baro, display over two wires, SDA/SCL. - SPI — a fast bus inside the board: gyro, OSD, flash for logs. Pads on the board Typical labels: VBAT battery voltage , 5V / 9V / 10V BEC outputs , GND , TX1 / RX1 UART1 , SDA / SCL I2C , CURR current sensor , LED addressable LEDs , BZ+ / BZ- buzzer , M1 – M4 or S1 – S8 outputs to ESCs/servos . Mounting Mounting standards are 30.5×30.5 and 20×20 mm whoops and some 3" use 25.5×25.5 . The frame sets the size: you fit the one the frame is drilled for; an AIO or a stack is chosen by ESC current, mounting and number of UARTs f-components-choice , Step 5a . The board sits on rubber dampers: the gyro should hear the frame's movement, not its vibration. The arrow on the board shows “forward”; if the board is rotated, the rotation is set in the firmware board alignment / AHRS_ORIENTATION . A closer look at the gyro: chips and rates The gyro is a MEMS chip on SPI. Common ones: MPU6000 old, 8 kHz output, low noise, discontinued , ICM20602/20689 noisier, more sensitive to power , ICM42688-P the modern standard: up to 32 kHz, a configurable hardware anti-aliasing filter — it suppresses frequencies above half the output rate before digitization, otherwise they “fold” into false low frequencies, — low noise , BMI270 an alternative; up to 6.4 kHz per the datasheet, but Betaflight reads it at 3.2 kHz by default, and the PID loop on it is no faster than 3.2 kHz; with gyro_hardware_lpf = EXPERIMENTAL — 6.4 kHz, but without the hardware LPF — the low-pass filter inside the chip; drivers/accgyro/gyro_sync.c . The firmware reads the chip over SPI at 8–24 MHz with DMA direct memory access: data goes into memory without the processor's involvement; the “Embedded” module and runs the PID loop synchronously with the gyro output always in 4.x; the PID loop divider is pid_process_denom : at 8 kHz — every 125 µs. The chain: chip → hardware LPF gyro_hardware_lpf → software filters the “Filters” module → PID. What PID loop rate to set and what it means when buying Betaflight 2025.12.5, config/config.c . PID loop = gyro rate / pid_process_denom . With the RPM filter it needs bidirectional DShot the rule is: on F405, F411 and G47x the firmware itself sets DSHOT300 and a 4 kHz PID loop with an 8 kHz gyro an F405 with cpu_overclock from 216 MHz is the exception ; on F7, H7 and AT32F435, DSHOT600 and an 8 kHz PID loop are available; with a BMI270 — 3.2 kHz on any MCU by default . 4 kHz with the RPM filter is a normal setup for 5" and larger, not a “cut-down” one bf-filters , “What the firmware will change by itself”; MCU table — f-micro-whoop . To check — status in the CLI: cycle time µs and GYRO rate — this is the gyro loop, the PID loop = GYRO rate / get pid_process_denom ; the CPU load is there too; the LOAD arming flag is a sign that the loop is too fast for the board. What to choose in DShot for this loop — f-motors-esc . Two gyros on a board dual gyro — averaging or selection; ArduPilot on H7 — up to three IMUs with separate EKF cores. {{diagram:fc-signal-path The signal path inside the FC: gyro → filters → PID → mixer → ESC; the RC command sets the target, Blackbox and OSD take a copy.}} What else sits on the board - OSD chip MAX7456 for analog or digital OSD over MSP DisplayPort DJI/Walksnail/HDZero; the protocol the FC uses to send OSD characters to a digital VTX — draws telemetry into the video. - Flash/SD for Blackbox: 16–32 MB of flash is enough for minutes at 2 kHz 16 MB — 2.7–4.6 min ; SD — hours. Log rate: 1 kHz — for PID analysis, 2 kHz 1.6 kHz with BMI270 — for noise and filters bf-blackbox . Written over SPI/SDIO, on F4 it sometimes has DMA conflicts with other functions. - BEC : 5 V typically 2–3 A total for all consumers and 9–12 V for VTX/digital, 2–3 A . Limits — in the board's description; a Raspberry Pi is not powered from an FC pad the “Connecting peripherals” module . - Current sensor on the PDB power distribution board /ESC → the CURR pad, the

summary: Half of all “tuning problems” are mechanical: an unbalanced prop, a loose motor, a frame that rings at a frequency where the motor harmonics land. Filters and PID treat the symptoms; this module is about the causes. Where vibration comes from, what frame resonance is, how to balance props and motors

Inspection Step 2. Balancing Step 3. Measure, don't feel Step 4. Wires Lab
text: summary Half of all “tuning problems” are mechanical: an unbalanced prop, a loose motor, a frame that rings at a frequency where the motor harmonics land. Filters and PID treat the symptoms; this module is about the causes. Where vibration comes from, what frame resonance is, how to balance props and motors, how to mount the flight controller and route the wires, and how to measure the result from the spectrum rather than by feel. theory Sources of vibration - Prop imbalance — the blade masses are not equal: force ~ m·r·ω², i.e. it grows with the square of RPM. The main source at the rotation frequency 1st harmonic . - Motor imbalance — the bell, the magnets; the same frequency. - Blade aerodynamics — thrust pulsations at the “RPM × number of blades” frequency 2nd, 3rd harmonics . - Play and flex — a bearing, an under-tightened motor, a flexible arm: they add broadband noise and can “ring” at their own frequency. - Prop wash and turbulence — low-frequency shaking at 20–70 Hz, aerodynamics, not mechanics. Frame resonance A frame has natural frequencies arms, FC mount, standoffs . When a motor harmonic passes through a natural frequency, the amplitude grows several times. In the spectrum it is a peak that does not move with RPM. A resonance is not filtered by the RPM filter that one tracks the motors ; it is caught by the dynamic notch or removed by changing the design: a stiffer arm, a different mass, a damper. How vibration spoils flight - The gyro sees vibration as angular rate → the PID “works off” movement that doesn't exist → hot motors, mushy response. - The accelerometer clips saturates → the ArduPilot EKF loses its altitude and position estimate VIBE , Clip . - The barometer “breathes” from the airflow. Mounting the flight controller The goal is to pass on the frame's movements but not high-frequency vibration. Standard practice: soft rubber grommets or standoffs with a damper, wires without tension a taut harness is a rigid link that bypasses the dampers . A mount that is too soft has its own low-frequency resonances and gyro lag. For large aircraft — damping plates. On racing 5" you also see hard mounting with filter tuning: the motors there spin fast, and the grommets add their own 50–150 Hz resonance section “Numbers” . The course rule for 5": start with the grommets that come with the stack — a 5" does have a soft-mount window subsection “FC damping” ; switch to hard mounting only if the spectrum shows a mount peak — a horizontal line below the motor harmonics that does not depend on throttle — and replacing the grommets with stiffer ones does not remove it. Numbers The motor's 1st-harmonic frequency = RPM/60. In hover a 5" is ~250–350 Hz 15–21 thousand rpm; a light aircraft is closer to 230 Hz — the 14,000 rpm used in the f-safety and f-physics calculations , 7" ~110–200 the 1.4 kg 7" LR from the bf-rpm-filter example — 110–130 , 10" ~80–100, 15" ~50–70. Carbon arm resonances are usually 100–400 Hz, FC mount resonances — 50–150 Hz. Natural frequencies: a rough estimate An arm as a cantilever beam: f₁ ≈ 0.56·√ E·I/ μ·L⁴ E — modulus of elasticity, I — second moment of area of the cross-section, μ — mass per meter, L — length ; for an engineering estimate it is easier to measure: a tap on the arm with the accelerometer/gyro logging LOG_DISARMED / blackbox_mode = ALWAYS gives decaying oscillations — the frequency of the peak in the spectrum is the resonance. Typical values: a 5" carbon arm of 4–5 mm — 300–500 Hz above the motor harmonics in hover, below them at full throttle ; 7" 5 mm — 150–250 Hz coincides with the 1st–2nd harmonics — the danger zone ; 10"+ tubular arms of 16–25 mm — 60–150 Hz. Stiffen the arm thicker, shorter, a tube instead of a plate → the frequency rises as √ stiffness/mass ; add mass at the tip a heavier motor → it falls. FC damping: how to choose A rubber grommet is a spring with a damper: the natural frequency of the “board on grommets” system is f₀ = 1/2π ·√ k/m . You want f₀ 3–5 times below the lowest motor harmonic, but above the control bandwidth ≥ 50–80 Hz : for a 5" motors 250+ Hz — f₀ ≈ 50–83 Hz 250 / 5 … 250 / 3 ; for an X8 motors 55 Hz dampers with an f₀ of 15–20 Hz are already “soft” and add lag — there you rely on balancing and notches, not on softness. Manufacturers usually do not publish the grommet stiffness k, so f₀ is not calculated but measured with the same tap as the arm: blackbox_mode = ALWAYS , a tap on the frame next to the stack, and the peak of the decaying oscillations in the gyro spectrum is the f₀ of the mount course method . The target for a 5" is 50–83 Hz the window in the diagram below ; higher — the grommets are too stiff for this stack, lower — too soft. The sign of a mount that is too soft: a low-frequency peak in the spectrum tens of hertz, below the motor frequency and a “mushy” feel. Wires and ribbon cables bypass the dampers if they are taut. {{diagram:chart-fc-damper-window A soft-mount window f₀ 3–5 times below the motor harmonic, but not below 50–80 Hz exists only for harmonics from 150–240 Hz: for a 5" 250 Hz it is 50–83 Hz; the 7" from the example 125 Hz , the 10" and the X8 have no window — there it is balancing and notches.}} Worked example: a 7" with a 180 Hz peak Spectrogram: a horizontal line at 180 Hz regardless of throttle, 25 dB above the noise floor; the motor harmonic in hover is 125 Hz, the 2nd is 250 Hz when throttling up it passes through 180 Hz — the resonance “rings” . Tap test on the arm — 182 Hz: it's the arm. Options: a 6 mm arm instead of 5 f ↑ ~20% → 215 Hz, moves away from the 1st harmonic, but the 2nd still passes through — not a solution; a dynamic notch at 180 helps, but adds delay — a temporary fix; the real fix — change the motor mounting point / shorten the arm f ↑ by 1.3–1.5 times or accept it and set a static notch gyro_notch1_hz = 180 , cutoff = 150 . Why not the bf-filters rule “ cutoff = frequency × 0.7”: cutoff is the lower edge of the notch, Q = f·f_c / f² − f_c² filterGetNotchQ

text: summary The PID controller is the core of stabilization in Betaflight. This article explains the physical meaning of the P, I and D gains, how they interact, how they affect the behavior of the drone, and how to tune them using Blackbox. After working through it the reader will be able to diagnose the typical problems oscillations, bounce-back, overheating motors and adjust the parameters purposefully instead of by trial and error. A separate block covers the throttle path in the mixer — dynamic idle, thrust_linear , vbat_sag_compensation , TPA, anti-gravity and throttle boost — with formulas from the source code and a calculation lab. theory The PID Proportional-Integral-Derivative controller receives the angular rate on the roll, pitch and yaw axes from the gyro and minimizes the error between the desired rate the setpoint, from the sticks or from navigation and the current rate of rotation. The controller output the PID sum is converted by the mixer into the motor signals. P term proportional reacts to the current error: the larger the error, the stronger the correction. It sets the basic stiffness of the drone. Its weakness: it cannot fully remove a steady-state error drift . When too high it causes fast oscillations tens of Hz; on a 5" roughly 30–80 Hz — a course estimate . I term integral accumulates the error over time and removes a constant offset drift from wind, an offset center of mass . It works more slowly than P. When too high it causes slow, wandering oscillations 1–5 Hz and windup. In 2025.12 this is handled by iterm_windup 80 by default, range 20–100 : it sets the I limit as a percentage of pidsum_limit . In 4.5 there were two variables and the meaning was different: iterm_windup 85 by default, % reduced I accumulation as the motors approached saturation a spread of motor commands above 85% , and iterm_limit 400 by default was the absolute I-term limit. iterm_limit was removed in 2025.12; this is not a rename. D term derivative reacts to the rate of change of the error and acts as a damper. It suppresses the oscillations caused by the P term. It is critically sensitive to gyro noise. Without filtering it produces high-frequency noise that overheats the motors. The rule: the D term is tuned after the P term; raising P requires raising D. Betaflight specifics 4.5 and 2025.12 : - Feedforward — an independent control path that drives the motors directly from the speed of stick movement. It speeds up the response without raising the P term. - TPA Throttle PID Attenuation — a reduction of the PID gains at high throttle. By default tpa_mode = D only the D term is reduced ; PD is also available, and from 2025.12 a WING build adds PDS together with the S term; it does not exist on a multirotor . - RPM Filtering — the use of data from the ESCs to suppress propeller noise. It places narrow filters at the motor rotation frequency, which allows a higher D term. The formula as implemented in flight/pid.c For every axis in every loop at the PID frequency : the error e = setpoint − gyro filtered ; - P = Kp·e; - I += Ki·e·dt with the iterm_windup limit % of pidsum_limit ; anti-windup and “relax” below ; in 4.5 — a reduction of Ki by iterm_windup on motor saturation and a separate iterm_limit ; - D = −Kd·d gyro_D /dt — the derivative of the gyro , not of the error stick movement produces no derivative kick , after the D filters the “Filters” module , with the multiplier of the D max logic before 2025.12 — d_min ; - FF = Kff·d setpoint /dt with averaging/smoothing feedforward_averaging , feedforward_smooth_factor , feedforward_jitter_factor , feedforward_boost — an addition from the second derivative, feedforward_max_rate_limit ; - the sum → TPA → pidSum → the mixer. The gains from the configurator “45” are multiplied by the scale factors in pid_init.c P ≈ 0.032, I ≈ 0.244, D ≈ 0.00053, FF ≈ 0.0138 — this is the “dimensionlessness” of Betaflight; the physical meaning is recovered only through the response the “Control theory” module . For FF the number from the configurator is additionally divided by 100: Kff = 0.0138 · f_ / 100 pidInitConfig in flight/pid_init.c , 2025.12.5; the same in 4.5 . Mechanisms that are not in a PID textbook - I-term relax iterm_relax = RP , iterm_relax_type = SETPOINT , iterm_relax_cutoff = 15 : during fast stick movements I accumulation is suspended — otherwise after a flip the I term adds extra rotation one of the kinds of bounce-back . A lower cutoff → more aggressive relax. - I-term rotation iterm_rotation : during yaw rotation the accumulated roll/pitch I terms are rotated together with the frame. - Anti-gravity anti_gravity_gain , anti_gravity_p_gain , anti_gravity_cutoff_hz : temporarily boosts I and P on sharp throttle changes — against the nose dip on a throttle punch. - D max d_ — the base, d_max_ — the peak, plus d_max_gain , d_max_advance ; in 4.5 it is the other way around: d_min_ — the base, d_ — the peak : D is low in calm flight less noise/heat and rises on fast movements and propwash, driven by the gyro/setpoint. - TPA tpa_mode = D by default, tpa_rate , tpa_breakpoint ; from 4.5 there is also tpa_low_ for low throttle : reduces D or PD above a throttle point — at high throttle the thrust per unit of command the loop gain and the noise both grow. - Thrust linearization thrust_linear and throttle boost : compensation for the nonlinearity of thrust versus throttle, and a short-term boost of the throttle response. - Air mode : PID works at zero throttle as well feature AIRMODE or the AIR MODE mode , with a minimum idle motor_idle ; before 2025.12 — dshot_idle_value — otherwise in a zero-throttle descent the aircraft is uncontrollable. A worked example: where bounce-back comes from A log: after a sharp stick stop in roll the gyro goes to −18% of the maneuver amplitude. Check in order: 1 the D filters are not too low delay — dterm_lpf1_dyn_max_hz 150 → OK; 2 is there enough D? the Damping slider 1.0 → 1.15 — bounce-back 18 → 11%, the motors are warm;

text: summary The tip of a five-inch prop moves at about 330 km/h and carries enough energy to cut skin down to the bone; a LiPo with an internal short delivers hundreds of amps and burns with its own oxidizer: the flame can be knocked down, but the burning resumes until the cells cool. The typical injury in the hobby happens not in the air but on the bench: the drone armed with props on during setup course guideline, not statistics . The module gives you the physics of the hazard in numbers, the mechanism of thermal runaway, the course's numbers for charging, storing and transporting batteries, the power-up order for a bench without props, what “armed” means in Betaflight, ArduPilot and PX4, the full list of Betaflight's arming disable flags from the source code, with explanations , pre-flight and post-flight checklists, and what to do in a battery fire. Lab: in ArduCopter 4.7.2 SITL, see the idle RPM after arming and the reaction to an RC loss on the ground and in the air, calculate a battery's energy and transport category, then — a failsafe test on your own aircraft without props. theory The hazard in numbers - Propeller. Tip speed = π · D · n. For a 5" D = 0.127 m in hover at 14,000 rpm 233 rev/s; this is a light aircraft, a heavy 5" hovers at up to ~20,000 — f-frame-mech : 0.40 m × 233 ≈ 93 m/s — about 335 km/h; at full throttle up to ~30,000 rpm course estimate — 200 m/s. The kinetic energy of a spinning prop in the thin-rod model E = ½ · I · ω², I = m · D² / 12: a 5" weighing 4 g at 14,000 rpm — 5.8 J, at 30,000 rpm — 26 J; a 7" 9 g at 9,000 rpm — 10 J; a 10" 18 g at 6,000 rpm — 19 J the calculation is in the practice; prop masses are an assumption, weigh your own; the rod model is an upper estimate . In the rod model the energy is mostly in the outer half of the blade, and that is the part that hits your hand. The scale of injuries is a course guideline, not statistics: 5" — deep cuts, 7–10" — broken fingers, 15" on an X8 — severe injuries. Energy grows with the square of RPM, so a 5" at full throttle 26 J is more dangerous than a 10" in hover 19 J . - Motors on the bench. A motor test in the configurator without removing the props is a classic injury. The firmware warns you, but it won't stop you. - LiPo. Internal resistance of 1–3 mΩ per cell: a fresh 6S has about 12 mΩ per pack f-power , and by Ohm's law a short circuit at 25.2 V gives up to 25.2 / 0.012 ≈ 2100 A; the wires and connector add only a few mΩ, so the current stays on the order of a thousand amps course estimate — a wire glows red-hot within a second. A cell punctured in a crash can catch fire minutes or hours after the impact. The burning is thermal runaway with oxygen released from the cathode: knock down the flame an ABC extinguisher, sand , then cool it with a large amount of water , or carry it outdoors in a non-flammable container and let it burn out. A class D extinguisher is designed for metallic lithium — there is none in LiPo or Li-Ion. A swollen pack is retired: discharge it to 0 through a load a resistor or a bulb, not salt water — the procedure is in f-power and hand it in for disposal. - Loss of link. If the failsafe has not been tested on this aircraft, it does something nobody chose the “Failsafe” module . - The first flight after any change — a swapped motor, the prop direction, a wrong mixer, an untested filter: the most dangerous flight course guideline: it reveals all the errors that are not visible on the bench . Why LiPo burns: thermal runaway step by step A LiPo or Li-Ion cell is a graphite anode, an oxide cathode in drone LiPos usually based on cobalt and nickel , a polymer separator tens of microns thick between them, and an organic electrolyte. The electrolyte is a mixture of carbonates: an EC/DMC mixture has a flash point of about 25 °C, i.e. there is always fuel inside the cell. The danger is not a “spark” but a chain of reactions, each of which heats the cell and starts the next one. The steps according to the review by Liu et al. Science Advances, 2018 : 1. At about 80 °C the rate of exothermic side reactions grows so much that the cell starts heating itself. Thermal runaway is defined as self-heating faster than 10 °C per minute. 2. From ~90 °C the protective film on the anode SEI decomposes, releasing flammable gases in an accident this is what swells the cell; ordinary “puffing over time” is gas from aging and over-discharge at normal temperature . Then the lithium in the anode reacts with the electrolyte solvent. 3. At ~135 °C a polyethylene separator melts, at ~165 °C — a polypropylene one. The anode and cathode touch, an internal short circuit begins, and the cell's entire energy is released inside it. 4. At 180–250 °C the review gives both figures for LiCoO2 the cathode decomposes and releases oxygen. Now the electrolyte no longer needs air to burn: smothering the flame does not mean putting it out. Three practical conclusions follow from the mechanism. First: you fight the temperature, not the flame. An ABC extinguisher or sand knock down the open burning, but as long as the cells are hotter than ~80 °C the reactions continue, so next comes a lot of water for cooling, or a non-flammable container outdoors and letting it burn out. Second: mechanical damage starts the same chain from step 3 — a crushed separator gives an internal short circuit without any overheating, which is why a pack can catch fire minutes after an impact hence the post-crash quarantine in ops-maintenance . Third: the charging “window”, 10–45 °C per the Gens Ace datasheet f-power , is only 35 °C away from the onset of self-heating. A pack is sometimes hot to the touch after an aggressive flight; charging it without letting it cool into the window means cutting into an already small 35 °C margin. {{diagram:safety-thermal-ladder The 10–45 °C charging window and the runaway steps on one scale: from the top of the window to self-heating is only 35 °C, and from 180 °C the cathode supplies its own oxygen.}} Charging, st

text: summary A UAV engineer is responsible not only for making the aircraft fly, but also for where and how it flies. Regulations differ by country and change every year, so this module does not retell them; it teaches you to find the current ones, to understand the common logic risk categories, zones, altitudes, registration, insurance and to keep the operator's documentation. This is not legal advice: the source of truth is your country's regulator. theory The common logic of regulation Most countries build their rules around risk : the aircraft's mass, proximity to people and infrastructure, altitude, visibility. Typical elements: - Registration of the operator and/or the aircraft above a certain mass. - Operation categories : from “open” small aircraft, within line of sight, away from people to “specific” and “certified” authorizations, risk assessment . - An altitude limit above the ground often around 120 m / 400 feet in the open category . - Zones : aerodromes, cities, infrastructure sites, borders, military sites — prohibited or permitted. - Visual line of sight VLOS as the basic requirement; flights beyond it BVLOS — separate authorizations. - Night flights, flights over people — separate conditions. - Liability insurance — mandatory or strongly recommended. What this means for an engineer - Test flights are flights too: the same rules apply. - Autonomous missions and BVLOS are almost always a separate category. Plan them legally or in a simulator. - RC and video frequencies are regulated separately: VTX power and bands, the permitted ELRS/900 MHz channels depend on the country. - Responsibility lies with the operator and the owner. The flight log is your protection in an incident. Operator documentation The minimum that professionals keep: - Operator log : date, location, aircraft, duration, purpose, incidents. - Aircraft log : configurations, repairs, replacements, motor/battery hours. - Build spec sheet from the “Foundation” capstone : mass, powertrain, frequencies. - Site risk assessment : people, obstacles, zones, weather, a plan for failure. How two “reference” systems work so you understand your own - EASA EU : three categories — Open up to 25 kg, VLOS, ≤ 120 m, subcategories A1/A2/A3 by proximity to people and by aircraft class C0–C4 classes C5/C6 are for the STS standard scenarios in the Specific category ; operator registration from 250 g or with a camera; an online A1/A3 exam, an additional one for A2 , Specific SORA risk assessment, an authorization from the national authority or the STS standard scenarios; this is where BVLOS, heavy aircraft and flights over assemblies of people fall — Open prohibits them, Regulation EU 2019/947, Art. 4 , Certified like crewed aviation . Home-built aircraft — Open only in A1 < 250 g or A3 away from people , otherwise Specific. - FAA USA : Part 107 — for any flights not for recreation: commercial, government, volunteer an exam, a Remote Pilot certificate, ≤ 400 feet, VLOS, registration of every aircraft regardless of mass, Remote ID ; Recreational — an exception for flights purely for fun the TRUST test, the rules of an FAA-recognized community-based organization CBO , registration from 250 g, 400 feet in class G, Remote ID for registered aircraft ; authorizations for flights in controlled airspace via LAANC or DroneZone; BVLOS — a waiver. Updates as of November 2026 — in the subsection below. What both have in common: registration and identification Remote ID / class C , a risk-based category, an altitude of ~120 m/400 feet, VLOS, zones, operator responsibility. Check your own country against the same structure: “what category, what registration threshold, what altitude, what identification, what about BVLOS”. What changed by November 2026: USA, United Kingdom, EU Checked against the regulators' pages on 2026-11-17. Rules change: before flying, open the official page from the table at the end of this subsection, not this text. This is an overview for an engineer, not legal advice. USA FAA . - Under 250 g and only for recreation — no registration. Under 14 CFR 48.15, registration is not required for an aircraft that flies exclusively under the recreational rules 49 U.S.C. 44809 and weighs no more than 0.55 lb 250 g at takeoff together with everything attached to it. No registration — no Remote ID requirement either. TRUST, 400 feet and the other rules still apply. - TRUST — a free online test, mandatory for any recreational flight; you must carry proof of completion. - Part 107 — everything that isn't recreation. The FAA's criterion is the purpose of the flight, not payment: according to the FAA Safety Briefing article, free services, volunteering and nonprofit organizations fall under Part 107 “goodwill and nonprofit operations fall under part 107” . An aircraft for Part 107 is registered regardless of mass, even under 250 g. On the FAA pages we checked there is no separate line about monetized video; by the purpose criterion, filming for channel income is not a flight “purely for fun” — in that case you fly under Part 107, and if in doubt you ask the FAA. - FPV in goggles — only with an observer. For recreation: the aircraft within the visual line of sight of the pilot or of an observer who stands next to the pilot and is in direct communication with them. Part 107: either the pilot or a visual observer must see the aircraft without instruments § 107.31, § 107.33 . A pilot in goggles does not see the aircraft, so an observer is mandatory. - Remote ID is in force: a registered aircraft broadcasts Remote ID or flies only within a FRIA details — the f-remote-id-security module . - Part 108 routine BVLOS operations is not yet in force. The proposed rule NPRM was published on 7 August 2025 90 FR 38212 , the comment period closed on 6 October 2025 and was reopened in January 2026 91 FR 3695 . In the regulatory agenda the rule is at the Final Rule stage with a target date of “July 2026”, but as of 2026-11-17 we did not find a published final r

text: summary Eighty percent of real engineering work is not tuning but selection: what to buy so that the aircraft does the job, stays within budget and doesn't fall apart. The module gives you a method: the mission in numbers → aircraft class → frame and props → motors and ESC → battery → FC and peripherals → mass and T/W check → two alternatives. With a T/W and flight-time calculator and a walkthrough of two specifications: a long-range 7" and a cargo 10". theory Step 0: the mission in numbers As long as the mission sounds like “I want to fly far”, there is nothing to choose. You need numbers: Parameter Example: long-range 7" Example: cargo 10" --- --- --- Payload camera 30 g cargo 1000 g Flight time ≥ 15 min ≥ 12 min with cargo Range 5 km 1 km Cruise speed 15–20 m/s 8 m/s Conditions wind up to 8 m/s wind up to 6 m/s Budget €400 €700 Constraints mass < 1 kg category foldable Each number will become a requirement with an ID in the engineering folder next module . Step 1: class and frame The prop size determines everything else. Rule: the payload mass and time set the required efficiency g/W , and the efficiency sets the prop diameter the aerodynamics module : 5" — 4–6 g/W, 7" — 8–10, 10" — 12–15, 15" — 15–20 for 10–15" this is the top of the range: a small fraction of maximum thrust; with cargo at working hover — 10–14, see f-aero-props . Long hover with cargo — large props; speed and maneuvering — small ones. Frame: 4–5 mm carbon arms for a 5" arm resonance 300–500 Hz — above the motor harmonics in hover , 5–6 mm or tubes for 10"+. On a 7" a 5 mm arm resonates at 150–250 Hz, within the band of the hover harmonics f-frame-mech , “Natural frequencies” , and 6 mm instead of 5 raises the frequency by only ~20 %: thickness alone does not solve this problem. The rule for a 7": after assembly — a tap on the arm method in f-frame-mech ; if it coincides with the 1st or 2nd hover harmonic — a static notch or a different motor mounting point worked example in f-frame-mech . Look at: weight, free space for the battery and payload, protection of the electronics, availability of spare parts an arm must be purchasable separately , a 20×20 or 30.5×30.5 mm stack. Step 2: motors and props From the manufacturer's thrust table for the chosen prop and voltage: the hover throttle must fall within the band for its class f-physics , “Hover throttle” : freestyle and racing T/W ≥ 6 — no higher than 30–41 %, long range and cinematic T/W 3–4 — 41–58 %, cargo T/W 2–2.5 — 56–71 %, and that is the limit; the current in hover — no higher than 40 % of the continuous rating. KV — by the rule from f-aero-props “KV for the prop and cell count” : a prop is designed for certain RPM, RPM ≈ k × KV × U, so with fewer cells the KV is higher. Oscar Liang's guidelines for 6S: 5" — 1700–2100 KV freestyle , 7" — 980–1300 long range or 1200–1400 freestyle , 10" — about 900; 2806/2807 motors for a 7", 3110/3115 for a 10". A 15" on 6S — 4008–4114 at 320–400 KV course estimate; example table — MN4006 380KV in f-aero-props . The motor mass goes into the mass budget. {{diagram:component-choice-tree Powertrain guidelines for typical aircraft classes.}} Step 3: ESC ESC continuous current ≥ 1.3 × the maximum motor current from the table course guideline: the thrust table is measured on a test stand with a fresh battery and a short run, while an ESC in the frame heats up and runs on a sagging battery; a smaller margin, like 45 A at a 38 A peak in the f-motors-esc example, only works because the peak lasts seconds, and counts as “cutting it close” ; voltage with margin 6S → an ESC rated for 6S, not “up to 6S” at the limit . 4-in-1 — compact, but one crash = replacing everything; individual ESCs — repairable, but you need to route the power. What to take course guideline : up to and including 7" — a 4-in-1 AIO or stack, Step 5a ; individual ESCs on the arms — on 10" and larger and on an X8, where the prop airflow cools them and replacing one channel is cheaper than a board. The firmware BLHeli_32/AM32/BLHeli_S determines telemetry and the RPM filter. Step 4: battery Capacity from current: I_avg from the table for cruise/hover × number of motors + electronics × t / 0.8. Chemistry: LiPo — current, Li-Ion — energy per kilogram but low current capability: the rated continuous current of a 21700 is 3–10C per cell, and for heat the average current is kept no higher than 1.5C, el-battery-packs . LiPo for current the rule — f-power , “Capacity and C rating” : capacity — by the average current, as above; label C × Q ≥ peak current — only a filter; the cell resistance decides: R_cell ≤ 0.5 V / I_peak. Check: does the battery mass fit the mass budget? Otherwise — iterate: heavier battery → more current → even more battery. This loop does not always converge; if it doesn't — change the class. Step 5: FC, receiver, video, GPS FC: an F4 is enough for Betaflight without extras. INAV 9.1.0 works in full on an F405 1 MB of flash; it is the most common MCU among INAV targets — 117 build targets in 88 board directories ; on boards with ≤ 512 KB of flash F411, F722 some features are disabled at build time, including geozones, and on F411 also the second mixer profile target/common.h . ArduPilot 4.7.3 — H7: for 65 of 82 flight controllers on F4 AP_Periph boards not counted the build is trimmed by minimize_ .inc files no built-in FFT, some GPS and telemetry drivers missing , for H7 — 2 of 118 hwdef . With GPS, compass and logs, the number of UARTs ≥ consumers + 1; a black box flash/SD for log-based tuning. Receiver: ELRS, the band — by the mission link-elrs , “Choosing a mode for the mission” : freestyle, racing, line of sight — 2.4 GHz; wing, forest, long routes — 900 MHz the longer wavelength diffracts around obstacles and penetrates foliage better; the price is a longer antenna and the regulatory domain for your country, link-elrs , “Regulatory domains” ; long-range 7–10" — 2.4 GHz 150 Hz or 900 MHz 100 Hz. Video — by the mission link-digital-video , “How to choose”

text: summary The first kit is five purchases that depend on each other: the radio, the video system with goggles, the aircraft, power and tools. A mistake in the order costs more than a mistake in the model: goggles of the wrong system make the next aircraft incompatible, and a receiver on the wrong ELRS version will not link with the radio. This module gives the order of decisions, class tables with price ranges as of November 2026, the DJI goggles compatibility matrix, a “do not buy first” list and a checklist for used gear. In the lab you put together a kit for a given budget and job, check compatibility against the table and calculate the total, the weight and the minutes in the air. theory The order of decisions: what outlives what Buy from the long-lived to the consumable: 1. The radio — lasts the longest: it does not crash, and it fits any aircraft with the same radio protocol. 2. The simulator — the radio connects to a PC over USB as a joystick. Oscar Liang guide updated in November 2026 advises at least 5–10 hours before the first real flight. Choosing a simulator and a training program with criteria are in ops-pilot-training . 3. The video system and goggles — choosing a system locks you into an ecosystem: the video transmitter of every later aircraft has to fit these goggles. 4. The aircraft — a consumable. You will crash the first one, and that is normal. 5. Batteries, charger, tools — chosen for the aircraft class cell count, connector . {{diagram:starter-kit-order You first buy what lives longer: the radio and the goggles stay for years, the aircraft and the batteries change. Goggles are chosen before the aircraft because the video transmitter has to match the goggles' system.}} A reference total Oscar Liang's estimate, November 2026 : aircraft $100–500, radio $50–300, goggles $50–900, batteries $20–100, charger $30–200 — about $250–2000 in all. A gamepad or keyboard instead of a radio? The simulator will accept them, but the stick travel and centering are different, and you will have to buy a radio anyway. Learn on it from the start. The radio: classes and what to look at Minimum requirements: EdgeTX firmware, a built-in ExpressLRS 2.4 GHz module, Hall-sensor gimbals, USB-C with joystick mode. The current stable EdgeTX is 2.12.5 October 17, 2026 . Radios on STM32F2 have stayed on the 2.11 branch 2.11.8, fixes only — this matters for used gear. Prices — the RadioMaster site and Oscar Liang's articles, November 2026, estimates without shipping and taxes. Class Example Price, $ Built-in RF Module bay For whom --- --- --- --- --- --- Mini gamepad RadioMaster Pocket 288 g, Hall gimbals, 2×18650 — not included 60–72 ELRS 2.4, up to 250 mW FCC or 100 mW EU LBT nano thumb grip, whoop and park, budget Ultra-budget RadioMaster T8L 35–40 ELRS 2.4 check the product page simulator and whoop; few switches Compact full-size RadioMaster Boxer, Jumper T20S 110–160 ELRS 2.4, up to 1 W on the Boxer JR Boxer full-size gimbals, pinch grip, long-range flights Full-size with a color screen RadioMaster TX15, TX16S MK3 154–200; MAX versions 220–270 ELRS 2.4 check the product page planes, many models, ArduPilot with telemetry Dual-band RadioMaster GX12 Gemini-X 170 ELRS 2.4 + 900 MHz check the product page long range, noisy RF environment DJI ecosystem radio DJI FPV Remote Controller 3 not verified DJI O4 only none flying O4 without a separate receiver - The form factor is chosen by grip. Thumbs on the sticks — a gamepad is more comfortable; a pinch grip — a full-size case and long sticks. There is no correct grip. - Gimbals. A potentiometer has a wiper rubbing on a track, and it wears. A Hall sensor is contactless: more durable, less signal jitter. A metal CNC gimbal housing feels stiffer; it does not change the accuracy of the electronics. - The external module bay JR — large, nano/Lite — small, not compatible with each other without an adapter is needed if you later want 900 MHz, Crossfire or more power. Which one to get course reference : ELRS and Crossfire modules are made in both formats, so what you already own decides: if you have a JR module — a radio with a JR bay; if not — either of the two, but the choice cannot be changed later without an adapter. - “Multiprotocol” 4-in-1, MPM — a module with four radio chips CC2500, NRF24L01, A7105, CYRF6936 running the MULTI-Module firmware: FrSky D8/D16, FlySky AFHDS 2A, Spektrum DSM and dozens of toy protocols. It cannot do ELRS. The “CC2500” version is one chip of the four the Pocket CC2500 is 100 mW . A beginner in 2026 needs the ELRS variant; a 4-in-1 is bought for a fleet of old receivers. - Power. Many radios are sold without 18650 cells — budget $10–15. Setting up models, mixes and modules is a separate module on EdgeTX link-edgetx . The video system and goggles: the ecosystem lock How the systems differ in principle is in link-digital-video “Four families”, “How to choose” .
