text: summary The overview of the four digital video families is in link-digital-video , and the analog VTX tables are in link-vtx . Here — how to connect a specific air unit to a Betaflight 2025.12 flight controller so that it does not burn out, the OSD appears in the goggles, and recording and power are set up. For DJI O3, O4, the old Air Unit and Vista , Walksnail Avatar and HDZero: power, wiring, the port mask, osd_displayport_device , vcd_video_system , the canvas, fonts and the boot logo analog and HD , the goggles side, the power-up order, heat, recording, power, latency and the equivalents in INAV and ArduPilot. The lab is a Python calculator following the firmware logic port masks, the isSerialConfigValid check, moving OSD elements between canvases per osd.h , then the bench: continuity checks, a fan, the link, OSD, recording. theory Who does what In a digital system the goggles draw the OSD. The flight controller only says which character to draw in which cell of the grid: the MSP DisplayPort commands MSP_DP_WRITE_STRING , MSP_DP_DRAW_SCREEN , heartbeat travel over a single UART. Over the same UART the air unit can control the VTX over MSP channel, power, pit mode and tells the flight controller the size of its grid — the canvas. So HD video needs three things: correct UART wiring, the correct port function mask and the HD mode of the OSD. If even one is missing, you get the number one forum question: there is video but no OSD. Three systems: power and wires The figures are taken from the manufacturers' documentation links in the references . Power is the main thing that sets models apart within one system. System / model Power per the specification Where to take it from UART air unit wire → FC pad RC from the goggles Latency claimed --- --- --- --- --- --- DJI FPV Air Unit 2019 7.4–17.6 V, 4–9 W VBAT 2S–4S MSP over a UART DJI radio → S.Bus < 28 ms 720p/120 Caddx Vista 7.4–26.4 V VBAT 2S–6S as for the Air Unit the same 21–28 ms 720p/120 DJI O3 Air Unit 7.4–26.4 V 2S–6S VBAT or a BEC white UART_RX → TX, gray UART_TX → RX, black and brown — grounds yellow DJI HDL/S.Bus → the S.Bus pad < 28 ms 810p/120 Goggles V2 , 30 ms 1080p/100 Goggles 2 DJI O4 Air Unit 3.7–13.2 V, BEC ≥ 10 W a BEC only 5 V/2 A the same colors the same from 20 ms 1080p/100 Goggles 3 DJI O4 Air Unit Pro 7.4–26.4 V, BEC ≥ 13.5 W VBAT or a 9 V/1.5 A BEC the same colors the same from 15 ms 1080p/100 Goggles 3 Walksnail Avatar HD Pro 6–25.2 V VBAT 6S — with a 50 V/47 µF capacitor air unit RX → TX, air unit TX → RX no, a separate receiver 22 ms on average Walksnail Avatar Mini V3 3.1–13 V 1–3S 4S and above — only through a BEC the same no 22 ms on average HDZero Race V3 4–12 V, 5–6 W a 5–12 V BEC white TX → RX, yellow RX → TX no model: ≈ 3 ms + the frame period 14 ms at 90 fps HDZero Freestyle V2 7–25 V, 6–15 W a BEC is recommended yellow RX → TX, white TX → RX no the same The rules that follow from the table: - Do not power an air unit with an upper limit of 13 V directly from 4S: a charged 3S LiHV is 13.05 V, a 4S is 16.8 V. HDZero says explicitly that, except for the Freestyle of the second batch and newer, their VTXs are not rated for 6S VBAT, and recommends a BEC: it suppresses the voltage spikes that kill VTXs. The “10V/12V HD” pad on a flight controller usually suits any air unit in the table, but its current has to be checked against the 13.5 W of the O4 Pro and the 15 W of the Freestyle V2. The calculation of the branch is in el-power-design . - TX↔RX are always crossed over, 3.3 V logic. DJI has two ground wires: power and signal. Both go to the flight controller. - Only DJI has control from the goggles. The yellow S.Bus wire is connected to the flight controller's S.Bus pad, serialrx_provider = SBUS , and on an F4 — the pad with an inverter bf-ports . If control goes over ELRS, the yellow wire is not connected, and the receiver goes on its own UART with CRSF. - SoftSerial is no good for DisplayPort: HDZero forbids it outright, and Betaflight strips MSP off SoftSerial ports when validating the config see below . {{diagram:bf-hd-wiring A worked example: ELRS on UART1, the air unit on UART4 with the mask 131073 = MSP + VTX_MSP; the air unit is powered per its specification — from VBAT or from a BEC only.}} The Betaflight side: the port mask The Ports tab stores for each port a line serial <id <mask <msp_baud <gps_baud <telemetry_baud <blackbox_baud id : 0 = UART1 … 9 = UART10, 20 = USB VCP, 30/31 = SoftSerial, 40 = LPUART1 . The mask is the sum of the serialPortFunction_e bits from io/serial.h . Four bits matter for video: MSP = 1, VTX SmartAudio = 2048, VTX Tramp = 8192, VTX_MSP = 131072 1 << 17 . The Peripherals item “VTX MSP + Displayport ” together with MSP enabled gives the mask 131073 . The value 131072 from the course audit is confirmed by the source 4.5 and 2025.12 , but it is the single VTX_MSP bit. The port must have 131073. What the firmware does with the mask at boot io/serial.c , config/config.c ; the logic is the same in 4.5 and 2025.12 : 1. isSerialConfigValid : VTX_MSP alone is not allowed, only together with MSP or Serial RX. MSP can be on no more than 3 ports, and MSP is mandatory on VCP. MSP and Serial RX on SoftSerial are silently removed. On any violation the whole port config is reset to the board defaults, and the receiver “disappears” together with the OSD. 2. The port for DisplayPort is found like this: the first port, other than VCP, that has both MSP and VTX_MSP set. There is no longer a separate variable for selecting the port. displayport_msp_serial existed in 4.2–4.3 and was removed in 4.4 it is not in settings.c of the 4.4, 4.5 and 2025.12 branches . The audit called it a 4.4 parameter — that is inaccurate. The DJI O3/O4 manuals and the old Walksnail quickstart still show it with the note “for 4.3”. On both 4.5 and 2025.12 the command set displayport_msp_serial returns the error INVALID NAME . 3. The baud rate is the msp_baud field, 115200. HDZero supports 115200 and 230400 the Race V

text: summary The RC link controls the vehicle, while telemetry connects it to the ground station: map, mission, parameters, warnings. On a 5" ELRS telemetry is enough; a vehicle flying a mission several kilometers out needs a MAVLink channel with known range, throughput and diagnostics. This module covers the SiK family 433/868/915 MHz, 100 mW and RFD900 up to 1 W , setting them up with AT commands and what each parameter means, RADIO_STATUS and fade margin, ELRS in MAVLink mode, IP radios and mesh for multiple vehicles and video, LTE for beyond-the-horizon flights — and how to pick a channel for the job. theory What you need from telemetry - Throughput. A typical set of ArduPilot MAVLink streams is a few kilobytes per second; parameter and mission uploads are bursts. 64 kbit/s over the air ≈ 8 KB/s is plenty, 2–8 kbit/s is enough only for a minimal set of messages. - Range is set by the link budget the “Radio Link Budget” module : power, antennas, frequency, receiver sensitivity. Sensitivity improves as you lower the air data rate — roughly 3 dB for every halving; 6 dB of margin means twice the range. - Latency and duplex. SiK is time-division TDM : the transmitters take turns, latency is tens of milliseconds. For real-time control a joystick over telemetry this matters, for missions it doesn't. - Legality. 433, 868 and 915 MHz have different power and duty-cycle rules in different regions; you configure the modem for your country MIN_FREQ , MAX_FREQ , TXPOWER , DUTY_CYCLE . SiK: the parameters you need to understand SiK firmware runs on most “3DR/Holybro telemetry radios” and on the RFD900x its own branch . Set it up in Mission Planner SiK Radio or by hand: +++ with a one-second pause before and after → OK , ATI5 — list the parameters, ATSn=x — write one, AT&W — save, ATZ — reboot; RT instead of AT does the same for the remote modem. Register Parameter Meaning --- --- --- S1 SERIAL_SPEED UART baud rate in “one-byte form” 57 = 57600 ; the same on the flight controller S2 AIR_SPEED air data rate, kbit/s; 64 by default, lower means farther but slower S3 NETID network ID, identical within a pair; different for neighboring vehicles S4 TXPOWER power, dBm 20 = 100 mW on SiK; up to 30 = 1 W on RFD900x S5 ECC error-correcting code: halves the useful data rate, not recommended S6 MAVLINK 1 — aligns to MAVLink packets and injects RADIO_STATUS ; 2 — also prioritizes RC_OVERRIDE S8/S9 MIN_FREQ / MAX_FREQ frequency range, kHz — per your country's rules S10 NUM_CHANNELS number of frequency-hopping FHSS channels S11 DUTY_CYCLE share of time spent transmitting, %; 100 if the rules don't limit it S15 MAX_WINDOW TDM window, ms; smaller means lower latency and lower throughput Both sides must match in AIR_SPEED , NETID , ECC , MIN/MAX_FREQ , NUM_CHANNELS , otherwise the modems won't link. {{diagram:chart-sik-airspeed Relative SiK range versus air data rate: going from 64 down to 16 kbit/s gains about 6 dB and roughly twice the range.}} RADIO_STATUS and fade margin With MAVLINK = 1 the modem injects the RADIO_STATUS message id 109 into the stream: rssi , remrssi signal at the local and remote end , noise , remnoise , txbuf free space in the transmit buffer, % , error counters. ArduPilot uses txbuf to lower stream rates on its own when the link can't keep up — which is why SERIAL_SPEED can be higher than what the air link carries. - Converting RSSI to dBm approximately : dBm ≈ RSSI / 1.9 − 127. - Fade margin ≈ RSSI − noise / 2, dB. Every 6 dB of margin is a twofold range reserve: 18 dB at the test distance ≈ ×8. - 1 m test: RSSI on both sides above ~190 on a standard SiK; lower means a damaged antenna or modem. Other options - RFD900x/ux — the same SiK logic, 900 MHz, up to 1 W, diversity antennas; for long-range planes and VTOL. More power also means tougher requirements on the power supply pulse current and on antenna separation from the GNSS. - ELRS in MAVLink mode ELRS 3.5+ — RC and MAVLink telemetry over one link; telemetry reaches the GCS through the TX Backpack over Wi-Fi UDP 14550 or over the transmitter's own USB 460800 . Pro: one radio channel and ELRS range; con: a narrow telemetry pipe, so streams get trimmed. In ArduPilot, the receiver port: SERIALn_PROTOCOL = 2 , SERIALn_BAUD = 460 , RSSI_TYPE = 5 , stream rates for that port — 1 Hz; receiver and transmitter on ELRS 3.5.0+, TX Backpack 1.5.0+ details on the MAVLink page of the ELRS documentation . - Herelink and similar “all-in-one” systems — RC, HD video and telemetry in one radio with an Android GCS. - IP radios and mesh Microhard, Doodle Labs, Silvus and others — an Ethernet bridge over radio: MAVLink over UDP, video, SSH to the companion, several vehicles on one network. Expensive, but the standard for serious systems; routing is covered in the mav-routing module. - LoRa — very long range at a few kbit/s: fine for a minimal set position, status , not for parameters and missions. - LTE/4G — beyond-the-horizon link through a carrier network the “Cellular Bridge” project : range is limited by coverage, latency is 50–200 ms with unpredictable dropouts; you need a VPN or a relay because of NAT, and a mandatory link-loss failsafe. {{diagram:chart-elrs-param-download Download time is proportional to the number of parameters parallel lines on log axes : 1000 parameters take 15.6 s at F1000 and 336 s at 50Hz, so parameters are downloaded in a fast mode on the ground.}} How to choose Task Channel --- --- Missions within 1–3 km, simple GCS SiK 100 mW, AIR_SPEED 64 Long-range plane, 10+ km RFD900x, directional antenna on the ground, lower AIR_SPEED FPV/small vehicle, a single radio channel ELRS in MAVLink mode Video + telemetry + several vehicles IP radio / mesh Beyond the horizon, within coverage LTE + VPN, backup radio channel Redundancy: two independent telemetry channels e.g. SiK + LTE on different flight controller ports — the GCS sees the vehicle through either one. practice Step 1. summary: Half of all “unexplained” aircraft losses are weather that nobody calculated: the wind at 100 m is twice as strong as at the ground, heat in the mountains ate the thrust margin, a cold battery sagged on takeoff, fog coated the propellers with ice. The module gives you the calculations you do before
headings: Wind: one thing at the ground, another aloft The wind limit for your aircraft Density altitude Cold and batteries Icing Reports: METAR and TAF The “go / no-go” sheet Place in the system Step 1. Wind profile Step 2. Your aircraft's limit Step 3. Density altitude Step 4. Decoding a report Step 5. Your own “go / no-go” sheet
text: summary Half of all “unexplained” aircraft losses are weather that nobody calculated: the wind at 100 m is twice as strong as at the ground, heat in the mountains ate the thrust margin, a cold battery sagged on takeoff, fog coated the propellers with ice. The module gives you the calculations you do before leaving for the field: the wind profile with height and gusts, the wind limit for your aircraft, density altitude and what it does to thrust and flight time, the battery in the cold, icing conditions, reading METAR/TAF aviation reports — and brings them together into a “go / no-go” sheet with numbers. theory Wind: one thing at the ground, another aloft - Profile. Friction with the ground slows the air: wind grows with height. A simple model is the power law v h = v₁₀· h/10 ^α, where v₁₀ is the wind at 10 m that is how weather stations measure it , α ≈ 1/7 for open terrain, more 0.2–0.3 over forest and buildings. Example: 7 m/s at 10 m → at 100 m 7·10^ 1/7 ≈ 9.7 m/s. - Gusts. The mean wind is not the maximum. Reports give gusts separately G in METAR ; if there are none, allow a factor of 1.3–1.5 over the mean. - Mechanical turbulence. Behind buildings, a tree line, a hill — eddies at a distance of several obstacle heights downwind. Taking off and landing on the lee side of an obstacle is the bumpiest place. - Thermals. During the day, rising currents over heated ground; for light aircraft and mapping, morning and evening are better. The wind limit for your aircraft - Multicopter. Flying into the wind, the aircraft is tilted; the stronger the wind, the greater the tilt and throttle. Rule of thumb course guideline : gusts no more than ~50–60 % of the aircraft's maximum horizontal speed in a position-holding mode — the rest is margin for maneuvering and the return. Where the number comes from: returning into the wind needs an airspeed of about 1.5 × the wind the same margin as in des-sizing , i.e. wind no more than 1 / 1.5 ≈ 67 % of maximum speed; 50–60 % leaves extra margin for a gust stronger than forecast. Check against the log: the mean tilt and throttle when hovering in wind; throttle above 65–71 % means T/W below 2, no margin for any class, and for a 5–7" 60 % is already a reason to be wary the bands by class — in f-physics , “Hover throttle” . - Plane. The wind must be noticeably below the cruise speed: with 15 m/s of wind and an 18 m/s cruise, the ground speed into the wind is 3 m/s, and the return will take six times longer. - Route planning. Fly out into the wind, come back downwind: on the way back, when the battery is weaker, the wind helps. Calculate the return time from the ground speed into the wind if the route is the reverse. {{diagram:chart-wind-profile Wind with height for 10 m/s at 10 m: at 100 m the mean is ~14 m/s, gusts ×1.4 — about 20 m/s.}} Density altitude A propeller's thrust is proportional to the air density ρ, and the power needed to hover at the same thrust — to 1/√ρ from the momentum theory of the propeller, the “Propeller aerodynamics” module . Density falls with altitude and with temperature. - Density altitude — the altitude in the standard atmosphere ISA: 15 °C and 1013.25 hPa at sea level, −6.5 °C per km at which the density is the same as now. Estimate: density altitude ≈ pressure altitude + ~36 m for every °C above the ISA temperature at that altitude. - Example. A site at 2000 m, +30 °C. The ISA temperature at 2000 m is +2 °C, a deviation of +28 °C → density altitude ≈ 2000 + 28·36 ≈ 3000 m. Density is ~74 % of sea level: maximum thrust drops to ~74 %, hover power grows by ~16 %, flight time drops by about the same, and a 2:1 thrust-to-weight ratio turns into ~1.5:1. - What to do. Recalculate the thrust-to-weight ratio and flight time, less payload, props with more pitch or diameter if the motors and ESCs allow it current-wise , a larger battery margin. {{diagram:chart-density-altitude Maximum thrust and hover power versus density altitude ISA : at 3000 m thrust is ~74 %, hover power ~116 %.}} Cold and batteries - The internal resistance of lithium cells grows several times in the cold: under load the voltage sags more, the flight controller sees “low voltage” sooner, and the capacity actually delivered falls. - Rules: keep batteries warm an inside pocket, an insulated bag, a heat pack at 20–25 °C before takeoff; the first 30–60 s — hover at low throttle while the cells warm up from their own current; do not lower the voltage warning threshold “so it stops beeping”; plan the flight time 20–30 % shorter than in summer. - Do not charge LiPo when cold below ~5–10 °C: the threshold depends on the manufacturer, Gens Ace — 10 °C, see f-power — lithium plates on the anode, the cell degrades and becomes dangerous. - Mechanics and electronics: thickened grease, brittle plastic, condensation when you bring a cold aircraft into the warmth — let it warm up in a closed case before powering it on. Icing - Conditions: visible moisture fog, drizzle, clouds, wet snow and a temperature from roughly +2 to −10 °C; the most dangerous is supercooled drizzle and fog around 0 °C. - Ice on the props builds up within minutes: thrust drops, vibration grows, the props become unbalanced; on a plane — the stall speed rises. Small UAVs without anti-icing systems do not fly in such conditions. - The sign in a report: a temperature/dew point spread of 0–2 °C at a negative or near-zero temperature — fog and icing are likely. Reports: METAR and TAF METAR is the actual weather at an aerodrome, TAF is the forecast. An example report: text METAR XXXX 081230Z 27012G22KT 9999 BKN015 04/01 Q1013 - 27012G22KT — wind from 270° westerly , 12 knots, gusts 22 knots 1 knot ≈ 0.51 m/s: 6 m/s, gusts 11 m/s ; - 9999 — visibility 10 km or more; BKN015 — broken clouds, base at 1500 feet ~450 m ; - 04/01 — temperature +4 °C, dew point +1 °C a 3 °C spread — damp, cold, fog possible toward evening ; - Q1013 — QNH pressure 1013 hPa for barometric altitude . text: summary Most accidents happen not because of the firmware but because of organization: nobody checked the neighbors' frequencies, nobody agreed who watches the aircraft, there was no plan for loss of link. This module is about operations as a discipline: sortie planning, roles in the team, frequencies and communication, the pre-flight and post-flight protocol, actions in an incident and searching for a crashed aircraft. Based on the practice of several pilots working at one site. theory Sortie planning Before leaving you know: the site and the zones the module on regulations , the weather wind by altitude, precipitation, temperature — cold cuts LiPo capacity , the goal of the sortie and the success criteria, who takes part and in what roles, which frequencies the neighbors occupy. Roles Even with two people it is worth naming the roles explicitly: - Pilot — flies, and does nothing else. - Observer spotter — watches the aircraft by eye and the surroundings: people, birds, other aircraft; talks to the pilot without distracting them. - Technician / GCS — telemetry, parameters, logs, battery swaps, the timer. - Lead — decides “go / no-go”, keeps the logbook. One person can combine roles, but a pilot in flight is only a pilot. Frequencies and communication - Video : a table of the channels occupied at the site; separation from the neighbors guideline ≥ ~37 MHz for analog: the signal occupies ~20–27 MHz around the carrier, so closer than that the bands overlap; with four or more aircraft there is also intermodulation, link-vtx ; a channel change — by the algorithm from the VTX module, on one aircraft first. - RC : the binding phrase is unique; packet rate for the mission link-elrs , “Choosing a mode for the mission”: freestyle and racing within line of sight — 2.4 GHz 250–500 Hz or F500, long-range 7–10" — 2.4 GHz 150 Hz or 900 MHz 100 Hz, wing and forest — 900 MHz 50–100 Hz ; with several ELRS radios — different phrases, otherwise the hopping patterns will coincide. - Voice : short standard phrases: “arming”, “taking off”, “link”, “low battery”, “landing”, “emergency”. The pilot confirms with one word. Protocols Pre-flight from the safety module, extended : frequencies agreed, roles named, battery voltage written down, failsafe tested on this aircraft, timer started at arming. Post-flight : disarm, battery disconnected, motor temperature, inspection of the props and frame, a logbook entry time, battery before/after, remarks , the log saved if it was a test sortie. Incidents - Loss of link : the pilot reports it, everyone watches the aircraft, nobody runs. The aircraft does what the failsafe is configured to do — that is why the failsafe is tested in advance. - Crash : the location from the last telemetry/video, the buzzer BEEPER , GPS coordinates from the GCS log. Approaching a crashed aircraft — the battery may be damaged: do not touch it if it is hot/swollen, do not charge it. - Injury : first aid, emergency services, then everything else. - Debrief : what happened, from the log, without looking for someone to blame; the conclusion goes into the logbook and the checklist. Searching for a crashed aircraft The search starts before the sortie: without coordinates and a buzzer, an aircraft in the grass is searched for for hours. Prepare in advance. - Coordinates to the radio and into the log. GPS on board and CRSF telemetry: the GPS sensors appear in EdgeTX after Discover new sensors. Recording — the SD Logs special function: the radio writes a CSV with radio and telemetry values to the LOGS folder on the SD card at a set interval at least 50 MB of free space needed . The last row with coordinates is the last known point. - Coordinates in the OSD and DVR recording in the goggles. Latitude and longitude on screen osd_gps_lat_pos , osd_gps_lon_pos in Betaflight end up in the goggles' recording; the last frame gives the point, heading and altitude. - A GCS recording a tlog for ArduPilot and PX4: the last position stays in the ground station's log even if the aircraft has lost power. - A buzzer on a switch BEEPER mode and a motor beacon over DShot : beacon RX_LOST and beacon RX_SET — both off by default; the beacon works only with the DShot protocol and stopped motors, and RX_LOST in 4.5 — only if the craft was armed after power-up, in 2025.12 — if the flight controller does not see USB in detail — the bf-led-buzzer module . - A standalone buzzer with its own battery — the only thing that works when the battery has been thrown off. The first minute after a crash. 1. Disarm. The pilot stays in place and says aloud the direction and a landmark where they last saw the aircraft; the observer points with their hand. Nobody runs. 2. Do not switch off the radio while there is telemetry: write down the coordinates and voltage, turn on BEEPER. If the link is already gone, the buzzer and the RX_LOST beacon work by themselves. If the link is there but there is no BEEPER switch, switching off the radio triggers them. 3. Stop the DVR recording and do not overwrite it; look at the last seconds: coordinates in the OSD, heading, altitude, what was under the aircraft. 4. The lead records the time of the crash and the remaining battery from the OSD — the time budget is counted from that. Where to get the last point in decreasing order of accuracy . Telemetry coordinates on the radio or in the CSV log → coordinates in the OSD on the last DVR frames → the last position in the ground station's tlog → without GPS: the direction of the last frame, the heading and the flight time from a known point. A correction for momentum: an aircraft that lost power at a height h at a speed v travels beyond the last point by about v × √ 2h/g . At 20 m/s and 30 m that is about 50 m forward along the heading. Search pattern. 1. Walk to the last point using a phone's navigator, start recording your own track — it will show what has already been covered. 2. Stop, 10–15 seconds of silence: listen for the buzzer. Repeat every 20–30 m. 3. Fi

text: summary Engineers learn from other people's crashes — if the crashes have been analyzed. This module takes three public investigations by government boards — the Matternet M2 in Zurich 2019, an ArduCopter-based platform, a failure caused by vibration and the EKF , the Alauda Airspeeder Mk II at Goodwood 2019, loss of link and a kill switch that did not work and the Freefly Alta X at Henley 2022, battery depletion — and analyzes each one with the same scheme: symptom → cause → what the log shows → consequences → what to change in the configuration and procedures. Each case ends with a line for your checklist. theory The analysis scheme Board reports AAIB in the UK, STSB/SUST in Switzerland, NTSB in the US follow the same logic, and it is also your tool: 1. Symptom — what the operator saw. 2. Sequence — events in time order from the logs and telemetry. 3. Cause — technical what failed and systemic why it was possible . 4. What the data shows — specific log messages, parameters, values. 5. Consequences — impact energy, who was nearby, what happened to the area. 6. Fix — configuration, design, procedure. Distinguish three types of cause: hardware failure a part broke , configuration error a parameter did not match the mission , operator error a procedure was not followed . In real accidents all three are almost always present. Case 1. Matternet M2, Zurich, 9 May 2019 STSB, final report No. 2390, aircraft SUI-9903 Context. A Swiss Post delivery quadcopter on a modified ArduCopter based on 3.5.0-rc5 , three IMUs, a flight termination system FTS with a parachute. A return flight without cargo. Sequence. Takeoff at 10:37:35. After ~50 s, vibration grew on all three IMUs accelerations in places 30 m/s² , and IMU3 showed sharp deviations, while IMU1 and IMU2 showed consistent values; the aircraft began to oscillate in pitch. At 10:38:46 the log shows EKFCHECK_BAD_VARIANCE ; the error handler activated the FTS at ~185 m above the takeoff point ~100 m above the ground : all four motors were stopped, the parachute was deployed. The parachute line broke at its attachment on the aircraft; an unbraked fall, destruction at 10:38:48. The location — a forest, ~50 m from a group of children with their teachers, who did not hear the warning signal. Causes. Technical: growing vibration of unknown origin probably a resonance from an external factor — prop damage or a bird strike combined with insufficient robustness of the firmware to such an event. Systemic: the modified ArduCopter could run only two EKF lanes, EK2_IMU_MASK = 5 IMU1 and IMU3, without IMU2 — the faulty sensor could not be isolated; the FTS triggered an uncontrolled descent immediately instead of attempting a controlled flight termination. The parachute line had been damaged by the sharp edge of the aluminum attachment even before deployment and did not withstand the jerk. What the log shows. VIBE grows on all IMUs, but the data of one IMU sharply diverges from the other two a sign of a local source or sensor, not of the frame as a whole ; the EKF innovations grow → EKFCHECK_BAD_VARIANCE ; switch to the FTS. Consequences. Impact energy ≈ 118 J without cargo above the 80 J accepted as the threshold of serious injury . The delivery program was suspended. Seven safety recommendations. Fixes actual . EK2_IMU_MASK = 3 two healthy IMUs + the ability to isolate , a check of both EKF lanes at arming, a second safety line and a redesigned attachment, a 100 dB siren, a log analysis tool, a parachute compliant with ASTM F3322, maximum speed reduced from 20 to 16 m/s. Board recommendation No. 591: pursue a redundant propulsion concept the analysis noted that configurations with 6 or more motors have a significantly lower probability of failure . Line for your checklist: “Vibration on each IMU in the log is checked after every mechanical change; the behavior on an EKF failsafe is known and tested in SITL”. Case 2. Alauda Airspeeder Mk II, Goodwood, 4 July 2019 AAIB, report 03/2021 Context. A 95 kg demonstration multirotor, a custom flight controller with two IMUs, no GNSS and no RTH, controlled from a FrSky Taranis X9D radio + an R9M module on 915 MHz 10 mW, FCC mode — a band not permitted for airborne use in the UK . A separate kill switch on 433 MHz LoRa with its own battery, cutting power to the controller through a relay. Sequence. ~65 s after takeoff — a sudden uncommanded transition to level attitude, then loss of link. On loss of link the controller froze the last throttle commands and held level attitude — the aircraft continued climbing at ~2000 ft/min, rotating at ~40°/s, for 4 min 12 s up to ~7900 feet, and entered the controlled airspace of a Gatwick holding area. On the “kill” command the observer activated the switch — with no effect. After the battery was depleted the aircraft flipped over and fell at ~4500 ft/min into a field 40 m from houses, 700 m outside the permitted area. Impact energy ≈ 24,800 J. No one was hurt. Causes. The exact cause of the loss of link was not established: there was no on-board recording , the boards were destroyed. Systemic causes established by the board: the loss-of-link failsafe was designed as “hold throttle” rather than “descend/land”; the kill switch had no feedback loss of its channel went undetected , with the relay in a normally closed state a switch failure goes unnoticed until the moment it is needed , on a prototyping board with jumper wires, activated by a voice command instead of automatically; in the wreckage the relay and the power wire were detached from the board. The aircraft was not designed or tested to any standard: mounting with Velcro and zip ties, Ethernet cables as ESC signal lines, soldering with jumper wires, a 42–58 V battery with no protection whatsoever; no vibration tests, no RF tests. Speed in flight up to 25 m/s against a declared limit of 11 m/s. What the data shows. Nothing — and that is the main lesson: without a log, an investigation ends with the words “not established”. Fixe

text: summary A hobbyist repairs the aircraft after a crash; an operator doesn't let it get to a crash. The difference is the logbook and the schedule: every flight is recorded, every battery has a history of cell resistance, props are replaced by a rule rather than “when they crack”, and trends of vibration and motor balance from the logs warn about wear before it becomes a failure. The module gives you the aircraft and battery logbooks, battery retirement criteria, an inspection schedule by flight hours, log analysis as a maintenance tool, and the basics of reliability — failure rate, MTBF, series and redundant systems — with a calculation that shows why six motors instead of four. theory Logbooks - Aircraft logbook : date, pilot, site, mission, flight time min , battery, remarks, a link to the log; separately — repairs and replacements what, why, serial numbers . The total flight time of the aircraft and its components motors, ESCs, props is the basis of the schedule. - Battery logbook : battery number a sticker , purchase date, cycles, voltage before/after the flight, the internal resistance of the cells by date, damage. A number on the battery is mandatory — otherwise the “bad battery” can never be pinned down. - Format : a table or CSV in git next to the aircraft's parameters the “Configs in CI” module — history and search for free. Battery life - Internal resistance IR of each cell is the main indicator. It is measured with a charger that has an IR function compare with the same instrument at the same temperature . Growing IR — less output under load, more heating. - Retirement criteria guidelines, check with the manufacturer : a cell's IR has grown about 1.5–2 times from new; cell imbalance after charging and resting of more than 0.05 V from 0.03 V — watch it; the script below flags from 0.04 V ; swelling; capacity below ~80 % of the rating; mechanical damage after a crash. A swollen or damaged battery — do not fly it and do not charge it, dispose of it by the procedure from the “Power” module discharge to ~0 V through a load outdoors, insulate the terminals, collection point . - Storage : 3.80–3.90 V per cell storage; Gens Ace datasheet, f-power , somewhere cool, in a fireproof bag or box; do not keep them fully charged for longer than a day course guideline . - Operating regime : do not discharge below the landing threshold the “Power” module , do not charge them hot or cold, balance charging. Inspection schedule When What Criterion --- --- --- Before every flight props, prop and motor mounting, battery and connector, antennas, straps cracks and chips, play, a hot connector After every flight motor and ESC temperature by touch, props, frame, logbook entry one motor noticeably hotter than the others — investigate After any impact props all of them, not just the broken one , frame, motors for play and binding, calibration check a prop after a strike — replace it Every ~10–20 h motor bearings spin by hand — rustling, play , frame screws, soldering and connectors, flight controller dampers rustling and play — replace the bearings or the motor Every ~50 h or per season full teardown: wiring, insulation, power connectors, firmware update as planned traces of heat, chafing The intervals are starting values; your own are determined from the logbook: if bearings die in 30 h, the schedule is 20. {{diagram:maint-inspection-timeline A schedule by flight hours: checks before and after every flight and after an impact always happen, the scheduled ones go by hours, and the bearing interval is adjusted from the logbook they die in 30 h — inspection every 20 h .}} Post-crash checklist The “after any impact” row of the schedule in expanded form. It is gone through in order, with an entry in the aircraft logbook; until the last row is done, the aircraft does not fly. Component What to check “Do not fly” criterion --- --- --- Battery — first disconnect it; dents, cuts in the wrap, swelling, heat, smell; cell voltages immediately and after 30 min of rest any damage to the wrap, swelling, heat; cell spread of more than 0.05 V; a cell below 3.0 V Battery — quarantine apart from the others, on a non-flammable surface, outdoors or in a fireproof box; watch it for at least 15 minutes, charge it only after inspection and under supervision; an entry in the battery logbook marked “impact” IR growth relative to the logbook, imbalance after the first charge, swelling during charging — retire it Frame plates and standoffs for cracks and carbon delamination against the light and by bending , all frame screws for tightness a crack, delamination, a stripped thread Arms each arm for bending and twisting by hand, the fit in the plates; text: summary Troubleshooting is not trying guesses one after another but eliminating the branches of a tree, where each step is confirmed by a fact: a multimeter reading, a firmware message, a line in a log. The module gives you a tree for six typical situations — “won't arm”, “motors don't spin or spin wrong”, “goes crazy on throttle”, “an ESC/board burns when the battery is connected”, “loses link or video”, “shut off in the air or flew away” — and a rule for adding your own cases to it. Tools: a smoke stopper, a multimeter, CLI status /pre-arm messages, Blackbox/DataFlash. theory Troubleshooting rules 1. Fact first, then hypothesis. The firmware almost always tells you what is wrong: Betaflight — status in the CLI the Arming disable flags line , INAV — the Status tab and status in the CLI, ArduPilot — PreArm messages in the GCS. Start with these, not with resoldering. 2. One change — one check. You changed two parameters and it started working — you don't know which one helped, and you don't know what you broke. 3. From cheap to expensive. Inspection and a multimeter come before an oscilloscope and replacing the board. 4. Safety at every step. Props off for everything to do with the motors. The first power-up after any soldering — through a smoke stopper. 5. Record the path. Steps with their results — in a note; the cause you found — into the tree and into the aircraft logbook. Tree 1. Won't arm Read the reason: Betaflight CLI → status → Arming disable flags: ... . The CLI prints the short names from runtime_config.c FAILSAFE, CALIB, NO_ACC_CAL, CMS, BOOTGRACE, MOTOR_PROTO, DSHOT_TELEM, ARM_SWITCH — before 2025.12 it was called ARMSWITCH ; below, some of the flags are named as in the documentation. The most common: - RXLOSS / RX_FAILSAFE — the receiver provides no channels. → The port and protocol UART, CRSF/SBUS, inversion for SBUS on F4 , the bind, receiver power 5 V with a multimeter , the Receiver tab — do the channels move. - THROTTLE — throttle above minimum. → Stick calibration in the radio, min_check , channel reversal. - ANGLE — the aircraft is tilted more than small_angle . → The surface, accelerometer calibration. - CALIBRATING / ACC_CALIBRATION / NOGYRO — the gyro is not calibrated or not found. → Keep it still at power-up; NOGYRO — a hardware problem or the wrong firmware target. - ARM_SWITCH — the arm switch was on when power was applied. → Switch it off, then on. - MSP / CLI / CMS_MENU — the configurator is connected or the OSD menu is open. → Disconnect USB, exit the menu. - NOPREARM — a prearm mode is configured but not activated. - DSHOT_TELEM before 4.5 — RPMFILTER — the RPM filter is enabled, but there is no ESC telemetry bidirectional DShot is not supported by the ESC firmware or not enabled . - BOOT_GRACE_TIME — just wait a few seconds after power-up. - MOTOR_PROTOCOL — no motor protocol selected. INAV: the Status tab shows the reasons Navigation is unsafe, Compass not calibrated, Hardware failure... . ArduPilot: PreArm: ... in the GCS — each line names the culprit Compass not calibrated, Gyros inconsistent, RC not calibrated, Throttle below failsafe, GPS: No Fix, Battery failsafe, etc. ; do not disable the checks in ARMING_SKIPCHK before 4.7 — ARMING_CHECK — fix the cause. {{diagram:arming-tree Tree 1 as a diagram: flag → cause → check.}} Tree 2. Motors don't spin / spin wrong Props off. - No motor responds on the Motors tab. → Do the protocol DShot300/600 and motor_pwm_protocol match the ESC? → Are the ESCs getting power voltage on the pads ? → Are the signal wires on the right pads resource MOTOR ? → Do the ESCs beep when power is applied the startup tune ? If not, the ESC is dead or has no power. - One motor doesn't spin, the others do. → Swap the signal wires with a working one: if the problem moved with the wire — it's the signal/the FC pad; if it stayed — the ESC or the motor. → Is the resistance of the motor's three phases equal? → Phase soldering a cold joint is typical . - A motor twitches and won't start. → Lost contact on one phase soldering, a chafed wire or a damaged ESC. → Check the phases for continuity, wiggle them. - They spin the wrong way / in the wrong order. → The Motors tab: check the number and direction one by one against the frame diagram; change the direction in the ESC firmware BLHeli Suite/Configurator or by swapping two phase wires. The “props in/out” direction — consistent on all four which layout to choose — f-physics , “Props in or props out” . - The drone flips over on takeoff. → This is tree 2: order/direction or a wrong mixer mixer not for your frame . Tree 3. “Goes crazy” on throttle Symptom: it hovers fine, above 60–70% throttle it shakes, the motors are hot, the drone behaves unpredictably. - Is there a Blackbox log? If not — record one, otherwise it's guesswork. The gyro spectrum: a huge peak at the motor frequency → mechanics imbalance, props, motor play ; broadband noise growing with throttle → vibration + insufficient filtering; a peak that doesn't move with throttle → frame resonance. - Did gyro noise grow after a replacement/repair? → Is there a capacitor on the power bus? The soldering of its leads, its capacitance. → The FC mounting dampers, taut wires . - ESC desync a motor suddenly loses RPM, a jerk, then it recovers; in the log — an eRPM dip on one motor : → ESC settings timing, demag , DShot too fast for long wires, a damaged motor; lower the protocol to DShot300, check the phases. - Voltage sag: in the log VBAT drops below the threshold on throttle → the BEC reboots the FC an instant loss of control or the ESCs go into protection. → Connector, battery, soldering. - PID/filters : too much D or P with insufficient filtering → oscillations at high throttle, where there is more noise. → Filters based on the spectrum, then lower D. - Interference to the receiver from a VTX at full power LQ drops with throttle — rare, but it happens with ripple on the VTX : → a VTX power filter, antenna separation. Tree 4. Something burns/

text: summary The picture in your goggles is a control channel, not footage: an analog DVR records a standard-definition frame with interference, a digital one records whatever made it through the radio. For a video you need a separate recording: an action camera, or the onboard recording of a digital video unit. The module covers camera classes with their mass and what that mass costs in flight time, stabilization in the camera and in Gyroflow the camera's gyro or the flight controller's Blackbox , exposure through shutter angle and ND filters with stop counting, vibration and "jello", camera tilt versus speed, DVR for crash analysis and searching, memory cards and camera power. After the module you can choose a camera, a filter and settings for the task, and find the cause of a defect from a description of the footage. The practice is computational: exposure, recording size, tilt geometry, and the analysis of four defects. theory Three recordings and what each is for Recording Where it is written What is in it What it is for --- --- --- --- Goggle DVR analog the SD card in the goggles or in the receiver module a PAL 576 / NTSC 480 line frame after the radio: snow, breakups, OSD flight review, search: the last frame and the coordinates in the OSD Goggle DVR digital the goggles HDZero: only there; DJI O4: per the Record With setting what made it through the radio, with OSD the same; you can see where the link degraded Onboard recording on the video unit the unit's internal memory or microSD DJI O3/O4, Walksnail the camera frame without radio losses, without OSD crash analysis, a mid-quality video Action camera its own microSD 4K, 10-bit on higher-end models, a gyro for Gyroflow the video The main consequence: the onboard recording stays on board. If the aircraft is lost, only what was recorded in the goggles and on the radio helps you find it ops-field . Power-on order, heating and recording for each system are in bf-hd-osd-video , and the comparison of systems is in link-digital-video . Camera classes and what they cost the aircraft Camera mass is flight time and tune. An estimate from disk theory f-aero-props : hover power grows as m^1.5, so with the same battery the hover time is t ∝ m^−1.5. For a 5" weighing 600 g without a camera: Class Example manufacturer's mass Price, as of November 2026 Gyro for Gyroflow Hover time, share of "no camera" --- --- --- --- --- Full-size action camera GoPro HERO13 Black 159 g with battery; DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro 146 g ~$300–500 estimate, not verified yes HERO 8+ even with HyperSmooth; DJI with EIS off 0.70 +159 g 360° Insta360 X5 200 g, 8K30, up to 180 Mbit/s not verified no Gyroflow does not support 360°; stabilization is in the manufacturer's app 0.65 +200 g "Naked" GoPro housing removed, powered from the flight battery Flywoo Naked V1/V2 based on HERO9–12: 45/49 g; GoPro HERO10 Bones 54 g, 5–27 V $350–590 Flywoo, Oscar Liang review yes, the same electronics 0.90 +45 g Lightweight FPV camera RunCam Thumb 2 27.8 g, 4K60 100 Mbit/s, 5 V only, up to 0.7 A ~$99 review yes, a separate .gcsv file 0.93 +28 g Magnetic mini camera Insta360 GO 3S 39.1 g, 4K30, 120 Mbit/s not verified yes 0.91 +39 g Onboard recording on the video unit DJI O4 Pro ≈32 g camera + unit , 4K120, 130 Mbit/s; O4 ≈8.2 g, 4K60, 100 Mbit/s; Walksnail HD Pro 1080p60, 32 GB of internal memory O4 Pro $229 Adorama, November 22, 2026 ; Walksnail HD Pro kit $159 caddxfpv yes, but the O3/O4 camera must be soft-mounted, or you need Optical correction replaces the FPV camera and VTX, adds almost nothing Mass is not only time. A camera on top at the front raises the center of mass and moves it forward, and increases the pitch moment of inertia: the same PID gives a different response, and the rear pair of motors is unloaded. After fitting a heavy camera, record a Blackbox log and check the tune bf-pid , bf-blackbox , just as after changing the battery. A "naked" GoPro loses the housing's protection and the built-in battery which is needed for firmware updates , and overheating is a frequent complaint about such builds per the Flywoo V2 review, the metal front helps . Stabilization: in the camera or in Gyroflow In the camera HyperSmooth on GoPro, RockSteady on DJI it is electronic: the frame is cropped and shifted by the gyro in real time. The upside: a finished file. The limits: the crop is chosen once and for all, the algorithm sees only the past, and the horizon is not held in every mode on the Osmo Action 5 Pro, HorizonSteady is 1080p/2.7K up to 60 fps only, HorizonBalancing up to 4K 60 fps; on the HERO13 Black, in-camera Horizon Leveling is not available in every mode . Sharp FPV flips and vibration are the worst case for any EIS. Gyroflow GPLv3, Windows/Linux/macOS/Android/iOS, plugins for DaVinci Resolve, Premiere, Final Cut stabilizes after the flight from the recorded gyro. What it needs: - Motion data. The camera's gyro in the file GoPro HERO 5+, but HERO5 and HERO7 are marked "Bad on FPV drone"; HERO 8+ can shoot with HyperSmooth on; DJI Avata/O3/O4/Action 4–6 need EIS off and FOV Wide, otherwise the gyro is not recorded; Insta360 GO/Ace: on some models, FreeFrame mode or an external log: Betaflight/INAV Blackbox .bbl , .bfl , .csv and ArduPilot logs .bin , .log . No gyro: Optical correction since 1.7.0 estimates the motion from the pixels, which is worse. - A lens profile. Built-in official profiles for GoPro, DJI, Sony, Insta360, RunCam Thumb/5 Orange; HERO11+ writes its calibration into the file. For your own camera, a chessboard calibration. - Synchronization. Not needed for the camera's gyro GoPro 8+, DJI, Insta360 . Needed for a flight controller log: Gyroflow compares the motion from the log with the video's optical flow; 2–3 points on stretches with motion in all axes are usually enough, and all the points should have similar offsets. - Camera tilt. In a flight controller log the gyro is in the frame axes while the camera is tilted: the angle goes into Motion data → Rotation → Pitch u

title: Onboard power circuit design
summary: An aircraft has several power buses with different requirements: the motor power bus tolerates sags and ripple, but the flight controller, receiver, GPS and camera don't. This module teaches you to compute the currents per branch, pick a BEC by current and voltage, pick wire gauge by current and len
headings: Load map Linear vs switching BEC Sag and internal resistance Ripple and the capacitor Protection Wire gauges Step 1. Power tree Step 2. Choosing BECs and wire gauges Step 3. Capacitor Step 4. Protection Step 5. Measure (link to the measurements module)
text: summary An aircraft has several power buses with different requirements: the motor power bus tolerates sags and ripple, but the flight controller, receiver, GPS and camera don't. This module teaches you to compute the currents per branch, pick a BEC by current and voltage, pick wire gauge by current and length, understand where sags and ripple come from and why a low-ESR capacitor on the bus isn't an option but part of the circuit. Separately — protection: smoke stopper, fuse, reverse polarity. theory Load map Before choosing components, draw the power tree: battery → power bus → ESC ×4…8, 5 V BEC, 9–12 V BEC → loads. Typical currents: {{diagram:power-tree Power tree: from the battery to the power bus and separate BECs; each load with its own current.}} Load Voltage Typical current --- --- --- FC + gyro 5 V 3.3 internal 0.1–0.2 A ELRS receiver 5 V 0.1–0.3 A on-board TX module up to 0.5 GPS with compass 5 V 3.3 0.05–0.1 A Digital video system air unit 9–12 V 0.5–1.2 A, higher peaks Analog VTX 800 mW–1 W 9–12 V / 5 V 0.4–0.7 A Servos wing 5–6 V / 7.4 V 0.5–1 A each while moving Companion Pi 4/5 5 V 1–3 A, peaks up to 5 Lighting/LEDs 5 V 0.06 A per LED Add them up with a 50% margin: a 5 V BEC on an aircraft with GPS, receiver and FC and no companion — 1 A is enough; with a Raspberry you need a separate 3–5 A BEC. Linear vs switching BEC - Linear LDO — dumps the excess voltage as heat: at 6S 25 V → 5 V and 0.5 A it dissipates 10 W. Unsuitable for high voltages and currents, but has no ripple — good for the gyro and RF. - Switching buck — 85–95% efficiency, but produces ripple at the switching frequency hundreds of kHz and its harmonics; a bad buck next to the receiver means lost LQ. Flight controllers have a filtered 5 V / 9 V buck. - A good trick: buck down to 5.5–6 V, then an LDO to 5 V for the sensitive part many FCs are built this way: 3.3 V for the gyro through an LDO . Sag and internal resistance Voltage under load U = E − I·R_int. R_int of a 6S 4P Li-Ion battery ≈ 20–40 mΩ per cell → 30–60 mΩ per pack R × 6 / 4 ; at 60 A the sag is 1.8–3.6 V. Plus the wires: 12 AWG ≈ 5.2 mΩ/m, 14 AWG ≈ 8.3, 16 AWG ≈ 13.2. 20 cm out and back of 14 AWG at 60 A is 0.2 V, which is small; but an XT60 connector with oxidized contacts can add more. The sag isn't dangerous in itself, but because the BEC on the flight controller gets an input voltage below its threshold some bucks shut off below 7–8 V on 2S — an FC reboot in flight. Ripple and the capacitor ESCs switch the windings at tens of kHz, and the current in the battery wires jerks. The inductance of the wires L ≈1 µH per meter turns dI/dt into voltage spikes: U = L·dI/dt. These are ripple and spikes on the power bus that pass into the FC supply, into the gyro noise in the log and into the video lines . The fix is a low-ESR electrolytic or polymer capacitor right on the ESC/PDB power pads: 470–1000 µF at 35 V for 4S, 1000 µF at 50 V for 6S ≥ 30% voltage margin . It acts as a local source: it delivers energy on the edge and absorbs the spike. Short leads — otherwise the lead inductance spoils the effect. {{diagram:chart-power-lc-filter A 22 µH + 470 µF LC filter attenuates the 24 kHz ESC ripple by tens of dB but amplifies at its 1.6 kHz resonance: a low ESR gives an +11 dB peak, an ESR of 0.15 Ω damps it at the cost of high-frequency attenuation.}} Protection - Smoke stopper — a bulb or a resistor/current limiter in series with the positive lead at the first power-up. A short circuit — the bulb lights up, the aircraft doesn't smoke. - Fuse — on large aircraft on the power bus not on the motors — the current is too high and pulsed and on the companion bus. - Reverse polarity — XT60/XT30 protect by their shape, but soldering one backwards kills the board in a second. A Schottky diode in series 0.3–0.5 V drop or a P-MOSFET ideal diode for low-voltage branches. - Connectors course rule — Amass datasheets, links in the references : continuous current is the datasheet's recommended current for your wire gauge at ≤ 60 K temperature rise; short-term up to 1 min — no more than the datasheet's instantaneous current. XT30 — 15 A on 18 AWG 20 A on 16 AWG , up to 30 A briefly; XT60 — 30 A continuous and 60 A instantaneous on 12 AWG datasheet V1.2 gives no conditions; Holybro gives the same 30 A for 4 h and 60 A for 1 min at < 60 K rise on 12 AWG ; XT90 — 45 A on 12 AWG, 50 A on 10 AWG, 55 A on 8 AWG, up to 60 A for 1 min UL1977 rating 30 A; 40 A appears only in retailer listings ; AS150 — 75 A on 8 AWG, the Amass catalogue maximum at < 85 K rise, with no 1-minute figure. The catalogue is older than the datasheets and gives other XT figures XT30 20 A, XT60 35 A, XT90 45 A — maximum at < 85 K ; for XT the course uses the datasheets. A connector overloaded for its current rated below the real current heats up, a hot one oxidizes, an oxidized one heats up even more. Wire gauges {{widget:wire-drop}} Rule of thumb for short runs on board — continuous cruise current: 12 AWG up to ~60–80 A, 14 AWG up to ~40–50 A, 16 AWG up to ~25 A, 18 AWG up to ~15 A course guideline , 20–22 AWG — signal and 5 V branches up to 2–3 A. Peak current a punch, seconds is checked not by this line but by the drop criterion: ≤ 1 % of the pack voltage on the power pair. So 14 AWG on a 5" with 60–100 A peaks f-power passes with short leads: a 0.2 m loop at 100 A gives 0.17 V, 0.75 % of 22.2 V. Long wires on a wing — one size up. practice Step 1. Power tree Draw the tree for your build with the current on each branch from the table and datasheets . The 5 V total and the 9–12 V total — separately. Step 2. Choosing BECs and wire gauges For each branch: BEC type buck/LDO , rating ≥ 1.5 × the total, input voltage with margin for a fully charged 6S 25.2 V . Wire gauge — from the table. summary: What separates an engineer from an assembler is that the engineer measures instead of assuming. This module is about three instruments: the multimeter (voltage, current, continuity, resistance), the oscilloscope (sags, ripple, PWM/DShot waveforms, noise) and the logic analyzer (decoding UART, I2C, S
headings: Multimeter Oscilloscope DShot on the oscilloscope Logic analyzer Measurement safety Step 1. Map of measurement points Step 2. Sag under load Step 3. BEC ripple Step 4. DShot and UART with the analyzer Step 5. Report A decoded DShot frame What you should get and what to record
text: summary What separates an engineer from an assembler is that the engineer measures instead of assuming. This module is about three instruments: the multimeter voltage, current, continuity, resistance , the oscilloscope sags, ripple, PWM/DShot waveforms, noise and the logic analyzer decoding UART, I2C, SPI, DShot . What to measure, how to connect, how not to fry the instrument or the aircraft, and how to read the result. theory Multimeter - Voltage — in parallel with the load. Useful: the voltage of each battery cell balance , 5 V and 9 V on the BEC under load. - Continuity — before applying power: + to − on the power bus, 5 V to GND. A beep = a short. With a capacitor the resistance rises as it charges — that's normal. - Current — in series, through the 10 A jack; anything more — only with a clamp meter or through the FC current sensor. Never measure voltage in current mode: that's a short circuit through the meter. - Resistance — checking motor windings three identical values of a few tenths of an ohm , a broken wire. - Limitation: a multimeter shows the average/RMS; it doesn't see brief sags and ripple. Oscilloscope Shows voltage over time. For on-board work 2 channels and 50–100 MHz are enough; a USB oscilloscope will do too. - Sag : a channel on the power bus, timebase 100 ms/div, trigger on the falling edge; punch the throttle — you see the depth and duration of the dip. - Ripple : AC coupling removes the DC component , 20–50 mV/div, timebase 10–50 µs/div — you see the ESC/BEC switching frequency and the p-p amplitude. Measure with a short ground spring instead of the long alligator clip — otherwise you pick up noise from the probe itself. - Signals : PWM servos — a 1–2 ms pulse every 20 ms 50 Hz ; UART — bursts of bits with idle at the high level; DShot — bursts of 16 pulses of different widths. - A ×10 probe reduces the load on the circuit and extends the bandwidth; for 3.3 V logic it's mandatory. {{diagram:chart-measure-current-calibration A calibration from one flight is accurate only at that flight's average current: a sensor with a 50 mV offset is off by +74 % at 2 A, while two clamp-meter points give < 0.5 % over the whole range.}} DShot on the oscilloscope A DShot frame is 16 bits: 11 throttle bits, 1 telemetry bit, 4 CRC bits. Each bit is a pulse: “1” is long ~75% of the bit period , “0” is short ~37% . DShot600 is 600 kbit/s, a bit ≈ 1.67 µs, a frame ≈ 27 µs. On screen — a burst of 16 pulses repeating at the PID loop rate for example, every 125 µs at 8 kHz . Problems you can see: ringing on the edges long wire, no termination , a level that doesn't reach 3.3 V weak driver , dropped frames. {{diagram:dshot600-pulse-train Frame 0x82C6 over time: the pulse width carries the bit — a “1” stays high for ~75 % of the bit, a “0” for ~37 %, and the 16 bits of DShot600 take ≈ 27 µs.}} Logic analyzer Records digital levels on many channels and decodes protocols. A cheap 8-channel 24 MHz one with software like PulseView/sigrok is enough for UART up to 1 Mbaud, I2C at 400 kHz, SPI up to a few MHz and DShot600 you need ≥ 4–5 samples per bit — 12–24 MHz is better . - UART : connect to the TX line and GND, set the baud rate 115200 for MSP, 420000 for CRSF! , the decoder shows the bytes. You can see: the wrong baud rate garbage , inversion SBUS is an inverted UART at 100000 8E2 . - I2C : SDA and SCL, the decoder shows addresses and ACK/NACK. A NACK on an address — the sensor isn't there or the address is different; no pull-up — the lines don't go high. - SPI : CLK, MOSI, MISO, CS — reading the gyro registers. - A common ground with the aircraft — always. Levels are 3.3 V; most analyzers tolerate 5 V lines, 12 V — no. Measurement safety - Props off for any measurement on ESCs/motors. - The oscilloscope ground is tied to protective earth: on a circuit that isn't referenced to earth battery powered that's fine; on a mains-powered supply you must not clip the probe ground to a point that carries a potential. - The probe never touches two pins at once: tiny FC pads are the number one way to cause a short with the instrument. {{diagram:measure-tools Which instrument for which question: values — multimeter, waveform — oscilloscope, protocol — logic analyzer.}} practice Step 1. Map of measurement points On the aircraft's schematic mark: the power bus, the 5 V output, the 9 V output, the receiver UART, DShot on one motor, the compass I2C. Find convenient pads. Step 2. Sag under load Without props the measurement is meaningless — use the log VBAT in hover or an oscilloscope on a test stand with a real load aircraft tied down, props on, short throttle pulses, extremely carefully and with an observer . Record: U with no load, U at maximum, duration of the dip. Step 3. BEC ripple AC coupling, 5 V under receiver/GPS load. Record p-p and frequency. Compare with/without a capacitor on the power bus. Step 4. DShot and UART with the analyzer Capture a DShot frame at low throttle without props: decode the 16 bits by hand, compute the throttle value DShot 48–2047 and check the CRC. Capture CRSF between the receiver and the FC at 420000 baud: find the channels frame type 0x16 . Calculation lab no hardware : calib_lab.py computes new voltage and current calibration values for Betaflight, ArduPilot and PX4 from bench measurements, compares a one-point mAh calibration with a two-point one and checks aliasing. The script and its real output: python calib_lab.py — FC voltage/current sensor calibration for Betaflight, ArduPilot and PX4. python3 calib_lab.py pure Python 3 . Inputs = bench measurements, props off. V_METER, V_FC = 24.12, 23.71 multimeter on XT60 vs FC reading all three FCs read the same I_CLAMP = 2.0, 10.0, 25.0 DC clamp meter, A bench load: resistor bank / motor test, props off BF_FC = 2.63, 8.13, 18.44 Betaflight OSD amps, ibata_scale 400, ibata_offset 0 AP_FC = 4.20, 13.00, 29.50 ArduPilot CURR, BATT_AMP_PERVLT 40.0, BATT_AMP_OFFSET 0 PX_FC = 3.82, 11.82, 26.82 PX4 battery_status.current_a, BAT1_A_P

title: Li-Ion and LiFePO4 packs: cells, welding, BMS
summary: LiPo is the norm for 5" and anything that needs 20C+, but long-range wings, 7–10" long range and heavy-lift X8s fly on Li-Ion 18650/21700, while ground stations and heavy platforms run on LiFePO4. This module compares the three chemistries in numbers, teaches you to work out the S/P configuration fo
headings: Three chemistries in numbers S/P configuration Spot welding BMS, balancer and the drone Internal resistance and health Step 1. Pick the chemistry for the job Step 2. S/P calculation Step 3. Welding design Step 4. Pack test
text: summary LiPo is the norm for 5" and anything that needs 20C+, but long-range wings, 7–10" long range and heavy-lift X8s fly on Li-Ion 18650/21700, while ground stations and heavy platforms run on LiFePO4. This module compares the three chemistries in numbers, teaches you to work out the S/P configuration for current and capacity with internal resistance in mind, build a pack by spot welding nickel strip without overheating the cell, pick a BMS and balancer so they don't cut power to the aircraft in flight, and measure the real capacity and sag with a cycle under load. theory Three chemistries in numbers Parameter LiPo graphite/LCO-NMC Li-Ion 18650/21700 NMC/NCA LiFePO4 --- --- --- --- Cell nominal 3.7 V 4.2 full, 3.3–3.5 land 3.6 V 4.2 full, 2.5–3.0 land 3.2 V 3.65 full, 2.5 land Specific energy 150–200 Wh/kg 220–270 Wh/kg high-capacity 21700 90–140 Wh/kg Continuous current 20–100C a 1300 mAh 75C pack ≈ 100 A 3–10C per cell P42A: 45 A at 4.2 Ah; 40T: 35 A at 4 Ah; VTC6: 15 A per datasheet, 30 A with an 80 °C cutoff, at 3 Ah 1–3C, high-current ones up to 10C Cycle life 150–300 cycles to 80% 300–500 2000–4000 Internal resistance 1–5 mΩ/cell 15–40 mΩ/cell 5–20 mΩ 26650 Safety catches fire easily, puffs burns, but protected by the can; CID/PTC in “protected” versions very tolerant of overcharge and temperature Where it fits racing, freestyle, anything with T/W 3 long range, wings, heavy-lift, companion power ground equipment, heavy slow platforms, stationary Rule: Li-Ion wins when the average current per cell is ≤ 1.5C the heating limit, “Heat” below , the peak is within the 0.6 rule practice step 2 and the flight is longer than 15 minutes. Between 1.5C and 3C — more P if the mass passes the flight-time calculation des-sizing , otherwise LiPo. If hover needs 3C, go LiPo. S/P configuration - S sets the voltage: 6S Li-Ion = 21.6 V nominal, 25.2 full, 18 V to land 3.0 V/cell , 15 V is the absolute limit. - P sets the current and capacity: 4P of P42A = 16.8 Ah, 4 × 45 = 180 A continuous per datasheet, but in practice limited by heating and sag. - Sag : R of the pack = R of the cell × S / P. 6S4P P42A ≈ 25 mΩ × 6 / 4 ≈ 38 mΩ plus strip and connections — +10–20 mΩ . At 60 A the sag is ≈ 2.3–3.5 V — almost 1 cell “lost” under load. That's why for the same job you size Li-Ion with margin on P, not “right at the datasheet current”. - Heat : P = I²·R on the pack: 60 A × 60 A × 0.05 Ω = 180 W over the whole pack — noticeable heating in 10 minutes. Rule of thumb: average current ≤ 1.5C for 21700 without forced cooling. - Mass budget : 6S4P 21700 ≈ 24 × 70 g = 1.7 kg + strip/case ≈ 1.85 kg for 363 Wh ≈ 195 Wh/kg including hardware . {{diagram:chart-pack-sag-sp Sag grows linearly with current and inversely with P; the curve ends at the limit of the 0.6 rule, and the 4P pack from the example loses 2.3–3.5 V at 60 A — almost a whole cell.}} Spot welding You must not solder to cells: overheating the terminal damages the separator and the protection. Weld with nickel strip: - Strip : pure nickel not nickel-plated steel — its resistance is several times higher and it rusts . A 0.15 × 8 mm cross-section carries roughly 7–10 A per path continuously; for high-current packs use 0.2 × 10 mm, “doubled” strip or a copper bus bar with a nickel layer, or parallel paths. - Welder : a capacitor/supercapacitor or transformer welder; tune it on scraps: a weld should tear the strip leaving a crater, not peel off. Two electrodes on the same side, 2–4 welds per cell. - Order : welding layout on paper → cells of equal capacity and voltage spread ≤ 0.02 V → insulator rings on the positive terminals → parallel groups → series links → balance wires from each group → heat shrink/case with air for cooling. - Safety : shorting a 21700 through nickel strip means hundreds of amps and a burn; work one connection at a time, no metal tools over the assembled part, safety glasses, sand nearby, a non-combustible box and a bucket of water for cooling class D is for metallic lithium, and Li-Ion has none . BMS, balancer and the drone A BMS protects against overcharge, overdischarge, overcurrent and temperature. For flight a classic BMS is dangerous: a discharge cutoff on current/temperature in the air = a crash. Options: 1. No BMS on board — balancing through the balance connector at charging like LiPo , voltage monitoring by the flight controller voltage failsafe . The standard for flying packs. 2. Charge-only BMS : balancer and protection while charging, discharge goes direct. Good for stationary and ground use. 3. Smart BMS with configurable thresholds JK/Jikong and similar, with a 1–2 A active balancer and Bluetooth : for ground stations and heavy slow platforms; for flight — only with discharge protection disabled and with an understanding of the consequences. An active balancer moves energy between groups is needed for large capacity and infrequent full charges; a passive one burns the excess on resistors is enough for 4–6S flying packs balanced regularly. Internal resistance and health The charger shows IR per cell: a new 21700 ≈ 15–25 mΩ; a rise to 50+ is end of life for high-current work. A difference between groups 30% means a weak group — check the welds/cells. LiPo: 1–3 mΩ new, 10+ — time to move it to ground duty. {{diagram:chemistry-choice Choosing a chemistry: LiPo when you need current, Li-Ion when you need energy, LiFePO4 when you need cycle life and safety.}} practice Step 1. Pick the chemistry for the job For your aircraft: average hover/cruise current from the log, the desired flight time, the mass. Work out the C-rate for the LiPo and Li-Ion candidates. If the average current is ≤ 1.5C on Li-Ion, go on with Li-Ion. Step 2. S/P calculation Pick a cell datasheet: capacity, continuous current, IR . P ≥ maximum current / 0.6 × cell current — a 40% margin for heating and sag. Work out the pack R, the sag at maximum and in hover, the heat, the mass and Wh/kg. Compare with LiPo. Step 3. Welding design Layout: cell arrangement, s

summary: The aircraft is a tightly packed box of interference sources (ESCs, power wires, buck converters, VTX, companion) and victims (compass, GPS, receiver, gyro). This module explains the mechanisms: the magnetic field of a current, radiation from switching edges, and conducted noise on the power and gro
headings: Three interference paths Worked example: the compass and a power wire Current-based compass compensation GPS: look at C/N0, not just the satellites Victims and their symptoms Techniques Measure, don't guess Step 1. A map of sources and victims Step 2. Compass Step 3. GPS Step 4. Fix and repeat
text: summary The aircraft is a tightly packed box of interference sources ESCs, power wires, buck converters, VTX, companion and victims compass, GPS, receiver, gyro . This module explains the mechanisms: the magnetic field of a current, radiation from switching edges, and conducted noise on the power and ground lines; it teaches three techniques twist, shield, separate and, most importantly, how to measure the effect from logs: the compass via MAG / compassmot , GPS via satellite count and HDOP, the receiver via LQ/RSSI. theory Three interference paths 1. The magnetic field of a current — around a wire carrying current I, at distance r, the field is B = μ₀·I/ 2π·r . At 60 A and 5 cm that's 240 µT, 5 times the Earth's magnetic field ~50 µT . A compass 5 cm from a power wire is useless on throttle. The field falls off as 1/r: twice as far means half as strong; a twisted pair with opposing currents cancels the field almost completely. 2. Radiation from switching edges — ESCs and bucks switch current in tens of nanoseconds; sharp edges contain harmonics up to hundreds of MHz. The wires act as antennas. Victims: GPS 1.5 GHz, signal at −130 dBm — the weakest on board , the 900 MHz/2.4 GHz receiver, analog video. 3. Conducted interference — through shared power and ground wires. Buck ripple gets into the receiver's supply; ESC current through a shared ground creates a potential difference between the FC ground and the camera ground — lines in the video. Worked example: the compass and a power wire Current 60 A, Earth's field ~50 µT. Single wire, B = 2·10⁻⁷·I/r: Distance to the compass Single wire Twisted pair 3 mm spacing --- --- --- 5 cm 240 µT ×5 the Earth's field 14 µT 10 cm 120 µT 3.6 µT 20 cm 60 µT 0.9 µT The field of a pair with opposing currents is the difference between the fields of the two wires: B ≈ 2·10⁻⁷·I·d/r², falling off as 1/r², not 1/r. Hence two rules that do more than any shielding: power + and − always run together twisted or tightly bundled , and the compass sits at least 10 cm from the power bus, preferably on a mast. The magnetic field of a DC current is not shielded by foil — only by distance, geometry or mu-metal. {{diagram:chart-emi-wire-field At 60 A a single wire gives a field stronger than Earth's even at 20 cm, while a twisted pair is below 30 % of Earth's field already at 5 cm: its field falls as 1/r², not 1/r.}} Current-based compass compensation If you can't separate them, ArduPilot can subtract the interference: compassmot with props on, the vehicle rigidly secured measures the field on board as a function of current and writes coefficients to COMPASS_MOT_X/Y/Z ; the mode is COMPASS_MOTCT 1 — by throttle, 2 — by current, needs a current sensor . This compensates the linear part of the interference; the nonlinear part saturation, eddy currents it does not. If the interference is above ~30 % of the Earth's field after compensation, the compass still has to be moved. GPS: look at C/N0, not just the satellites Satellite count and HDOP drop late. The first thing to react to interference is the signal-to-noise ratio of each satellite C/N0, dB·Hz : under open sky, 35–45 dB·Hz for visible satellites. If turning on the VTX or companion lowers the C/N0 of all satellites by 5–10 dB at once, that's interference on board, not the sky. To look: u-center through the flight controller passthrough SERIAL_PASS1 / SERIAL_PASS2 and SERIAL_PASSTIMO in ArduPilot, the serialpassthrough command in Betaflight/INAV , the Satellite Level view. Victims and their symptoms - Compass : heading changes with throttle; in ArduPilot compassmot shows the % of interference; in the log MAG.MagX/Y/Z correlate with CTUN.ThO . Above 30% is bad, you need to separate. - GPS : satellite count drops when the VTX/companion is turned on, HDOP rises, GPS.NSats , GPS.HDop . Typical culprits: USB 3.0 harmonics at 1.5 GHz , cameras, HDMI, a buck next to the GPS antenna. - Receiver : LQ drops while RSSI is normal — a wideband noise source near the antenna VTX, companion . Sometimes RSSI “rises” from interference: the receiver sees the noise as signal. - Gyro : noise in the log at the buck switching frequency — rare, but it happens with poor layout. - Video : lines on throttle — conducted ripple; “snow” — radiation. Techniques - Twist the power + and −: opposing currents cancel the magnetic field; twisting signal wires with ground reduces pickup. - Separate : compass and GPS on a mast pointing up 10–15 cm of distance gives ×3–5 on the field , receiver antennas away from the VTX and companion, preferably at the other end of the frame. - Shield : copper foil/shielding fabric on the companion and camera, grounded at a single point; ferrite rings on USB/HDMI cables turns through the ring — more turns, stronger suppression . - Filter : an LC filter on the VTX/camera supply how to choose L, C, ESR and the inductor saturation current — el-power-design , “LC filter for video”; check — an oscilloscope at the VTX input before and after the filter under throttle, el-measure , a capacitor on the power bus see power circuit design , an LDO for the receiver. - Single ground : a star from the PDB, not a daisy chain; a cable shield grounded at one end otherwise — a ground loop . Measure, don't guess One change at a time, with a before/after measurement: - compass: compassmot or the correlation of MAG with throttle in the log; - GPS: NSats/HDOP at rest for 5 minutes with the loads turned on and off one by one; - receiver: LQ at 50–100 m with the VTX off/on, companion off/on; - video: an oscilloscope in AC mode on the camera supply. {{diagram:emi-paths Three interference paths and their typical victims: the magnetic field of a current — compass, radiation from switching edges — GPS and receiver, conducted — video and RX power.}} practice Step 1. A map of sources and victims On the aircraft wiring diagram, mark the sources ESCs, power wires, buck, VTX, companion, USB and the victims compass, GPS, RX antennas, camera with distances. St
