text: summary Blackbox is the flight data recorder in Betaflight; it can capture the state of the flight controller on every control loop iteration up to 8 kHz . A log contains the gyro, the accelerometer, the stick signals, the PID controller terms, the motor outputs and the filter parameters. This article gives a complete picture of how to set up logging, read the graphs and use the tools Blackbox Explorer, PIDscope for diagnostics and tuning. After working through it you will be able to identify the noise structure of a drone, estimate filter delay, and tune PIDs and filters from objective data rather than by trial and error. {{lesson:bf-motor-balance The first thing worth extracting from a hover log: the balance of the four motors — center of gravity, a weak motor, a yaw offset, with a ready-made Python script.}} theory Purpose and architecture of Blackbox Blackbox records the internal state of the flight controller at the highest possible rate so that control algorithms can be simulated offline, debugged and analyzed on data from real flights. A log is built from frames of several types: - I frames intra — complete frames that can be decoded independently. - P frames inter — delta frames that rely on prediction. - G/H frames — for GPS data. - S frames slow — state that changes rarely. - E frames event — state transitions. Predictors and variable-length encoding are used for compression, which makes it possible to store a large amount of data at a moderate data rate. What exactly is logged Blackbox captures: - time, - the P/I/D values and the summed output, - the setpoint sticks , - gyro and accelerometer data, - voltage/current, RSSI, - the commands to the ESCs, - GPS frames if present . Log format and storage devices Logs can be written to: - onboard flash usually 2–16 MB , - an SD card preferable for long sessions , - an external logger over a UART. For an SD card, FAT32 and a card with low write latency are recommended. How the settings affect log quality - 1 kHz — basic PID analysis; - 2 kHz or 1.6 kHz for the BMI270 — detailed noise/filter analysis. If the looptime is short a high PID rate , you may need to raise the baud rate or lower the logging rate, otherwise frames can be dropped. The physical meaning of the noise spectrum - <20 Hz — useful dynamics; - 20–100 Hz — vibration/propwash/PID problems; - 100–250 Hz — frame resonances/play; - 250 Hz — motor/prop noise and harmonics. The goal of filtering is to suppress high-frequency noise without adding unnecessary delay in the useful band. Recording parameters blackbox_device SPIFLASH / SDCARD / SERIAL; from 2025.12 also VIRTUAL — for SITL , blackbox_sample_rate 1/1, 1/2, 1/4, … of the PID rate: with an 8 kHz PID and 1/4 — a 2 kHz log , blackbox_mode NORMAL — on arming; MOTOR_TEST; ALWAYS — on the ground too: for measuring gyro noise/bias , blackbox_high_resolution finer gyro/setpoint resolution , blackbox_disable_ disable groups of fields: acc , rc , gyrounfilt , rpm , gps … — saves data rate , debug_mode which 8 debug values to log: RPM_FILTER , D_LPF , DSHOT_RPM_TELEMETRY , FEEDFORWARD , GPS_RESCUE_ , AUTOPILOT_ALTITUDE before 2025.12 — GPS_RESCUE_THROTTLE_PID , RTH …; the GYRO_SCALED mode — the raw gyro before the filters — does not exist in 2025.12, where the gyroUnfilt field replaces it; 4.5 has it . Data rate: 2 kHz with the full set of fields is on the order of 60–100 KB/s → 16 MB of flash lasts 3–4 minutes; an SD card lasts hours. An external logger is the Blackbox logging function on a UART in the Ports tab serial <id 128 … with the blackbox baud rate ; there are no separate blackbox_uart / blackbox_baud settings in 4.5 or 2025.12. {{diagram:chart-blackbox-flash-minutes At 60–100 KB/s 2 kHz, all fields 16 MB of flash lasts 2.7–4.6 minutes, 8 MB at 80 KB/s — 102 s, 2 MB — 26 s; long sessions need an SD card.}} Field groups and blackbox_disable_ cli/settings.c ; in 2025.12 two were added to those listed in the table: blackbox_disable_attitude — the imuQuaternion 0..2 field, when an accelerometer is present, and blackbox_disable_servos — servo 0..7 , only with servos in the mixer; the field conditions are in testBlackboxConditionUncached in blackbox/blackbox.c . Everything is enabled by default fields_disabled_mask = 0 ; a group without its sensor is not logged anyway. The number is how many values are in each main frame for a quadcopter, 4 motors : Parameter What it disables Values When to disable --- --- --- --- blackbox_disable_pids axisP , axisI , axisD , axisF up to 12 axisD on yaw — only with d_yaw ≠ 0 almost never: without them the tune cannot be analyzed blackbox_disable_rc rcCommand 0..3 4 if setpoint is there and the sticks are not needed blackbox_disable_setpoint setpoint 0..3 4 never for tuning blackbox_disable_bat vbatLatest , amperageLatest 2 rarely: needed for sag blackbox_disable_mag magADC 0..2 3 if there is a compass there is a compass, but it is not being analyzed blackbox_disable_alt baroAlt , surfaceRaw 1–2 baro/rangefinder no altitude-related work blackbox_disable_rssi rssi 1 — blackbox_disable_gyro gyroADC 0..2 after the filters 3 never blackbox_disable_gyrounfilt gyroUnfilt 0..2 before the filters 3 after the filters are tuned, to save data rate blackbox_disable_acc accSmooth 0..2 3 the first candidate when data rate is short on an acro quadcopter blackbox_disable_debug debug 0..7 8 only with debug_mode ≠ NONE debug_mode = NONE gives the same result blackbox_disable_motors motor 0..3 4 never blackbox_disable_rpm eRPM 0..3 4 only with DShot telemetry after the RPM filter has been verified blackbox_disable_gps the separate GPS frames G/H — no GPS analysis Storage maintenance from the CLI: flash_info — the size and usage of the onboard flash; flash_erase — erase it prints dots until done; the same as the Erase flash button in the Blackbox tab or the BLACKBOX ERASE mode, id 31 ; sd_info — the SD card state Not configured , None inserted , Startup failed , or the card's manufacturer, capacity and manufacture

This module gives a method. You pic
headings: Why mechanics come before PID Quad X: numbers, log fields, rotation What is in `motor[0..3]` and how to convert it to percent The method: segment, medians, three indices Signatures of the causes Diagnostic table A case: a 10" with a yaw imbalance The order of work before tuning Reference table (Betaflight 4.5) Place in the system Step 1. The range and percent Step 2. The script Step 3. A run on synthetic data Step 4. Your own log Moving to real hardware
text: summary Before tuning PID it is worth checking the mechanics. In level flight, unequal motor outputs show that the controller is constantly compensating for a physical imbalance: an offset center of gravity CG , a weak motor, a damaged prop, a tilted motor or a bent arm. This module gives a method. You pick a steady 10–20 s segment of the log, take the median of each motor 0..3 and convert it to percent of travel using the motorOutput header. Three imbalance indices are computed from the medians: rear–front, left–right and diagonal yaw . Their combination points to the cause, and a swap test confirms it. The lab is a Python script. It finds the steady segment in the CSV from blackbox_decode by itself. You check the script on synthetic logs with defects injected in advance: the CG 4 % to the rear and motor 4 at +6 %. Then you do the same on your own aircraft, with a bench procedure and a field procedure. theory Why mechanics come before PID In a steady hover the angular rates on all axes are near zero, and the P and D terms do almost nothing. A constant disturbance torque is held by the I term: it accumulates a correction until the error is zero and then keeps it. That is why a mechanical imbalance always looks the same in the log: a non-zero median of axisI 0..2 and a constant difference between motor 0..3 with the sticks centered. Raising yaw I is useless here: I will reach the same correction faster, but the correction itself will remain. You pay for it with control headroom: - The mixer adds the correction to the throttle: motor = motorOutputMin + motorOutputRange · throttle + Σ pidSum/1000 · mixer coefficient flight/mixer.c , applyMixToMotors , PID_MIXER_SCALING = 1000 . A motor that already needs 8 % more in hover will be the first to hit 100 % in a punch-out. If the spread of the corrections motorMixRange is greater than 1, the LEGACY mixer compresses the corrections on all axes together applyMixerAdjustment , and all axes lose part of their authority at once. - iterm_windup = 85: when motorMixRange exceeds 0.85, the I term starts to accumulate more slowly, and at 1.0 it stops altogether flight/pid.c , dynCi . Part of this window is already spent on the mechanical imbalance. - Yaw has the least headroom. Yaw torque is produced only by the reaction torque of the props: the reaction-torque arm K_M = Q/T is 1–2 cm against a 15–25 cm arm in roll and pitch the estimate is below . In addition, pidsum_limit_yaw = 400 against 500 for roll and pitch. A constant diagonal imbalance eats exactly this headroom, which is why the heading “drifts” in a sharp turn at full throttle. A motor that constantly needs a higher command than the others runs hotter — a frequent answer to the question “why is one motor hotter”. A weak motor or prop also produces vibration that the filters will not remove bf-filters . Hence the order: mechanics and balance, then filters, then PID. Quad X: numbers, log fields, rotation In Betaflight 4.5 the Quad X motors are numbered as follows: 1 — rear right RR , 2 — front right FR , 3 — rear left RL , 4 — front left FL . In the log the indices start from zero: motor 0 = motor 1, …, motor 3 = motor 4. The mixerQuadX table flight/mixer_init.c , the columns throttle, roll, pitch, yaw sets the signs as follows: Motor Log field roll pitch yaw Rotation, props-in --- --- --- --- --- --- 1 RR motor 0 −1 +1 −1 CW 2 FR motor 1 −1 −1 +1 CCW 3 RL motor 2 +1 +1 +1 CCW 4 FL motor 3 +1 −1 −1 CW The default rotation is props-in: the front props at the camera spin inward. The Betaflight page “Running with Reversed Motors” describes the opposite: with props-out the front left spins counterclockwise and the front right clockwise. For props-out, set yaw_motors_reversed = ON . The parameter changes neither the table nor the numbers; it only inverts the sign of the yaw PID before the mixer if !mixerConfig - yaw_motors_reversed scaledAxisPidYaw = -scaledAxisPidYaw; . The motors themselves are not reversed by it: the direction is changed in the ESC configurator or by swapping two phase wires. The yaw pairs: motors 1 and 4 spin one way, motors 2 and 3 the other. text: summary Filters sit between the gyro and the PID controller and decide what the controller “sees”: the useful motion of the frame, or motor noise, resonances and vibration as well. Without them the D term turns noise into motor jitter and heat; with too many, every filter adds delay, the aircraft becomes “mushy” and the stability margin melts away. This module goes through the filter chain of Betaflight 2025.12 it is the same in 4.5 in the order in which the code applies it LPF2 at downsampling → RPM notches → static notches → LPF1 → dynamic notch for the gyro; notch → LPF1 → LPF2 for the D term , explains every parameter with its default numbers, gives a tuning method based on the Blackbox spectrum with specific “enough” criteria, and shows where filters do not help mechanics, propwash . The interactive part is the frequency response and group delay of the chain. theory What exactly is filtered and why The gyro signal = frame motion 0–100 Hz, useful + noise. The noise sources and where they sit in the spectrum details are in the modules “Frame and vibration”, “Signals and spectra” : {{diagram:fc-signal-path Where the filters sit in the chain: between the gyro and the PID; everything they let through reaches the D term and the motors.}} Source Frequency on a 5" 6S Appearance on the spectrogram What deals with it --- --- --- --- Motor fundamental imbalance 250–450 Hz in hover, up to 700+ on throttle a sloped line that tracks the throttle RPM filter 2nd, 3rd harmonics blades, aerodynamics ×2, ×3 parallel lines RPM filter harmonics Frame / FC mount resonance 100–300 Hz a horizontal line mechanics, dynamic notch, static notch Broadband noise play, bad bearings, electrical the whole range a “cushion” mechanics, LPF Propwash 20–80 Hz bursts on sharp maneuvers not filters: D term, mechanics, props Other classes. The frequencies in the table are for a 5" 6S. The motor fundamental in hover: 7" — 110–200 Hz f-frame-mech , “Numbers”; a 1.4 kg 7" LR in hover — 110–130 Hz, the example in bf-rpm-filter , 10" — 80–100 Hz, 15" — 50–70 Hz f-frame-mech . On 7–15" builds motor noise lies where a 5" has only propwash and frame motion, so the boundary “below 100 Hz is not a filter problem” does not apply to them. The order for 7" and larger: first bf-rpm-filter — rpm_filter_min_hz by class 7" — 70, 10" — 50, the “measure, then set” procedure is there too , then the steps of this module; lower dyn_notch_min_hz default 100, range 20–250, cli/settings.c below 100 only if the frame resonance found by tapping an arm f-frame-mech lies below 100 Hz. The sliders and LPF frequencies below are reference values for a 5"; on large aircraft they are changed only from the spectrum, one step at a time. The main victim of noise is the D term : a derivative amplifies a signal in proportion to frequency 40 times more at 400 Hz than at 10 Hz , so the motors “buzz” and heat up, while P and I hardly notice the noise. Hence two chains: a gentle one for the gyro it feeds all three terms and a stricter one for D. Filter types and the cost of each - PT1 — a first-order filter: −3 dB at the cutoff frequency fc, then −20 dB/decade; the group delay at low frequencies ≈ 1/ 2π·fc PT1 100 Hz → 1.6 ms; 250 Hz → 0.64 ms . The “cheapest” in delay. - PT2, PT3 — cascades of PT1: −40/−60 dB/decade, a delay of ×1.6/×2.2 relative to a PT1 of the same fc. They are used when noise above the band has to be cut off sharply at a moderate delay the D term LPF is PT1 by default, and the type is changed with _lpf1_type / _lpf2_type : PT1, BIQUAD, PT2, PT3 . - BIQUAD second-order, Butterworth — steeper than PT1, with a delay between PT1 and PT2. - Notch — a dip around a center frequency with a width set by Q the higher the Q, the narrower ; outside the band the delay is almost zero. That is why narrowband motor noise is properly cut with notches rather than by lowering the LPF. The cost of filtering is delay; the cost of delay is phase margin the module “Control theory” : with a total gyro+D chain delay of about 1–2 ms a good 5" tune holds P/D 30–50% higher than with 4–6 ms. {{widget:filter-response}} The gyro chain in Betaflight 2025.12 parameters; the real order in filterGyro : LPF2 → RPM → static notches → LPF1 → dynamic notch 1. Q = 500 means a width of ≈ f/5: narrow and precise. min_hz — below this frequency no notch is applied so as not to cut useful signal at low throttle , fade_range_hz — a smooth fade-in above min_hz. A separate module — “RPM filter”. 2. Dynamic notch dyn_notch_count = 3 range 0–7; in 4.5 — 0–5 , dyn_notch_q = 300 , dyn_notch_min_hz = 100 , dyn_notch_max_hz = 600 : an FFT of the gyro finds the strongest peaks in the min..max range and places notches on them. It catches what the RPM filter does not know about — frame resonances. With the RPM filter, count = 1–2 and q = 300–500 are enough; without the RPM filter — count = 4–5 , q = 250–300 wider . Why a course guideline : with the RPM filter the motors are already notched out, and the dynamic notch is left with one or two frame resonances — extra notches only add delay, and a high Q makes each one narrow; without the RPM filter it also has to catch the motor harmonics, which move with the throttle — more and wider notches are needed. Start at the low end: count = 1 , q = 500 with the RPM filter; +1 to count only if a peak remains in the spectrum after the filters. 3. text: summary An electronic speed controller is a separate computer with its own firmware, and the RPM filter, the sound of the motors, heating and even whether a motor will start after a crash all depend on it. The “Motors and ESCs” module explained what an ESC does; here — which firmware to put on which hardware, what bidirectional DShot and EDT are, which ESC settings really change the flight PWM frequency, timing, demagnetization, startup power , how to flash through the flight controller in Betaflight and ArduPilot, and how not to turn a 4-in-1 into a brick. theory Who is who Firmware Hardware Status What matters --- --- --- --- BLHeli_S 8-bit EFM8 BB1/BB2/BB21 factory firmware on cheap ESCs, not developed no bidirectional DShot in its original form Bluejay 8-bit EFM8 BB21 and BB51 BB1/BB10 — only up to version 0.18.1 open source, developed bidirectional DShot, EDT, PWM frequency 24/48/96 kHz, startup tunes BLHeli_32 32-bit ARM closed; development and support ended in 2024 works, but there will be no updates and no new configurator AM32 32-bit ARM STM32F051, G071, AT32F421, GD32 and others open source, developed the replacement for BLHeli_32 where there is a target for the board The firmware name on the box tells you about the ESC's microcontroller: “BLHeli_S” — 8 bit, “BLHeli_32” or “AM32” — ARM. Bidirectional DShot and EDT - DShot — a digital command protocol from the flight controller → ESC: DShot300/600 — the speed in kbit/s; no throttle range calibration, with a checksum. - Bidirectional DShot bidir — over the same wire the ESC replies with the electrical RPM eRPM . This is the input of the Betaflight RPM filter and the ArduPilot harmonic notch. Mechanical RPM = eRPM / number of poles / 2 , so the motor's number of poles usually 14 for 22xx–28xx must be set in the flight controller. - EDT Extended DShot Telemetry — the same replies additionally carry the ESC's temperature, voltage, current and status — without a separate telemetry wire. Supported by Bluejay and AM32; enabled in the flight controller. {{lesson:bf-rpm-filter What Betaflight does with eRPM: notches on the harmonics, the lower limit rpm_filter_min_hz for large props, and diagnosing telemetry errors.}} Settings that change the flight - PWM frequency. Lower 24 kHz — more thrust and braking at low throttle, cooler ESC switches; higher 48–96 kHz — smoother current in a low-inductance motor, a softer sound and less vibration. The smaller the motor and the higher its RPM, the higher the frequency needed. The selection rule, a table by class and the calculation — in the subsection “PWM frequency: how to choose for the aircraft” below. - Timing advance . The commutation advance angle. Higher — more RPM and current, heating; lower — more efficient, but a risk of losing sync on a sharp throttle input. Auto/medium is a sensible start. - Demagnetization demag compensation . Protection against losing sync on sharp throttle changes with large motors. Sync losses “desyncs” — a motor twitches or stops in flight — are treated first of all by raising the compensation. - Startup power startup/rampup power . Too high — the windings burn if the motor is jammed; too low — a heavy motor won't start. - Spin direction. Changed in the ESC firmware or with a DShot command from the flight controller — no need to resolder wires. - Tunes and beacon. The “lost aircraft” sound after a crash is a useful feature, not a toy. PWM frequency: how to choose for the aircraft An ESC does not change the voltage on the winding smoothly but with switches: in a period T = 1/f the phase is connected to the battery for a fraction D of the period the duty cycle , and for the rest of the time it is connected to ground. The average voltage on the motor is D·U. The frequency f of these switchings is the PWM frequency. It does not affect throttle; it determines how smooth the current will be and how much the ESC pays for it. The rule. The PWM frequency must be high enough for the current in the winding to be smooth at hover RPM, and no higher than that. A small motor with a high KV few turns — low inductance, high RPM needs a high frequency. A large low-KV motor is smooth already at a low frequency, and its ESC, with a high current and voltage, pays more than anyone for every switching. Hence the direction: the smaller the aircraft, the higher the frequency; the bigger and heavier, the lower. The four mechanisms this follows from: Mechanism Formula What follows from it --- --- --- Current ripple in the winding the winding is an R–L load peak-to-peak ΔI ≈ U·D· 1 − D / L·f ; the addition to copper losses ≈ ΔI²/ 12·I² of I²·R torque is produced by the average current I, but heating by the RMS current; the lower L, the more “extra” motor heating at a low frequency; doubling f reduces the addition fourfold Switching losses in the switches P ≈ ½·U·I·t_sw·f per switch t_sw — the MOSFET transition time grow in proportion to f and to the product U·I: at 1S and 2 A it is milliwatts, at 6S and 40 A — watts Dead time the pause between the half-bridge switches fraction of the period = t_d·f by this fraction the actual voltage is lower than commanded when driving and higher when braking: both thrust and braking at low throttle weaken as f grows The number of PWM periods per commutation step N = 10·f/eRPM f in Hz at N around 1–2 the duty cycle “doesn't have time” to take effect within a step: jerky torque, beating, a rough sound The ripple formula is the triangular approximation; it holds when T is much less than L/R. For the smallest motors this condition is violated at 24 kHz, and the formula gives an upper estimate. L and R here are between two phase wires. Throttle resolution also depends on the frequency. In Bluejay the PWM counter has 1024 steps at 24 kHz, 512 at 48 kHz and 256 at 96 kHz in builds with dead time greater than 0, i.e. with center-aligned PWM; with dead time 0 — twice as many , and the dead time is subtracted from them. text: summary An analysis of a real case: a 10-inch quadcopter's motors “whistle” and it flies unevenly. The cause turned out to be not PID but one line of the config: the lower limit of the RPM filter was above the motor rotation frequency, and for most of the flight the filter simply did not work. This module teaches you to check whether the RPM filter covers the real RPM range from Blackbox data, not by eye. The theory follows the Betaflight code: the path eRPM → frequency → notch weight, the role of motor_poles , rpm_filter_ , the connection with dynamic idle and the dynamic notch, and the diagnostics of telemetry errors; a calculation lab shows which harmonics work at your RPM. theory How the RPM filter works With bidirectional DShot every ESC reports the eRPM of its motor to the flight controller. Betaflight converts eRPM to RPM using motor_poles and places narrow notch filters exactly on the rotation frequency of each motor and its harmonics. By default that is 12 notch filters per axis 4 motors × 3 harmonics on roll, pitch and yaw. A notch “follows” the RPM in real time, so it cuts motor noise with almost no extra delay. Why the math is different for large props The fundamental frequency of a motor: f = RPM / 60 . A five-inch in hover spins at tens of thousands of RPM, and the fundamental lies in the hundreds of hertz. A 10-inch has low-RPM motors low KV, heavy props , and the fundamental in hover can drop to 50–100 Hz. The rpm_filter_min_hz parameter sets the lower limit: a notch does not go below it and is turned off weight 0, details below . If the limit is above the real motor frequency, the filter sits “beside” the noise. That is exactly what happened in the case below. From eRPM to notch: the chain in the code Below is the path of one number from the ESC to the gyro filter. The references are to Betaflight 4.5.3. In 2025.12.5 the chain is the same with one difference: the notch update takes the actual scheduler cycle time into account schedulerGetCycleTimeMultiplier in rpmFilterUpdate . 1. eRPM. The ESC answers every DShot frame with an eRPM number in units of 100 ERPM_PER_LSB = 100, drivers/dshot.c:56 . eRPM is electrical RPM: one mechanical revolution corresponds to motor_poles /2 electrical ones. 2. The motor frequency. erpmToHz = 100 / 60 / motor_poles / 2 dshot.c:160 . In every loop the frequency of each motor passes through a PT1 with a cutoff of rpm_filter_lpf_hz dshot.c:165, 333 . The minimum over the motors goes to dynamic idle getMinMotorFrequencyHz . A raw 350 with 14 magnets is 83.3 Hz. If motor_poles = 12 is set by mistake, the result is 97.2 Hz, that is, all the notches shift by a factor of 14/12 = 1.17. 3. Initialization flight/rpm_filter.c:71–110 . Without telemetry or with rpm_filter_harmonics = 0 the filter is off. The upper stop maxHz = 0.48 · f_loop : 3840 Hz at 8 kHz, 1920 Hz at 4 kHz. Q = rpm_filter_q /100, and the weights are clipped to 0…1. Each axis gets motors × harmonics notches: 4 × 3 = 12, and three axes — 36. 4. The update rpm_filter.c:112–168 . All the notches are retuned within 1 ms RPM_FILTER_DURATION_S , several per loop: 2 at 8 kHz, 3 at 4 kHz, 4 at 3.2 kHz. For harmonic k the frequency f_k = k · f_motor is constrained to the range rpm_filter_min_hz ; maxHz . Margin = f_k − min_hz. If the margin is less than rpm_filter_fade_range_hz , the weight is multiplied by margin/fade, then by rpm_filter_weights k . The coefficients are computed for roll and copied to pitch and yaw. 5. Application. The filter sits right after the downsampling of the samples with gyro_lpf2 enabled, that is the downsampling filter, gyro_filter_impl.c:37–40 , before the static notches, LPF1 and the dynamic notch sensors/gyro_filter_impl.c:52–53 ; the order is as in bf-filters : LPF2 → RPM → static notches → LPF1 → dynamic notch. Every notch mixes its input and output by the weight: output = w · notch x + 1 − w · x common/filter.c:227–234 . Item 4 implies a non-obvious detail. Below rpm_filter_min_hz a notch does not disappear; it sits at min_hz with weight 0, that is, it does nothing. With rpm_filter_fade_range_hz = 0 the condition “the margin is less than fade” is never met. Then the notch of a slow motor stays parked at min_hz at full depth, like a static notch. This is an inference from the code; it was not verified on an aircraft. Low RPM, dynamic idle and harmonic coverage The weight is computed from the frequency, and the frequency from the mechanical RPM, so coverage is conveniently measured in RPM. With the defaults min 100 Hz, fade 50 Hz : - the 1st harmonic works at full strength only above 150 Hz = 9000 RPM and is off below 6000 RPM; - the 2nd works at full strength above 4500 RPM; - the 3rd — above 3000 RPM. Hence the main conclusion. At idle, in falls and on a throttle chop the propwash zone the fundamental is often not filtered at all, and on a 10″ hover at 5000–5800 RPM — not in hover either. On a 7″ hover at 110–130 Hz, 6600–7800 RPM the 1st harmonic works only partially in hover: a weight of 0.2–0.6. Dynamic idle bf-pid-reg-in-bf keeps the slowest motor no lower than dyn_idle_min_rpm × 100 RPM and thereby sets the lower edge of the filter's working range. With dyn_idle_min_rpm = 30 3000 RPM and the defaults only the 3rd harmonic 150 Hz works fully, and the 2nd sits exactly at min_hz with weight 0. With rpm_filter_min_hz = 50 at the same 3000 RPM the 2nd and 3rd harmonics work at full strength, and the 1st turns on from 3000 and reaches full strength by 6000 RPM. There is a second effect too: dynamic idle does not let the RPM collapse toward zero, so eRPM at low throttle is more stable and the notch jumps less. {{lesson:bf-pid-reg-in-bf How the dynamic idle controller uses the same eRPM to raise the lower motor limit, its P/I/D and the limits on the ground and in the air — with formulas from mixer.c .}} The price of a low min_hz is that a notch of width f/5 at 50–100 Hz 10–20 Hz of bandwidth lies close to the band where PID works and adds phase delay. text: summary PID tuning without theory is trial and error. This module explains, at a level sufficient for an engineer, what closed-loop stability is, why delay eats the phase margin and leads to oscillations at high P, how the step response relates to poles and damping and why bounce-back is an underdamped pole , and why the autopilot builds an angle → angular rate cascade with an inner loop several times faster than the outer one. The formulas are kept to a minimum, and each one is tied to what you see in the PID simulator and in the log. theory Plant, controller, loop The plant is the vehicle: the input is the motor command, the output is the angular rate. The controller is the PID: the input is the error setpoint − gyro , the output is the command. The closed loop: the output affects the input through the measurement. The whole point of the theory is to predict the behavior of the loop without closing it. A first-approximation model of one axis The motor torque creates angular acceleration: J·ω̇ = M − b·ω, where J is the moment of inertia and b is the aerodynamic damping. The transfer function from torque to ω is a first-order lag 1/ J·s + b — a “leaky integrator”: ω grows as long as torque is applied. Plus the delays : the motor current/RPM, τ ≈ 10–30 ms for a 5" , the gyro and D filters 1–5 ms , the loop period and the ESC protocol 0.1–0.5 ms . The total pure delay T_d is the main enemy. Stability and phase margin A loop with a P controller: at low P it's sluggish, at high P it oscillates, at even higher P the oscillations diverge. The boundary is where the loop gain equals 1 at the frequency where the phase shift reaches −180°. A pure delay T_d gives a phase shift of −360°·f·T_d: at 50 Hz with T_d = 5 ms that's −90°, and the plant pole adds another −90° — and there's your −180°. Therefore: - Phase margin — how many degrees remain to −180° at the frequency where the gain = 1. 45–60° is a good tune small overshoot ; 20–30° — ringing and bounce-back; 0 — sustained oscillations. - The delay T_d eats the margin linearly with frequency: the faster you want the loop higher P , the more you lose. Doubling the delay at the same P loses ~half the margin. - Hence the limit “P no higher than the delay allows.” Reducing the delay higher filter cutoffs, an RPM notch instead of a wide LPF, a fast ESC protocol, light props is the only way to raise P without oscillations. Step response, poles, damping A second-order closed loop is described by its natural frequency ωₙ and damping ζ: - ζ 1 — overdamped, slow; - ζ ≈ 0.7 — fast with ~5% overshoot; this is the goal; - ζ = 0.4 — ~25% overshoot, ringing; - ζ → 0 — oscillations. Overshoot ≈ exp −π·ζ/√ 1−ζ² : 0.7 → 4.6%, 0.5 → 16%, 0.3 → 37%. Settling time ≈ 4/ ζ·ωₙ . Bounce-back after the stick stops is the same underdamped pole, just excited by a “downward” step: large bounce-back = low ζ = either too little D, or too much P/delay. The D-term increases the damping ζ — that's why “lots of D” removes the bounce, but D amplifies noise ∝ frequency, and the D filters add delay, which again reduces the margin. That's the tuning trade-off. I-term: steady-state error and windup I removes steady-state error wind, asymmetry . It pays in phase: an integrator gives −90° at low frequencies, so too much I means slow oscillations 0.5–3 Hz, “wandering” . Windup is I accumulating while the outputs are saturated stick at the endpoint, motors at the ceiling : firmware limits it iterm_limit , iterm_relax , in ArduPilot ATC_RAT_ _IMAX . Feedforward FF applies a command proportional to the derivative of the setpoint, bypassing the error: the output starts moving before the error has built up. It doesn't affect stability it's outside the loop , but too much of it gives overshoot on sharp stick moves. Good FF means low response delay at the same P. Cascade: angle → rate The outer loop angle computes the desired angular rate from the angle error; the inner loop rate tracks it. The rule: the inner loop must be 3–10 times faster than the outer one in bandwidth , otherwise the outer loop “sees” the dynamics of the inner one and the cascade oscillates. In ArduPilot: ATC_ANG_RLL_P outer, ~4.5–12 and ATC_RAT_RLL_P/I/D inner ; on top of that, the position loop PSC_ is slower still. In Betaflight angle mode: angle_p_gain default 50 on top of the rate PID. In PX4: MC_ROLL_P → MC_ROLLRATE_P/I/D . Autotune tunes the inner loop first, then the outer one — for the same reason. What this means for tuning 1. First reduce the delay mechanics, filters , then raise P. 2. P — until ringing starts, then back off by 20–30% phase margin . 3. D — until bounce-back is < 10% and the motors don't heat up. 4. I — until the drift disappears, without “wandering.” 5. The outer loop — after the inner one. Where the total delay T_d comes from and which link weighs the most — compute it for your own setup: {{widget:link-latency}} {{diagram:angle-rate-cascade The “angle → angular rate” cascade: the outer P on angle sets the setpoint for the inner PID on the gyro.}} {{diagram:chart-step-responses Step response of a second-order system: ζ = 0.7 gives ~5 % overshoot and fast settling — the target for the rate loop; ζ = 0.3 rings, ζ = 1 is sluggish.}} practice Step 1. Simulator: the P limit at two delays In the interactive PID simulator the “PID Controller in Betaflight” module : with a 2 ms delay, raise P until sustained oscillations start, and write down P_max and the frequency; with a 5 ms delay, repeat. Expected: P_max is noticeably lower, and the oscillation frequency is lower. Step 2. ζ from overshoot From the log data-python → step_metrics : overshoot → ζ via the formula; settling time → ωₙ. title: System identification: chirp, frequency response, a model for tuning
summary: Tuning “by eye,” and even AUTOTUNE, answers the question “which gains,” but not “why.” System identification answers it: you feed the vehicle a known signal (a chirp — a sine wave with rising frequency), record the response, compute the frequency response, and fit a model with meaningful parameters
headings: Why a model The chirp and the requirements for the experiment SYSID mode in ArduCopter Frequency response from spectra Fitting the model Model → tuning Step 1. Synthetic check Step 2. Phase margin from the model Step 3. SYSID in SITL Step 4. Change and compare
text: summary Tuning “by eye,” and even AUTOTUNE, answers the question “which gains,” but not “why.” System identification answers it: you feed the vehicle a known signal a chirp — a sine wave with rising frequency , record the response, compute the frequency response, and fit a model with meaningful parameters to it — the motor time constant, the delay, the gain. With a model, tuning becomes a calculation: phase margin, crossover frequency, what a filter will cost. This module covers the chirp and the requirements for the experiment, the SYSID mode in ArduCopter, estimating the frequency response from spectra, fitting a first-order-plus-delay model, and using the model to choose gains. The code is checked on synthetic data first, then on a SITL log. theory Why a model - A controller is tuned for a plant. The plant of a copter's rate loop is “torque command → angular rate”: the body inertia, the motor time constant prop spin-up , the delays filters, ESC, the computation loop . - A model of the form G s = K·e^ −sτ / Ts + 1 or with an integrator, to go to the angle describes this chain with three numbers. Knowing them, you can compute the phase margin for any gains, see how much phase a new filter will “eat,” and compare two vehicles objectively. - The “Control Theory” module gave you the language transfer functions, margins ; here you learn how to get a model from a flight. The chirp and the requirements for the experiment - A chirp is a sine wave whose frequency rises from f₀ to f₁ over the recording time. An exponential logarithmic chirp spends the same time on every octave — convenient for a logarithmic frequency axis. - Frequency range : from below the expected loop bandwidth 1–2 Hz to above the crossover frequency 30–60 Hz for small copters , but below the frequencies where the noise and frame resonances are. - Amplitude : large enough for the signal to be above the noise, and small enough not to drive the motors into saturation and nonlinearity. The sign of saturation is motors at their limit in the log. - Duration : tens of seconds — more periods at low frequencies, a more accurate estimate. - Closed loop. The vehicle flies with the controllers running, so input and output are coupled through the controller. It matters where the signal is injected and what is taken as the “input”: you estimate the ratio of the output to the actual signal at the plant input for example, to the controller/mixer output , not to the setpoint. SYSID mode in ArduCopter - A mode “like STABILIZE” that injects a chirp at a selected point in the loop and writes the data to the log SIDD messages — time-domain data, SIDS — settings . - SID_AXIS — where to inject angle, rate or mixer on roll/pitch/yaw, etc.; the values are per the list for your version . While SID_AXIS = 0 , you can't enter the mode; in addition, the vehicle must be airborne, and you can switch to SYSID for axes 1–13 only from a manual-throttle mode STABILIZE, ACRO , and for axes 14–19 only from LOITER. - SID_MAGNITUDE — amplitude, SID_F_START_HZ and SID_F_STOP_HZ — the range, SID_T_REC — recording duration, SID_T_FADE_IN / SID_T_FADE_OUT — smooth ramp-up and ramp-down of the amplitude. - Safety: altitude, open space, the pilot ready to take over by switching modes; start with a small amplitude, and in SITL first. - Betaflight and PX4: Betaflight since 2025.12 has a CHIRP mode build option USE_CHIRP , parameters chirp_ , the settings are written to the Blackbox header ; 4.5 has no built-in chirp analysis is done from Blackbox with manual disturbances ; in PX4 the copter autotune identifies the model online by itself, and for manual identification there are signal generators in test builds — see the documentation for your version. Frequency response from spectra For a linear system Y f = H f ·U f . The estimate is H = Y·U / U ², averaged over frequency bands: divide the cross-spectrum by the input spectrum. Averaging over a band suppresses noise; where there is little energy in the input outside the chirp , the estimate is meaningless. - Coherence the quality of the estimate — how much of the output is explained linearly by the input: close to 1 — good; dropping — noise, nonlinearity, another input wind, pilot . - The result is points on a Bode plot: gain in dB and phase in degrees. Fitting the model Model G s = K·e^ −sτ / Ts + 1 : - at low frequencies the gain ≈ K; - at the corner frequency 1/ 2πT the gain is −3 dB, the phase −45° without delay ; - the delay τ doesn't change the gain but adds −360°·f·τ of phase, growing with frequency. So T is seen from the gain, τ from the “extra” phase at high frequencies. The fit minimizes the difference between the complex H and G over the points grid search over T and τ, K analytically . On the module's example T = 20 ms, τ = 10 ms, noise on the output the fit returns T = 20 ms and τ ≈ 9 ms: the model is continuous while the data are discrete with a 2.5 ms step, so half a step of delay gets “lost.” {{diagram:chart-sysid-bode Frequency response from a chirp: points computed from spectra and a first-order-plus-delay model; the gain corner is at 8 Hz, and the phase drops off because of the delay.}} Model → tuning - Phase margin. For a proportional controller Kp the open loop is L = Kp·G. The crossover frequency is where L = 1; the phase margin is 180° + ∠L at it. The larger Kp, the higher the crossover frequency and the smaller the margin because of the delay. - The cost of a filter. A low-pass filter with frequency f_c adds approximately −arctan f/f_c of phase: at a 20 Hz loop crossover, an 80 Hz filter takes away ~14°. This is the “filters eat the margin” from the “Filters” module — now as a number. - Comparing vehicles and changes. New props, motors, frame — a new model: you can see whether the time constant or the delay changed, and how much in gains it costs. {{diagram:chart-sysid-phase-margin With the step 1 model the phase margin falls with the crossover frequency: at 20 Hz it is 47°, an 80 Hz LPF takes 14°

The baseline Step 2. Four profiles Step 3. The flight program Step 4. The metrics Step 5. One step at a time
text: summary “Sharper”, “softer”, “it wobbles”, “it runs hot” — these are a pilot's impressions, and they can be turned into numbers from the log so that profiles are compared fairly. This module gives a working method: filters before PID, one parameter per step, four profiles — four short flights in a row with one program, five metrics computed per maneuver. The case is an experiment on two identical 7" quads: four profiles, what matched the impressions and what did not, and why the outcome was not a new PID but new filters. theory The order: filters first, then PID PID amplifies everything that comes from the gyro, including noise. Choosing PID gains on bad filters is tuning an amplifier against a background of interference. So: the RPM filter and the dynamic notch are working, the spectrum is clean the modules on filters and the RPM filter , and only then — PID. {{lesson:bf-motor-balance Even before the filters come the mechanics: the motor medians from the log reveal an offset center of gravity, a weak motor and a yaw imbalance that PID only “holds with current”.}} The Betaflight 4.3+ sliders The simplified tuning mode moves groups of parameters at once: - Damping D — resistance to fast movements, damps overshoot; higher — the motors run hot. - Tracking P and I — how accurately the aircraft follows the stick and rejects disturbances; higher — oscillations. - Stick Response FF — the reaction to fast stick movements; higher — overshoot at the end of a flip. - Dynamic Damping D max — how much D may rise on fast movements. - Drift - Wobble I — holding in turns and at zero throttle. - Master Multiplier — everything at once; it is touched when the others run out of travel. In the CLI these are simplified_pi_gain , simplified_d_gain , simplified_feedforward_gain , simplified_d_max_gain before 2025.12 — simplified_dmax_gain , simplified_i_gain , simplified_master_multiplier plus simplified_tuning apply . There are four PID profiles and four rate profiles. Only the rate profile can be switched in flight the RATE PROFILE adjustment . The PID profile is changed only on the ground while disarmed: with the sticks, through the OSD menu, in Betaflight App or in the CLI with the profile N command N = 0–3 — there is neither a mode nor an adjustment for it. {{widget:pid-sim}} Symptoms - P too high — twitchy, overcorrects, fast oscillation. Too low — sluggish, slow wobble. - I too high — “robotic”, low-frequency oscillation. Too low — drifts, “slides as if on ice”. - D too low — bounce-back after flips, propwash in descents. Too high — hot motors, a mushy response. - FF too high — overshoot at the start of a flip, shake on stick movements. Check the motor temperature after every change of D or the filters: a short flight, land, a finger on a motor. If you cannot hold it — roll back. Five metrics per maneuver A maneuver is a segment where setpoint is above a threshold for example, 200 °/s for longer than 50 ms. For each: Impression Metric How to compute it --- --- --- runs hot motor noise the std of the motor commands above 40 Hz, averaged over the motors shakes in descents propwash RMS the gyro RMS in the 20–70 Hz band over the descent segments wobbles after a stop bounce-back the gyro peak of the opposite sign within 150 ms after the stop / the maneuver amplitude, % slow on the stick entry lag the time from the start of the setpoint movement to 50% on the gyro, ms undershoots / overshoots peak tracking max gyro / max setpoint, % The median over 10–20 maneuvers is robust; the mean is spoiled by one bad snap. The classic step response Blackbox Explorer; PID-Analyzer — not developed since 2019, PIDscope is good on long freestyle logs, but on short logs of 1–2 minutes per profile it is noisy to ±40% — direct metrics are more honest. A case: four profiles on two 7" quads Two almost identical 7" quads the same frame, motors, props, FC , brought to a common baseline. The four profiles differed only in the sliders, with identical filters; each profile had its own short flight, four flights in a row with one program: COOL SHARP WASH FLOAT --- --- --- --- --- Tracking 1.00 1.15 1.00 1.00 Damping 1.00 1.00 1.20 0.85 D max 1.00 1.00 1.20 1.00 Feedforward 1.00 1.15 1.00 0.80 The result drone A, four flights, medians : motor noise 16.1 / 23.3 / 18.0 / 14.6; bounce-back 6.0 / 8.5 / 9.4 / 14.9%; entry lag 38 / 31 / 40 / 44 ms. - SHARP “sharper” — yes: the lag is 7 ms shorter. The price is +45% motor noise. That is P: it raises the gain at all frequencies. - FLOAT “softer” — yes, the quietest. But bounce-back is almost 15%: after a stop the drone rolls back by 1/7 of the amplitude. That is bad for filming. - WASH “felt no difference” — and the numbers confirmed it: propwash is 0.97 of COOL, within the noise. At 1.4 kg under 7" props propwash is aerodynamics, not underdamping. The profile was dropped. - Two “identical” drones gave a different bounce-back for SHARP 2.9% against 8.5% : on the second one the pilot flew more sharply, and D max had time to kick in. The conclusion about the method: compare profiles only within one series of flights one pilot, one program, one charge window or normalize by the maneuver amplitude. The outcome: COOL is the best compromise. Sharpness was restored not through P but through the filters: simplified_gyro_filter_multiplier 1.00 → 1.10 and dyn_notch_q 400 → 450, with PID as in COOL. That is how the CRISP profile appeared. The first proposal was more aggressive 1.25 and one notch ; it was rejected in favor of small steps: 1.10 → a flight → 1.20 on success. The tuning protocol from data, not from impressions 1. Baseline : the 2025.12 defaults D: d_roll 30 — the base, d_max_roll 40 — the peak; in 4.5 the same numbers were called d_min_roll and d_roll , the filters per the “Filters” module, a clean spectrum, cool motors. Log A: 30 s of hover + 10 maneuvers with a sharp stop in roll/pitch + 3 descents with propwash. 2. The metrics from log A data-python : step_metrics , bounce_back , motor nois

The limit of the test and the plan Step 2. The script Step 3. A run on synthetic data Step 4. Your own logs Moving to real hardware
text: summary “It got softer with the new D” is a hypothesis, not a result. This module turns the comparison of two settings into an experiment: one change, one flight program, the ABBA order within one window of conditions, log metrics with exact definitions and a minimum of statistics — the spread, the ratio of the effect to the standard error, and a permutation test. It covers what Betaflight 4.5 can switch in flight: the rate profile — yes, the PID profile — not by any standard means, a single PID gain — yes, with an absolute adjrange slot. The lab is a Python script: the CSV from blackbox_decode → maneuvers → five metrics → a verdict with p. On synthetic data with a known effect −15 % propwash one pair of flights decides nothing, five pairs in ABBA order find the effect, and the same amount flown in blocks AAAAA BBBBB loses it. theory Why one flight proves nothing The propwash metric from two flights with the very same setting differs by 5–15 % a course guideline; in the lab model CV ≈ 8 % : a different gust, a different pack, the pilot caught the throttle earlier. One flight of A against one flight of B gives no estimate of the spread within an arm, and a difference of 13 % cannot be told from noise. In the lab one pair of flights shows −32 % in overshoot and −33 % in motor headroom, although B does not change them at all. Impressions are a source of hypotheses, not a decision. A pilot who knows that the “new, better” profile is on flies and judges differently placebo . In the bf-pid case one flight per profile the log supported “sharper” for SHARP and showed its price of +45 % motor noise, which cannot be felt by hand; by the standards of this module that is a hypothesis for an A/B test with 4–5 flights per arm. Confounders change together with the setting and shift the metric by themselves: Factor How it distorts How to control it --- --- --- Battery: charge, sag on an empty pack delay and propwash grow one batch, the same charge and landing voltage; ABBA; the same vbat_sag_compensation Motor and ESC heating the metrics drift toward the end of the session the same pause between flights, ABBA Wind propwash and tracking error up to 5 m/s bf-pid , an entry in the log, ABBA Props a nick or a different batch changes the vibration one set of props per session; if you changed them — start the session over Pilot different sharpness of the maneuvers one program, one pilot, blind selection Aircraft “identical” drones have different CGs and motors A and B on one aircraft bf-motor-balance {{lesson:bf-motor-balance A motor imbalance and an offset CG shift all the metrics more than a slider step does: mechanics first, then A/B.}} The design of the experiment 1. A hypothesis with a target metric and a threshold — before the flights. An example: “B d_roll / d_pitch 40/46 → 46/52 in 4.5 will reduce propwash by at least 10 % without raising the hover noise by more than 10 %”. A threshold written down in advance keeps you from later picking the metric that “worked out”. 2. One change. A is the control without edits, and B differs in one parameter or slider. 3. A flight program that is the same for all the flights below ; each maneuver feeds its own metric. 4. The order. ABA: the average of the two A flights cancels linear drift. ABBA ABBA…: the arms get almost the same drift. ABAB works too, but B always has one flight's worth more drift. The blocks AAAAA BBBBB are the worst option: the whole drift of the session falls on the difference. 5. An A/A test. A against A with the same program shows the metric's own noise. If it is comparable with the expected effect, more flights or a larger step are needed. 6. Blind selection. A helper sets the profile on the ground, and the pilot does not know what is being flown and writes down a 1–5 rating before the log is analyzed. {{diagram:bf-ab-order The number of flights is the same; the order decides: in the blocks AAAAA BBBBB the wind drift added an extra +15 % of propwash to B and ate the −15 % effect, while in ABBA order the drift was split almost evenly +13.2 % and +13.8 % .}} The flight program about 30 s, repeated in every flight; the segmentation thresholds are course guidelines, and the lab script uses them : Maneuver How Metric How the script finds the segment --- --- --- --- Hover 5 s at 1.5–2 m, sticks centered gyro noise \ setpoint\ < 20 °/s on all axes, throttle 1300–1600, ≥ 2 s Roll snaps 5 full-stick snaps of 0.25 s, a 0.75 s pause, alternating sign tracking error, overshoot \ setpoint 0 \ 200 °/s for longer than 50 ms Punch-out 100 % throttle for 1–1.5 s motor headroom rcCommand 3 1900 for longer than 0.3 s Descents 3 times: throttle to zero for 1–1.5 s, a catch at 70 % propwash rcCommand 3 < 1150 for longer than 0.5 s The first and last 3 s of the log are discarded takeoff and landing , as in bf-pid . How to switch between A and B in Betaflight 4.5 The best conditions are A and B in one flight: one pack, one wind. What the firmware can do verified against the source : - There is no standard way to switch the PID profile in flight. There is no such function in fc/rc_adjustments.h and no such mode in fc/rc_modes.h 4.5.3 and 2025.12 ; MSP_SELECT_SETTING silently ignores the PID profile while armed msp/msp.c , and the stick commands and entering the OSD menu with the sticks work only while disarmed. On the ground: with the sticks throttle down + yaw left + roll left / pitch forward / roll right → profiles 1/2/3 in the App numbering, that is, profile 0 / 1 / 2 , fc/rc_controls.c , the OSD menu, Betaflight App or profile N N = 0–3; the fourth profile — only the CLI, the OSD or the App . A comparison of PID profiles means separate flights. The gains themselves can be written over MSP in flight MSP_SET_PID , MSP_SET_PID_ADVANCED , MSP_SET_SIMPLIFIED_TUNING , for example by a Lua script on the radio : only to RAM, with no Blackbox event — that is not a method for A/B. 4.5.3 also has a hole: the OSD menu opened through CRSF telemetry does not check the arm st

text: summary This module follows a command from the stick to the setpoint — the desired angular rate that PID compares the gyro against. It covers channel calibration rxrange , the formulas of the five rate types from fc/rc.c , the throttle curve, rate profiles, RC smoothing with its cutoff frequency chosen automatically from the receiver rate, and feedforward with its anti-jitter filters. The lab is a Python port of the firmware formulas. It converts rates between Actual, Betaflight and Quick while keeping the center and the maximum, and models the PT3 smoothing of a stick step on ELRS at 50…1000 Hz; a second script reproduces the 4.5.3 feedforward pipeline jitter, duplicates, boost, the limit near the maximum rate and teaches you to read debug_mode = FEEDFORWARD . Then on hardware: checking rxrange , reading rc_smoothing_info with a real link, and a blind comparison of rate profiles switched in flight. theory The chain from the stick to PID The processing order rx/rx.c , fc/rc.c , flight/mixer.c ; the same in 4.5 and 2025.12 : 1. The receiver delivers a channel in microseconds. CRSF/ELRS: 172…1811 → 988…2012 µs rx/crsf.c . 2. rxrange stretches the first four channels after map from min…max to 1000…2000. AUX channels are not scaled. 3. The validity check: outside rx_min_usec … rx_max_usec 885…2115 a channel is considered bad. It holds the last value for 300 ms, then gets the value from rxfail , and for channels 0–3 Betaflight declares signal loss failsafe . 4. Roll/pitch/yaw: rcCommand = rcData − mid_rc with deadband yaw_deadband subtracted, limited to ±500. The deflection x = rcCommand / 500 − deadband ∈ −1; 1 . In this module “full travel” is from stop to stop, 1000 units of rcCommand ; “half travel” is from center to stop, 500 units, x = 1. 5. applyRates x gives °/s, followed by the _rate_limit limit 1998 by default . The result is rawSetpoint. 6. Feedforward is computed from rawSetpoint on every new RC packet. 7. RC smoothing PT3 smooths the setpoint and feedforward at the PID loop rate. From there PID takes them. 8. Throttle: rcData − min_check ·1000/ 2000 − min_check → the thr_mid / thr_hover / thr_expo curve → the throttle PT3 → throttle_limit_ in the mixer. {{diagram:chart-bf-rates-curves The center and the maximum do not yet define the stick feel. Actual 20/67/54 and Betaflight 1.01/0.70/0.01 agree to within 4 °/s. The default Actual 7/67/0 70 → 670 °/s , with the same center and maximum in Betaflight, differs by up to 151 °/s in the middle of the travel.}} The five rate types rates_type , ACTUAL by default Which type to choose: Actual — its center, maximum and expo are independent, it is the default, and the same type is set in the simulator so that the skill carries over ops-pilot-training , the starting numbers are there too . Another type — only if you are carrying over someone else's profile: the numbers are not converted when the type is changed. The values are stored as integers: rc_rate , srate , expo per axis roll_ / pitch_ / yaw_ . Below, x is the stick deflection and e = expo/100 . The formulas are taken from the apply Rates functions. text: summary The Adjustments tab and the CLI command adjrange let you change PIDs, rates and profiles from the radio — without a laptop, right in the air. This is convenient and dangerous at the same time: a change applies immediately, it is not written to EEPROM by itself, and the function number in the CLI does not match the number in the source. This module goes through fc/rc_adjustments.c from Betaflight 2025.12 the file differs from 4.5 only by the added function 31 LED_DIMMER : 30 slots, two channels per slot, three modes step, absolute, select , the full function table with CLI numbers, the 500 ms timing and the ±200 µs thresholds, saving with the sticks, the OSD and Blackbox. Separately — the vtx command for the power, band and channel of the video transmitter on a switch, vtxtable and vtx_low_power_disarm . The lab: a Python model that repeats the firmware logic the run and its output are in the text , then the bench without props and a short hover session with a D adjustment and a save. theory Why this is needed and what it cannot do Typical jobs: tweak P/D/FF in the field when there is no laptop; switch rate profiles for different pilots; an OSD profile “race / long range / empty”; the LED strip color; VTX power “low on the bench, working in the air”. The last one is served by a separate command, vtx , not by adjrange . What Adjustments cannot do neither in 4.5 nor in 2025.12 : switch the PID profile there is no such function, and no such mode in Modes either , change D max d_max_ ; in 4.5 it was d_min_ that was unavailable , filters, the simplified_ sliders, anti-gravity, the VTX band/channel/power. The PID profile changes only while disarmed: with the sticks throttle down + yaw left + roll left / pitch up / roll right → profile 1/2/3, fc/rc_controls.c , from the OSD menu, with the CLI command profile or through auto_profile_cell_count . In flight — not at all. The profiles that are switched in the air: rates function 12 , OSD 29 , LED 30 ; from 2025.12 the strip brightness changes the same way 31, LED_DIMMER . The two-channel model: slot, range, function There are 30 slots MAX_ADJUSTMENT_RANGE_COUNT 30 , indices 0…29; the official In-flight Adjustments page says “12” — that is outdated . Each slot stores: - the range channel auxChannelIndex , AUX1 = 0 and the range start..end 900–2100, step 25, as for aux . The slot is active if start ≤ channel < end the end is not included, isRangeActive in fc/rc_modes.c ; - the function — a number from the table below; - the adjustment channel auxSwitchChannelIndex , AUX1 = 0 — the switch or pot that changes the value. It may be the same as the range channel; - center and scale — for absolute mode. All active slots are processed at the same time: you can turn four parameters with four channels. An inactive slot changes nothing, so the simplest way to have a “safe position” of the selector is to leave it without a slot. Adjustments are processed in the RC receive task fc/core.c , both armed and disarmed , but not in CLI mode and not with PARALYZE active while disarmed. Three modes - Step STEP — center = 0 , the function is not from the select group. The adjustment channel above mid_rc + 200 1700 µs with mid_rc 1500 → +1, below mid_rc − 200 1300 → −1. The step equals 1 for all functions. While held, the value repeats every 500 ms RESET_FREQUENCY_2HZ ; a return to center “re-arms” the slot immediately, so quick taps are faster than holding. The beeper: 2 short — up, 1 equally short — down beeperConfirmationBeeps 2 / 1 . - Absolute ABSOLUTE — center ≠ 0 , a step function. The value = center + rc − 1500 × scale / 500 C integer division, truncates toward zero , applied on every change of the channel. A pot at 1000 gives center − scale , at 2000 — center + scale . While the slot is inactive, the “last channel value” is reset to 0 — at the moment the slot turns on, the value jumps to the pot position. - Select SELECT — functions 12, 24, 25, 29, 30 in 2025.12 also 31 . The 900–2099 range is divided into N equal parts: position = rc − 900 / 1200 / N . RATE_PROFILE: N = 3, or 6 with rate_6pos_switch = ON but there are 4 rate profiles — positions 5–6 have nothing to switch to . OSD_PROFILE: N = 3, position + 1 is written osd_profile 1…3 . LED_PROFILE: N = 3 RACE / BEACON / STATUS . PID_AUDIO: N = 7. HORIZON_STRENGTH: N = 255. Limits: P/I/D 0–200 although set p_roll accepts up to 250 , F 0–2000 set f_roll — up to 1000 , RC rate 1–255, expo 0–100, super rate 0–255, thr_expo 0–100, feedforward_transition 1–100. The 2025.12 function table: CLI number ≠ enum number The CLI number is the position in the defaultAdjustmentConfigs array plus 1, not the value of adjustmentFunction_e . In the enum, positions 25–28 hold ROLL/PITCH RC RATE/EXPO, which are not in the array, so from number 25 on everything is shifted by 4. The table below was printed by the lab script from the 4.5.x source branch 4.5-maintenance , commit 7dcc851 : version.h says 4.5.6, but there is no such release; the latest release is 4.5.5, and the src/ code matches it except for the version number in version.h and checked against 2025.12.5: rows 1–30 match, and row 31 was added in 2025.12. CLI Function Mode What it changes Code in Blackbox --- --- --- --- --- 0 none — — — 1 RC_RATE step/abs. roll_rc_rate and pitch_rc_rate 25, 26 2 RC_EXPO step/abs. roll_expo and pitch_expo 27, 28 3 THROTTLE_EXPO step/abs. thr_expo 3 4 PITCH_ROLL_RATE step/abs. pitch_srate and roll_srate 13, 14 5 YAW_RATE step/abs. yaw_srate 5 6 PITCH_ROLL_P step/abs. p_pitch and p_roll 15, 18 7 PITCH_ROLL_I step/abs. i_pitch and i_roll 16, 19 8 PITCH_ROLL_D step/abs. d_pitch and d_roll in 2025.12 this is the base D, in 4.5 — the peak 17, 20 9 YAW_P step/abs. p_yaw 9 10 YAW_I step/abs. i_yaw 10 11 YAW_D step/abs. d_yaw 11 12 RATE_PROFILE select 3/6 rate profile 12 13 PITCH_RATE step/abs. pitch_srate 13 14 ROLL_RATE step/abs. roll_srate 14 15 PITCH_P step/abs. p_pitch 15 16 PITCH_I step/abs. i_pitch 16 17 PITCH_D step/abs. d_pitch 17 1

text: summary The Betaflight command line interface CLI is a text interface that gives access to the flight controller configuration at a level the graphical interface does not reach. From the CLI you can change any setting, including those not exposed in the configurator tabs, check the hardware state, manage resources microcontroller pins and make backups. The key practical goal of this article is to give you a confident working knowledge of resource and pin remapping without reflashing, and to teach you how to find out what a firmware build contains and how to restore a configuration after a failure. theory CLI architecture The CLI runs over a serial port UART , using the same channel as the configurator MSP , MultiWii Serial Protocol . To enter the CLI from a terminal for example, PuTTY/screen you send the character — it switches the controller into command mode. Key commands and what they are for - Session control: save , exit , batch start , batch end - Viewing the configuration: get , diff , dump , status , version - Changing settings: set , feature , profile , rateprofile - Resource remapping: resource , timer - Diagnostics and debugging: tasks , flash_info , dma Diff vs Dump: what to use and when diff all prints only the settings that were changed. It is the main format for backups and for a safe transfer within one firmware version. dump all prints a complete snapshot of the configuration, including default values. It suits deep diagnostics but is dangerous for a transfer between different versions. It is recommended to save separately: - diff all - resource show - status version/build diff / dump scopes and flags The syntax the same in 4.5 and 2025.12 : diff master profile rates hardware all {defaults bare} , and dump takes the same words printConfig in cli/cli.c . What goes into the output: Command What it prints Wrapper --- --- --- diff = diff master the common settings resource, timer, dma, feature, serial, mixer, beeper, map, led, aux, adjrange, rxrange, vtxtable, vtx, rxfail, all master-level set lines plus only the current PID profile and only the current rate profile batch start … batch end , without defaults nosave and without save diff profile only the current PID profile no wrapper diff rates only the current rate profile no wrapper diff hardware resource, timer, dma, feature, serial and the “hardware” set lines blackbox_device , sensor buses… , without profiles batch diff all everything from master , mcu_id and signature , all 4 PID profiles and all 4 rate profiles , and at the end — a return to the active profiles profile N , rateprofile N batch start , defaults nosave , …, save without batch end : it is printed only for diff / dump without all the defaults flag adds to every changed line a commented-out line with the default value — the bare flag removes batch / defaults nosave / save , mcu_id , signature and the restoring of the profile selection — The trap: diff without all loses three profiles out of four. A backup “with profile 2 for Li-Ion” made with diff while profile 1 is active will be pasted back without profile 2. For a backup — only diff all ; for comparing versions — diff all defaults you can see what default a changed setting had . The defaults and bare flags do not work together: only the first one is processed. {{diagram:bf-diff-scopes A plain diff writes only the active PID and rate profile; all 4 + 4 profiles, mcu_id and the wrapper with save are only in diff all.}} All CLI commands The priority A/B commands cmdTable in cli/cli.c , 59 in total — the set is the same in 4.5 and 2025.12; text:
summary Once you have more than one drone, configuring them by clicking through the Configurator is a recipe for mistakes. The Betaflight CLI is available over an ordinary serial port, so it can be scripted, and a board can be identified without the CLI at all — over the MSP protocol. This module shows how the firmware switches a port between MSP and the CLI, what format the CLI replies in and how to tell a reply from the prompt, and collects the pitfalls of bulk configuration: floating COM ports, save and exit that reboot in 4.5.3 — even with noreboot , “silent” value fixes on save and at boot, the substring search in get , batch mode, and the incompatibility of diff all between 4.5 and 2025.12. The lab needs no hardware: on SITL builds of Betaflight 4.5.3 and 2025.12.5 made from source, a Python script does everything it would do with a board over USB and catches real value fixes made by the firmware. theory How entering the CLI works A flight controller on USB is a virtual COM port USB CDC . The baud rate in the port settings does not matter for USB CDC; 115200 is the convention. The character puts the controller into the CLI, exit leaves it with a reboot. The mechanism comes from the sources msp/msp_serial.c , cli/cli.c , the same in 4.5.3 and 2025.12.5 unless stated otherwise . By default the port listens for MSP. Every byte that is not part of an MSP frame is treated by the firmware as “non-MSP data”: a byte queues a request to enter the CLI, a reboot_character byte R by default, code 82, range 48–126 queues a request to reboot into the bootloader. The request is executed only once the port has been silent for 100 ms, and the versions behave differently: in 4.5.3 any byte that arrives before those 100 ms have elapsed, on the next pass of the task, cancels the entry msp_serial.c:519–522 : “abort pending request” — followed immediately by a command gives “the CLI did not open”; in 2025.12 only $ clears the request msp_serial.c:535–539 , but bytes that arrive before the entry are lost. The order for both: , wait for the prompt, then the commands. While the aircraft is armed, non-MSP bytes are ignored fc/tasks.c : ARMING_FLAG ARMED ? MSP_SKIP_NON_MSP_DATA : on an armed drone does nothing, and that is a protection, not a bug. The same mechanism gives a pitfall: a script that sends arbitrary text to the port before entering the CLI may accidentally send R and drop the board into DFU. After the entry the firmware prints Entering CLI Mode, type 'exit' to return, or 'help' in 2025.12 — ... to reboot ... , sets the CLI arming disable flag and prints the prompt — exactly the 4 bytes 
 . The CLI echoes every character it receives, so the reply to a command is the echo, a line break, the output and 
 again. A line longer than 256 characters CLI_IN_BUFFER_SIZE is silently truncated, and everything after in a line is treated as a comment so if the board is already in the CLI from a previous session, a lone starts a comment and swallows the next command: in testing the short script below, that is how the version command was lost; the safe entry is 
 sent in a single write to the port: then both bytes arrive in one pass, and it works in both states , and errors are printed in the format ERROR IN <command : <text . In the CLI all bytes of the port go to the CLI: MSP does not answer on this port in 4.5.3 — on any port: fc/tasks.c returns before mspSerialProcess ; in 2025.12 the CLI state is kept per port, and the other MSP ports work , Blackbox does not log fc/core.c : if !cliMode && blackboxConfig - device , and the telemetry task does not run fc/tasks.c : if !cliMode && featureIsEnabled FEATURE_TELEMETRY . The Configurator shows “no connection” during this time — that is normal. MSP: identify a board without entering the CLI MSP v1 is the Configurator's binary protocol: a request is $M< , a size byte, a command byte, the payload and a checksum — the XOR of the size, the command and the payload; a reply starts with $M , and an unsupported command gives $M! . Five commands are enough to find the right board, and none of them requires the CLI, reboots, or sets an arming block: Command number Reply 4.5.3 SITL 2025.12.5 SITL --- --- --- --- MSP_API_VERSION 1 protocol, major, minor 1.46 1.47 MSP_FC_VARIANT 2 4 characters BTFL BTFL MSP_FC_VERSION 3 3 version bytes in 2025.12 — also a Pascal string 4.5.3 25.12.5 year − 2000, month, patch + 2025.12.5 , 13 bytes in total MSP_NAME 10 craft_name string string MSP_UID 160 3 × uint32, the unique ID of the MCU 12 bytes 12 bytes The pitfall is in the third row: with the move to calendar versioning, MSP_FC_VERSION in 2025.12 returns 25, 12, 5 msp.c : FC_VERSION_YEAR - FC_CALVER_BASE_YEAR . A script with the check “major ≥ 4 means new” will take 2025.12 for version 25, and a script with “major == 4” will take it for unknown firmware. Compare versions by MSP_API_VERSION , by the full string from version , or by the string that 2025.12 appends to the MSP_FC_VERSION reply after the three bytes sbufWritePString FC_VERSION_STRING , msp.c:646 . On a real board MSP_UID is the factory serial number of the microcontroller, and it does not change on reflashing or defaults ; in SITL it is fixed 000000000100000002000000 in both versions , so in the lab identification goes by name. Pitfall 1: the COM port is not permanent If several identical boards are connected to the computer, they share one USB VID/PID, and the COM port number changes after every reboot. You cannot bind to COM8 . The reliable identifier is craft_name inside the config, and it should be read over MSP MSP_NAME , not by entering the CLI on every port: entering the CLI sets an arming block until reboot, and on 4.5.3 you cannot leave the CLI without a reboot. Hence the rule: all drones have different craft_name values before the work starts; for a fleet of identical boards, also store MSP_UID next to the name — it catches a cloned config where two aircraft got the same name. Pitfall 2: exit noreboot reboot

text: summary On Betaflight, GPS is needed for GPS Rescue, the home arrow and the speed in the OSD. What matters is not “there are satellites” but “home is recorded correctly and the heading is known”. This module covers choosing and connecting a u-blox M8 or M10, what Betaflight writes to the receiver with gps_auto_config = ON from the code of io/gps.c , which disagrees with the documentation in four places , the gps_ and mag_ variables, the GPS arming flag, recording home, heading without a compass, the OSD, gpspassthrough with u-center, cold, warm and hot start, DOP and CEP. A Python lab: a UBX parser following the 4.5 rules is checked on a real M8030 recording DOP matched the receiver to within 0.02 , then six synthetic logs show the effect of constellations and VTX noise, plus the UART load. On hardware — satellites with the VTX off and on, timing a cold start and checking home. GPS Rescue itself is in bf-failsafe and bf-setup-scratch . theory What GPS gives Betaflight 2025.12 Betaflight 2025.12 does not fly waypoints that is INAV and ArduPilot, inav-gps . 2026.6 brought the AUTOPILOT permanentId 56 and WP CAPTURE 57 modes and the waypoint CLI command, but all of it is under ENABLE_FLIGHT_PLAN , and in tag 2026.6.2 USE_FLIGHT_PLAN is defined only in the SITL target target/common_post.h , platform/SIMULATOR/target/SITL/target.h : on flight controllers it is an experimental feature, not for flying. From 2025.12 it can hold position the POS HOLD mode, id 11, the pos_hold_ and ap_position_ variables; a build option and altitude ALTHOLD ; 4.5 does not have these modes. The coordinates go to GPS Rescue, to home, the distance and the OSD arrow, to the speed and coordinates in the OSD and telemetry, to the altitude flight/position.c blends GPS with the baro with a weight of gpsTrust = min 1/PDOP, 0.9 and to the lap timer gps_lap_timer_ . Without a compass GPS also provides the heading; POS HOLD without a compass is allowed by pos_hold_without_mag OFF by default . In 2026.6 pos_hold_without_mag was removed: GPS-based POS HOLD and GPS Rescue require a trustworthy heading POS HOLD on optical flow alone does not, positionEstimatorIsHeadingRequired in flight/pos_hold_multirotor.c — from the compass only if trust_mag = ON OFF by default, flight/imu.c , sensors/compass.c , otherwise from GPS after gaining speed; the position source is selected by poshold_position_source AUTO, GPS_ONLY, OPTICALFLOW_ONLY . The line set pos_hold_without_mag from an old diff gives INVALID NAME in 2026.6. The module: M8 or M10 Parameter u-blox M8 NEO-M8N, FW 3.01 u-blox M10 MAX-M10S, ROM SPG 5.10 --- --- --- Default constellations GPS + GLONASS + SBAS, QZSS , Galileo disabled GPS + Galileo + BeiDou B1I + QZSS, SBAS Cold start 26 s GPS+GLO , 29 s GPS only 27 s by default, 23–28 s in other sets Hot start 1 s 1 s CEP accuracy 24 h, static 2.5 m 2.0 m with SBAS 1.5 m Max navigation update rate NEO-M8N: 5 Hz with two systems, 10 Hz with one 3 Hz by default GPS+GAL+BDS , 10 Hz for GPS+GAL, 6 Hz for GPS+GAL+GLO; 18 Hz with a single system Supply of the module itself 2.7–3.6 V 1.76–3.6 V, 9.5 mA at 3 V GPS+GAL+BDS Default UART 9600 8N1, NMEA 9600 8N1, NMEA The figures are from the u-blox datasheets. The M10 is more accurate, more economical and sees more satellites, but a factory MAX-M10S with GPS+GAL+BDS does not deliver the 10 Hz that Betaflight configures it for: the ceiling is 3 Hz. The M10 defaults depend on the firmware: for ROM 5.00 it is GPS+GAL, for the SAM-M10Q — GPS+GAL+GLO+BDS B1C. Look up the version and the constellation set in u-center MON-VER, MON-GNSS . An FPV module is a receiver, an LDO, a patch antenna, sometimes a capacitor or a battery on V_BCKP and a compass on I²C. “5 V” on the silkscreen is the LDO input; the chip itself runs on 3.3 or 1.8 V; without an LDO you need the 3.3 V pad — the board marking decides. Power on V_BCKP keeps the ephemeris and the clock — a restart takes seconds. The inrush current of the SAM-M10Q is up to 100 mA. Wiring and installation - UART crossed over: module TX → flight controller RX, RX → TX, common GND. Both wires are needed: Betaflight sends configuration to the module. A hardware UART only: on SoftSerial the baud rate is capped at 19200 serial.c , which is not enough step 3 . The compass SDA/SCL goes to the I²C pads. - The antenna faces the sky, with nothing conductive above it. The SAM-M10Q gives its optimal pattern on a 50 × 50 mm ground plane; the board of an FPV module is 20–25 mm, so a large module on a mast is usually better than a small one inside the frame. - Interference: L1 signals at the Earth's surface are about −130 dBm at 1561–1602 MHz BeiDou B1I 1561.098, GPS and Galileo 1575.42, GLONASS ≈ 1602 . Keep the module away from the VTX and its antenna, a digital air unit with its camera, the ESCs and the power wires; 1.2–1.3 GHz video is the closest of all to the L band. How much your VTX interferes is shown by the bench test in the practice. - Tilt: the documentation advises tilting the aircraft 45° in all directions — the satellites must not be lost, since the aircraft flies home tilted. summary: A servo on a Betaflight quad is not “plug in and it works”: the firmware has to support servos (in Cloud Build — the SERVOS option), the output has to sit on a timer that is not used by DShot, the power has to come from a separate BEC, and `smix` is not applied on a quad at all. This module separate
