headings: The MAVLink 2 frame seq and packet loss CRC and CRC_EXTRA Zero truncation in the payload Field order on the wire Dialects and mavgen Packet signing Where it fits in the system Step 1. A decoder by hand Step 2. CRC_EXTRA by hand Step 3. Your own dialect Step 4. Loss from seq
text: summary In the comp-mavlink module, MAVLink was "a library that sends messages". Here it becomes a protocol you can read by eye in a hex dump. We take v1 and v2 frames apart byte by byte, look at the sequence number and how to count packet loss from it, at CRC-16/MCRF4XX and why a CRC_EXTRA byte is mixed into it, and at why MAVLink 2 truncates trailing zeros in the payload and what that breaks in home-made parsers. Then we look at where messages come from: XML dialects, mavgen , the field order on the wire not the XML order , extension fields, and compatibility. The last part is packet signing: what the 13 bytes are made of, how the key gets into the autopilot, and what signing protects against and what it does not. Lab: a frame decoder without the pymavlink parser, your own dialect with a new message, automated tests in examples/mavlink/ . theory The MAVLink 2 frame Byte Field Meaning --- --- --- 0 STX = 0xFD start of frame v1: 0xFE 1 len payload length after zero truncation 0–255 2 incompat_flags bit 0: the frame is signed; an unknown bit → the frame is dropped 3 compat_flags an unknown bit can be ignored 4 seq sequence number 0–255 from this sender 5 sysid sending system 6 compid sending component 7–9 msgid 24 bits, little-endian 10… payload len bytes +2 checksum CRC-16/MCRF4XX, little-endian +13 signature only if incompat_flags & 1 The v2 header is 10 bytes, v1 is 6 no flags, a 1-byte msgid, so only messages with IDs < 256 . All multi-byte numbers are little-endian. The minimum v2 frame is 12 bytes, the maximum 280. {{diagram:mavlink2-frame A MAVLink 2 frame: a 10-byte header, the payload, the CRC, and the optional signature.}} seq and packet loss Every sender a sysid/compid pair increments seq modulo 256. A receiver that sees seq_new ≠ seq_old + 1 knows that seq_new − seq_old − 1 mod 256 frames were lost. That is exactly how QGC and Mission Planner compute "link quality" and the loss percentage, with no feedback from the radio at all. The trap: if one link carries two different senders with the same sysid/compid two copies of the same script, for example , the loss count becomes meaningless and routing becomes unpredictable. Note that seq counts per sending channel: a router that filters messages by msgid mav-routing makes the GCS see "loss" that is not real. CRC and CRC_EXTRA The checksum covers every byte after STX up to the end of the payload the header without STX + the payload , using CRC-16/MCRF4XX polynomial 0x1021 in reflected form, initial value 0xFFFF; the check value for "123456789" is 0x6F91 . Then one more byte is "fed" into the CRC: CRC_EXTRA , computed from the message definition, that is, its name and the list of fields with their types. It is not in the frame. Why: if the sender and the receiver have different definitions for the same msgid a field added, a type changed , the length may match while the meaning does not. CRC_EXTRA makes such frames invalid, and the receiver silently drops them. Hence the classic symptom "the link is up, the heartbeat is there, but this one message never arrives": the dialects diverged on a single message. python def x25_crc data: bytes, crc: int = 0xFFFF - int: for b in data: tmp = b ^ crc & 0xFF tmp = tmp ^ tmp << 4 & 0xFF crc = crc 8 ^ tmp << 8 ^ tmp << 3 ^ tmp 4 & 0xFFFF return crc Zero truncation in the payload MAVLink 2 drops trailing zero bytes of the payload before sending: a COMMAND_LONG with confirmation = 0 goes out as 32 bytes instead of 33 param1–param7 come first on the wire, so their zeros never end up at the tail . The receiver must pad the payload with zeros up to the full struct size before unpacking. A home-made parser that checks len == sizeof struct will drop half the messages, and it will look like "random packet loss". At least one payload byte is always kept. {{diagram:mav-rx-frame-flow Receiving a frame step by step: a corrupted byte and diverged dialects both end in a silent drop at the CRC check with CRC_EXTRA, while truncated zeros must be padded back, not rejected.}} Field order on the wire In the XML, fields are listed in an order that suits humans. On the wire they are sorted by type size, largest first uint64/double → uint32/int32/float → uint16 → uint8/char , stable within one size, and extension fields after the <extensions/ tag go at the end in XML order. That way the struct is aligned with no gaps. In pymavlink this is ordered_fieldnames ; in the C headers it is the field order in mavlink_ _t . CRC_EXTRA uses the fields in wire order, without the extension fields: that is why adding an extension field does not break compatibility, while changing an existing field does. Dialects and mavgen Messages are defined in XML: minimal.xml HEARTBEAT ⊂ standard.xml ⊂ common.xml ⊂ ardupilotmega.xml through <include . Your own dialect is an XML file that includes common.xml and adds its own messages in a dedicated ID range. mavgen generates a library from it: bash python -m pymavlink.tools.mavgen --lang=Python3 --wire-protocol=2.0 --output=mydialect.py mydialect.xml python -m pymavlink.tools.mavgen --lang=C --wire-protocol=2.0 --output=generated/ mydialect.xml Rules that save days of debugging: the msgid of a new message must not collide with existing ones; after changing the XML, rebuild every side autopilot, companion, GCS ; check the generated CRC_EXTRA in both places. For experiments without rebuilding the autopilot there are ready-made general-purpose messages: NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT 251 , NAMED_VALUE_INT 252 , DEBUG_VECT 250 , TUNNEL 385, arbitrary bytes with a payload type . Packet signing A signed frame incompat_flags bit 0 carries 13 bytes: link_id 1 , timestamp 6 bytes, in units of 10 µs since January 1, 2015 , signature the first 6 bytes of a SHA-256 hash of "secret key + header + payload + CRC + link_id + timestamp" . The receiver checks the signature and that the timestamp increases monotonically: this protects against both spoofing and replay of a captured frame. The key 32 bytes reaches the autopilot in

text: summary MAVLink is not a set of messages but a set of exchanges microservices : who starts, who answers, what to do on loss. Almost every companion integration bug is a violation of one of these exchanges: a command sent without waiting for the ACK, a parameter "written" without an echo, a mission uploaded halfway. The module walks through the main microservices: heartbeat and state, commands COMMAND_LONG / COMMAND_INT , ACK, IN_PROGRESS, the confirmation counter , parameters reading the list, writing with confirmation, type encoding , missions upload, download, partial update, geofences and rally points as separate mission types , telemetry stream control, MAVFTP, camera/gimbal, and Remote ID, at the level of "which exchange it is and where it breaks". Lab: a mission client with retries that passes its tests at 25 % packet loss. theory Heartbeat and state HEARTBEAT 0 goes out once a second from every component: the type MAV_TYPE , the autopilot, base_mode the arming flag is MAV_MODE_FLAG_SAFETY_ARMED , custom_mode the mode number, specific to each firmware , system_status . The heartbeat is participant discovery, the source of addresses for routing, and the basis of failsafes: an autopilot that stops hearing the GCS heartbeat triggers the GCS failsafe if enabled ; a companion that stops hearing the autopilot must stop sending setpoints. The rule: send addressed commands only after the first heartbeat from the target. Commands: COMMAND_LONG, COMMAND_INT, and the ACK COMMAND_LONG 76 : target_system , target_component , command MAV_CMD , confirmation , seven float parameters. COMMAND_INT 75 : the same addressing and param1–4, but no confirmation field instead there are current / autocontinue , both unused ; parameters 5–6 are the integers x , y latitude/longitude × 10⁷ without float precision loss , and there is a frame field; prefer it for commands with coordinates. The reply is COMMAND_ACK 77 with a result : result Meaning What the client does --- --- --- ACCEPTED 0 executed/accepted done TEMPORARILY_REJECTED 1 not possible right now retry later DENIED 2 not allowed in this state read STATUSTEXT, do not retry UNSUPPORTED 3 command not supported do not retry FAILED 4 attempted, and failed analyze the cause IN_PROGRESS 5 long-running command, progress 0–100 wait for the final ACK The protocol prescribes: if no ACK arrives within the timeout, resend the command with confirmation incremented . That lets the receiver tell a retry from a new command. Without waiting for the ACK a command is hope; without a retry limit it is a hang. {{diagram:mavlink-command-seq An acknowledged command: a retry when the ACK is lost, an intermediate IN_PROGRESS, the final result.}} Parameters - The list: PARAM_REQUEST_LIST 21 → a stream of PARAM_VALUE 22 with param_count and param_index . Gaps are filled by index with PARAM_REQUEST_READ 20 and param_index . - Reading one: PARAM_REQUEST_READ by name 16 characters, with no terminating null when the name is 16 long! or by index. - Writing: PARAM_SET 23 . There is no separate ACK : the confirmation is a PARAM_VALUE with the same name and the new value. If the echo carries the old value, the write was rejected a read-only parameter, for example ; on an error no such name, read-only, a NaN value ArduPilot 4.7 and PX4 1.18 send PARAM_ERROR 345 ; for an unknown name or a NaN value ArduPilot sends only PARAM_ERROR and no echo at all, so a client waiting only for PARAM_VALUE times out. - Every value travels in the float param_value field. ArduPilot sends integer types as a number converted to float C cast , PX4 byte-wise the integer's bits in the float's bits . A flag in AUTOPILOT_VERSION.capabilities tells which scheme the autopilot uses MAV_PROTOCOL_CAPABILITY_PARAM_ENCODE_C_CAST or ..._BYTEWISE ; ArduPilot 4.7 does not set ..._C_CAST and reports the deprecated MAV_PROTOCOL_CAPABILITY_PARAM_FLOAT instead, so the sign to look for is the absence of ..._BYTEWISE . Getting the scheme wrong turns MAV_SYSID = 1 SYSID_THISMAV before ArduPilot 4.7 into 1.4e-45. For bulk parameter download, so you do not run 1000 exchanges over the radio, there is MAVFTP: ArduPilot serves the whole @PARAM/param.pck file. Missions: an exchange driven by the receiver Upload client → vehicle : 1. Client: MISSION_COUNT 44 with the number of items and the mission_type . 2. The vehicle requests items one by one: MISSION_REQUEST_INT 51 with a seq ArduPilot 4.7 sends the old MISSION_REQUEST 40 ; answer it with MISSION_ITEM_INT as well . 3. The client replies with MISSION_ITEM_INT 73 carrying that seq . 4. After the last item the vehicle sends MISSION_ACK 47 with the result. The key idea: the receiving side holds the initiative . It requests the items, and it repeats a request on a timeout. The sender answers every request, repeated ones included, and never sends items "ahead". Download vehicle → client is symmetric: MISSION_REQUEST_LIST → MISSION_COUNT → the client requests with MISSION_REQUEST_INT → MISSION_ITEM_INT → the client finishes with MISSION_ACK . mission_type : 0 is the mission, 1 the geofence fence , 2 rally points, 255 all of them for clearing with MISSION_CLEAR_ALL . Item 0 in ArduPilot is the home position; uploading from item 1 in Mission Planner is just the interface, and on the wire home is still seq 0. Avoid the deprecated MISSION_ITEM 39 with float coordinates float precision at a given latitude is about a meter ; never send the deprecated MISSION_REQUEST 40 yourself, but accept it ArduPilot sends it during upload . In flight: MISSION_CURRENT 42 is the current item, MISSION_ITEM_REACHED 46 means an item was reached, MAV_CMD_DO_SET_MISSION_CURRENT 224 jumps to an item the MISSION_SET_CURRENT 41 message was superseded by this command in 2022 . Partial update: MISSION_WRITE_PARTIAL_LIST 38 with an index range; not supported everywhere, so it is safer to re-upload the whole mission and verify it by downloading. {{diagram:mavlink-mission-seq Mission upload: the vehicle requests items one

text: summary After four modules "on the wire" you can choose your tool deliberately. pymavlink gives direct access to every message; MAVSDK gives ready-made actions arm , takeoff , upload_mission , offboard on top of the same microservices; MAVROS is a MAVLink ↔ ROS bridge; DroneKit is historical and unmaintained. Since autumn 2026, MAVSDK for Python has a new architecture: the mavsdk 4.x package is a native binding to the C++ core, with no gRPC and no mavsdk_server , and with its own API; the old code lives on in the mavsdk-grpc package. The module compares the libraries by layer, covers the MAVSDK 4 asynchronous model subscriptions, cancellation, timeouts , five pitfalls of MAVSDK + ArduPilot 4.7 found by running it in SITL, and what happens on a link loss at each level. The lab: a script on MAVSDK 4.2.1 against ArduCopter 4.7.2 SITL: connection, health, mission, takeoff in GUIDED, progress and RTL, with an analysis of the raw mission contents. theory Layers Layer What it gives you What it does not When to use it --- --- --- --- Raw protocol mav-protocol everything nothing ready-made a driver on an MCU, your own dialect, debugging pymavlink codec, connections, recv_match , tlog the dialog logic missions, ACKs, retries are on you scripts, log analysis, tests, non-standard messages MAVSDK C++, Python, Kotlin, … actions and microservices: action, telemetry, mission, offboard, param, ftp, camera, gimbal exotic firmware messages through the MavlinkDirect plugin; MavlinkPassthrough is deprecated applications on a companion, automated flight tests MAVROS MAVLink ↔ ROS 1/2 topics/services, TF, setpoints ROS independence; overhead a ROS system with ArduPilot; for PX4 + ROS 2, uXRCE-DDS is preferred the px4-ros2 module DroneKit-Python — not developed, problems with modern Python and firmware reading old code only All the upper layers implement the same dialogs you wrote by hand: inside, upload_mission is MISSION_COUNT/REQUEST_INT/ITEM_INT/ACK with retries. You need to understand the lower layer to read a tlog when the upper layer says "timeout" or, worse, silently does the wrong thing. {{lesson:mav-services The mission, parameter and command dialogs with ACKs and retries: what MAVSDK hides inside; without them you cannot read a tlog.}} MAVSDK 4: a native binding instead of gRPC Up to and including version 3.x, pip install mavsdk installed MAVSDK-Python: an asynchronous wrapper that launched a bundled mavsdk_server process and talked to it over gRPC. Since MAVSDK v4, the mavsdk name on PyPI belongs to a different product: a native binding that calls the C++ core directly inside the Python process ctypes through the C wrapper libcmavsdk . PyPI releases: 3.17.4 on September 17, 2026 the last of the old kind , 4.0.0 on September 22, 2026, 4.2.1 on November 17, 2026 the lab was recorded on it; the core reports MAVSDK v4.2.1 , 4.3.0 on November 27, 2026. The old gRPC client continues to be developed under the name mavsdk-grpc imported as mavsdk_grpc , also 4.2.1 . What this means in practice: - No second process. No mavsdk_server , no port 50051, no grpcio dependency. Fewer moving parts on the companion, but also less isolation: a crash in the core takes down the Python process. - Two interfaces from one package. mavsdk is a synchronous, callback-based API, mavsdk.asyncio an asynchronous one. The asyncio wrapper moves blocking calls into a thread pool run_in_executor , and callbacks from the core arrive on its own thread and are handed to the event loop with call_soon_threadsafe read from the code of package 4.2.1, mavsdk/asyncio/plugins/ . - System discovery is separate from connecting. add_any_connection url only opens the channel; the vehicle shows up through first_autopilot timeout_s or get_systems . This matters when there is more than one vehicle on the network. - Plugins are constructed explicitly. drone.action.arm becomes ActionAsync drone .arm . - Subscribing and one-off reads are separate. In the gRPC package, telemetry.position was an endless stream; in 4.x the stream is subscribe_position , and position returns the latest value once. A loop async for p in telemetry.position carried over "as is" will fail. Old code does not break silently: the 4.x package intercepts imports of the old modules and calls to System and prints a hint checked: TypeError: System is not constructed directly, get it from Mavsdk instead… . Three ways forward: change the import to import mavsdk_grpc as mavsdk touch nothing else , pin mavsdk<4 in requirements.txt no more updates , or rewrite on the native API, which wins on a companion: no extra process, and a synchronous variant for simple utilities. Before gRPC, mavsdk<4 After mavsdk.asyncio , 4.x --- --- drone = System sdk = Mavsdk Configuration.create_with_component_type ComponentType.GROUND_STATION await drone.connect system_address=url await sdk.add_any_connection url implicit inside connect drone = await sdk.first_autopilot timeout_s → System or None drone.core.connection_state drone.is_connected_state drone.action , drone.telemetry ActionAsync drone , TelemetryAsync drone async for p in drone.telemetry.position async for p in tel.subscribe_position e._result.result in ActionError e.result The same scenario as in the old edition of this module a three-waypoint mission, arm, start, progress, RTL , on the 4.x API: python import asyncio from mavsdk.asyncio import Mavsdk, Configuration, ComponentType from mavsdk.asyncio.plugins.action import ActionAsync from mavsdk.asyncio.plugins.telemetry import TelemetryAsync from mavsdk.asyncio.plugins.mission import MissionAsync, MissionItem, MissionPlan async def main : cfg = Configuration.create_with_component_type ComponentType.GROUND_STATION async with Mavsdk cfg as sdk: await sdk.add_any_connection "udpin://0.0.0.0:14540" older gRPC package: drone.connect ... drone = await sdk.first_autopilot timeout_s=10.0 if drone is None: raise SystemExit "no autopilot in 10 s" tel, act, mis = TelemetryAsync drone , ActionAsync drone , Miss

text: summary The ESP32 is an ideal "small companion": UART, Wi-Fi, BLE, a display, a price of pocket change and a boot time of a fraction of a second. The module covers three typical roles: onboard peripheral sensors, indication , a Wi-Fi ↔ FC MAVLink bridge, and a radio companion. The last one is shown on a project for the RadioMaster TX16S: an ESP32-S3 with a screen that shows telemetry in flight and brings up an access point on the ground for configuration from a phone. The pitfalls covered: the EdgeTX Lua widget lifecycle, UART levels, the power budget and a verifiable radio shutdown. theory Three roles for an ESP32 1. Onboard peripheral. Polling I2C sensors, addressable LEDs, servos, relays. The link to the FC is a UART carrying MAVLink or a simple text protocol. 2. MAVLink bridge. The ESP32 receives MAVLink from the FC over UART and serves it over Wi-Fi UDP to a phone or laptop. Many off-the-shelf Wi-Fi telemetry modules work this way; your own version is a few dozen lines. 3. Radio companion. The ESP32 is connected to the AUX port of an EdgeTX radio; a Lua script on the radio sends it the state mode, arm, telemetry , and the ESP32 shows it on its own display and provides a configuration interface. UART: levels and wiring The ESP32 runs at 3.3 V. Flight controllers and EdgeTX radios also use 3.3 V on their UARTs, but check with a multimeter before you connect them. TX goes to RX and RX to TX, and a common GND is mandatory. The baud rate to the radio is whatever is set in the port settings, usually 115200. EdgeTX: the AUX port and Lua In the radio's Hardware settings, the AUX1/AUX2 ports have a "Lua" mode: scripts then get access to serialWrite str , serialRead num and setSerialBaudrate baudrate . Without an argument, serialRead reads up to and including the first newline, so a line-based protocol "one line, one message" maps onto it naturally. Pitfall: the widget lifecycle An EdgeTX widget has two functions: refresh is called while the widget is visible on screen, background while it is hidden. If you put the heartbeat only in refresh , the companion loses the link as soon as the pilot switches screens. The fix: a shared tick function that both of them call. Safe by default A design decision of the project: an undefined state = FLIGHT mode with Wi-Fi off. The access point comes up only after the ESP32 has received an explicit "disarmed" from the radio. Every settings write goes in two steps: STAGE prepare → APPLY apply with an automatic backup , and the in-flight write protection is duplicated on both sides, in the Lua script and in the ESP32 firmware. Turning the radio off must be verifiable: WiFi.mode WIFI_OFF plus esp_wifi_stop , not the assumption "we never turned it on". Power An ESP32-S3 with Wi-Fi active draws peaks of hundreds of milliamps. From the radio battery or a BEC that is noticeable; in FLIGHT mode with the radio off it is several times less. You budget power per mode, not by the average. A minimal MAVLink bridge on an ESP32 the code idea UART2 Serial2.begin 921600, SERIAL_8N1, RX_PIN, TX_PIN ↔ WiFi UDP: everything that arrives from the FC goes out over UDP to the address of the last client or broadcast 14550 ; everything that arrives over UDP goes to the UART. 1 KB buffers, no MAVLink parsing the bridge is transparent ; a task on the second FreeRTOS core the "Embedded" module : core 0 runs the Wi-Fi stack, core 1 the UART copying at a priority above loop . The latency of such a bridge is a few ms; packets get lost when Wi-Fi is congested 2.4 GHz shares the air with ELRS 2.4, so on board a Wi-Fi bridge belongs to ground configuration only and is switched off in flight . An onboard sensor over MAVLink The ESP32 as a system component: it sends HEARTBEAT with its own component_id: MAV_COMP_ID_PERIPHERAL 158 or one from the USER1–USER75 range 25–99 , data as NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT visible in the GCS and, in ArduPilot, in the NVAL log; NAMED_VALUE_INT is shown by the GCS but ArduPilot does not log it , or DISTANCE_SENSOR 132 for your own rangefinder, which ArduPilot accepts as RNGFND1_TYPE = 10 MAVLink and uses in the EKF and for landing. Library: the mavlink C headers from the generator common.xml ; header-only, so only the messages you call end up in flash: a few KB for HEARTBEAT, a couple of data messages and the parser , or a minimal hand-written frame builder with CRC the "MAVLink protocols" module . Worked example: the radio companion the TX16S project Line protocol: radio → ESP32 S,<mode ,<armed ,<vbat ,<rssi \n every 500 ms; ESP32 → radio A,<cmd ,<arg \n . ESP32 states: FLIGHT radio off; the default, and also on a line timeout 2 s → GROUND the radio has sent armed=0 for ≥ 3 s in a row: Wi-Fi AP, web settings → FLIGHT on any armed=1 . Settings: STAGE JSON in RAM → APPLY an NVS write keeping a copy of the previous version , only in GROUND; the Lua script on the radio blocks APPLY if telemetry shows the vehicle armed. Testing: a line emulator on a PC over a USB-UART, scenarios for transitions and timeouts, then the real radio without a vehicle. {{diagram:esp32-tx-companion-states Radio companion states: by default and after more than 2 s of silence, FLIGHT with the radio off; GROUND and the settings only after 3 s of armed=0 in a row.}} {{diagram:esp32-roles The three ESP32 roles in the course: a UART ↔ Wi-Fi/BLE bridge, a MAVLink component of its own, and a radio companion on the AUX port.}} The ESP32 as a flight controller: what exists and what to expect Whether an ESP32 can replace a flight controller is not decided by the board's price but by whether your chip is in the target list of the firmware version you actually fly . summary: An STM32 flight controller polls the gyro 8000 times a second, computes the PID loop, sends DShot to four ESCs, receives CRSF, writes a log, and draws the OSD, all on a single core. That is only possible because hardware does the work without the CPU (DMA, timers) and events arrive as interrupts. Th
headings: What the flight controller's CPU is busy with Interrupts Timers DMA RTOS: tasks, priorities, queues Jitter and blocking Watchdog Where it fits in the system Step 1. Two tasks and a queue (ESP32, ESP-IDF or Arduino-FreeRTOS) Step 2. Jitter Step 3. Break it and fix it Step 4. Read the firmware
text: summary An STM32 flight controller polls the gyro 8000 times a second, computes the PID loop, sends DShot to four ESCs, receives CRSF, writes a log, and draws the OSD, all on a single core. That is only possible because hardware does the work without the CPU DMA, timers and events arrive as interrupts. This module explains these mechanisms at the level you need to read firmware and build your own devices: interrupts and priorities, timers with capture and generation, DMA, the Betaflight scheduler, FreeRTOS on the ESP32 and NuttX in PX4, jitter, and why a delay in the main loop is a disaster. The lab on an ESP32: two FreeRTOS tasks, a queue, a hardware timer, a jitter measurement, and a blocking call, shown and then fixed. theory What the flight controller's CPU is busy with At 8 kHz the budget is 125 µs per loop. Reading 14 bytes from the gyro over SPI at 8+ MHz takes ~15 µs if you wait in the loop; with DMA it takes 0 µs of CPU time. The PID on three axes on an F4 168 MHz takes ~10–20 µs, the filters about as much, DShot goes through timer+DMA 0 µs , CRSF through a UART with an interrupt/DMA. What is left goes to lower tasks src/main/fc/tasks.c : TASK_RX runs on events, when a frame arrives, with a fallback period of 33 Hz, TASK_SERIAL at 100 Hz, TASK_BATTERY_CURRENT at 50 Hz, TASK_OSD at osd_framerate_hz , TASK_GPS at 100 Hz 500 Hz while the receive buffer has bytes waiting , and blackbox on a divider of the PID loop. Betaflight uses a cooperative scheduler without an RTOS scheduler.c : each task has a desired period, a priority, and an execution time estimate; the critical tasks gyro/PID preempt nothing; the scheduler simply does not start a lower task if its estimated execution time anticipatedExecutionTime does not fit before the next gyro cycle; the rest wait for a "gap". Interrupts An interrupt is a hardware signal that suspends the running code and calls a handler ISR . Sources: a UART byte is ready, a DMA transfer completed, a timer fired, an edge on a pin EXTI: that is how the gyro says "data ready", Betaflight gyro_sync on EXTI . ISR rules: keep it short microseconds , no blocking calls and no printf , no memory allocation; hand heavy work to a task through a flag/queue. Priorities the NVIC on Cortex-M : a higher-priority interrupt preempts a lower-priority ISR; the gyro/DShot are higher, UART logging is lower. On an ESP32: ESP_INTR_FLAG_LEVEL1..3 , the ISR in IRAM IRAM_ATTR , work on the other core through a queue. Timers A counter clocked from a bus that can: generate an interrupt every period the scheduler, periodic tasks , produce PWM compare , capture an input edge input capture: measuring the pulse width from a PWM receiver , and trigger DMA on an event DShot: the timer + DMA write a sequence of durations into the compare register, so one 16-bit DShot frame goes out with no CPU involvement . The resolution is one timer clock: at 84 MHz, 12 ns. DMA A direct memory access controller copies data between peripherals and memory on events, without the CPU: UART reception into a ring buffer, reading an SPI gyro, DShot output, writing to the SD card. Limitations: the number of channels/streams and how they are tied to peripherals on the STM32F4, DMA stream conflicts are the real reason some boards cannot run DShot on every motor and, say, an LED strip at the same time; Betaflight target files describe exactly this , and cache coherence on the F7/H7 buffers in non-cacheable memory, or SCB_Clean/InvalidateDCache . RTOS: tasks, priorities, queues FreeRTOS ESP32; PX4 runs on NuttX, a different RTOS with the same concepts of tasks, priorities, and queues : tasks with priorities and their own stacks; a preemptive scheduler, so a higher-priority task always gets the core when it is ready; equal-priority tasks share it by time slices the tick defaults to 100 Hz in ESP-IDF, CONFIG_FREERTOS_HZ ; 1000 Hz in Arduino-ESP32 . Primitives: the queue ISR → task, task → task; copies the data, thread-safe , the semaphore/notification an "event" signal , the mutex protecting a shared resource, an I2C bus , and the timer a software timer, running in the daemon task's context; not for precise periods . For a precise period: vTaskDelayUntil a fixed period from the last wake-up, not from the end of the work or a hardware timer + a notification. Jitter and blocking Jitter is the spread of the actual period. Causes: an ISR doing long work, a higher-priority task, cache misses, delay /waiting in a loop busy-wait , printf logging from a critical task, flash operations on an ESP32 a flash write stalls code executing from flash on the other core unless it is in IRAM . For a control loop, jitter should stay < 5–10% of the period; PX4 and Betaflight measure and log it DEBUG_CYCLETIME , PX4 perf . Why blocking in the main loop is a disaster : the control task waits 50 ms on a UART → 400 missed loops at 8 kHz → the gyro data is stale, the D-term jumps, the motors "twitch"; in the worst case the watchdog reboots the controller in flight. Hence the rule: the control loop never waits for anything; it only reads data that is already there. {{diagram:emb-blocking-timeline 50 ms of waiting on a UART is 400 loops not run at 8 kHz; a correct loop never waits, and an interrupt or DMA collects the bytes into a ring buffer.}} Watchdog A hardware timer that resets the MCU if it is not "fed". Betaflight/ArduPilot/PX4 use it: a hang means a reboot better than motors stuck at their last value forever ; ArduPilot controls it with BRD_OPTIONS bit 0 on by default on ChibiOS boards and logs the details in a WDOG message. On an ESP32 there is the task watchdog on the idle tasks: a task without vTaskDelay starves idle → the TWDT fires. {{diagram:fc-loop-125us One 8 kHz loop: gyro read by DMA, filters, PID and mixer, a DShot frame by DMA; a UART interrupt squeezes in, and the rest of the loop goes to slow tasks orders of magnitude, not an exact profile .}} Where it fits in the system - Takes in: the gyro's "data ready" signal and the

text: summary The "Connecting Peripherals" module taught you to connect ready-made parts; this one teaches you to build your own: what bits look like on the wire, why there is a start bit and an ACK, where framing errors and NACKs come from, how timing is computed and bus length is limited, and how to write a sensor driver from scratch an I2C barometer/IMU on an ESP32: registers, block reads, error handling, timeouts . It ends with DroneCAN: CAN 2.0 frames, arbitration, node IDs, why large vehicles need it, and what a DroneCAN packet looks like in an analyzer. theory UART Asynchronous: there is no clock line; both sides know the baud rate. A frame: a start bit 0 , 5–9 data bits LSB first , an optional parity bit, 1–2 stop bits 1 . 8N1 at 115200 → 10 bits per byte → 11 520 bytes/s. The receiver samples in the middle of each bit usually with ×16 oversampling ; a baud rate error up to ~3–5% is tolerated, beyond that you get a framing error . Errors: framing the stop bit is not 1: wrong baud rate/inversion , overrun a byte was not collected in time: you need DMA/interrupts , noise. Inversion SBUS : the levels are flipped, idle = 0. Levels are 3.3 V TTL; RS-232/RS-485 use other levels/a differential pair long lines . The driver: a receive ring buffer fed by an interrupt/DMA, a protocol frame parser CRSF: address length type payload CRC8 0xD5 ; MAVLink: magic 0xFD, length, seq, sysid/compid, msgid, CRC16 with CRC_EXTRA , and an inter-byte timeout for resynchronization. I2C Synchronous, two open-drain lines with pull-ups: SCL and SDA. The master generates the clock; a transaction: START SDA↓ while SCL=1 → a 7-bit address + the R/W bit → an ACK from the target SDA↓ on the 9th clock → data bytes with ACK/NACK → STOP. Reading a register: START, address+W, the register number, a repeated START , address+R, the data, NACK on the last byte, STOP. Speeds: 100/400 kHz Fast-mode , 1 MHz Fast-mode Plus . Limits: bus capacitance ≤ 400 pF up to Fast-mode; 550 pF in Fast-mode Plus → wires up to ~30–50 cm, pull-ups of 2.2–4.7 kΩ lower values give sharper edges and more current . Errors: NACK on the address no device/wrong address/no power , NACK on data, a stuck bus the target holds SDA=0 after a master glitch; fixed by clocking SCL 9 times by hand, "bus recovery" , clock stretching the target holds SCL low, and the master must be able to wait; some MCUs/sensors have trouble with this . {{diagram:i2c-transaction Reading a register over I2C: the address with the write bit, the register address, a repeated start, the address with the read bit, the data.}} SPI Synchronous, full duplex: SCLK, MOSI, MISO, CS one line per device . No addresses and no ACK: the master pulls CS low and clocks, and every clock shifts one bit in each direction. The CPOL/CPHA modes 0–3 set the clock polarity/phase and must match the datasheet ICM42688: mode 0 or 3 . Speeds up to tens of MHz a gyro at 8–24 MHz, flash at 50+ . Reading a register: an address byte with the R bit often the top bit = 1 , then N dummy bytes on MOSI while the data comes back on MISO. A burst read of 14 IMU bytes in one transaction is what every firmware does. There are no "protocol" errors: integrity can only be checked by meaning the WHO_AM_I register, values within range . Keep traces short: SPI is rarely routed off the board. What a 14-byte IMU block costs. SPI: an address byte + 14 bytes at 8 clocks each = 120 clocks: 15 µs at 8 MHz, 5 µs at 24 MHz. I2C: address+W, register, address+R, and 14 bytes at 9 clocks each 8 bits + ACK , plus START, repeated START, and STOP ≈ 156 clocks: 390 µs at 400 kHz, 156 µs at 1 MHz, 1.56 ms at 100 kHz. UART 8N1: 10 bits per byte: 1.2 ms at 115200, 152 µs at 921600. The whole 8 kHz loop is 125 µs emb-basics , which is why an 8 kHz gyro is connected only over SPI, while I2C is left to the barometer and the compass with their tens of hertz. {{diagram:chart-bus-imu-read-time A 14-byte IMU block: SPI fits in 5–15 µs, while I2C even at 1 MHz 156 µs and a UART at 921600 152 µs take longer than the whole 8 kHz loop.}} CAN and DroneCAN CAN 2.0: a differential pair, CAN_H/CAN_L, 120 Ω terminators at both ends, up to 1 Mbit/s up to 40 m at 1 Mbit/s; longer runs need lower rates . A frame: an 11-bit or 29-bit extended identifier, the DLC, up to 8 data bytes, CRC15, and an ACK from any receiver. Arbitration : everyone transmits at once, a dominant 0 beats a recessive 1, and the lower ID wins with no time lost; the priority is built into the ID. The CAN controller in the MCU receives/sends frames in hardware and filters by ID; errors are counted error passive once an error counter reaches 128, bus-off once the transmit error counter reaches 256: the node disconnects itself . DroneCAN formerly UAVCAN v0 : on top of CAN, a 29-bit ID with the priority, the message type, and the source node ID 1–127 , multi-frame messages with a transfer CRC and a toggle bit, dynamic node ID allocation DNA , and standard types: uavcan.equipment.gnss.Fix2 , ahrs.MagneticFieldStrength2 , esc.RawCommand/Status , power.BatteryInfo , range_sensor.Measurement . Why large vehicles use it: one twisted pair for every device, the noise immunity of a differential pair and the CRC, telemetry from every ESC, hot-swappable nodes, long runs a 2 m wing , and no more "one UART, one device". The tool: DroneCAN GUI Tool with an SLCAN adapter, or the flight controller as a bridge with CAN_SLCAN_CPORT shows the nodes, node parameters, and messages. A driver: what it must have 1. Bus initialization and a device check WHO_AM_I/chip id . 2. Configuration registers : range, rate, filters. 3. Block reads with a timeout; return an error, never hang. 4. Conversion of raw units to physical ones LSB → °/s, Pa . 5. Error handling: counters, reinitialization after N errors in a row, bus recovery for I2C. 6. Thread safety: a mutex on the bus if there are several devices. Where it fits in the system - Takes in: levels, pull-ups, and bus wiring el-peripherals ; interrupts and DMA for lossless recept

text: summary A Raspberry Pi on board is the classic first companion: Linux, Python, a camera, Wi-Fi. This module takes you from the wire to a working service: connecting to an ArduPilot telemetry port, setting up the UART on the Pi, checking with MAVProxy, routing MAVLink to several consumers at once, the power budget and throttling checks, protecting the SD card from power loss, and your own script as a system service with a watchdog. theory Wiring An FC telemetry port TELEM2 = SERIAL2 , for example ↔ the Pi UART: TX → RX, RX → TX, common GND. 3.3 V levels on both sides. On the FC: - SERIAL2_PROTOCOL = 2 : MAVLink 2; - SERIAL2_BAUD = 921 : 921600 baud; normal for short wires and heavy telemetry traffic; for long wires use 57 57600 . Power the Pi from a dedicated 5 V BEC with current headroom a Pi 4/5 under load draws more than an amp , not from the FC telemetry port. The UART on a Raspberry Pi By default the UART is taken by the Linux console. In raspi-config → Interface Options → Serial Port: login shell over serial, no ; serial port hardware, yes . After a reboot the port is available as /dev/serial0 , on a Pi 3/4. On a Pi 5 , /dev/serial0 points to the debug connector /dev/ttyAMA10 , while the UART on GPIO 14/15 is enabled with the line dtoverlay=uart0-pi5 as the Raspberry Pi documentation has it; dtparam=uart0=on is also used in /boot/firmware/config.txt and is called /dev/ttyAMA0 ; substitute it in the examples below. On a Pi 3/4 the primary UART is given to Bluetooth by default, which leaves the mini UART on the GPIO, and its baud rate "drifts" with the core clock: for a stable 921600, put enable_uart=1 and dtoverlay=disable-bt in config.txt . Routing One UART, several consumers: a GCS over Wi-Fi, your script, tlog recording. The answer is a MAVLink router: mavlink-router or mavp2p reads the port and hands the stream out over UDP/TCP to everyone connected. Your scripts then connect to a local UDP port instead of /dev/serial0 directly, and they do not get in each other's way. {{diagram:mavlink-routing mavlink-router hands one FC UART stream to several consumers: the GCS, your scripts, and a logger.}} Power: a budget, not "some BEC" A Raspberry Pi 5 is specified for 5.1 V / 5 A 27 W : it draws about 3 W idle and 7–8 W under full CPU load, plus the camera, a USB modem, or a Wi-Fi adapter on top. An example budget: Consumer Power Current at 5 V --- --- --- Pi 5 under load 8 W 1.6 A CSI camera 1.5 W 0.3 A USB Wi-Fi / LTE modem 2.5 W 0.5 A Total 12 W 2.4 A Pick a BEC rated at one and a half to two times the load at the very least 5 A , and keep the wire short and thick: 30 cm of a 22 AWG pair ≈ 53 mΩ/m per conductor, ≈ 32 mΩ out and back loses ≈ 0.08 V at 2.4 A. Peak surges the camera starting, the modem transmitting pull the voltage down further than the average, which is why the Pi connector should see no less than ~4.9 V under load. Overheating and undervoltage show up in numbers vcgencmd get_throttled returns a bit mask: bit 0 is undervoltage right now, 1 frequency capped, 2 throttled, 3 soft temperature limit; bits 16–19 are the same flags as "has occurred since boot". 0x0 means all is well, 0x50000 means there was undervoltage and throttling; 0x50005 means it is happening right now. Temperature is vcgencmd measure_temp ; without a heatsink and airflow a Pi 5 under load starts throttling within minutes, and even more so inside a drone body with no airflow. A vision algorithm that "suddenly got slower in flight" almost always comes down to this. {{diagram:rpi-throttled-bits The get_throttled mask bit by bit: the high nibble repeats the low one as "has occurred since boot", so 0x50000 means it happened, and 0x50005 means it is happening now.}} Losing power without breaking the SD card On a drone, power goes away without a shutdown : after a crash, on a battery swap. A write at the moment of power loss corrupts the SD card's file system. Two approaches that work: - Overlay File System raspi-config → Performance Options → Overlay File System : the root is read-only, changes live in RAM and vanish after a reboot. The system is indestructible, but logs and recordings have to go to a separate partition or a USB drive. - Writing properly : logs on a separate partition or a USB SSD, f.flush + os.fsync for anything important, and the systemd journal in RAM Storage=volatile in /etc/systemd/journald.conf so it does not wear out the card. A service instead of "started it by hand", with a watchdog A script started from a terminal over SSH dies with the session. On board, everything must start by itself: a systemd unit with Restart=always , logs in journalctl . If the script can hang rather than crash a socket, a camera, an infinite loop , you also need a watchdog: Type=notify and WatchdogSec= , and systemd restarts the service when it stops reporting "I'm alive". Without those reports from the script, WatchdogSec simply kills it every N seconds; almost everyone falls into this trap. A working setup is in the practice section, step 3. Time and logs A Pi without an RTC and without a network boots with a stale clock the time saved at the last shutdown by fake-hwclock, or 1970 on a bare system : there is no accurate time after boot, and absolute timestamps before synchronization are meaningless. A practical approach: at startup the script records a pair SYSTEM_TIME.time_unix_usec from MAVLink, the flight controller's GPS time, and its own time.monotonic and from then on uses monotonic timestamps a TimeUS -like counter plus the recorded synchronization moment ; during analysis the companion logs are matched to the flight controller's DataFlash log using that pair. The Pi 5 has an RTC battery connector; with a battery, the time survives a power-off without a network. Where it fits in the system - Takes in: MAVLink from the FC telemetry port at 921600 comp-mavlink ; 5 V from a dedicated BEC with current headroom el-power-design ; GPS time through SYSTEM_TIME . - Puts out: one FC stream to several clients th

title: Jetson Nano as a companion: what it can do, what it can't, and how to get the most out of it
summary: A "Jetson Nano" in a shop is two different boards: the original 2019 Nano (Maxwell, 4 GB, JetPack 4, end of life) and the Jetson Orin Nano (Ampere, 8 GB, JetPack 6, Super mode). This module covers both honestly: what each one can and cannot compute, how much it really draws and why 5 V is the main t
headings: Two boards under one name Power modes: nvpmodel and jetson_clocks Power: what it really draws, and the 5 V traps Heat and throttling Carrier boards and mass Cameras and video The inference stack and benchmarks What the Nano can run at the same time UART, MAVLink, ROS 2 Storage, headless, autostart, shutdown What to choose Where it fits Step 1. A tegrastats sample Step 2. The parser Step 3. The bridge to MAVLink, and SITL Step 4. A unit with a watchdog Moving to real hardware
text: summary A "Jetson Nano" in a shop is two different boards: the original 2019 Nano Maxwell, 4 GB, JetPack 4, end of life and the Jetson Orin Nano Ampere, 8 GB, JetPack 6, Super mode . This module covers both honestly: what each one can and cannot compute, how much it really draws and why 5 V is the main trap, how it heats up and throttles, which cameras and video pipeline to use, how the inference stack differs, how to connect the UART to the flight controller and run everything as a service. The course has no Jetson, so all hardware figures come from NVIDIA documentation and published benchmarks with links, not from our own measurements. The lab needs no hardware: a parser for a tegrastats line and a "companion health → MAVLink" bridge that, in SITL, writes the temperature and load into the flight controller's log as NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT . Then, the order of steps for moving to a real board. theory Two boards under one name The boundary of responsibility is the same as in the "Companion: why, and where the boundary is" module: the flight controller flies and returns by itself, the Jetson only watches and advises. Jetson Nano 2019 Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB Super --- --- --- CPU 4 × Cortex-A57, 1.43 GHz 6 × Cortex-A78AE, 1.7 GHz GPU Maxwell, 128 cores, 472 GFLOPS, no Tensor Cores Ampere, 1024 cores, 32 Tensor Cores, 67 TOPS INT8, sparse Memory 4 GB LPDDR4, shared by CPU and GPU 8 GB LPDDR5, shared Power modes 10 W MAXN , 5 W 15 W, 25 W, MAXN_SUPER without the Super configuration: 15 and 7 W Hardware encoder yes: 4Kp30 or 4 × 1080p30, H.264/H.265 no NVENC : 1080p30 in software, ≈ 2 CPU cores System JetPack 4.6.6, L4T 32.7.6, Ubuntu 18.04, kernel 4.9 JetPack 6.2, L4T 36.4.3, Ubuntu 22.04 the course's version; JetPack 7.2.x, Jetson Linux 39.2, Ubuntu 24.04 also supports Orin since 2026 CUDA / TensorRT 10.2 / 8.2.1 12.6 / 10.3 JetPack 7.2.1: 13.2 / 10.16 Devkit power 5 V: micro-USB 2 A or barrel jack 4 A barrel jack 9–20 V 19 V supply in the box Module 69.6 × 45 mm, SO-DIMM 260 the same form factor Status module in production until January 2027; devkit discontinued module until January 2032 What "end of life" means in practice. JetPack 4.6.6 November 22, 2024 is the last in the series: there will be no more critical updates, and JetPack 5/6 do not exist for the Nano. Ubuntu 18.04 means Python 3.6, while current ultralytics needs a newer Python, so on the Nano it is run in the ready-made ultralytics/ultralytics:latest-jetson-jetpack4 container. For TensorRT 8.x, Q-engineering exports ONNX with opset=11 ; DeepStream is 6.0.1 and no newer. Bottom line: the Nano is fine if it is already sitting in a drawer and the task is one small detector; there is no reason to buy one for a new project. Orin on PX4 has its own module, "PX4 + Jetson Orin". Power modes: nvpmodel and jetson_clocks nvpmodel sets the ceiling: how many cores are online and the maximum CPU/GPU frequencies. sudo nvpmodel -q shows the current mode, sudo nvpmodel -m <ID switches it. Board Mode ID CPU cores CPU max, MHz GPU max, MHz --- --- --- --- --- --- Nano MAXN 10 W 0 4 1479 921.6 Nano 5 W 1 2 918 640 Orin Nano 8 GB Super 15 W 0 6 1497.6 612 Orin Nano 8 GB Super 25 W default 1 6 1344 918 Orin Nano 8 GB Super MAXN_SUPER 2 6 1728 1020 The Nano's "10 W" is the budget for the CPU and GPU rails only, not for the whole board. jetson_clocks pins the CPU, GPU and memory clocks to the maximum of the current mode: latency is more stable, consumption higher; since release 32.4 it no longer turns the fan on by itself jetson_clocks --fan . On Orin, a mode change that alters the GPU TPC mask requires a reboot, and nvpmodel will offer one itself. In 5 W mode the Nano loses two cores and a third of its GPU clock, so the detector, mavlink-router and the encoder end up sharing two cores. Power: what it really draws, and the 5 V traps Real tegrastats lines from the NVIDIA forum Jetson Nano, field POM_5V_IN , the 5 V input, in mW : with a CSI camera running and no load, 2.9 W; under TensorRT, a peak of 7.7 W with an average of 4.5 W. The devkit carrier adds 0.5–1.25 W, and USB peripherals add their own watts. Budget for the BEC: 10 W module + 1.25 W carrier + camera and USB Wi-Fi/LTE ≈ 15 W → 3 A; get a 5 A BEC. The Orin Nano idles at about 4 W an NVIDIA employee's answer on the forum; the thread author's devkit drew 6.1 W in the default 25 W mode , and the ceiling is the selected mode. Nano traps: - The module needs 4.75–5.25 V at its input, and the devkit expects exactly 5 V: "5.3 V" from an adjustable BEC and a sag to 4.6 V are both out of range. - Micro-USB is rated for 2 A. The 5.5 × 2.1 mm barrel jack is rated for 4 A, but works only with jumper J48 fitted; without it the board is powered from micro-USB. - Pins 2 and 4 of the J41 header take 2.5 A each 5 A in total , which is convenient on board, but it is a direct 5 V input. - Voltage drop in the wire: U = U_BEC − I· 2·L·r + R_connector . A meter-long micro-USB cable at 28 AWG 0.213 Ω/m, connector taken as 0.10 Ω : R = 0.53 Ω, so at 1.54 A 7.7 W the board sees 4.19 V, and the 4.75 V threshold is already crossed at 0.48 A. A short 0.3 m at 24 AWG: 4.77 V at 1.54 A and 4.55 V at 3 A. The barrel jack, 0.3 m at 20 AWG connector 0.03 Ω : 4.85 V at 3 A. {{diagram:chart-jetson-brownout With 5.0 V at the BEC, a meter-long micro-USB cable drops the Jetson Nano input below 4.75 V at just 0.5 A; a short 20 AWG pair into the barrel jack holds 4.8 V up to 4 A.}} The Orin Nano devkit accepts 9–20 V: 4S up to 16.8 V is formally within range, while 3S under load sags to 9–10 V and below, so feed it a regulated 12 V. Power either board from a separate BEC with a common ground to the flight controller, as in the "Raspberry Pi + ArduPilot" module. The cost in flight. A 2.0 kg quadcopter hovers at 300 W, the battery is 4S 5 Ah, the usable 80 % = 59.2 Wh → 11.84 min. Add only 10 W: 59.2 / 310 → 11.46 min −3.2 % . Add 200 g as well devkit carrier 77 g + module with heatsink 61 g + BEC, camera, mounting; hover power ∝ m^1.5 →

title: MAVLink routing and transport: radio, 4G, multiple GCSs
summary: As soon as more than one participant is connected to the vehicle (a GCS over a radio, a companion, a second GCS over 4G, a camera), the question is who receives which packets. MAVLink has no "network layer": routing rests on sysid/compid conventions and on tables that every node builds from the pack
headings: Addressing: sysid and compid Forwarding rules (as in ArduPilot) Tools Transports Link metrics and how to measure them Link security Where it fits in the system Step 1. A router with three clients Step 2. RTT and loss under netem Step 3. UDP vs TCP Step 4. A diagram of your system
text: summary As soon as more than one participant is connected to the vehicle a GCS over a radio, a companion, a second GCS over 4G, a camera , the question is who receives which packets. MAVLink has no "network layer": routing rests on sysid/compid conventions and on tables that every node builds from the packets it has seen. The module goes through these rules in the ArduPilot source, the tools mavlink-router, MAVProxy, mavp2p , the transports UART, UDP, TCP, SiK radios, 4G/LTE through NAT and VPN , and the link metrics latency, loss, jitter , measured under artificial impairment with tc netem . Lab: a router with three clients, and heartbeat RTT measured as the network degrades. theory Addressing: sysid and compid - sysid is a vehicle or a station. Vehicles: usually 1…250 the spec allows any ID 1…255; unique within one network! , a GCS usually 255 a second one 254, and so on . - compid is a component within a system: autopilot 1, cameras 100–105, gimbal 154, onboard computer 191–194, peripheral 158, GCS application 190. Your own script on the companion gets its own compid in the same system as the autopilot. - A message either has target_system / target_component fields addressed or does not telemetry, broadcast in nature . A target of 0 means "everyone". Forwarding rules as in ArduPilot The source file libraries/GCS_MAVLink/MAVLink_routing.cpp states the rules explicitly. The autopilot processes a packet itself if it has no target, has target_system 0, or is addressed to it, including to its own sysid with target_component 0 or with no such field, and also to its own sysid with a compid that has not been seen on any port. It forwards the packet to another port if: 1. the message has no target_system, or target_system = 0: to every port where at least one packet has been seen HEARTBEAT is handled separately and goes out to every active port, which is how routes can appear in the first place ; 2. target_system is someone else's, and packets from that sysid have already been seen on that port; 3. target_system is its own: if target_component is set ≠ 0 , to the port where packets from that sysid/compid pair have been seen; if target_component = 0 or the field is missing, to every port where any component of its own sysid has been seen a camera, a script , while also processing it itself. Consequences to know by heart: - A route appears only after the first packet from the target. A silent script on the companion will not receive a single addressed command from the GCS, so have it send its own heartbeat. - A packet is never sent back to the port it came in on. - The routing table is reset on reboot; a GCS must notice a decrease in time_boot_ms in SYSTEM_TIME and relearn the routes. - A port can be excluded from forwarding: in ArduPilot, MAVn_OPTIONS bit 1, "Don't forward mavlink to/from" SERIALn_OPTIONS bit 10 before 4.7; on upgrade the bit is moved over automatically, and one left set in SERIALn_OPTIONS fails a pre-arm check . You need this, for example, for a port with a "chatty" device on it. {{diagram:mav-forward-tree The forwarding rules as a tree: a broadcast packet goes to every port where someone has been seen, an addressed one only to where the target has been seen; a silent component is unreachable.}} {{diagram:mavlink-topology A typical topology: the autopilot and a companion router connect GCSs over radio and 4G with the onboard components.}} Tools - mavlink-router C++, a systemd service : one or more UARTs + UDP/TCP endpoints, routing by the same rules, filtering by msgid, tlog recording. The standard on a Raspberry Pi/Jetson; configuration is covered in the comp-raspberry module. - MAVProxy Python : both a router --out and a console GCS with modules. Handy for debugging, heavier for permanent use on board. - mavp2p Go : a lightweight router with the same purpose, a single binary. - In the autopilot itself: every port with SERIALn_PROTOCOL = 2 MAVLink2 takes part in forwarding. Sometimes you do not need the companion as a router at all; two autopilot ports are enough. Transports Transport Latency Loss Notes --- --- --- --- UART to the companion < 1 ms ~0 921600 baud ≈ 90 KB/s; needs a common GND and 3.3 V levels SiK radio 433/868/915 30–100 ms 0–10 % air rate 64 kbit/s by default, half-duplex TDM; RADIO_STATUS 109 with RSSI/noise/free buffer space txbuf ; ECC halves the throughput ELRS/Crossfire MAVLink 10–50 ms depends on the rate telemetry shares the air with control: a narrow link Wi-Fi 2–20 ms bursts range of hundreds of meters; UDP broadcast is convenient but noisy 4G/LTE 50–300 ms, jitter 0–5 %, dropouts the modem has a private IP behind the carrier's NAT: no incoming connections NAT and 4G. A vehicle behind NAT does not accept incoming connections. text: summary Two questions a UAV engineer must close before series operation: “can the regulator see who is flying” and “can a stranger control my aircraft”. The first is Remote ID: the aircraft in flight broadcasts its identifier, its position and the pilot's position, and in a number of countries this is a mandatory condition for flying. The second is the attack surface: the RC link, MAVLink telemetry, GNSS, the companion computer's network and the firmware itself. The module covers what Remote ID transmits and how, how it is connected to ArduPilot and PX4, how MAVLink 2 signing works and what it does not do, where the companion is exposed, and how firmware is protected against substitution. The lab — enable signing in SITL and prove that unsigned commands are rejected. theory Remote ID: what is transmitted Remote ID Drone ID is an on-board broadcast that an ordinary smartphone near the aircraft can receive. Under the ASTM F3411 standard the basis of the US rules and the European standard ASD-STAN EN 4709-002 the messages contain: - the aircraft identifier serial number and/or the operator registration number; - the aircraft's position, altitude, speed and heading; - the position of the controller/pilot or of the takeoff point — depending on the rules ; - a timestamp and status including emergency . The transport is Bluetooth 4 legacy and 5 long range and Wi-Fi NAN and Beacon . It is a broadcast , with no connection to a server, so it works without internet. Who must comply and when Checked against the regulators' pages on 2026-11-17; the rules change, check the official page before you fly. This is not legal advice. Where Who must comply How to comply Dates --- --- --- --- USA FAA, Part 89 every aircraft that must be registered: any flight under Part 107 and recreational flights with an aircraft heavier than 250 g built-in Remote ID, an external broadcast module, or flying only in designated FRIA zones in force mandatory for most flights since March 2024 USA, exception an aircraft of no more than 0.55 lb 250 g that flies only recreationally is not registered 14 CFR 48.15 — Remote ID is not required — — EU EASA direct Remote ID is part of the requirements for classes C1–C3 and for the specific category; the operator registration number is uploaded to the aircraft's Remote ID system built-in or a module in force United Kingdom CAA UK1, UK2, UK3, UK5, UK6 the built-in Direct Remote ID function: enter your Remote ID and enable it before the flight from 1 January 2026 United Kingdom, second stage UK0 from 100 g with a camera; UK4 models , unless exempt; home-built and legacy aircraft from 100 g with a camera built-in or a module from 1 January 2028 For a home-built FPV aircraft this means: in the US — a broadcast module or a FRIA if the aircraft is registered; in the UK — the deadline is 1 January 2028 if the aircraft is 100 g or more and has a camera; in the EU — by class and operation category. Other countries have their own rules, and they change — check with your aviation regulator before your first flight; the f-regulations module is the starting point and has the table of official pages. Remote ID on ArduPilot and PX4 - A module over MAVLink or DroneCAN takes the position from the autopilot and broadcasts it. Ready-made modules Cube ID, Holybro and others with OpenDroneID support or the open ArduRemoteID — ArduPilot firmware for ESP32-S3/ESP32-C3 boards connected over MAVLink or DroneCAN CAN needs an external transceiver . - A standalone broadcast module — with its own GPS and battery; not connected to the autopilot. - What to choose course guideline : on ArduPilot and PX4 — a module over MAVLink or DroneCAN: the position comes from the autopilot, and a certified ArduPilot build will not let you take off without a working Remote ID. Betaflight and INAV have no OpenDroneID subsystem it is not in the 2025.12.5 and 9.1.0 sources , so there — a standalone broadcast module. The check in both cases — a Remote ID scanner app on a phone sees the aircraft before takeoff. - ArduPilot : the OpenDroneID subsystem — DID_ENABLE , the port DID_MAVPORT or DID_CANDRIVER , DID_OPTIONS . Certified configurations use a special firmware build with tamper protection and pre-takeoff checks: without a working Remote ID the aircraft won't arm. ArduRemoteID can lock its parameters against changes changes only through signed commands . - PX4 : supports OpenDroneID messages and external modules; enabling and checks — per the Remote ID section of the documentation for your version. - MAVLink messages: the OPEN_DRONE_ID_ family OPEN_DRONE_ID_BASIC_ID , _LOCATION , _SYSTEM , _OPERATOR_ID ; the pilot's position is sent to the module by the GCS OPEN_DRONE_ID_SYSTEM . {{diagram:remote-id-data-path The Remote ID module doesn't know the position by itself: the autopilot provides it over MAVLink or DroneCAN, the pilot's position comes from the GCS; on a certified build a non-working module blocks arming.}} Attack surface Channel Threat Protection --- --- --- RC link someone else's transmitter with the same binding, jamming a unique binding phrase in ELRS it is a pair identifier, not encryption , a well-thought-out failsafe MAVLink telemetry foreign commands: mode change, disarm, mission upload MAVLink 2 signing, separate keys per aircraft, MAVLink 1 disabled on radio ports GNSS jamming, spoofing EKF checks, navigation without GNSS, assessment per nav-resilience Companion open Wi-Fi, default password, SSH, UDP telemetry to the whole segment, DDS without protection SSH keys instead of passwords, a firewall, telemetry only to the required address, limited discovery and SROS2 Firmware substitution of the firmware or parameters signed firmware and a secure bootloader, version control of parameters MAVLink 2 signing: how it works - The aircraft and the GCS share a 32-byte secret key . 13 bytes are appended to each packet: link ID 1 byte , timestamp 6 bytes, in units of 10 µs since 1 January 2015 and the signature 6 bytes — the fir

Component tests Step 2. ArduPilot SITL accepts the rangefinder Step 3. A component parameter Step 4. ESP32
text: summary So far the companion has been a client: it read telemetry and sent commands. Here it becomes a participant in the system : a component with its own compid, heartbeat, parameters, and messages that the autopilot uses as sensor data. This is how rangefinders, obstacle sensors, external navigation, gimbals, and payloads connect to ArduPilot and PX4. The module covers a component's duties heartbeat, answering requests, parameters , sensor messages DISTANCE_SENSOR , OBSTACLE_DISTANCE , ODOMETRY / VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE , debug messages NAMED_VALUE_ , DEBUG_VECT , and two implementations: Python on a companion and C on an ESP32. Lab: a virtual rangefinder that ArduPilot SITL accepts as RNGFND1 , then the same component on an ESP32. theory What makes a component "well-behaved" 1. Heartbeat at 1 Hz with its own MAV_TYPE for a sensor, MAV_TYPE_GENERIC or a specific one , MAV_AUTOPILOT_INVALID it is not an autopilot! , the sysid of its system the same vehicle , and a unique compid. Without a heartbeat, routing to the component does not work the mav-routing module . 2. Answers requests addressed to it : a COMMAND_LONG with its compid → a COMMAND_ACK even UNSUPPORTED is better than silence, which leaves the client hanging until its timeout ; MAV_CMD_REQUEST_MESSAGE for a COMPONENT_INFORMATION / AUTOPILOT_VERSION -style description, where possible. 3. Its own parameters , if it needs them, over the parameter protocol: it answers PARAM_REQUEST_LIST / PARAM_REQUEST_READ / PARAM_SET from the GCS addressed to its compid, and stores the values in non-volatile memory. QGC and Mission Planner show them in a separate group for the component. 4. Does not duplicate other components' messages and does not send the autopilot commands that conflict with the operator. 5. Degrades honestly : when it loses measurements, it stops sending the message or flags it as invalid instead of repeating the last value. The autopilot detects the timeout and disables the source. Distance sensor: DISTANCE_SENSOR 132 Fields: time_boot_ms , min_distance / max_distance / current_distance in centimeters , type MAV_DISTANCE_SENSOR_LASER , _ULTRASOUND , _RADAR … , id , orientation MAV_SENSOR_ROTATION_PITCH_270 = down, _NONE = forward… , covariance 255: unknown , and in the extension fields horizontal_fov , vertical_fov , quaternion , signal_quality 0: unknown, 1: invalid signal … 100: perfect . ArduPilot: RNGFND1_TYPE = 10 MAVLink , RNGFND1_ORIENT = 25 down , RNGFND1_MIN / RNGFND1_MAX meters; before 4.7, RNGFND1_MIN_CM / RNGFND1_MAX_CM in centimeters . The autopilot treats values outside min, max as "out of range", not as a measurement. Rate: 10–50 Hz; ArduPilot's MAVLink rangefinder timeout is 500 ms: if packets arrive slower than ~2 Hz or with gaps longer than 0.5 s, the sensor is considered lost. A downward rangefinder is used for height above ground RFND in the log, the EKF POSZ source = rangefinder, landing, terrain following ; sensors in other orientations are used for obstacle avoidance PRX proximity, PRX1_TYPE = 2 MAVLink . {{diagram:mav-rangefinder-timeout The 0.5 s timeout only works for an honest component: a sensor that goes silent is dropped after 0.5 s, one that repeats its last value is never dropped, and a pause longer than 0.5 s causes "flickering".}} Obstacles and external navigation - OBSTACLE_DISTANCE 330 : an array of 72 distances by sector increment degrees per sector, angle_offset , for 2D lidars and stereo cameras → proximity in ArduPilot PRX1_TYPE = 2 , collision prevention in PX4. - VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE 102 , VISION_SPEED_ESTIMATE 103 , ODOMETRY 331 : pose/velocity from VIO or motion capture → the ArduPilot EKF as ExternalNav EK3_SRC1_POSXY = 6 , PX4 as external vision EKF2_EV_CTRL . Time matters here usec timestamps, TIMESYNC , and so do coordinate frames FRD/NED vs FLU/ENU: the math-linalg-rot module . Debug messages To show your own value in the GCS and in the log without a dialect of your own: NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT 251 , a name of up to 10 characters and a float; NAMED_VALUE_INT 252 ; DEBUG_VECT 250 , a name and three floats. Mission Planner shows them in the Quick tab and graphs, ArduPilot writes received NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT messages to the log NVAL , PX4 writes them to the ulog as debug topics. For a permanent integration, use your own dialect the mav-protocol module or TUNNEL 385 . A Python implementation examples/mavlink/virtual_rangefinder.py is a complete component: its own compid MAV_COMP_ID_PERIPHERAL , a heartbeat, reading GLOBAL_POSITION_INT to simulate a measurement, publishing DISTANCE_SENSOR at a set rate, range clamping. The structure polling, sending at a fixed rate, the heartbeat separately is the same for any sensor: replace measurement_cm with reading a real lidar over UART/I2C, and you have a working driver. An ESP32 implementation C On a microcontroller you use a generated C library the header-only c_library_v2 or your own from mavgen : c include <common/mavlink.h static void send_distance uart_port_t uart, uint16_t dist_cm { mavlink_message_t msg; uint8_t buf MAVLINK_MAX_PACKET_LEN ; mavlink_msg_distance_sensor_pack 1, MAV_COMP_ID_PERIPHERAL, &msg, esp_timer_get_time / 1000, 20, 4000, dist_cm, MAV_DISTANCE_SENSOR_LASER, 0, MAV_SENSOR_ROTATION_PITCH_270, 255, 0, 0, NULL, 0 ; / fovs, quaternion, signal_quality: extensions / uint16_t len = mavlink_msg_to_send_buffer buf, &msg ; uart_write_bytes uart, const char buf, len ; } Receiving is byte by byte with mavlink_parse_char chan, byte, &msg, &status in the task that reads the UART. A separate FreeRTOS task sends the heartbeat once a second; sending from several tasks needs a mutex, or frames get interleaved on the UART. The ESP-IDF and UART details are in the comp-esp32 module. text: summary Inspection, mapping, tracking: in every project of the course the camera has to look where the task needs it, not wherever the vehicle happens to be pointing. That is the gimbal's job, and today the usual way to talk to it is MAVLink Gimbal Protocol v2. This module covers who in the system is the "manager" and who is the "device", how to connect a gimbal to ArduPilot MNT1_ and PX4 MNT_ , how to control it from the transmitter, from a mission and from companion code, how to tie the camera CAM1_ to distance-based capture, and how not to lose the vehicle together with a dropped payload, from the center of gravity to testing the release mechanism. theory Why a gimbal, and which one - Stabilization. A brushless gimbal holds the camera using its own IMU, damping vibration and body tilt; in wind the vehicle banks 10–20°, the picture does not. - Pointing. The camera looks at a point ROI regardless of the vehicle heading: orbiting a tower, tracking a target, nadir for mapping. - Types. A servo gimbal two servos, cheap, pointing with no or rough stabilization , a brushless gimbal with its own controller SimpleBGC/STorM32 and similar , a "smart" gimbal with a camera Siyi, ViewPro, Gremsy and others with its own protocol or MAVLink. Gimbal Protocol v2: manager and device The old protocol MOUNT_CONTROL , DO_MOUNT_CONTROL sent commands straight to the gimbal: the transmitter, the GCS and the companion fought over who sent the last command. In v2 the roles are separated: - Gimbal device : the gimbal itself: motors, IMU, stabilization. It accepts GIMBAL_DEVICE_SET_ATTITUDE and reports its orientation in GIMBAL_DEVICE_ATTITUDE_STATUS quaternion, flags, errors . - Gimbal manager : usually the autopilot. It knows the vehicle attitude, turns "look at a point" into angles, decides who is in control right now primary/secondary control and sends commands to the device. - Clients : the GCS, the companion, a mission, the transmitter send commands to the manager: MAV_CMD_DO_GIMBAL_MANAGER_PITCHYAW or a stream of GIMBAL_MANAGER_SET_PITCHYAW ArduPilot; as a stream PX4 accepts only GIMBAL_MANAGER_SET_ATTITUDE , and taking control is done with MAV_CMD_DO_GIMBAL_MANAGER_CONFIGURE . The angle flags matter: yaw can be set "relative to the vehicle" follow or "relative to north" lock . Orbiting an object needs lock or an ROI, otherwise the camera turns along with the vehicle. text: summary GUIDED mode is the door through which a companion computer controls the vehicle: "fly to this point", "hold this velocity", "look over there". This module shows how to set position and velocity targets from Python on a companion, how ArduPilot protects itself from a companion that has gone silent or gone haywire, and how to build a control loop that you can debug safely in SITL. Before that comes the wire: which FC port to give the companion, which SERIALn_ parameters to set, which parameters were renamed in 4.7.2 SRn_ → MAVn_ , SYSID_THISMAV → MAV_SYSID , why ArduCopter 4.7 sends a companion no telemetry by default, and which participant on the network counts as the ground station for the failsafe. The lab was run on ArduCopter 4.7.2 SITL through a MAVProxy router: a parameter audit, a GUIDED arm and takeoff with COMMAND_ACK checks, a stream of velocity targets, a measurement of the stop after the companion goes silent the drop starts after 3.2–3.3 s, and the stop at < 0.2 m/s comes after 4.3 s , and the pilot taking over control. The result is a framework for the track's capstone: your own logic on board. theory The companion ↔ FC link: port, protocol, baud rate A companion is connected to a free telemetry UART of the flight controller usually TELEM2 = SERIAL2 ; the FC's USB is left for configuration . On the FC side there are three port settings: the protocol SERIALn_PROTOCOL = 2 MAVLink2; 1 is MAVLink1, 45 is DDS XRCE for ROS 2 , the baud rate SERIALn_BAUD , and hardware flow control BRD_SERn_RTSCTS . The baud rate is set as a code, not as a baud number: 57 = 57600, 115 = 115200, 460 = 460800, 921 = 921600, 1500 = 1.5 Mbaud AP_SerialManager.cpp , the @Values of SERIAL1_BAUD . The 4.7.2 defaults for SERIAL1 and SERIAL2 are MAVLink2 at 57 AP_SerialManager.cpp:47–64 , confirmed by the parameter audit in SITL . For a companion 57600 is too slow, and the arithmetic shows it. An 8N1 UART sends 10 bits per byte, so 921600 baud is 92 160 bytes/s and 57600 baud is 5 760 bytes/s. A MAVLink2 frame adds 12 bytes to the payload a 10-byte header and a 2-byte CRC; a signature adds another 13 . LOCAL_POSITION_NED and ATTITUDE each carry 28 bytes of payload, so up to 40 bytes each on the wire. A companion that needs position and attitude at 50 Hz each for a tracking loop takes 2 × 50 × 40 = 4000 bytes/s: that is 69% of a 57600 link and 4.3% of a 921600 link. At 57600 the GCS stream through the router, parameters, and missions come on top of that, the link overflows, messages start getting lost, and the failure looks like "random timeouts" in the code. A course guideline: 921 for a companion on a short wire up to ~30 cm , link load no higher than 50%, and 1500 only with BRD_SERn_RTSCTS = 1 and a check for losses. Flow control: BRD_SER1_RTSCTS is 0 Disabled, 1 Enabled, 2 Auto, and 3 uses the RTS pin as an RS-485 driver enable; BRD_SER1_RTSCTS … BRD_SER3_RTSCTS default to 2, Auto AP_BoardConfig.cpp ; the parameter does not exist if the port has no RTS/CTS lines on that board HAL_HAVE_RTSCTS_SERIALn . If the RTS/CTS lines are not wired to the companion, set 0 explicitly so you do not depend on auto-detection. UART levels are 3.3 V on the FC and on a Raspberry Pi; the ground is shared, and the wiring is FC TX → companion RX and the other way around. In 4.7 two bits of SERIALn_OPTIONS moved to MAVn_OPTIONS : "don't forward mavlink to/from this port" it was bit 10, now bit 1 and "ignore stream rate requests" it was bit 12, now bit 2 ; bit 0 of MAVn_OPTIONS accepts unsigned MAVLink2 messages GCS_MAVLink_Parameters.cpp , the @Bitmask of _OPTIONS . The conversion on update is done once the hidden MAVn_OPTIONSCNV . {{lesson:comp-raspberry The Raspberry Pi UART, the mavlink-router configuration, the power budget, and a systemd watchdog: the companion side of the same wire.}} MAVn channels and telemetry streams in 4.7 In 4.7 the MAVLink channel parameters are collected in the MAV group: MAV1_ , MAV2_ …, one block per channel. The channel number is not the SERIALn number: channel 1 is the console SERIAL0 , USB , and after that channels are handed to the ports with a MAVLink protocol in order of their numbers a conclusion from the code: the console in GCS::setup_console , GCS_Common.cpp:2808–2819 ; the rest in GCS::setup_uarts , GCS_Common.cpp:2844–2853 . If MAVLink is on SERIAL0 , SERIAL1 , and SERIAL2 , a companion on SERIAL2 is MAV3_ ; if you switch SERIAL1 to GPS, the same wire becomes MAV2_ . Each block holds the rates of the stream groups _RAW_SENS , _EXT_STAT , _RC_CHAN , _RAW_CTRL , _POSITION , _EXTRA1 , _EXTRA2 , _EXTRA3 , _PARAMS , _ADSB before 4.7, SR0_ … SR6_ , numbered from zero . On Copter every default is 0 the APM_BUILD_COPTER_OR_HELI block in GCS_MAVLink_Parameters.cpp , on Plane they are mostly 1 Hz PARAMS 10, ADSB 5 , and on Sub 2…10 Hz for the main groups RAW_CTRL, PARAMS, ADSB are 0 . The SITL 4.7.2 audit confirms it: MAV1_EXT_STAT = 0 , MAV2_POSITION = 0 , while SR0_EXT_STAT and SYSID_THISMAV answer "no such parameter". The practical conclusion: a companion that silently listens to an ArduCopter 4.7 port gets neither position nor mode beyond HEARTBEAT. The options: a request the messages you need with MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL 511 after connecting; the request applies to the channel it arrived on and lasts until a reboot; b set MAVn_ for your channel these require a reboot ; c get the stream through a router for which the ground station has already requested it, but then the GCS decides the rates, not your loop. Who is who: sysid, compid, and the GCS failsafe A companion is part of the vehicle: the same sysid as the autopilot MAV_SYSID , before 4.7 SYSID_THISMAV , default 1 and its own compid, by convention 191 MAV_COMP_ID_ONBOARD_COMPUTER . ArduPilot always accepts packets from its own components GCS_Common.cpp:7181 , "accept packets from our own components e.g. mavlink-connected companion computers " ; it also accepts them from other sysids as long as bit 0 of MAV_OPTIONS accept M

title: Multiple vehicles: addressing, separation, formation and a supervisor
summary: A second vehicle in the air is not "the same thing, twice".
