This module is the theory
headings: Addressing and routing Several vehicles in SITL Separation: do not rely on luck Formation One failure is not everyone's failure Where it fits in the system Step 1. Three vehicles in SITL Step 2. Routing Step 3. Supervisor Step 4. FOLLOW Step 5. The distance calculation
text: summary A second vehicle in the air is not "the same thing, twice". New questions appear: addressing who the command went to , routing how one GCS sees all of them , separation how they avoid hitting each other , and responsibility who answers when one vehicle loses its link . This module is the theory behind the "Fleet telemetry" project: unique sysids and ports, running several vehicles in SITL, separation strategies by altitude, sector, and time with a minimum-distance calculation, FOLLOW mode and formation flying from companion code, and a supervisor that watches the distances and stops a conflict. theory Addressing and routing - A unique sysid on every vehicle: ArduPilot MAV_SYSID SYSID_THISMAV before 4.7 , PX4 MAV_SYS_ID . Two vehicles with sysid 1 on one network: the GCS sees "one" vehicle that jumps around, and commands go to both. - The GCS and scripts are participants too: a GCS is usually 255, and a second station or a supervisor needs its own sysid 250, for example . pymavlink identifies itself as 255 by default, so set source_system for the supervisor. - target_system in every command is the vehicle number. target_system = 0 is a command to everyone ; in a fleet that is a deliberate tool a common stop , not a default value. - Routing : every vehicle has its own link a telemetry radio with a unique NETID , a separate UDP port , and everything is merged in mavlink-router or MAVProxy, which the GCS, the supervisor, and the logger connect to the mav-routing module . - Failsafe on its own GCS : a vehicle must know which GCS is "its own" MAV_GCS_SYSID , SYSID_MYGCS before 4.7 ; otherwise another station's heartbeat keeps it "connected". Several vehicles in SITL - ArduPilot: sim_vehicle.py -v Copter --count 3 --auto-sysid --location CMAC --auto-offset-line 90,10 --mcast --map --console gives three copters in a line 10 m apart, sysid 1…3; --mcast passes MAVLink between the vehicles without it, the follower in FOLLOW from step 4 never hears the leader . Only one vehicle type per command. Without a start-point offset, they all spawn in the same place. - PX4: start each instance with -i N ; it sets MAV_SYS_ID = N + 1 and shifts the UDP ports by N offboard 14540 + N, 18570 + N towards the GCS , see Multi-Vehicle Simulation in the docs for your version. Separation: do not rely on luck The minimum distance is made up of errors and reaction time: - Position error : GNSS without RTK is on the order of 1–3 m horizontally, and worse vertically; for two vehicles the errors add up. - Detection and reaction delay : telemetry 0.2–1 s , the supervisor's decision, the braking time. - Closing speed : two vehicles head-on at 10 m/s each close at 20 m/s. With 0.5 s of telemetry + 0.5 s of decision + ~1.5 s of braking, ~50 m are covered in that time; with position errors 3 m for each vehicle, the upper end of the range above, +6 m in total the minimum trigger distance is 56 m, that is, about 60 m. The lab's threshold MIN_H = 15 m, with the same 0.5 + 0.5 + 1.5 s, is only enough up to 15 − 6 / 2 · 2.5 = 1.8 m/s per vehicle. Hence the rule: the faster the vehicles, the earlier the supervisor must step in. {{diagram:chart-fleet-min-separation The trigger distance grows linearly with speed: at 10 m/s and 0.5 s of telemetry you need 56 m, while the lab's 15 m threshold is only enough up to 1.8 m/s.}} Strategies, from simple to complex: 1. Altitude layers : each vehicle has its own altitude, with ≥ 10 m separation plus the altitude error. Works as long as the vehicles do not change altitude takeoff and landing are handled separately, one at a time . 2. Sectors and corridors : each vehicle in its own geofence FENCE_ on each , with transitions along dedicated corridors. 3. Time separation : takeoff, landing, and passing shared points on a schedule. 4. Supervisor : watches pairwise distances in real time and stops a conflict LOITER/BRAKE for the lower-priority vehicle . 5. Built-in avoidance : ArduPilot can avoid aircraft using ADS-B AVD_ , ADSB_VEHICLE messages ; feeding it the positions of your own fleet from the companion is a workable technique that you must test in SITL before flying. Formation - FOLLOW ArduPilot : the follower holds an offset from the leader: FOLL_ENABLE = 1 , FOLL_SYSID is the leader's sysid, FOLL_OFS_X/Y/Z the offset in meters, FOLL_OFS_TYPE 0 for north-east-down or 1 relative to the leader's heading, FOLL_DIST_MAX the distance beyond which the follower stops following and holds position. The follower needs the leader's positions: GLOBAL_POSITION_INT over a shared MAVLink bus better: FOLLOW_TARGET from a Lua script on the leader . - Formation from code : the companion sends each vehicle in GUIDED its own target SET_POSITION_TARGET_GLOBAL_INT at 2–4 Hz: the formation center + the vehicle's offset. More flexible than FOLLOW, but all the logic is yours, including the behavior when the link to the companion is lost. One failure is not everyone's failure - Every vehicle must have its own link, battery, and geofence failsafes; the supervisor is an extra layer, not a replacement. - Several vehicles on RTL to the same point means a collision over home. Use a different RTL_ALT_M RTL_ALT before 4.7 or different return points rally for each vehicle. - Regulations: in many countries, one pilot controlling several vehicles needs a separate authorization; check before flying. {{diagram:multi-vehicle A fleet: the GCS and the supervisor connect to a router, each vehicle has its own sysid, link, and altitude layer; a follower in FOLLOW tracks vehicle 2.}} Where it fits in the system - Takes in: a unique sysid and its own link for each vehicle mav-routing ; the GNSS position with its error est-gnss ; each vehicle's own failsafes ap-safety-fs . - Puts out: GUIDED targets for each vehicle ap-companion ; the supervisor's LOITER/BRAKE commands to the lower-priority vehicle; altitude layers and return points for the system documentation eng-systems . - If you get this wrong: two vehicles with the same sysid →

text: summary A flight controller's flash memory is not elastic: you cannot enable everything at once, so firmware for your aircraft is a matter of choice. This module goes through Cloud Build in Betaflight using the 4.5.3 and Configurator 10.10 sources: what is sent to the build server, which option groups exist, what Core Only and Custom Defines do, where the build key can be seen on the board and how to check what is inside the firmware. Separately — why a missing option disappears silently and how to move a diff all into a build with a different set of options without losing half of the settings. For ArduPilot — building from source with subsystems disabled the HeeWing F405 case . The lab without hardware is a Python port of the 4.5.3 CLI logic that predicts which diff all lines will not be accepted and whether the config will be saved. theory Why build at all - On an F411/F405 the standard firmware with all options does not fit, or fits without the feature you need. - You need an option that is not in the standard set a rangefinder, a transponder, an exotic protocol . - You need to remove what is not on board and never will be GPS, compass, OSD chip , freeing up flash and memory. How much space there really is 4.5.3 linker scripts : the F411 and F722 have 512 KB of flash, the F405 has 1 MB, the H743 — 2 MB. After the config sector 16 KB and the first 16 KB sector the vector table, and on the F411 also the initialized data the main code .text must fit into the FLASH1 region on the F722 it is called AXIM_FLASH1 : 480 KB on the F411/F722 and 992 KB on the F405. The sum of the code regions is larger 496 and 1008 KB , but a build usually runs out of room in FLASH1 ; from here on the course counts by it. A “classic” build without the cloud this is how the project's CI and a local make without options build includes almost all features only on boards with 1024 KB of flash or more. On 512 KB boards that block of common_pre.h is skipped entirely: no GPS, LED strip, transponder, rangefinder or MAVLink telemetry. That is why GPS on an F411 is possible only through a custom build. Betaflight: Cloud Build Starting with 4.4 the firmware is built by the server build.betaflight.com for your list of options. Betaflight firmware consists of two parts: - the target — the processor family STM32F405 , STM32F411 , STM32H743 … , the common code; - the board config config.h from the betaflight/config repository : pins, gyro, flash, OSD chip. The drivers for a specific board come from it automatically; you do not select them. What happens when the build button is pressed per firmware_flasher.js of Configurator 10.10 : 1. The Configurator sends a request with three fields to /api/builds : target the board , release the version and options — a list of strings in Expert Mode for Development also commit . The first string is CLOUD_BUILD , followed by the values of the selected items of all the lists, for example USE_SERIALRX_CRSF , USE_DSHOT , USE_OSD_SD , USE_GPS . 2. The server builds the firmware with these flags. In the sources CLOUD_BUILD turns off the classic set common_pre.h:52–272 : the firmware gets what came in the list and what those options pull in. In addition, the server explicitly adds base flags that are not in the Configurator list for example, without USE_SERIALRX and USE_TELEMETRY , common_post.h would strip CRSF out entirely ; which ones exactly is not visible in the open code — this is the course's inference from the fact that cloud builds with CRSF work. The exact set is shown by /api/builds/<key /json and the build log. For example, USE_GPS adds GPS Rescue and the NMEA/UBLOX drivers, and USE_OSD_SD or USE_OSD_HD adds the OSD, CMS and the menus. 3. The build key BUILD_KEY is embedded in the firmware build/version.c:33–43 . It is 32 characters by which the server finds the request and the build log. An identical request is served from the cache: status success cached . 4. Flashing. If Expert Mode is off, the Configurator always erases the whole flash Full chip erase, firmware_flasher.js:581–585 : the config is gone, so diff all is needed before flashing, not after. If a board is connected to the Firmware Flasher, the Configurator reads its key and fills the lists with the options of the current build loadOptionsByBuildKey . This is the simplest way to “repeat it, but add one option”. {{diagram:bf-cloud-build-pipeline The Cloud Build path: an option that was not in the request is absent from the code — the setting, the CLI command and the tab disappear without a single error message.}} The build types in the version list: Release , Release And Release Candidate , Development . For Development in Expert Mode you can select a specific commit. Option groups Configurator 10.10 ↔ Betaflight 4.5 The list comes from the server /api/options/<version . The 4.5 firmware keeps a copy of it in msp/msp_build_info.h : from it the board tells the Configurator what was built into it MSP_BUILD_INFO, API 1.46 . Group in the interface 4.5 options USE_ + name Notes --- --- --- Radio Protocol SERIALRX_CRSF, SERIALRX_FPORT, SERIALRX_GHST, SERIALRX_IBUS, SERIALRX_JETIEXBUS, RX_PPM, SERIALRX_SBUS, SERIALRX_SPEKTRUM, SERIALRX_SRXL2, SERIALRX_SUMD, SERIALRX_SUMH, SERIALRX_XBUS for CRSF, FPort and GHST the telemetry field is locked with the label Automatically Included Telemetry Protocol TELEMETRY_FRSKY_HUB, TELEMETRY_HOTT, TELEMETRY_IBUS_EXTENDED, TELEMETRY_LTM, TELEMETRY_MAVLINK, TELEMETRY_SMARTPORT, TELEMETRY_SRXL ELRS/CRSF telemetry is not selected separately Other Options ACRO_TRAINER, AKK_SMARTAUDIO, BATTERY_CONTINUE, CAMERA_CONTROL, DASHBOARD, EMFAT_TOOLS, ESCSERIAL_SIMONK, FRSKYOSD, GPS, LED_STRIP, LED_STRIP_64, MAG, OSD_SD, OSD_HD, PINIO, RACE_PRO, SERVOS, VTX the OSD is here too: OSD_SD — analog MAX7456 , OSD_HD — digital over MSP DisplayPort Motor Protocol BRUSHED, DSHOT, MULTISHOT, ONESHOT, PROSHOT, PWM_OUTPUT with CLOUD_BUILD DShot is not enabled automatically common_pre.h:52–53 : without DSHOT in the list ther

text: summary Documentation describes what a parameter "does"; only the code shows what it actually does, including the order of operations, the limits and the side effects. This module teaches you to find your way around two large codebases without reading all of them: how to trace the path from the gyro to the motors, where the PID controller and the filters live, how to check the implementation against theory and spot where they disagree , and how to make a minimal change, build it and test it in SITL without touching a real aircraft. The lab: a patch and a write-up page in your own repository. theory Tools for reading code git clone + grep -rn / rg + an editor with go-to-definition VS Code with clangd, or just rg "pidController\ " . For C/C++ firmware the main technique is to start at the scheduler entry point and follow the calls down, and to go from a parameter its name in the code to the places where it is used. git blame / git log -S "name" shows when and why a line was added; the PR discussion often explains more than the wiki. Betaflight: the gyro → PID → mixer path Repository betaflight/betaflight , code in src/main/ : 1. Scheduler : scheduler/scheduler.c picks tasks from the table in fc/tasks.c . The task TASK_GYRO taskGyroSample and TASK_FILTER / TASK_PID taskMainPidLoop in fc/core.c . 2. Gyro : sensors/gyro.c : gyroUpdate reads the driver drivers/accgyro/accgyro_spi_icm426xx.c and others, via DMA , and LPF2 common/filter.c : PT1/PT2/PT3/biquad is applied while still at the gyro sample rate; then gyroFiltering sensors/gyro_filter_impl.c applies the chain: RPM notch flight/rpm_filter.c , static notches 1 and 2, LPF1 and, last, the dynamic notch flight/dyn_notch_filter.c . The filter order is defined right here, and you cannot tell it from the Configurator. 3. PID : flight/pid.c , pidController : for each axis error = setpoint − gyro, P, I with anti-windup and iterm_relax, D on the filtered gyro D-term LPF, D max: d_max_ in 2025.12, d_min_ in 4.5 , feedforward flight/pid_init.c , fc/rc.c : FF is computed from the setpoint derivative with interpolation/smoothing , TPA, anti-gravity, and pidSum in pidData axis .Sum . 4. Mixer : flight/mixer.c , mixTable : per-axis pidSum × the mixer matrix mixer_init.c / mixer_tricopter.c + throttle → motors, airmode , limiting mixer_type : LEGACY/LINEAR/DYNAMIC/EZLANDING , idle motor_idle ; before 2025.12, dshot_idle_value , motorOutputLimit . 5. Output : drivers/dshot.c frame encoding , drivers/pwm_output.c ; the platform part on current master is src/platform/STM32/dshot_bitbang.c , src/platform/common/stm32/dshot_dpwm.c and pwm_output_dshot_shared.c , which generate DShot frames with a timer + DMA; bidirectional DShot eRPM decoding is in drivers/dshot_bitbang_decode.c in 4.5, dshot_dpwm.c lived in src/main/drivers/ . 6. Blackbox : blackbox/blackbox.c : what gets logged and how the field table blackboxMainFields is in the same file . Checking against theory: in pid.c , find how D is computed: - gyroRateDterm axis - previousGyroRateDterm axis pidFrequency , where gyroRateDterm is the gyro already passed through the D-term notch and D-term LPF1/LPF2 the filters come before the differentiation , then multiplied by pidCoefficient axis .Kd and dMinFactor in 4.5; dMaxMultiplier from 2025.12 . D is taken from the gyro , not from the error so there is no "derivative kick" when the stick moves , and the gain scaling is a set of constants in pid.h applied in pid_init.c PTERM_SCALE , ITERM_SCALE , DTERM_SCALE : this is where the "dimensionless" values in the Configurator come from . ArduPilot: the IMU → rate → motors path Repository ArduPilot/ardupilot , vehicle code in ArduCopter/ , libraries in libraries/ : {{diagram:ardupilot-fast-loop The ArduCopter fast loop: the tasks the scheduler calls on every tick, and the slower tasks with their own rates.}} 1. Scheduler : ArduCopter/Copter.cpp , the scheduler_tasks table: FAST_TASK_CLASS AP_InertialSensor, &copter.ins, update → FAST_TASK run_rate_controller_main → FAST_TASK motors_output_main → FAST_TASK read_AHRS → … → FAST_TASK update_flight_mode ; slower tasks such as SCHED_TASK rc_loop, 250, 130, 3 with a rate, a time budget µs and a priority. Newer versions can run a dedicated rate thread ArduCopter/rate_thread.cpp , FSTRATE_ENABLE at the gyro rate. 2. IMU and filters : libraries/AP_InertialSensor/ : AP_InertialSensor.cpp update , the backend drivers AP_InertialSensor_Invensensev3.cpp , the harmonic notch libraries/Filter/HarmonicNotchFilter.cpp , the LPF Filter/LowPassFilter2p.cpp . 3. Rate loop : ArduCopter/Attitude.cpp : run_rate_controller_main → attitude_control- rate_controller_run in libraries/AC_AttitudeControl/AC_AttitudeControl_Multi.cpp : for each axis _motors.set_roll get_rate_roll_pid .update_all target, gyro, dt, _motors.limit.roll, … in libraries/AC_PID/AC_PID.cpp P, I with limit, D with the FLTD filter, FF, the error through FLTE , the target through FLTT → _motors.set_roll ... . 4. Angle loop : AC_AttitudeControl.cpp : input_euler_angle_roll_pitch_euler_rate_yaw_rad and others → quaternion attitude error → rate_target_ang_vel with ATC_ANG_ _P and the acceleration limits ATC_ACC_ _MAX , before 4.7 ATC_ACCEL_ _MAX : this is the input shaping implementation. 5. Motors : ArduCopter/motors.cpp motors_output_main → libraries/AP_Motors/AP_MotorsMulticopter.cpp output throttle filter, lift_max from battery voltage, spool logic → AP_MotorsMatrix.cpp output_armed_stabilizing mixing roll/pitch/yaw/throttle through the matrix with priorities and MOT_YAW_HEADROOM → output_to_motors → SRV_Channel / AP_HAL RCOutput DShot/PWM . 6. EKF : libraries/AP_NavEKF3/ : AP_NavEKF3_core.cpp UpdateFilter , one file per measurement type _PosVelFusion.cpp , _MagFusion.cpp , _OptFlowFusion.cpp , sources in AP_NavEKF/AP_NavEKF_Source.cpp . 7. Parameters : ArduCopter/Parameters.cpp and the _Params.cpp files in the libraries: the // @Param: blocks with description, range and @Values are what the parameter wiki is generated fr

text: summary "Engineering method 101" introduced the requirements → architecture → tests → documentation cycle on a single build. This module is the same cycle at full scale, for a vehicle or system that someone else will carry on: how to write requirements that can be verified with an ID, a criterion and a method , how to trace them to tests, how to run a system-level FMEA with mitigations and their verification, how to build a verification plan SITL → bench → field , and how to document so that a handover takes an hour instead of a month. The lab: a complete documentation package for your own project. theory Requirements A good requirement is unambiguous, verifiable and has a source . Structure: ID statement acceptance criterion verification method analysis/simulation/bench/flight source task, rule, standard priority . - Bad: "The drone shall fly for a long time." Good: R-PWR-03 Hover endurance with a 500 g payload of at least 25 min at 20 °C log: hover current, capacity calculation ≥ 25 min; flight: ≥ 25 min until BATT_LOW flight customer task §2 . - Classes: functional what it does , performance how much , constraints mass, budget, law , safety failsafe, zones , interfaces MAVLink, payload power , operational battery swap ≤ 2 min without tools . - Safety requirements are derived from the FMEA and the rules , not made up out of thin air. - Every requirement has an owner and a status draft/approved/verified/not met . How to check the wording: INCOSE and EARS The INCOSE Guide to Writing Requirements v4, 2023 defines nine characteristics of an individual requirement: necessary, appropriate for its level , unambiguous, complete, singular one thought , feasible, verifiable, correct, and conforming to the project's patterns C1–C9 . A set of requirements has its own characteristics: complete, consistent, feasible, comprehensible, able to be validated, and correct C10–C15 . Of the guide's 42 rules, five catch almost every beginner mistake: - R7, vague terms: "fast", "reliable", "user-friendly", "enough", "long": replace with a number. - R8, escape clauses: "where possible", "if necessary", "as a rule": a requirement you are allowed not to meet is not a requirement. - R18, single thought: "shall hold altitude and return on link loss" is two requirements and two tests. - R26, absolutes: "always", "never", "100 %" cannot be verified; give a probability, a condition or a time. - R33–R34, range of values and measurable performance: "±2 m in winds up to 8 m/s", not "holds altitude accurately". To keep the condition from getting lost, the EARS syntax Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax; Mavin et al., Rolls-Royce, RE'09 conference, 2009 is handy. Five patterns, with an example on a vehicle: Pattern Keyword Example --- --- --- Ubiquitous — The vehicle shall record a flight log on board. State-driven WHILE While the vehicle is in AUTO mode, it shall hold altitude within ±2 m in winds up to 8 m/s. Event-driven WHEN When the RC signal has been absent for more than 1 s, the vehicle shall switch to RTL. Unwanted behavior IF … THEN If the voltage stays below 3.5 V per cell for more than 10 s, then the vehicle shall switch to RTL. Optional feature WHERE Where an airspeed sensor is fitted, the autopilot shall use it in TECS. The unwanted-behavior pattern is a direct bridge from the FMEA: every FMEA row with a "detection + response" mitigation becomes an IF … THEN requirement with a number in both the condition and the response. Combining WHILE + WHEN gives the complex pattern: "While the vehicle is airborne, when the geofence is breached, …". Architecture and interfaces The system diagram: blocks FC, companion, power, RC, video, payload , the interfaces between them with protocol, power and direction the interface table is the main document during integration , and budgets: mass with a 10% margin , power per branch, from the power module , link the link budget , compute companion CPU . Decisions with their alternatives and the reason for the choice ADR, architecture decision record: context, options, decision, consequences , so that a year from now you do not argue it all over again. System-level FMEA The difference from the failsafe module: it covers not only in-flight failures but also integration failures a firmware bug after an update, an incorrect build, human error during preparation , and for each one a mitigation elimination, redundancy, detection, procedure and how the mitigation was verified a link to the test . The RPN is recalculated after the mitigations. The table is a living document, updated after every incident review → a new row or an updated mitigation . Worked example: a three-row FMEA Ratings on a 1–10 scale: S is the severity of the effect, O the likelihood of occurrence, D how hard it is to detect before harm is done 10 means we will not detect it . RPN = S·O·D gives the order in which to close risks; it is not an absolute measure. Failure Effect S O D RPN Mitigation Requirement / test --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- RC loss at a distance uncontrolled flight 9 4 2 72 FS_THR_ENABLE = RTL, RTL altitude above obstacles R-SAF-01 / SITL SIM_RC_FAIL Cold solder joint on a motor phase crash quad , yaw departure X8 8 3 7 168 load check and vibration test in the build checklist R-MFG-04 / voltage-drop test A new firmware renamed parameters failsafe silently stops working 9 3 8 216 invariants in CI, parameter diff after an update R-PRC-02 / check_params.py The surprise in this example is typical: the risk that feels "scariest" link loss is the best covered, and the highest RPNs belong to the build and the process, where detection is poor. That shift of attention is exactly what makes an FMEA valuable. {{diagram:eng-trace-chain The FMEA row with RPN 216 goes through the chain mitigation → requirement R-PRC-02 → test check_params.py → record → matrix; the test result comes back to the FMEA as a recalculated RPN.}} The S, O, D scales and the weak spots of the RPN Ratings mean nothing until the scale has

This module sets that up for a single vehicle or a fleet: Betaflight `

Repository Step 2. Export by script Step 3. Invariants + CI Step 4. Run CI locally: five cases Step 5. A SITL failsafe test on the fleet config Moving to real hardware
text: summary A drone's configuration is code: whether it flies depends on it. So everything engineers have long done with code applies to it: a change history with explanations, review before applying, automated checks, releases and rollback. This module sets that up for a single vehicle or a fleet: Betaflight diff all and ArduPilot .param files in git with meaningful commits, a fleet manifest under a JSON Schema, an invariant-check script that knows about parameter renames between versions and about the firmware's "silent" fixes, GitHub Actions with action versions pinned to a commit SHA, a SITL failsafe autotest that loads the fleet's actual config, a pull request as the form of review, release tags and rollback. The lab runs locally with the same commands as CI, on real exports: a diff all from Betaflight 4.5.3 SITL and 1015 parameters from an ArduCopter 4.7.2 SITL log; CI must go red on a broken failsafe and green once it is fixed. theory What to store fleet/ repository root: CI runs every path below from here fleet.yaml manifest: site, craft list, firmware versions, config paths schema/fleet.schema.json JSON Schema for fleet.yaml viking2/ README.md what the aircraft is, hardware, firmware version betaflight/diff-all.txt diff all after every change hex1/ ardupilot/params.param full parameter list Mission Planner / mavproxy param save notes/CHANGELOG.md what changed and why, with dates tools/ export_bf.py takes diff all over MSP/CLI check_configs.py invariant checks sitl_fs_test.py failsafe autotest in SITL .yamllint .github/workflows/config-ci.yml Rules: one commit is one change with a reason "D roll 38→42: bounce-back 18%→9%, log 2026-11-08-03" ; no reason, no commit. Binary logs do not go into the repository Git LFS or releases . The fleet.yaml manifest is the only place that records which aircraft flies which firmware and which file is its config. The check script takes the firmware version and the site's obstacle height from there instead of guessing them; that is why the manifest is itself validated against a schema, and a typo in it breaks CI before the config checks even run. Exporting the config automatically Betaflight: over USB in CLI mode not MSP: you enter the CLI with the character , diff all from Python pyserial : → wait for → diff all → read until the \r\n prompt plus 0.3 s of silence after it , or the export from betaflight-configurator . The board is identified by MSP_NAME , and the end of the output is detected by the prompt and the pause; the details and the pitfalls are in the CLI automation module. ArduPilot: in MAVProxy, param fetch , wait for the download to finish the command is asynchronous: the received-parameter counter in the console has to reach the total , then param save params.param ; or pymavlink param_fetch_all , checking that exactly param_count parameters arrived, → a sorted text file. A param save right after param fetch can write an incomplete list: that is exactly the "200 lines" case below. Sort and normalize strip the comments with the date , otherwise the diff is noisy. {{lesson:bf-cli-automation How to take a diff all reliably from a script without losing the end of the output or rebooting the board needlessly: covered there.}} What counts as a complete export. In the lab, the ArduCopter parameters were taken from the PARM messages of a SITL 4.7.2 log: 1370 lines, and 1015 remained after removing 355 SIM_ simulator parameters. If the file suddenly has 200 lines, that is not "the config got simpler" but a truncated export, and the check script must catch it the rule "at least 300 parameters" is a course guideline for Copter . For Betaflight, the sign of a complete file is the final save line of the diff all . Invariants: checking configs A script that reads a config and fails on any violation of the rules known from the course: - Betaflight: failsafe_procedure is set, failsafe_delay is within reasonable limits, motor_poles = 14 for a 2207, dshot_bidir = ON with the RPM filter, vbat_min_cell_voltage ≥ 330, no set debug_mode in the flight profile. - ArduPilot: FS_THR_ENABLE ≠ 0 , BATT_FS_LOW_ACT ≠ 0 , FENCE_ENABLE = 1 for flights under the rules, RTL_ALT_M meters; before 4.7, RTL_ALT in centimeters ≥ the site's obstacle height in the README , ARMING_SKIPCHK = 0 before 4.7, ARMING_CHECK = 1 , INS_HNTCH_ENABLE = 1 if a notch is needed, BRD_SAFETY_DEFLT per your policy. Implementation: JSON Schema or plain Python with a rules table; the output is a list of violations, each with a reference to a course module. A rule is only worth something if it knows the firmware version. Both renames above were checked in the ArduCopter 4.7.2 source unchanged in 4.7.3 : RTL_ALT_M is declared in ArduCopter/mode_rtl.cpp with the conversion table entry "RTL_ALT moved to RTL_ALT_M" default 15 m, config.h , and ARMING_SKIPCHK in libraries/AP_Arming/AP_Arming.cpp default 0, "no checks skipped" . The script keeps both names: if the file has RTL_ALT_M , it takes that in meters, otherwise it divides RTL_ALT by 100. For Betaflight the same thing happens at a different level: the version string at the top of the diff all Betaflight / <board <id 4.5.3 … is compared with the version in fleet.yaml , and if they differ the check fails immediately: applying 4.5 rules to a 2025.12 file makes no sense. For 2025.12 a separate rule catches d_min_<axis , which no longer exists it is now d_max_<axis , with the opposite meaning . The second class of rules predicts the firmware's "silent" fixes. text: summary The course teaches UAV engineering, but until now it left the question "what job do I do with this" to the reader. This module breaks the industry down into twelve roles: what each one does on an ordinary day, which course tracks and modules cover it, and what a candidate should be able to show at the door. Then: how to turn the capstone and the course projects into a portfolio that can be checked without the author; how to make a first contribution to ArduPilot, PX4, Betaflight or INAV; which pilot certificates you need in the EU using Czechia as the example , the UK and the US, and what is known about Ukraine, from official sources only, as of November 2026; and what can and cannot be said about salaries. The practice needs no hardware and no simulator: you pick a role, compute in percent how much of its skill set your completed modules cover, draw up a plan of three portfolio pieces, and write down the steps to a certificate in your country. theory How to read the industry: a role is a set of verifiable skills Job ads give the same work different names, so in this module a role is described not by its title but by what the person does and how they prove it. The twelve roles below cover almost everything you meet around small UAVs, from pilot to safety engineer. The further from flying, the less a pilot certificate matters and the more the artifacts do: code, logs, calculations, documents. A pilot certificate Part 107, A2 CofC, Flyer ID is permission to fly, not a profession. When money is involved, the customer pays for a result in their niche: an inspection report with georeferenced findings, an orthomosaic with measured accuracy, a tuned vehicle with an analyzed log. So the answer to "should I become a pilot" is: yes, if the permission comes with data-processing skill in a specific niche mapping, thermal inspection, agriculture, filming . On its own, the certificate is an entry ticket. text: summary A customer does not come for a “drone” but for a job: treat 40 ha, find an overheated contact, carry 2 kg over 8 km, draw a picture of 231 points in the sky. This module goes through six application segments — spraying and spreading, mapping and multispectral, inspection thermal camera, lidar , delivery, light shows, public safety — the same way: the job → the requirements payload weight, time, position accuracy, wind, redundancy → the aircraft class and the stack firmware, course modules → where to look in the rules of the EU, the United Kingdom and the USA → typical failures. The main tool is the selection rule: from the mission description to a requirements table and a class. The practice needs no hardware: four missions for which you calculate GSD, the thermal measurement distance, the number of show aircraft and the delivery radius, and choose the class; the answers are unambiguous and given in the reference. theory How to read a segment: job → requirements → class The professions and the way into the industry are in eng-career “Niches for an operator” ; here — what the aircraft must be able to do. The typical mistake is starting from the aircraft “I have a 7", what can I do with it?” . The order is the reverse. The selection rule course, 5 steps . 1. Describe the job in one sentence with numbers: what, where, how much, how accurately, over whom. “Spray 40 ha of wheat at a rate of 15 L/ha, with a road nearby” will do; “agricultural survey” will not. 2. Derive six requirements: the payload weight m_pl including consumables: liquid, cargo ; the working time t_work from the segment's productivity formula; the position accuracy σ; the design wind at the working height v h = v₁₀· h/10 ^α, ops-weather ; the consequences of a failure over people, BVLOS, expensive cargo, takeoff weight 25 kg ; whether hovering over a point is needed. 3. The class by the layouts from des-sizing : t_work ≤ 40 min → a multirotor 20–40 min . t_work 40 min and hovering is not needed or is needed for minutes → a VTOL no runway or a plane 1–3 h ; hovering is the main work → several multirotor flights. Serious consequences of a failure → a hexa or an octo, which survive a motor failure el-redundancy . In terms of energy a wing is also better on short missions without hovering des-sizing ; a quad is taken there for the simplicity of launch. 4. Positioning: ordinary GNSS gives 2–3 m, RTK — 1–10 cm Skybrush FAQ . The course rule estimate : the tolerance σ the job needs is at least three times the navigation error; otherwise — RTK nav-rtk , and for absolute map accuracy — ground control points as well per-mapping . 5. The regulatory corridor: takeoff weight up to 25 kg in the USA — less than 55 pounds , VLOS, not over people, nothing is dropped or sprayed → Open EU, United Kingdom or Part 107; commercial VLOS work in the United Kingdom often goes under PDRA01 — that is already a simplified Specific. Any “no” → Specific, a waiver, an exemption or an operator certificate. The specifics are in the rules table below and in f-regulations . {{diagram:apps-selection-tree The class is chosen by the job, not by the aircraft at hand: the working time and the share of hovering set the type, the consequences of a failure set the number of motors, and a weight 25 kg and BVLOS take you straight out of the “open” rules.}} Summary table of requirements by segment The ranges are the course's engineering estimate; products are named only as an example of the class manufacturer specifications as of November 2026 , not as a recommendation. Segment Payload Time / productivity Position accuracy Wind Redundancy Class and stack Course modules --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- Spraying 10–50 kg of liquid 10–20 min per flight; ha/h = B·v·0.36 RTK; track error ≤ 10 % of the swath estimate T50: up to 6 m/s; drift — per the product label MTOW 25 kg → hexa/octo heavy multirotor; AC_Sprayer , ZigZag ap-heavy , ap-payload , nav-rtk , nav-terrain Spreading T50: 50 kg, 75 L hopper, MTOW 103 kg as for spraying, the weight drops in jerks RTK as above as above a spreader on a servo output ap-heavy , ap-outputs Mapping, multispectral camera 0.2–1 kg Mavic 3M — MTOW 1050 g ha/h = line spacing · v · 0.36 RTK for georeferencing, GCPs for absolute accuracy Mavic 3M: 12 m/s takeoff, landing usually not needed a quad up to 40 min, a VTOL/plane beyond per-mapping , ap-payload , ap-quadplane Thermal camera 0.3–1 kg Matrice 4T — 1219 g, MTOW 1420 g hovering at the object; distance by the 3 × 3 px rule GNSS degrades near structures M4T: 12 m/s takeoff, landing over people and near power lines — yes a quad with a gimbal payload-gimbal , per-depth-avoid , nav-resilience Lidar about 1 kg ρ = PRR/ v·W RTK FIX for the datasheet accuracy as for the carrier expensive cargo → hexa/octo medium multirotor nav-rtk , ap-heavy Delivery 1–3 kg estimate radius from the flight time with a reserve landing or drop at the point per-landing along the route BVLOS over people → high a multirotor with a winch or a VTOL ap-payload , ap-quadplane , ap-safety-fs , el-redundancy Light show a light quad with an RGBW light 10–20 min estimate RTK 1–10 cm stronger at 120 m than near the ground geofence and failsafe on each one Skybrush fork of ArduCopter mav-multi-vehicle , nav-rtk , ap-notify Search and rescue thermal camera area coverage ordinary GNSS any by the job a quad or a VTOL ops-field , ops-weather Agriculture: spraying and spreading The job. Apply a product at a rate q L/ha evenly, without gaps or overlaps, and keep the droplets from drifting beyond the edge of the field. Requirements from the formulas. The swath width B m and the speed v m/s give the productivity P = B·v·3600/10,000 ha/h; the tank V L — the area per flight S = V/q; the pump flow Q = q·B·v·60/10,000 L/min. Example the tank and the swath are within the T50 specification: 40 L, 4–11 m : B = 7 m, v = 6 m/s, q = 15 L/ha → P = 15.12 ha/h, with a utilization factor of 0.7 turns, refilling; estimate — 10.58 ha/h; S = 2.

headings: Cameras and interfaces Capture with minimal latency Measuring latency Streaming to the GCS Camera and autopilot Sensor and lens: focal length, field of view, pixel GSD, footprint and pixels on the object Exposure and motion blur Rolling and global shutter in numbers Distortion and calibration: what to check in the result Reference table: formulas and tools Where it fits in the system Step 1. Optics in numbers Step 2. Calibration on a synthetic board Moving to real hardware: calibrating your own camera Step 3. Capture Step 4. Glass-to-glass latency Step 5. Stream to QGC Step 6. RTSP
text: summary Onboard vision starts with a frame that reached the program on time. This module is about the path camera → memory → algorithm → GCS: CSI versus USB, formats MJPEG/YUV/H.264 , capture in Python with minimal latency libcamera/V4L2 through OpenCV or GStreamer , measuring the real latency and FPS, and sending the stream to QGroundControl over RTSP/UDP through GStreamer with hardware encoding. The second half is optics in numbers: focal length in pixels, field of view, GSD and pixels on target, blur from speed and from rotation, rolling shutter skew, and what to check in a calibration besides the RMS. Lab: optics calculations and a real OpenCV calibration on a synthetic checkerboard no camera needed , then frames in OpenCV with an FPS measurement, an RTSP stream in QGC, and a measured latency. theory Cameras and interfaces - CSI Raspberry Pi Camera v2/v3, HQ; Jetson IMX219/IMX477 : a direct interface to the ISP, minimal latency 1–2 frames , high frame rates 120 fps at low resolution , a short ribbon cable up to ~30 cm without a repeater, which is a real constraint on a drone . Controlled through libcamera Pi / Argus Jetson . - USB UVC : any webcam; higher latency buffers, the USB controller , often MJPEG only at high fps decoding costs CPU , but the cable can be 3–5 m and you can swap cameras without drivers. Global shutter USB cameras for example, OV9281-based ones are for fast motion and VIO. - IP cameras/HDMI capture : for heavy platforms; a latency of 100+ ms is fine for a picture for the operator, not for a control loop. - Shutter : rolling rows exposed at different times, "jello" under vibration and fast rotation; breaks VIO versus global the whole frame at once . For navigation, use global. - Formats : YUV420 is raw and cheap for algorithms; MJPEG is compressed, every frame independent, decoded on the CPU; H.264/H.265 are for transmission and should be encoded in hardware Pi 4: H.264 up to 1080p30; Jetson: NVENC . {{diagram:camera-choice-tree Choosing a camera starts with whether the frame goes into a control loop: a picture for the operator can live with an IP camera at 100+ ms, navigation needs a global shutter, and CSI versus USB is decided by the cable length, about 30 cm versus 3–5 m.}} Capture with minimal latency Principles: 1 do not copy more than necessary, 2 a short buffer queue 1–2 frames , 3 take the latest frame, not the first one in the queue, 4 the resolution the task needs a detector is fine with 640×480 , 5 fixed exposure/gain, otherwise auto exposure causes jumps. OpenCV + V4L2 USB : python import cv2, time cap = cv2.VideoCapture 0, cv2.CAP_V4L2 cap.set cv2.CAP_PROP_FOURCC, cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc "MJPG" cap.set cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 640 ; cap.set cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, 480 cap.set cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS, 60 ; cap.set cv2.CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE, 1 t0 = time.perf_counter ; n = 0 while True: ok, frame = cap.read with BUFFERSIZE=1 this is the latest frame if not ok: break n += 1 if n % 60 == 0: print f"{n / time.perf_counter - t0 :.1f} fps" Pi CSI: picamera2 Picamera2 .configure create_video_configuration main={"size": 640, 480 , "format": "RGB888"}, buffer_count=2 , capture_array ; Jetson: the GStreamer pipeline nvarguscamerasrc ! nvvidconv ! video/x-raw,format=BGRx ! videoconvert ! video/x-raw,format=BGR ! appsink drop=true max-buffers=1 through cv2.VideoCapture pipeline, cv2.CAP_GSTREAMER . Measuring latency "Glass-to-glass": a stopwatch with milliseconds on a phone screen or a blinking LED with a timer , the camera looks at it, the program shows the frame next to it; a photo of both gives the difference = capture + processing + display latency. For the stream to the GCS, do the same with the GCS screen. Typical values: CSI + OpenCV locally 30–60 ms; USB MJPEG 60–120 ms; RTSP H.264 to QGC over Wi-Fi 150–300 ms the player buffering is the main contribution; reduce latency in QGC and in the GStreamer receiver . Compute FPS from the time between frames, not from the declared value; detect drops from gaps in frame numbers/timestamps. Streaming to the GCS GStreamer on board Pi 4 with hardware H.264 through v4l2h264enc ; Jetson with nvv4l2h264enc : bash UDP/RTP to the GCS QGC: Video Source = UDP h.264, port 5600 gst-launch-1.0 libcamerasrc ! video/x-raw,width=1280,height=720,framerate=30/1,format=NV12,interlace-mode=progressive \ ! v4l2h264enc extra-controls="controls,repeat_sequence_header=1,video_bitrate=2000000" ! 'video/x-h264,level= string 4' \ ! h264parse ! rtph264pay config-interval=1 pt=96 ! udpsink host=192.168.1.10 port=5600 sync=false On a Pi 5 no hardware encoder replace v4l2h264enc and the video/x-h264,level= string 4 caps after it with x264enc tune=zerolatency speed-preset=ultrafast bitrate=2000 . An RTSP server QGC: RTSP URL : gst-rtsp-server test-launch from its examples or mediamtx with the same pipeline; RTSP is convenient for several clients and reconnections, UDP gives the minimum latency. The bitrate follows the link budget 2–4 Mbit/s for 720p30 over Wi-Fi/4G; 0.5–1 Mbit/s at 480p for long-range links . More frequent keyframes iframe period 1 s mean faster recovery after losses. Camera and autopilot The frame time has to be matched with the flight data: a frame timestamp monotonic clock + MAVLink SYSTEM_TIME / TIMESYNC to synchronize with the FC; the offset and orientation of the camera relative to the IMU CAM_ /extrinsics for any geometry VIO, tracking . The companion is powered from its own BEC the peripherals module , and the camera and its ribbon cable are kept away from power wiring. {{diagram:glass-to-glass What makes up the video latency from light on the sensor to the screen typical shares; measure your own chain .}} Sensor and lens: focal length, field of view, pixel You choose a camera for a task by three numbers. The first is the pixel size p the sensor pitch, µm . The second is the lens focal length f mm . The third is the mode resolution W×H that the algorithm actually runs at. Everything else follows from them: - active sensor width

title: Camera geometry: from a pixel to a point on the ground
summary: The detector has found an object in the frame, in pixels (u, v). The autopilot needs a point in meters: "12 m north and 3 m west of me". Between the two sit the pinhole camera model, the intrinsic parameters (focal length and principal point), lens distortion, the camera mount on the frame and the v
headings: The pinhole camera Distortion Calibration Camera mount (extrinsics) Pixel → point on the ground Error budget Stereo and known size Camera and IMU in time Where it fits in the system Step 1. Calibration Step 2. Synthetic check of the chain Step 3. Real-world check
text: summary The detector has found an object in the frame, in pixels u, v . The autopilot needs a point in meters: "12 m north and 3 m west of me". Between the two sit the pinhole camera model, the intrinsic parameters focal length and principal point , lens distortion, the camera mount on the frame and the vehicle attitude. This module builds the whole chain: checkerboard calibration and what its results mean, pixel → ray → intersection with the ground, back-projection as a check, stereo and baseline, PnP for known objects, and where along the chain accuracy is lost. The lab uses the ready-made library examples/perception/camgeo.py with a synthetic "ground → pixel → ground" check: if your chain does not close on synthetic data, it will be even further off on real video. theory The pinhole camera An ideal camera projects a point P = X, Y, Z in the camera frame onto the image plane by similar triangles: x = X/Z, y = Y/Z normalized coordinates , and then into pixels: u = f_x·x + c_x, v = f_y·y + c_y. The intrinsic matrix camera matrix : K = f_x, 0, c_x , 0, f_y, c_y , 0, 0, 1 f_x, f_y are the focal lengths in pixels not millimeters : f_x = f_mm · W_px / sensor_width_mm. The link to the field of view: f_x = W/2 /tan HFOV/2 . A 1280 px camera with an HFOV of 90° has f_x = 640 px. c_x, c_y is the principal point, usually close to the image center but not exactly on it. The OpenCV camera frame: x to the right in the image, y down in the image, z forward along the optical axis. Remember it: it differs from both FRD and ENU. The key consequence: a single pixel gives you only a ray , a direction, not a point. The distance along the ray is unknown. To get a point you need extra information: the height above flat ground, a second camera stereo , the known size of the object, or a rangefinder. {{diagram:pixel-ground-chain The "pixel → ground" chain: K⁻¹ and undistortion give a ray in the camera frame, the mount rotates it into FRD, the attitude into NED, and the intersection with the ground plane gives meters.}} Distortion A real lens bends straight lines, especially a wide-angle FPV lens. The standard model Brown–Conrady in normalized coordinates: radial x_d = x· 1 + k₁r² + k₂r⁴ + k₃r⁶ , where r² = x² + y², plus tangential terms p₁, p₂ that arise because the lens is not exactly parallel to the image plane. Barrel distortion has k₁ < 0, pincushion has k₁ 0. For a fisheye lens 120° this model does not work and you need a separate one cv2.fisheye , the Kannala–Brandt model . The direction matters: the model describes how an ideal point gets distorted . We need the inverse: remove the distortion from a measured pixel. There is no closed-form formula, so it is solved iteratively cv2.undistortPoints , or a fixed-point iteration x ← x_d / 1 + k₁r² + … , 5–20 iterations . At the edge of a wide-angle frame, the "forgot about distortion" error is tens of pixels, which means meters on the ground. Calibration A checkerboard with a known square size is shot 20–40 times at different angles and distances, covering the whole frame, especially the edges. cv2.calibrateCamera finds K, the distortion coefficients and the board pose in every frame by minimizing the reprojection error RMS . What to look at in the result: - Reprojection RMS < 0.5 px is good, 0.5–1 is acceptable, 1 means bad frames blur, too little tilt, a board that is not flat . - f_x ≈ f_y for square pixels; a mismatch of 1–2 % is suspicious. - c_x, c_y within ~5 % of the center. - A calibration is valid for one specific resolution and focus. Switch the camera mode from 1080p to 720p with a crop and K is different. Autofocus and electronic image stabilization break the calibration; on board you turn them off. Camera mount extrinsics The ray in the camera frame has to be rotated into the body frame FRD. For a camera on the nose looking forward: camera z = body x, camera x right in the image = body y, camera y down in the image = body z. A camera pitched down by an angle τ adds a rotation about the body y axis by −τ. A camera looking straight down nadir has τ = 90°: the top of the image points forward along the heading. Add the camera offset from the center of gravity PLND_CAM_POS_X/Y/Z in ArduPilot exist exactly for this ; at 50 m a 10 cm offset is negligible, at 1 m just before touchdown it is noticeable. The gimbal is a separate trap: if the camera is stabilized, its orientation is the gimbal's orientation, not the vehicle's. In that case the chain uses the gimbal angles from GIMBAL_DEVICE_ATTITUDE_STATUS or MOUNT_STATUS , not ATTITUDE . Pixel → point on the ground The full chain: 1. u, v → normalized coordinates: x_d = u − c_x /f_x, y_d = v − c_y /f_y. 2. Remove the distortion → x, y ; the ray in the camera frame r_c = x, y, 1 , normalized. 3. Into FRD: r_b = R_bc · r_c. 4. Into NED: r_n = R_nb φ, θ, ψ · r_b, where R_nb = Rz ψ ·Ry θ ·Rx φ . 5. Intersect with the ground plane h meters below the camera: t = h / r_n,z; point = t · r_n. If r_n,z ≤ 0, the ray points at the horizon or above it and there is no point on the ground. 6. Convert to latitude/longitude: Δlat = N / R_Earth, Δlon = E / R_Earth · cos lat , R ≈ 6 378 137 m. Example: a nadir camera, f = 800 px, altitude 100 m, the object 80 px above the image center in level flight → 100·80/800 = 10 m ahead along the heading. With 10° of roll, the same point in the image center moves 100·tan 10° = 17.6 m sideways: attitude matters more than it seems , and a 1° attitude error at 100 m is 1.7 m on the ground. Error budget The error of the ground point is the sum of: - Attitude: δ_ground ≈ h · δθ / cos² angle from nadir . 1° at 100 m straight down is 1.7 m; looking 60° away from nadir it is 7 m. - Altitude: the point scales proportionally: a 5 % altitude error → a 5 % range error. title: Computer vision: from OpenCV to neural networks
summary: An onboard detector is not "just run YOLO". It is a choice between classical methods (color, contours, markers: cheap, predictable, brittle) and a neural network (robust, expensive, needs acceleration), followed by measurement: FPS on the target hardware, accuracy (precision/recall/mAP) on **your ow
headings: Classical methods: when they are enough Neural networks: detection Metrics that make sense Worked example: metrics from the counts A tracker on top of the detector The onboard pipeline Where it fits in the system Step 1. Classical methods Step 2. Data and fine-tuning Step 3. On board Step 4. Evaluation How to measure and what to record
text: summary An onboard detector is not "just run YOLO". It is a choice between classical methods color, contours, markers: cheap, predictable, brittle and a neural network robust, expensive, needs acceleration , followed by measurement: FPS on the target hardware, accuracy precision/recall/mAP on your own data, false positives and what they cost inside the control loop. The module walks both paths with code, shows how to run a model on a Jetson TensorRT and a Pi NCNN/ONNX Runtime/Coral , and teaches you to judge the result honestly. theory Classical methods: when they are enough - Markers ArUco/AprilTag : a known object carrying a code → detection plus a 6DoF pose with subpixel accuracy, tens of FPS on a Pi, robust to lighting. The best choice for precision landing, calibration and control-loop tests ArduPilot precision landing accepts AprilTag through a companion computer: PLND_TYPE = 1 MAVLink, message LANDING_TARGET . - Color + contours : HSV threshold → morphology → findContours → filter by area/shape. 2–5 ms per frame. Breaks when the lighting changes; thresholds are tuned on site. - Background/motion : background subtraction createBackgroundSubtractorMOG2 works only with a static camera; from a drone you need optical flow and motion compensation, which is hard. - Templates/features ORB + matching : for a known object; brittle under scale and rotation changes. Neural networks: detection Single-shot detectors the YOLO family, SSD, NanoDet take a 320–640 px input and output boxes with a class and a confidence score, followed by NMS. Facts that matter on board: - Model size : nano/small 2–10 M parameters is the only realistic option on a Pi/Jetson Nano/Orin Nano; medium needs an Orin NX/AGX. - Acceleration : on a Jetson, export to TensorRT FP16/INT8, ×3–10 over PyTorch ; on a Pi 4/5, NCNN or ONNX Runtime on the CPU a nano model at 320 px: 5–15 fps on a Pi 5 , a Coral USB Accelerator INT8 models , and on a Pi 5 only PCIe a Hailo-8L Raspberry Pi AI Kit / AI HAT+ 13 TOPS , a Hailo-8 AI HAT+ 26 TOPS or a Hailo-10H AI HAT+ 2, 40 TOPS INT4 for tens of fps; ARM laptops/mini PCs with a GPU run any stack. - Fine-tuning on your own data is mandatory: a model pretrained on COCO "sees" people and cars, but not your marker or object. 300–1000 labeled frames from the aircraft different altitudes, lighting, backgrounds , augmentations, 50–100 epochs on a PC/Colab; export to ONNX → TensorRT/NCNN. - INT8 quantization : ×2–4 faster than FP32 on hardware with integer units, −1–5 points of mAP50-95; the calibration set comes from your own data. The gain over FP16 depends on the board: 17–39 % on an Orin Nano Super and zero on the original Jetson Nano comp-jetson-nano . Metrics that make sense - Precision = TP/ TP+FP , the share of correct detections among everything found; Recall = TP/ TP+FN , the share of true objects that were found; the confidence threshold trades one for the other the PR curve . - mAP@0.5 is the area under the PR curve at IoU ≥ 0.5; it is the standard, but on board two things matter more: recall at a fixed precision the cost of an FP is a false maneuver! and the latency of the full cycle capture → inference → NMS → command . - Evaluate on held-out frames from the aircraft, not on training frames, and separately per condition altitude, lighting : a model that scores "0.9 on average" can drop to 0.5 at sunset. - FP analysis : classify the false positives similar object, shadow, frame edge, glare ; each group has its own fix: more data, the threshold, a geometric filter object size for the flight altitude , temporal filtering the object must appear in N consecutive frames, i.e. a tracker . Worked example: metrics from the counts Held-out set: 200 frames containing 250 objects. At a confidence threshold of 0.5 the detector output 230 boxes: 210 matched the labels at IoU ≥ 0.5 TP , 20 were false FP , and 40 objects were missed FN . - Precision = TP / TP + FP = 210/230 = 0.91 : of what was found, 91 % is real. - Recall = TP / TP + FN = 210/250 = 0.84 : of what was there, 84 % was found. - IoU = intersection area / union area of the two boxes; 0.5 means "matched", 0.75 means "matched tightly". A threshold of 0.3 gives, say, precision 0.80 and recall 0.93; a threshold of 0.7 gives 0.96 and 0.70. The cost of an error picks the point, not how nice the number looks: in a search for a person a miss costs more than a false alarm lower threshold, the operator checks the false alarms ; for an automatic action on a target it is the other way round higher threshold plus confirmation over several frames . {{diagram:chart-cv-threshold Raising the threshold lifts precision 0.80 → 0.91 → 0.96 and drops recall 0.93 → 0.84 → 0.70 : the cost of an error picks the point, a low threshold for a person search, a high one plus multi-frame confirmation for an action on a target.}} A tracker on top of the detector Per-frame detection is noisy and expensive. A tracker SORT/ByteTrack: a Kalman filter + IoU matching gives stable IDs, smooths the boxes, survives missed detections and lets you detect only on every 2nd–3rd frame. The control loop takes its commands from the tracker, not from the raw detector. The onboard pipeline Capture a thread, latest frame → preprocessing resize, letterbox, normalization; on the GPU or in hardware where possible → inference → NMS → tracker → publishing a ROS 2 topic / MAVLink / ZeroMQ with the frame timestamp. Profile every stage time.perf_counter ; typical proportions on a Jetson Orin Nano for YOLO-nano at 640: capture 3 ms, preprocessing 2, TensorRT FP16 inference 8–12, postprocessing 2 → 15–20 ms, 50 fps in theory, 30 with headroom. Inference time depends on the model and the board power mode: this is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a measurement; YOLO26n on an Orin Nano Super takes 4.57 ms TensorRT FP16, inference only, Ultralytics benchmark, comp-jetson-nano . {{diagram:cv-pipeline The onboard vision pipeline: the detector at 5–10 Hz, the tracker at the camera rate, quality metr

title: Onboard ML: budget, quantization, evaluation, maintenance
summary: A model that gives 0.9 mAP and 60 frames per second on a laptop turns, on board, into 6 frames per second with throttling five minutes into the flight and silent degradation over snow. This module is about preventing that: a latency and energy budget derived from the task, not from the model; what q
headings: A budget derived from the task Where to compute Quantization Profiling honestly Evaluation: your own data and the cost of an error Maintaining a model across a fleet Where it fits in the system Step 1. Pipeline profile Step 2. Heat and quantization Step 3. Per-slice evaluation
text: summary A model that gives 0.9 mAP and 60 frames per second on a laptop turns, on board, into 6 frames per second with throttling five minutes into the flight and silent degradation over snow. This module is about preventing that: a latency and energy budget derived from the task, not from the model; what quantization FP16, INT8 is and what it costs; how to profile honestly warm-up, percentiles, thermal behavior, the whole pipeline rather than just inference ; how to evaluate a model on held-out data from your own conditions and pick a threshold for the cost of an error; and how to maintain a model across a fleet: versions, rollback, drift monitoring. Lab: profile the pipeline with examples/perception/latency_bench.py on your compute board and write a record with a verdict against the budget. theory A budget derived from the task First what the task needs, then which model fits: - Latency : tracking a target moving at 10 m/s needs ≤ 100–150 ms from frame to command in 150 ms the target moves 1.5 m ; for mapping and search, seconds are fine. Latency means p99, not the mean: one 500 ms frame in the middle of a maneuver is a lost target. - Rate : a tracker between detections the tracking module lets you detect at 5–10 Hz and track at the camera rate. - Energy and heat : a 10–15 W computer on a vehicle that uses 300 W to hover costs 3–5 % of the flight time; but in a closed enclosure with no airflow it will overheat and drop its clocks. - Mass : a Jetson Orin Nano with a heatsink is 100–180 g; a Raspberry Pi 5 + an accelerator is 60–100 g. A budget statement for a requirements spec: "detect class X with recall ≥ 0.9 at distances up to 50 m, p99 camera → bbox latency ≤ 80 ms, on computer Y at 35 °C, no throttling for 30 minutes". Where to compute Computer What it accelerates Typical path --- --- --- CPU Pi 5, x86 nothing special ONNX Runtime, OpenCV DNN, small models YOLO-n at 320 px: from a few to about ten frames/s GPU Jetson FP16/INT8 on CUDA and Tensor Cores TensorRT from ONNX, several times faster than "raw" PyTorch NPU/TPU Hailo, Coral, built-in NPUs INT8 vendor compiler, supported layers only The general rule: exporting to ONNX is the standard hand-off between the training framework and the inference engine. No engine supports every operator; an unsupported layer falls back to the CPU and eats the whole gain, and the profiler shows that right away. Quantization Weights and activations are converted from FP32 to FP16 or INT8. INT8: a value x ≈ s· q − z , where q is an 8-bit integer, s is the scale and z is the zero point, both chosen from the value range. The gain: 4 times less memory, 2–4 times the speed of FP32 on accelerators with integer units NPU, Edge TPU, DSP , lower energy; on a Jetson GPU the gain over FP16 is modest or zero figures in comp-jetson-nano . The cost: lost accuracy, typically 1–5 points of mAP50-95 with plain PTQ YOLO26 on an Orin Nano Super: −1.8 to −4.7, comp-jetson-nano , more on small objects and in difficult conditions. - Post-training quantization PTQ : the ranges are calibrated on 200–1000 representative frames. If you calibrate on daytime frames, the activation ranges at night are different, and accuracy drops more than it did in the test. - Quantization-aware training QAT : quantization is simulated during fine-tuning; more accurate than PTQ, more expensive. - FP16 on a GPU costs almost nothing in accuracy, so it is always the first step. Check: the same held-out set before and after quantization, comparing metrics per slice distance, lighting, background , not just the overall mAP. Profiling honestly - Warm-up : the first 10–50 runs are slower memory allocation, kernel compilation, clocks . - Percentiles : p50, p95, p99, max. The mean hides the tails, and the tails break the control loop. - The whole pipeline : frame capture → decoding → resize and normalization → inference → postprocessing NMS → tracker → sending the command. Inference can be half the time, not all of it. - Thermal behavior : a 20–30 minute run inside the enclosure at a temperature close to the field one; log clocks and temperature tegrastats on a Jetson, vcgencmd measure_temp and get_throttled on a Pi . If p99 after 20 minutes is twice as bad as in the first minute, the budget is not met. - Concurrent load : video recording, MAVLink and ROS 2 run on board at the same time, so profile together with them. {{diagram:edge-budget-verdict The budget is met only if all three checks pass: p99 of the whole pipeline under load, 20–30 minutes in the enclosure without p99 doubling, and per-slice metrics after quantization.}} Evaluation: your own data and the cost of an error A model trained on an open dataset sees the world "from eye level", while a drone camera looks from above, at an angle, at small objects with motion blur. So: - A held-out set from your own conditions : frames from your vehicle, your camera, your altitudes and seasons that did not take part in training, split by flight not by frame: neighboring frames of one flight are almost identical, and such a split inflates the metrics . - Slices : metrics separately by distance, lighting, background. An overall mAP of 0.8 can hide a recall of 0.3 at distances 50 m. - A threshold for the cost of an error : in a search for a person a miss costs more than a false alarm, so a lower threshold, higher recall, and the operator checks the false alarms; for an automatic action on a target a false positive costs more, so a higher threshold plus confirmation over several frames and by the tracker. - Metrics the customer understands : not only mAP but "93 of 100 people in the field found, 4 false alarms per minute". Maintaining a model across a fleet A model is an artifact just like firmware and needs the same discipline: - Version of the model, the training data and the thresholds: in the metadata and in the log of every flight without it, incident analysis is impossible . - Rollback : the previous verified version is kept on board; switching is don

title: Visual navigation: optical flow, VIO, SLAM overview
summary: Optical flow gives velocity, visual-inertial odometry (VIO) gives position and attitude without GPS, and SLAM adds a map. This module explains what each method computes and what to expect from it (drift, scale, failures), how to feed VIO into ArduPilot EKF3 as an external navigation source (`VISION_
headings: Three levels How VIO works What VIO fundamentally cannot observe Ready-made solutions Into the autopilot Source failure What SITL showed: three failures in numbers Where it fits in the system Step 1. SITL on external navigation Step 2. Baseline hover Step 3. Frozen pose Step 4. Stopped feed Step 5. A 5 m jump Step 6. Freeze detector on the companion Moving to real hardware
text: summary Optical flow gives velocity, visual-inertial odometry VIO gives position and attitude without GPS, and SLAM adds a map. This module explains what each method computes and what to expect from it drift, scale, failures , how to feed VIO into ArduPilot EKF3 as an external navigation source VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE / ODOMETRY , EK3_SRC = ExternalNav, VISO_ and into PX4 EKF2_EV_CTRL , vehicle_visual_odometry , which cameras/modules do it out of the box T265 class, stereo + IMU, ZED , and where the limits are: lighting, texture, dynamics, latency. Lab: ArduCopter 4.7.2 SITL on external navigation and three source failures with real numbers: a frozen pose, a stopped feed, a 5 m jump. theory Three levels Method What it gives From what Drift Load --- --- --- --- --- Optical flow + rangefinder velocity in the plane, position by integration image shift between frames, height, gyro the position drifts integral of velocity , the velocity does not a few % CPU, a dedicated sensor VIO visual-inertial odometry 6DoF position + attitude feature tracks across frames + IMU scale and dynamics 0.5–2% of the distance traveled; grows without loop closure Pi 4/5 at the limit mono, low resolution , Jetson yes; ready-made modules run on their own chip SLAM the same + a map + loop closure VIO + place recognition, graph optimization jumps at loop closure, bounded on average Jetson/PC class Optical flow is covered in the module "Altitude and position without GPS". This one is about VIO/SLAM. A drift of 0.5–2 % of the path is a course guideline for good texture and calibration, not a guarantee: on a 200 m route that is 1–4 m. How VIO works 1. A feature detector FAST/ORB/Shi-Tomasi → tracking between frames KLT or descriptor matching. 2. Geometry: from point correspondences across several frames, the camera motion and the 3D points triangulation . A monocular camera does not know the scale everything could be twice as far and twice as large ; the scale comes from the IMU accelerations in m/s² or from stereo a known baseline . 3. Optimization: an EKF MSCKF or a sliding window bundle adjustment: VINS-Mono/Fusion, OpenVINS, ORB-SLAM3 in VIO mode, Kimera . 4. Output: pose and velocity with covariance in the frame of the first image the "odom" frame , at the camera rate 20–60 Hz with a latency of 20–80 ms. What breaks VIO: too little texture a white wall, water, snow, featureless grass , bad light night, glare, exposure changes , fast rotation blur, features leaving the frame; a global shutter and the IMU help , rolling shutter , moving objects in the frame people, cars; rejected by RANSAC , bad calibration the camera intrinsics, distortion and, above all, the camera pose relative to the IMU and the time synchronization; a 5 ms timing error means noticeable drift . What VIO fundamentally cannot observe A camera + IMU determine the scale, roll and pitch unambiguously: gravity gives the vertical, and accelerations in m/s² give meters. Four quantities are unobservable: the position x, y, z and the heading relative to the outside world. VIO knows them only relative to the first frame, and their error grows without bound; that is the drift. Three practical consequences follow. - Scale needs acceleration. In a hover and in flight at constant velocity the accelerometer sees only gravity, and the scale of monocular VIO rests on past data. That is why initialization is done with motion rock the vehicle, travel a few meters while accelerating , while stereo VIO gets its scale from the baseline even without motion. - Heading drifts just like position. If you feed the VIO heading into EKF3 EK3_SRC1_YAW = 6 , the compass no longer holds the heading, and the angle wanders together with the VIO map. On a long flight the compass is the more stable heading source, if the magnetic environment allows it. - A timing error turns into an attitude and position error. When rotating at 180°/s π rad/s , a 5 ms offset between the camera and IMU timestamps assigns the frame a rotation of π × 0.005 = 0.016 rad ≈ 0.9°. A feature 3 m away then "moves" by 4.7 cm. The filter explains this with wrong motion, hence drift during maneuvers course calculation, derived from the geometry . Ready-made solutions - Modules with onboard VIO the Intel RealSense T265 class, discontinued but the principle is the same; ModalAI VOXL; ZED stereo + IMU, needs a GPU machine ; Luxonis OAK-D stereo, VIO in firmware : they output the pose over USB/UART, and the companion translates it into MAVLink. - Open software: VINS-Fusion, OpenVINS, ORB-SLAM3, Kimera-VIO, for ROS/ROS 2, camera + IMU with synchronization a hardware trigger is ideal . Into the autopilot ArduPilot EKF3 ExternalNav : the companion sends MAVLink VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE position + angles, 20–50 Hz and/or VISION_SPEED_ESTIMATE , or ODOMETRY everything together, with covariances ; parameters VISO_TYPE = 1 MAVLink , VISO_POS_ camera offset from the IMU , VISO_ORIENT , VISO_DELAY_MS source latency ; sources EK3_SRC1_POSXY = 6 , EK3_SRC1_VELXY = 6 only if the companion sends a velocity, VISION_SPEED_ESTIMATE or ODOMETRY ; with VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE alone, as in the lab below, set 0, as in nav-indoor , EK3_SRC1_POSZ = 6 or baro 1 , EK3_SRC1_YAW = 6 or the compass ; EK3_SRC2_ is a backup set on GPS, switched with a switch/script; with bit 1 of EK3_SRC_OPTIONS AlignExtNavPosWhenUsingOptFlow , while the EKF flies on optical flow the ExternalNav position is pulled toward its estimate so that switching to ExternalNav causes no jump AP_NavEKF_Source.cpp:136–139 . Check: XKF4.SP/SV are normal, the VISP / VISV log messages are present, the XKF1 position follows the source. PX4 EKF2 : EKF2_EV_CTRL a bitmask: horizontal position, vertical position, velocity, yaw , EKF2_EV_DELAY , EKF2_EV_POS_ offset , EKF2_HGT_REF ; the ROS 2 topic /fmu/in/vehicle_visual_odometry uXRCE-DDS or MAVLink ODOMETRY through MAVROS /mavros/odometry/out . Coordinate frames: PX4 expects FRD/NED, ROS gives FLU/ENU, so a conversion is mandatory

title: Navigating by terrain with a camera: frame vs map, visual odometry and return without GNSS
summary: GNSS is gone, and you still need to get home. A downward-looking camera gives two different measurements: **visual odometry** (VO), the shift between consecutive frames, which accumulates error, and **map matching**, a comparison of the frame with a georeferenced orthophoto, which gives absolute lat
headings: Why odometry drifts and the map does not The frame-matching pipeline Coarse localization: VPR What breaks map matching How a fix gets into the autopilot Where it fits Step 1. Camera, route, run Step 2. Odometry and its drift Step 3. Map matching Step 4. Fusion and search without a prediction Step 5. SITL: the vision node as a second GPS Step 6. GNSS loss, a false fix, the return Step 7. Four ways to break it: real runs Moving to real hardware
text: summary GNSS is gone, and you still need to get home. A downward-looking camera gives two different measurements: visual odometry VO , the shift between consecutive frames, which accumulates error, and map matching , a comparison of the frame with a georeferenced orthophoto, which gives absolute latitude and longitude, but not every time. The module builds the whole pipeline: rectifying the frame by altitude and heading, ORB/AKAZE features and the learned SuperPoint/LightGlue , a homography with RANSAC, coordinates and their σ, coarse localization by a global descriptor VPR , fusion with VO, and the input into the autopilot through GPS_INPUT ArduPilot or VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE / EKF2_EV_CTRL PX4 . The lab: a Python test bench on a synthetic map with known ground truth, then a closed loop in ArduCopter 4.6.3 SITL: a 1.3 km route, of which 900 m and the landing happen after GNSS is switched off. theory Why odometry drifts and the map does not VO adds up increments, so it also adds up their errors. Three sources: - scale : meters = pixels · h / f per-geometry ; if the altitude is overestimated by e %, the path is overestimated by e %, an error Δ = D · e/100; - heading : the shift is computed in the frame axes and rotated into NED; a heading error δψ gives a sideways drift of D · sin δψ, so 1° is 1.7 % of the path; - matching noise : a random walk that grows as √N frames. VIO per-visual-nav takes the scale from the accelerometer, but drift still accumulates with distance. Map matching works the other way around: each fix is independent, and its error does not depend on the distance flown fractions of a meter at a GSD of 0.2–0.25 m , but a fix does not always come, and sometimes it lies. The conclusion is the same as for an inertial system and GNSS est-gnss : VO carries you between fixes, and the fixes reset the drift . Source What it gives Error When it fails --- --- --- --- VO mono + AGL a position increment in the frame axes grows with distance: e % of scale + sin δψ water, snow, motion blur VIO the same + scale from the IMU grows with distance, more slowly the same; a poor camera–IMU calibration Map matching absolute lat/lon, heading bounded: GSD + the map's georeferencing season, uniform terrain, an outdated map VPR "which tile am I on": hundreds of meters coarse, no σ similar fields; needs a geometric check The frame-matching pipeline {{diagram:vtrn-pipeline The frame is rectified by AGL and heading, matched against a map window around the prediction, the homography goes through checks and only then updates the filter; the autopilot gets a smoothed 5 Hz estimate, not the raw fixes.}} 1. Camera pointing down , a global shutter or a short exposure; undistortion from the calibration per-geometry . Tilt is compensated by a gimbal or by rotating the frame using ATTITUDE . 2. Rectification : a scale s = h_AGL / f / GSD_map and a rotation by the heading, so the frame becomes "north up, pixels like the map's". The features then only have to find a shift, not a scale and a rotation. 3. Features. ORB is FAST + rotated BRIEF, 32 bytes, Hamming distance; AKAZE is more robust to blur but slower and gives fewer points. The learned SuperPoint a detector-descriptor and LightGlue a matcher : according to their papers, SuperPoint is more accurate than ORB at homography estimation on HPatches illumination and viewpoint changes , and LightGlue is a fast learned matcher; check robustness to seasonal change on your own frames. The price is a GPU on board per-edge-ml . 4. Matching only against map features within a 3σ window around the predicted position; Lowe's ratio test at 0.8. 5. Homography + RANSAC cv2.findHomography , a 3 px threshold : 4 pairs per hypothesis, the number of iterations N = ln 1 − p / ln 1 − w⁴ , p = 0.99; with an inlier ratio w = 0.5 that is 72, with 0.2 it is 2900. Checks: inliers ≥ 15, homography scale 0.8–1.25 otherwise the altitude is wrong or the match is false . 6. Coordinates : frame center → map pixel → meters → Δlat = N/R, Δlon = E/ R·cos lat . The homography's residual rotation is an absolute heading correction. 7. Covariance : σ ≈ 3 · RMS_inliers · GSD / √n + a fraction of the search window, with a floor of 0.5 m. This is a lower bound: a match against a repeating pattern gives a small RMS and a wrong point, which is why innovation gates sit on top of it. A homography assumes flat ground: a height difference Δh within the frame shifts points by a fraction Δh/h of the footprint, so over buildings and slopes you fly higher or use an elevation map. Coarse localization: VPR If there is no prediction a cold start, a minute over water , the search window is the whole map. Visual place recognition compresses each map tile into a single vector NetVLAD, AnyLoc on DINOv2; a home-made miniature in the lab , the frame looks up the k nearest tiles, and geometry makes the decision: a homography around each candidate. VPR itself gives no coordinate and does not know when it is wrong. What breaks map matching Factor Mechanism What to do --- --- --- Season, lighting, shadows the tone of the fields changes, descriptors stop matching, w drops a map from the same season; learned features; roads and buildings as anchors Uniform terrain water, snow, a flat field: no features, and VO goes blind too a route along landmarks; an honest σ; a time limit without fixes Low altitude the footprint of 0.96·h is small, and the camera pixel is finer than the map pixel matching only above a threshold; below it, optical flow and a rangefinder nav-indoor High altitude the GSD is coarser than the map's, haze a longer focal length; a map with resolution to spare Repeating patterns crop rows, city blocks: false matches with a small RMS a window from the prediction, gates, a scale check Compute on the x86 test bench: VO 13 ms, matching 22–107 ms, the whole map 248 ms matching in a separate thread, latency accounted for How a fix gets into the autopilot ArduPilot, path 1: GPS_INPUT 232 . The companion pretends to be
