title: Mapping: surveying, georeferencing, photogrammetry
summary: An orthomosaic and an elevation model are the most widespread civilian drone product, and also a place where quality is decided before takeoff. This module walks the whole pipeline: the requirement for the result (centimeters per pixel, accuracy) → altitude, overlap and speed calculation → a mission
headings: Start with the requirement GSD and altitude Overlap Speed, shutter, interval Distance-based triggering in ArduPilot Georeferencing Processing: OpenDroneMap Accuracy assessment Where it fits in the system Step 1. Open dataset Step 2. Experiment Step 3. Your own mission Step 4 (optional). Linear inspection
text: summary An orthomosaic and an elevation model are the most widespread civilian drone product, and also a place where quality is decided before takeoff. This module walks the whole pipeline: the requirement for the result centimeters per pixel, accuracy → altitude, overlap and speed calculation → a mission with distance-based triggering CAM1_TRIGG_DIST , DO_SET_CAM_TRIGG_DIST → georeferencing the frames from the log TRIG versus CAM → processing in OpenDroneMap → accuracy assessment on check points. Lab: the full cycle on an open dataset and the calculation of your own survey mission, verified in SITL. theory Start with the requirement The customer does not need "a flyover" but a product with measurable properties: - GSD ground sample distance : how many centimeters of ground one pixel covers. For a cadastre 2–3 cm, for agricultural monitoring 5–10 cm, for an overview map 10–20 cm. - Accuracy : relative dimensions within the map and absolute coordinates versus reality . The first is set by the survey geometry, the second by georeferencing the vehicle GNSS, RTK/PPK, ground control points . - Product : orthophoto GeoTIFF , DSM/DTM surface/terrain model , point cloud, 3D model. GSD and altitude GSD = H · w_sensor / f · W_px . A 1" class camera 13.2 mm sensor width, 8.8 mm focal length, 5472 px gives 2.74 cm/px at 100 m; to get 2 cm/px you need 73 m. The same formula through the FOV: footprint width = 2H·tan HFOV/2 , GSD = footprint / W_px. A 1280 px FPV camera with a 120° HFOV at 100 m gives 27 cm/px: practically useless for a map, not because it is "bad" but because of the field of view and the resolution. Terrain changes the GSD: over a 30 m hill, flying 100 m above the takeoff point, the GSD at the top is 30 % better and the overlap is worse. For noticeable relief the mission is built to follow the terrain terrain following on a DEM, TERRAIN_ENABLE and altitudes in the Terrain frame . Overlap Photogrammetry finds the same point in several frames and recovers its 3D position from the different viewpoints structure from motion . Hence the requirement: every ground point in 5–9 frames. Typical values: frontal overlap along the survey line 75–80 %, side overlap between lines 65–70 %; for forest, uniformly textured fields and water 85/75 % and more, because there are few reliable points there. Calculation: distance between shots = footprint_along · 1 − frontal_overlap ; distance between lines = footprint_across · 1 − side_overlap . At 100 m with an HFOV of 84° and a VFOV of 62°: the footprint is 180 × 120 m; at 80/70, a shot every 24 m and lines 54 m apart. Camera orientation: the long side of the frame across the line means fewer lines. {{diagram:survey-overlap Survey geometry: the frame footprint, the frontal overlap sets the trigger distance, the side overlap sets the distance between lines.}} Speed, shutter, interval - Motion blur : during the exposure the vehicle must not move more than ~0.5 GSD. At 10 m/s and 1/1000 s the shift is 1 cm, which is borderline for a 2 cm GSD. Hence a short exposure 1/1000 and shorter and a flight speed tied to the GSD. - Minimum camera interval : if the camera needs 1.5 s to write a frame and the trigger distance is 24 m, the speed must not exceed 16 m/s. The CAM1_INTRVAL_MIN parameter stops the autopilot from triggering faster than the camera can keep up: the shot is postponed until the interval has elapsed the frame is taken later and the trigger distance grows , and the vehicle does not slow down. - Wind : lines across the wind mean a smaller difference in ground speed between the two directions. - Rolling shutter distorts the geometry at speed; ODM can compensate for it the --rolling-shutter option , but a global shutter is better. Distance-based triggering in ArduPilot Camera: CAM1_TYPE 1 Servo, 2 Relay, 5/6 MAVLink cameras, 4 gimbals with a built-in camera . Distance-based triggering: CAM1_TRIGG_DIST m in the parameters or, better, the mission command DO_SET_CAM_TRIGG_DIST at the start of the survey leg and with zero at the end, so that you do not shoot the turns and the transit to the area. CAM_AUTO_ONLY : trigger only in Auto. CAM_MAX_ROLL : do not trigger when the roll is larger than set the frames in a turn are oblique . Two messages in the log, and the difference between them is fundamental: - Without feedback the log has only CAM , and that is the moment the autopilot sent the trigger. - With feedback CAM1_FEEDBAK_PIN , CAM1_FEEDBAK_POL there are two records: TRIG is the trigger moment, CAM is the moment the shutter actually fired, from the hot shoe signal. Between them is the camera latency, tens to hundreds of milliseconds; at 10 m/s that is meters. Without feedback the frame coordinates are an estimate. The ArduPilot camera parameters, commands and survey errors are covered in detail in ap-payload . In PX4 the same is done by the camera_trigger driver TRIG_MODE , TRIG_DISTANCE , TRIG_INTERVAL and camera_capture feedback , with the ULog records camera_trigger and camera_capture ; the details are in px4-camera-gimbal . Note the difference: PX4 skips a trigger that comes too early, while ArduPilot postpones it. Georeferencing The options, in order of increasing accuracy: 1. Vehicle GNSS in EXIF a camera with its own GPS, or coordinates from the log written into EXIF by time : 2–5 m of absolute error. The relative accuracy of the map can still be at the centimeter level. 2. Coordinates from the CAM log with shutter feedback + the position interpolated to the frame time: 1–3 m. 3. RTK/PPK : camera center coordinates accurate to 2–5 cm; PPK needs raw GNSS observations recorded on board and on the base station. 4. Ground control points GCPs : 5–10 targets with RTK-measured coordinates, spread evenly over the area and over the elevations. They give an absolute accuracy of 1–3 GSD regardless of the onboard GNSS. Another 3–5 check points are not used in processing and serve for an honest assessment. Matching frames to the log: by image number Img in CAM

title: Precision landing on a marker: ArUco, LANDING_TARGET, PLND
summary: GPS lands a vehicle to within a meter or two; a charging station, a truck bed or a small pad needs 10–15 cm. Precision landing closes the loop through a camera: a marker (ArUco/AprilTag or an IR-LOCK infrared beacon) → the marker pose relative to the camera → the direction to the target in the vehic
headings: How the target is marked From pixels to LANDING_TARGET ArduPilot: PLND PX4: precision landing Landing phases and timing What breaks precision landing Where it fits in the system Step 1. Detector and pose Step 2. LANDING_TARGET in SITL Step 3. Failures
text: summary GPS lands a vehicle to within a meter or two; a charging station, a truck bed or a small pad needs 10–15 cm. Precision landing closes the loop through a camera: a marker ArUco/AprilTag or an IR-LOCK infrared beacon → the marker pose relative to the camera → the direction to the target in the vehicle frame → the autopilot descends while holding over the target. This module covers every link: which markers and why nested ones, how to turn the marker pose into a LANDING_TARGET message and what its fields mean, how ArduPilot uses it PLND_ , the target filter, landing retries and how PX4 does PLD_ , Required/Opportunistic modes , and, most importantly, what the system does when the marker disappears at 3 m and at 0.5 m. Lab: SITL with a camera in Gazebo or on recorded video, the landing error over 10 approaches. theory How the target is marked - IR-LOCK : an IR beacon + a dedicated camera that outputs the beacon coordinates in the frame. Works at night and in sunlight narrow IR filter , gives no heading. Supported by the autopilots directly PLND_TYPE = 2 in ArduPilot; the standard path in PX4 . - ArUco / AprilTag : black-and-white square markers carrying a code. The detector finds the 4 corners with subpixel accuracy, and given the marker side length solvePnP returns the full pose: position and heading. They need light and contrast and work with any camera through a companion computer. AprilTag the 36h11 family is more resistant to false detections; ArUco is faster and ships with OpenCV cv2.aruco . - Nested marker : a large marker 80 cm for acquisition from 10–15 m and a small one 10–15 cm inside or next to it for the last meter, when the large one no longer fits in the frame. Without it the landing loses the target at about 1 m, exactly when it is needed most. Marker size and acquisition range: the marker side should span ≥ 20–30 pixels. At f = 600 px a 0.5 m side gives 30 px at 10 m. So the large marker is for altitude and the small one is for the ground. From pixels to LANDING_TARGET LANDING_TARGET ID 149 is a message from the companion to the autopilot. The key fields: - angle_x , angle_y : the angular offset of the target from the optical axis along the x and y axes of the image rad . This is the minimal variant: the autopilot converts the angles into meters itself using its own altitude rangefinder! and attitude. - distance : the distance to the target m , if known from PnP or a rangefinder . - size_x , size_y : the angular size of the target. - frame : the coordinate frame usually MAV_FRAME_BODY_FRD for the angle variant . - The extended variant: position_valid = 1 and the fields x, y, z give the target position in meters in the specified frame, plus q , the target orientation. You fill it in when PnP gives a full pose. With position_valid = 1 ArduPilot requires distance 0 otherwise the message is dropped and does not use q ; according to its documentation PX4 accepts only x, y, z in MAV_FRAME_LOCAL_NED in the 1.18 code it turns the angle variant with position_valid = 0 into an irlock_report , as if from IR-LOCK, with the receive time instead of time_usec . - time_usec : the frame exposure time on the companion's monotonic clock not the send time . ArduPilot does not require clock synchronization: its jitter correction correct_offboard_timestamp_usec_to_ms estimates the offset between the companion clock and its own from the fastest messages. A consequence worth understanding: the variable part of the latency processing that takes 30 ms one time and 90 ms the next is removed this way, while the constant part is indistinguishable from the clock offset, so you set it with the PLND_LAG parameter. Without a correct timestamp and PLND_LAG , a 50–100 ms camera latency turns into oscillation over the target. Angles for a downward camera: angle_x = atan x_n , angle_y = atan y_n , where x_n, y_n are the normalized coordinates of the marker center after undistortion. The landing_target_angles function in examples/perception/camgeo.py does exactly that. {{diagram:landing-loop The precision landing loop: camera → detector → pose → LANDING_TARGET with the exposure timestamp → target filter in the autopilot → position loop during descent.}} ArduPilot: PLND Enabling: PLND_ENABLED = 1 , source PLND_TYPE 1 MAVLink from a companion, 2 IR-LOCK, 3/4 SITL . Landing on the target works in LAND, in the landing phase of RTL, and in a mission on a LAND command. The parameters that decide the outcome: - PLND_EST_TYPE : 0 RawSensor, 1 KalmanFilter the target filter smooths and survives short dropouts; recommended . - PLND_CAM_POS_X/Y/Z : the camera position relative to the vehicle center; PLND_YAW_ALIGN : the camera rotation relative to the nose in centidegrees . - PLND_LAG : the measurement lag s , used to line up with the history of inertial data. - PLND_XY_DIST_MAX : if the horizontal error is larger than this, the vehicle does not descend but first centers over the target. - PLND_STRICT : what to do when the target is lost: 0 land vertically right away not strict ; 1 default keep descending for another PLND_TIMEOUT s, then retry the landing, and if the target is still not found, hover for 7 s time to take over and land vertically; 2 the same retry, but never land without the target, hover instead very strict . That is how AC_PrecLand_StateMachine works in ArduPilot 4.7. - PLND_TIMEOUT : how many seconds default 4 to keep descending without the target before a retry with STRICT 1 and 2 ; PLND_RET_MAX : how many retries per mode default 4; 0 means no retries, go straight to hovering or landing according to STRICT ; PLND_RET_BEHAVE : where to go back to the last location where the target was detected, or toward its estimated location . - PLND_ALT_MIN : below this height by rangefinder the landing continues even without the target: at 50 cm the camera often no longer sees the whole marker, and abandoning the landing there is more dangerous than finishing it. title: Depth and obstacle avoidance: sensors, OBSTACLE_DISTANCE, algorithms
summary: Obstacle avoidance is not a single feature but a chain with honest limits at every link: the sensor does not see everything everywhere, the data arrives late, the vehicle does not stop instantly, and the avoidance algorithm runs only in some modes. This module covers depth sensors (stereo, ToF, lida
headings: Depth sensors and their honest limits OBSTACLE_DISTANCE: the common language Physics: how much distance you need to stop ArduPilot: two levels PX4: Collision Prevention Where avoidance is actually useful Where it fits in the system Step 1. Sector map Step 2. Speed budget Step 3. SITL: stop in front of a wall
text: summary Obstacle avoidance is not a single feature but a chain with honest limits at every link: the sensor does not see everything everywhere, the data arrives late, the vehicle does not stop instantly, and the avoidance algorithm runs only in some modes. This module covers depth sensors stereo, ToF, lidar, radar and their blind spots, turning a depth image into the 72 sectors of OBSTACLE_DISTANCE , the physics of braking which gives the maximum safe speed for a given sensor , and what the autopilots actually do: ArduPilot simple avoidance AVOID_ in pilot-controlled modes, the BendyRuler and Dijkstra path planners OA_ in automatic modes, and Collision Prevention in PX4 CP_ . Lab: a sector map from a depth image with examples/perception/obstacles.py , and a SITL scenario where the vehicle must stop in front of a wall at a set distance. theory Depth sensors and their honest limits Sensor Range Strengths Where it goes blind --- --- --- --- Stereo camera 0.3–10 m accuracy falls as Z² dense map, cheap smooth uniform walls, darkness, glare, thin wires ToF camera 0.1–5 m dense map, no texture needed sunlight IR washout , black surfaces Single-beam lidar / rangefinder up to 40–100+ m accurate, long range one direction only Spinning 2D lidar 360° 8–40 m all-round view in a plane everything above and below the plane: wires, branches Radar 30–100+ m rain, fog, dust, night low angular resolution, false reflections Two things you have to accept: 1 almost nothing sees wires : not stereo no texture , not a 2D lidar a thin target outside the scan plane , and radar only sees thick ones; 2 a forward sensor does not see what is to the side or behind, while the vehicle flies in every direction. So the avoidance system has to know where it is not looking and must not treat "no data" as "clear". OBSTACLE_DISTANCE: the common language The OBSTACLE_DISTANCE message ID 330 carries up to 72 distances in centimeters over equal sectors: increment or increment_f degrees per sector, angle_offset is the angle of the first sector, frame is usually MAV_FRAME_BODY_FRD 0° is forward, clockwise: 90° is right . Special values: UINT16_MAX 65535 means unknown/not used for that sector, max_distance + 1 means no obstacle is present within range. The difference is fundamental: the first means "I don't know", the second means "I know it is clear". For single sensors there is DISTANCE_SENSOR with its orientation field. Depth image → sectors: every image column has a bearing atan u − c_x /f_x ; for each column take the minimum depth in the working band of rows no floor, no sky , convert the depth along the optical axis into slant range divide by the cosine of the bearing and put it into its sector, keeping the minimum per sector. Sectors outside the camera field of view stay at 65535. That is what depth_to_sectors in examples/perception/obstacles.py does. {{diagram:sector-map The OBSTACLE_DISTANCE sector map: 72 sectors of 5°, the camera fills only its own field-of-view sector; the rest is "no data", not "clear".}} Physics: how much distance you need to stop Stopping distance = distance traveled during the latency + braking distance + margin: d_stop = v·L + v²/ 2a + d_margin, where L is the total latency frame, processing, transmission, velocity loop; usually 0.2–0.5 s and a is the deceleration actually achievable limited by the lean angle and the acceleration parameters: 2–5 m/s² for a multicopter . This gives the maximum safe speed for a sensor with range R: v_max = −a·L + √ a·L ² + 2a· R − d_margin . Example: a stereo camera with a reliable range of 6 m, a 2 m margin, a = 3 m/s², L = 0.3 s → v_max ≈ 4.1 m/s. Fly faster and avoidance turns into hope. PX4 states it plainly: collision prevention may restrict the maximum speed if the sensor range is not large enough; in ArduPilot the same follows from AVOID_ACCEL_MAX and AVOID_MARGIN . {{diagram:chart-avoid-stop-distance v_max is where the stopping distance reaches the sensor range: with 6 m and a 2 m margin, a 0.3 s latency lowers the limit from 4.9 to 4.1 m/s, and 0.5 s lowers it to 3.6 m/s.}} ArduPilot: two levels Simple avoidance works in pilot-controlled modes Loiter, PosHold and others; AltHold has a caveat at the end of this paragraph : the vehicle will not let itself get closer to an obstacle than AVOID_MARGIN m , either sliding along it AVOID_BEHAVE = 0 , Slide or stopping AVOID_BEHAVE = 1 , Stop . The sources are enabled by the bits of AVOID_ENABLE : 0 UseFence, 1 UseProximitySensor, 2 UseBeaconFence. In non-GPS modes AltHold the push-back is done by leaning: AVOID_DIST_MAX is the distance at which it starts, AVOID_ANG_MAX is the maximum lean angle degrees; before ArduPilot 4.7 it was AVOID_ANGLE_MAX in centidegrees . Since 4.7 this part is left out of standard Copter builds: there is no avoidance in AltHold unless the firmware is built on the custom build server with that option; in Loiter and the other position modes everything works as before. There is an acceleration limit AVOID_ACCEL_MAX and back-away parameters AVOID_BACKUP_SPD . Path planners object avoidance, OA_ work in automatic modes Auto, Guided, RTL : the vehicle changes its own path. OA_TYPE : 1 BendyRuler, 2 Dijkstra, 3 Dijkstra with BendyRuler. - BendyRuler is local: it probes the bearings around the course out to OA_BR_LOOKAHEAD and picks the one closest to the destination whose clearance is larger than OA_MARGIN_MAX . It works with proximity sensors through the obstacle database OA_DB_ and with the fence. Fast, but it can get stuck in a "pocket". - Dijkstra is global over a known map: it builds a path around the polygon fence inclusion and exclusion zones , keeping the OA_MARGIN_MAX margin. It does not use sensors; it is meant for no-go zones known in advance. - Dijkstra with BendyRuler combines a global path over the fences with local avoidance of whatever appears in flight. The data source is PRX1_TYPE 2 MAVLink, in which case the companion sends OBSTACLE_DISTANCE or DISTANCE_SENSOR ; there are also di

title: Tracking and target-based control
summary: Closing the "camera → error in the frame → velocity command" loop is easy; making it not oscillate and not fly away when the target is lost is an engineering problem. This module builds it from what you have already covered: the detector and tracker (per-cv), the latency of the chain (camera → infer
headings: From a pixel to a command Latency is the main limit Interfaces Safeguards (mandatory) Test plan Where it fits in the system Step 1. A simulated target in SITL Step 2. The gain limit: calculation and simulation Step 3. The loop in SITL Step 4. Safeguards Step 5. Analysis
text: summary Closing the "camera → error in the frame → velocity command" loop is easy; making it not oscillate and not fly away when the target is lost is an engineering problem. This module builds it from what you have already covered: the detector and tracker per-cv , the latency of the chain camera → inference → command → autopilot → response , control theory phase margin with a 100–200 ms delay , the GUIDED interface ArduPilot SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED with velocities and the Offboard interface PX4 TrajectorySetpoint , and the safeguards velocity/acceleration limits, a detection watchdog, a target-loss timeout → hover, the geofence, manual takeover . The lab runs in SITL with a simulated target; the starter code is in examples/ros2-skeleton . theory From a pixel to a command The error in the frame e_x, e_y is in normalized coordinates −1, 1 from the center. For a downward camera, the target offset in meters ≈ h · tan e·FOV/2 : for small angles it is linear in e and proportional to the height h. The velocity command: v = K_p · offset , limited to v ≤ v_max. For a forward or tilted camera the geometry is more complex: you need the camera angle and the height or the range to the target from the box size , otherwise K_p "drifts" with distance. A gimbal that tracks the target ArduPilot MNT1_ / GIMBAL_MANAGER splits the job: the gimbal keeps the target centered, and the vehicle flies on the gimbal angles. The loop structure: the outer loop ours, 10–30 Hz, on the image error outputs a velocity → the inner loop the autopilot: velocity → angles → rates, 50–400 Hz . The cascade rule from control theory: our loop must be noticeably slower than the autopilot velocity loop, and it will be, because of the latency. Latency is the main limit The chain: exposure + capture 10–30 ms → inference 10–50 → tracker/command 1–5 → MAVLink/DDS 2–10 → the autopilot accepts the velocity setpoint and tracks it the velocity loop PSC_NE_VEL_P before 4.7, PSC_VELXY_P , time constant 0.3–1 s . In total 50–150 ms of pure delay plus the dynamics. With a delay T_d and a gain K_p, a P-type loop starts to oscillate at a frequency of about 1/ 4·T_d −90° of phase from the delay + −90° from the "velocity → position" integrator : at T_d = 100 ms that is about 2.5 Hz, and the K_p limit ≈ π/ 2·T_d ≈ 15 1/s in the ideal case. But the autopilot does not change velocity instantly: with a velocity response τ ≈ 0.4 s the limit drops to ~10 1/s at 100 ms and ~3.7 1/s at 300 ms, and with velocity and acceleration limits saturation even lower: ~7.8 and ~2.8 1/s the simulation in the practice section . The working K_p is chosen 3–5 times below the limit for phase margin, hence the typical 0.5–2 1/s m/s per meter of error . Techniques: predicting the target position T_d ahead with the tracker, filtering the command, a D term on the target velocity from the tracker , limiting the acceleration, and above all reducing the latency. {{diagram:chart-tracking-kp-limit The K_p limit falls as the latency grows, and the autopilot dynamics and limits push it even lower: 7.8 1/s at 100 ms and 2.8 1/s at 300 ms; the working K_p is 3–5 times lower.}} Interfaces ArduPilot GUIDED : SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED with a type_mask that enables only the velocities 0b110111000111 = 3527: position, acceleration, yaw and yaw rate are ignored, vx, vy, vz are used , frame MAV_FRAME_BODY_OFFSET_NED velocity in the vehicle axes, convenient for tracking or LOCAL_NED ; send at ≥ 2–3 Hz, otherwise after GUID_TIMEOUT 3 s the targets are cleared the vehicle stops and hovers, which is exactly the safeguard . The pilot always takes over by switching the mode on the transmitter. ArduCopter does not limit the speed in GUIDED with velocity targets. WP_SPD m/s; before Copter 4.7, WPNAV_SPEED in cm/s is the speed for flying to waypoints and has no effect on a velocity command: ModeGuided::velaccel_control_run passes the target to AC_PosControl::input_vel_accel_NE_m in 4.6, input_vel_accel_xy , which shapes the trajectory with acceleration and jerk limits only, without a speed limit. Vertically it is the same: WP_SPD_UP/DN are not applied to a velocity target. Checked in ArduCopter 4.6.3 SITL: with WPNAV_SPEED = 300 in 4.7 that is WP_SPD = 3 a 6 m/s command gave 6.1–6.2 m/s; in the 4.7.3 source this path is unchanged. The input filter only rejects NaN and components larger than 1000 m/s. What the autopilot actually enforces on this path: - acceleration: WP_ACC 2.5 m/s²; before 4.7, WPNAV_ACCEL , 250 cm/s² , vertically WP_ACC_Z 1 m/s²; before 4.7, WPNAV_ACCEL_Z , 100 cm/s² ; jerk: PSC_NE_JERK 5 m/s³; in 4.6, PSC_JERK_XY ; - lean angle: PSC_ANGLE_MAX 0 = use ATC_ANGLE_MAX , 30°; before 4.7, ANGLE_MAX , 3000 centidegrees : this is an acceleration limit, not a speed limit; the steady-state speed is limited only by air drag; - GUID_TIMEOUT : the target is cleared when no new commands arrive; GUID_OPTIONS has no speed limits; - the geofence is the only boundary that stops a velocity command. With FENCE_ENABLE = 1 and bit 0 set in AVOID_ENABLE default 3: fence and proximity sensors , AC_Avoid::adjust_velocity cuts the velocity component toward the boundary so that the vehicle stops FENCE_MARGIN 2 m short of the FENCE_RADIUS circle, a polygon or FENCE_ALT_MAX ; the braking is no harder than 1 m/s². With AVOID_BEHAVE = 0 default the vehicle slides along the boundary, with 1 it stops. The companion keeps sending a velocity outward meanwhile, and the error in the frame grows; the companion has to notice that itself. If the boundary is crossed anyway wind, overshoot , braking for that boundary is turned off and FENCE_ACTION fires default 1: RTL, or Land if RTL is not possible . Hence the rule: the companion clips v_max and a_max before sending ; the autopilot parameters are the second line of defense, not the first. PX4 Offboard : OffboardControlMode velocity=true + TrajectorySetpoint velocity, position NaN at ≥ 2 Hz 10+ recommended , COM_OF_LOSS_T offboard loss timeout and COM_OBL_RC_ACT

summary: The perception modules take the links one at a time: the frame (per-camera), geometry (per-geometry), the detector (per-cv), the tracking loop (per-tracking), profiling (per-edge-ml). Here they are assembled into a "light on the sensor → command to the autopilot" pipeline, where every stage has a la
headings: The pipeline and its budget Capture: V4L2, CSI, GStreamer Undistort: the frame or a point A detector for the task The tracker and ID persistence Georeferencing and time What to send the autopilot Interlocks in three layers Where it fits Step 1. Data Step 2. The pipeline and latency by stage Step 3. Scoring by slices Step 4. Time Step 5. Replay in SITL: tracking and timeouts Step 6. Autopilot interlocks Moving to real hardware
text: summary The perception modules take the links one at a time: the frame per-camera , geometry per-geometry , the detector per-cv , the tracking loop per-tracking , profiling per-edge-ml . Here they are assembled into a "light on the sensor → command to the autopilot" pipeline, where every stage has a latency budget and a described failure. After the module you can measure glass-to-command by stage, evaluate a detector and a tracker by slices, turn a detection into a point on the ground with an honest timestamp, and close the loop through the autopilot so that a lost target, a hung process or a false target ends in a hover rather than a flyaway. The lab: the pipeline on a synthetic flight 40 s, 1200 frames with a log of latencies and target coordinates, then a replay in ArduCopter SITL with GUIDED tracking, FOLLOW mode, and checks of the timeouts and the geofence. theory The pipeline and its budget The exposure timestamp travels with the frame through every stage: it is used to pick the attitude and to compute the age of the data. Stage What it does Typical latency Failure → what the next stage must see --- --- --- --- Sensor exposure + readout 10–30 ms overexposure, blur → no detections Capture V4L2/CSI → memory 1–10 ms; USB MJPEG +10–20 frame did not arrive → age grows, watchdog Undistort a point or the whole frame ≈ 0.02 / 1–5 ms wrong calibration → a systematic error at the edges Detector bbox + confidence HSV 1–5 ms; YOLO-n on a CPU 25–300 ms x86 and 320 px in the lab, a Pi 5 and 640 px at Ultralytics , several times less with an accelerator per-edge-ml a miss or a false target Tracker association, ID, prediction < 1 ms an ID switch → the target "jumps" Georeferencing pixel → ray → ground < 1 ms ray above the horizon → None , not a point Command velocity/target, interlocks < 1 ms NaN, an outlier → discard Link + FC MAVLink, the autopilot loop 3–20 ms dropout → autopilot timeout The sum is the glass-to-command latency T_d . It, not the FPS, limits the loop gain: K_p,max ≈ π/ 2·T_d without the vehicle dynamics the derivation is in per-tracking . The budget is allocated from the task per-edge-ml . {{diagram:vision-pipeline-budget The budget from the lab: on 2 x86 cores the whole pipeline with the HSV detector takes 3.3 ms p95 , and the 36 ms of glass-to-command come from the sensor and the link; with YOLO11n on the CPU it is 65 ms, and inference becomes the main item.}} Capture: V4L2, CSI, GStreamer The interfaces are in per-camera. Three things matter for the pipeline. A fresh frame, not a queue: appsink drop=true max-buffers=1 in GStreamer or CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE = 1 in OpenCV, otherwise you process a frame that is a second old. Raw format: v4l2src device=/dev/video0 ! video/x-raw,width=640,height=480,framerate=30/1 ! videoconvert ! appsink drop=true max-buffers=1 ; on a Pi with CSI the source is libcamerasrc , on a Jetson nvarguscamerasrc comp-jetson-nano . The timestamp: a V4L2 buffer timestamp usually runs on CLOCK_MONOTONIC the V4L2_BUF_FLAG_TIMESTAMP_MONOTONIC flag and with most drivers is taken when the last pixel of the frame is received TSTAMP_SRC_EOF ; a few take the start of exposure TSTAMP_SRC_SOE . The middle of the exposure is in neither, so check the buffer flags of your camera. The difference is nearly constant: you measure it once and subtract it. time.time after cap.read is a processing timestamp, not a frame timestamp. Undistort: the frame or a point A full cv2.remap of 640×480 took 0.9 ms p50 in the lab, and on a single-board computer it will be several times more, so measure it; cv2.undistortPoints for one point takes about 0.02 ms. Distortion usually does not bother a bbox detector, and geometry needs only the corrected point; a full undistort is justified for lines and markers near the edge of the frame. A side effect with a number, in the lab : remap stretches objects near the edges, and the size gate lets the wrong things through. A detector for the task Task Detector What you get --- --- --- Your own marker, landing ArUco/AprilTag per-landing pose and ID, almost no false positives; needs contrast and ≥ 20 px per marker A bright object of known color and size HSV + contours + an area gate from AGL < 1 ms; goes blind in shadow and blur, but it stays silent rather than lying People, cars, arbitrary classes YOLO-n, fine-tuned on your own frames per-cv robust to lighting and blur; 25–300 ms on a CPU, produces confident false targets A target of diameter D at altitude h takes up s = D·f/h pixels; below 8–10 px a neural network is unreliable, and area gates become meaningless. You choose by slices lighting, blur, occlusion, background , not by average mAP: a miss costs a second of hovering, a false target costs a flight to the wrong place. The tracker and ID persistence - SORT: a constant-velocity Kalman filter per object + the Hungarian algorithm on IoU; hundreds of Hz, but the ID is lost when the detector misses. - ByteTrack: a second association pass for low-confidence detections: a target in shadow stays in its track, while the background is filtered out. - KCF, CSRT OpenCV : single-object template trackers between runs of a slow detector. KCF is fast but does not follow scale; CSRT is more accurate and slower. Both silently "drift" onto the background, so the detector rechecks them every 5–10 frames. The autopilot needs one object with an ID that survives misses. Four rules: track confirmation 3 frames in the lab , life without detections max_age 15 frames = 0.5 s , an association gate 30 px , and target lock: keep the selected ID, and after a loss take a new track only within a radius of the last position better in meters on the ground: pixels depend on altitude and roll . Georeferencing and time The "pixel → ray → R_bc → R_nb roll, pitch, yaw → intersection with the ground at h " chain is in per-geometry camgeo.pixel_to_ground . Here: where to get the attitude and altitude at the moment of exposure : - ATTITUDE 50 Hz via MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL and GLOBAL_P

text: summary INAV grew out of the same codebase as Betaflight but went in a different direction: navigation. It is the firmware for people who need position hold, return to home and missions on an inexpensive flight controller — and for fixed wings, which Betaflight does not support at all. This module explains where INAV sits between Betaflight and ArduPilot, what a Betaflight pilot will recognize, what is fundamentally different platform, arming, navigation modes, safehomes and how to prepare the first flight. theory Where INAV fits - Betaflight — manual flight only, minimum latency. - INAV — manual flight plus navigation: POSHOLD, RTH, missions, fixed-wing autolaunch, autoland. It runs on the same F4/F7/H7 boards, with the same configurator approach and a similar CLI. - ArduPilot — a full autopilot with an EKF, Lua, companion computers, a thousand parameters and hardware requirements to match. INAV is the compromise: navigation without moving to an H7 and without learning ArduPilot. Platform The first decision is platform_type : MULTIROTOR, AIRPLANE, TRICOPTER the values HELICOPTER, ROVER and BOAT are in the list but are not fully implemented . The platform determines the available modes, the mixer presets, whether flaps exist and the navigation logic. A fixed wing and a quadcopter behave like different firmware, even though it is one binary. What is familiar after Betaflight The Ports, Receiver, Modes and OSD tabs, the CLI with set / get / save / diff all , Blackbox. A CRSF or SBUS receiver is connected the same way. The Configurator 9.x tab names that differ from Betaflight locale/en/messages.json : the first tab after connecting is called Status Setup in older versions and in older guides ; accelerometer and compass calibration is a separate Calibration tab; aligning an external compass at an arbitrary angle is the Alignment Tool inav-gps ; PIDs and rates are on Tuning , filters on Filtering , plus Advanced Tuning , Mission Control , Programming and JavaScript Programming inav-ipf . What is different - Arming with a switch only. Stick arming was removed back in INAV 2.2. The fixed-wing exception: fixed_wing_auto_arm OFF by default with motorstop enabled arms on throttle above min_check , and the only way to disarm is a power cycle. - Arming is blocked without a GPS fix if navigation modes are configured nav_extra_arming_safety can bypass this, but that is a deliberate risk . - Navigation modes : NAV ALTHOLD, NAV POSHOLD, NAV RTH, NAV WP, NAV CRUISE for fixed wings . A multirotor needs a valid heading for POSHOLD and RTH: a calibrated compass or, without a compass since 7.1 , the GPS heading after a short straight-line flight; in 9.1 the heading can also be set on the ground — nose pointing north and the compass calibration stick command see the section on moving to 9.1 . - Home is the arming point the first arm by default: inav_reset_home = FIRST_ARM; EACH_ARM and NEVER also exist ; safehomes are up to 8 predefined safe landing points. The nearest one within safehome_max_distance is selected at the moment of arming and replaces home when RTH is activated. - Failsafe with the procedures DROP, LAND emergency landing , RTH, NONE. RTH as the failsafe procedure is the main reason to run INAV. - Programming Framework — logic conditions right in the firmware, without Lua. Requirements Navigation means GPS mandatory , a compass strongly recommended for a multirotor: without one the heading comes only from GPS while moving, and a position hold without a compass lasts minutes and a barometer practically mandatory for a multirotor: without one altitude is held from GPS and the accelerometer only, noticeably worse . A fixed wing can estimate heading from GPS; a compass is desirable. Under the hood: an estimator, not an EKF INAV computes position and altitude with a weighted complementary estimator inav_w_ , not an EKF — simpler and lighter for an F4, but without automatic trust or distrust of sensors the module “INAV: GPS and RTH” . Hence the requirements: a compass and a baro are practically mandatory for a multirotor without a baro altitude comes from GPS only, without a compass heading exists only as GPS course while moving ; GPS quality matters more than in ArduPilot, where the EKF “survives” bad frames. Why it will not arm: reading the OSD The reason for the block is visible in three places: as text in the OSD lines such as “WAITING FOR GPS FIX”, “AIRCRAFT IS NOT LEVEL”, “COMPASS NOT CALIBRATED” — the texts from io/osd.h 9.1.0, the same in 8.0.1 , on the Status tab of the configurator and in the CLI with the status command the Arming disabled flags: line . Typical reasons: no GPS fix with navigation modes configured nav_extra_arming_safety , the accelerometer or compass is not calibrated, throttle is not at minimum, tilt is greater than small_angle , the arm switch was on at power-up, the CLI or the OSD menu is open, the first mission waypoint is farther than nav_wp_max_safe_distance , a sensor failure. The same principle as in Betaflight the “Safety” module : you remove the cause, you do not bypass it. The procedure: status → flag names → look the flag up in the full table of 24 flags bit, name, what blocks in inav-cli-backup → fix the cause → status again, until the line is empty. The flags whose cause is a setting rather than “wait” conditions from fc/fc_core.c and navigation.c 9.1.0 : Flag What sets it Setting What to do --- --- --- --- NAV navigation modes are configured or failsafe may require RTH, and the position is not usable; a navigation mode is already switched on; the first mission waypoint is farther than nav_wp_max_safe_distance 100 m ; a JUMP error nav_extra_arming_safety = ALLOW_BYPASS default wait for the fix; without a fix — arm with yaw held right ALLOW_BYPASS only ; a distant first waypoint — yaw right while arming with any value of the setting; turn the NAV switch off; fix the JUMP inav-missions ROLL/PITCH fixed wing, NAV LAUNCH enabled by a switch or by feature FW_LAUNCH

text: summary INAV navigation rests on three sensors: GPS provides position and velocity, the compass provides heading, the barometer provides altitude. This module covers how to connect and check them, how ALTHOLD, POSHOLD and RTH work inside, the five RTH altitude modes, safehomes and what INAV does when GPS is lost in flight. The RTH setup is the most important safety setup in INAV: it is also the failsafe. theory Three sensors and their roles - GPS — horizontal position and velocity. A 3D fix is required; the quality is the satellite count and HDOP in the OSD. - Compass — heading. A multirotor needs it for POSHOLD and RTH: without a heading the controller does not know which way to tilt the aircraft to fly north. If a compass is connected, arming is blocked until it is calibrated. Without a compass since 7.1 the navigation modes become available only after the heading has been obtained from GPS by flying in a straight line; in 9.1 it can be set on the ground: point the nose north and give the compass calibration stick command throttle high, yaw right, pitch back . Without a compass the position holds for a few minutes, then the heading drifts and the “toilet bowl” begins. - Barometer — altitude. Strongly recommended on a multirotor for ALTHOLD/RTH: without it altitude is taken from GPS and held noticeably worse. How inav_default_alt_sensor default GPS; BARO, GPS_ONLY, BARO_ONLY splits the trust between baro and GPS is covered in inav-sensors-extra . A fixed wing can get its heading from the GPS ground course while moving: INAV uses it with a 3D fix, at least 6 satellites and a ground speed of 3 m/s or more. Until the first acceleration there is no heading. The 9.1 “heading = north” stick command works only on a multirotor without a compass; a plane has no way to set the heading by hand. GPS receiver setup: the 9.1.0 table and what to do when there is no fix INAV configures u-blox modules itself at every power-up: you do not need to write anything to the receiver in u-center beforehand, and whatever you wrote will be overwritten. The values from settings.yaml 9.1.0: Setting Default in 9.1.0 Values When to touch it --- --- --- --- gps_provider UBLOX UBLOX, MSP, FAKE MSP — the position is sent by an external device over MSP; FAKE — SITL only gps_auto_config ON ON / OFF OFF — only if the module is configured by hand and must stay that way gps_auto_baud ON ON / OFF — gps_auto_baud_max_supported 230400 9600 … 921600 M8 — up to 460800, M10 — up to 921600 gps_ublox_use_galileo / _beidou / _glonass ON / ON / OFF in 8.x Galileo and BeiDou were OFF ON / OFF each constellation is enabled at the expense of the others the description in settings.yaml : a u-blox M8 module receives no more than three at once, an M10 — four gps_ublox_nav_hz 8 10 in 8.x 5–200 an M9 at 10 Hz or higher tracks only 16 satellites, below 10 Hz — 32 gps_sbas_mode NONE AUTO, EGNOS, WAAS, MSAS, GAGAN, SPAN, NONE EGNOS in Europe, WAAS in the USA; AUTO chooses by itself gps_dyn_model AIR_2G PEDESTRIAN … AIR_4G, SEA, MOWER AIR_4G — an aggressive aerobatic aircraft; PEDESTRIAN and AUTOMOTIVE on a fast aircraft cause flyaways gps_min_sats 6 5–10 the minimum for a fix, not for navigation The procedure if the fix does not come or comes after 10 minutes: 1. The link to the module. status in the CLI, the Sensor status line: GPS=OK — the module answers; UNAVAILABLE or FAILING — the wrong UART, the wrong port function, or TX/RX swapped. The baud rate is taken from Ports: auto-configuration switches the module to it, and gps_auto_baud_max_supported limits the baud rates the firmware tries while searching for the module. 2. The sky. The gpssats command the command list is in inav-cli-backup prints the u-blox satellites with their signal level. If satellites are visible but weak and disappear when the VTX is on, that is interference from the VTX or the power wires: move the module away, check with the VTX off. 3. Constellations and update rate. Few satellites with a good signal — check that the constellations are enabled for your module; for an M9 use a rate below 10 Hz. 4. Cold start. The first fix of a new module without a backup battery takes minutes; a repeat fix with a live battery takes seconds. If it is slow every time, the module has no backup power. 5. u-center. If you need direct access to the module to update the module firmware, to read its config : gpspassthrough , then u-center on the flight controller's COM port; the only way out is a power cycle. The check: in an open area, 1–3 minutes after a cold start, there is a 3D fix, at least 10 satellites and an HDOP of no more than 2 the same norms as in inav-setup-scratch before the first hover . A compass on a mast and at an angle The compass alignment is set in two ways, and they do not add up: - align_mag — presets in 90° steps CW0, CW90 … CW270FLIP ; they work together with align_board_ ; - align_mag_roll , align_mag_pitch , align_mag_yaw — arbitrary angles in tenths of a degree −1800…3600, default 0 . If any of the three is not 0, the firmware assumes the compass is externally mounted and ignores both align_board_ and align_mag the description in settings.yaml . These three numbers are what the Alignment Tool tab of Configurator 9.x writes tabs/magnetometer.js reads and writes exactly align_mag_roll/pitch/yaw : you set the angles so that the module model on the screen sits the way the module sits on the aircraft. The procedure: the module on a mast at 45° → Alignment Tool → save → compass calibration → a check at the four cardinal points: the heading in the Configurator matches a paper compass within ±10° the same norm as in the ground check of inav-setup-scratch , and the heading does not move noticeably when the aircraft is tilted. An error of exactly 90° or 180° is a wrong yaw rotation; a heading that is right on a level aircraft but drifts when it is tilted is a wrong roll or pitch of the module. text: summary One GPS quadcopter goes all the way from a blank board to a logged hover, POSHOLD and RTH — in an order of 17 setup steps. The other INAV modules explain individual parts: what RTH is, how the estimator works, how to write missions. Here the whole chain is assembled, including the steps the course did not have before: bind and the channel map, the motor protocol, motor order and direction, ESC calibration, voltage and current calibration vbat_scale , current_meter_scale , current_meter_offset , failsafe with the RTH procedure, ground checks of navigation and the first flight with abort criteria. The main path is INAV SITL: everything that concerns the configuration you do without hardware. The steps that require real hardware are laid out separately for the bench and for the field. The lab: a diff all from SITL and from the real aircraft, the battery calibration calculation, a hover log and a recorded failsafe → RTH. theory The step map: what, where and with what {{diagram:inav-setup-flow The 17 steps go strictly in order: everything that concerns the configuration is checked in SITL; bind, motors, ESCs and the battery — only on the bench without props; the props go on at step 15, not earlier.}} Step Where INAV: tab / CLI In detail --- --- --- --- --- 1 Firmware, backup of the old config SITL, bench Firmware Flasher, diff all inav-intro 2 Platform, mixer SITL Mixer, platform_type , mmix inav-intro 3 UART ports SITL Ports, serial here 4 Receiver, bind bench Receiver, receiver_type , serialrx_provider link-elrs 5 Channel map, endpoints, centers SITL + bench map , rxrange , min_check / max_check here 6 Motor protocol bench Outputs, motor_pwm_protocol f-motors-esc 7 Motor order and direction bench, no props Outputs motor test , Motor Mixer Wizard here 8 ESC calibration PWM only bench, no props Outputs, the Master slider here 9 Accelerometer, compass bench, field Status / Calibration, align_mag inav-gps 10 Voltage and current bench + flight vbat_scale , current_meter_scale , current_meter_offset here 11 Modes, arming, arming blocks SITL Modes, aux , status inav-intro 12 Failsafe: set up and test SITL + bench + field failsafe_procedure = RTH here, bf-failsafe 13 OSD and video bench OSD, osd_video_system bf-modes-osd, link-vtx 14 GPS, home, RTH SITL + field nav_rth_ inav-gps 15 Preflight check, first hover field — here 16 First tuning field nav_mc_hover_thr , filters, EZ Tune here, inav-mc-tuning , bf-filters 17 Log, diff all , restore SITL + field Blackbox, CLI here What INAV SITL can and cannot do SITL is the same INAV firmware compiled with an ordinary gcc for a PC cmake -DSITL=ON . You can run the build by hand or from the SITL tab in the Configurator. The sensors gyro, accelerometer, baro, compass, GPS work in FAKE mode: the simulator supplies their data. The UARTs are replaced with TCP ports: UART1 = 5760, UART2 = 5761 and so on. The Configurator connects by selecting “SITL” or over TCP to localhost:5760 . Without a simulator SITL runs in “Configurator only” mode: the mixer, ports, modes, failsafe and diff all are configured as on a real board, but the aircraft does not fly. Flight comes only from an external simulator: RealFlight 9.5S / Evolution or X-Plane. For a quadcopter only RealFlight really works paid, Windows : the INAV-X-Plane-HITL plugin supports only the Airplane platform checked on 8.0.1; the 9.1 documentation also names the INAV-X-Plane-XITL plugin — its multirotor support has not been checked . What SITL cannot do in principle: - DShot. SITL has no USE_DSHOT , and config.c silently changes DSHOT300 to MULTISHOT at load — this is verified below, in step 6. - Bind, motor direction, ESCs, the voltage divider, the current shunt, the compass on the real airframe. All of this is the physics of a particular aircraft, and SITL does not have it. - Analog OSD. There is only MSP DisplayPort through INAV-Sim-OSD. Battery calibration: the formulas from the source src/main/sensors/battery.c INAV 9.1.0; the formulas are the same in 8.0.1 computes: - voltage: V = ADC · vbat_scale · 3300 / 4095 · 1000 , that is, the reading is directly proportional to vbat_scale . Hence new = old × V_multimeter / V_INAV ; - current: I = U_sensor − offset / scale . current_meter_scale is set in 0.1 mV/A 400 = 40 mV/A . The reading is inversely proportional to scale, so new = old × mAh_INAV / mAh_charger — this is the formula from docs/Battery.md; - offset: in the code offset × 100 µV is subtracted from the sensor voltage, so the actual unit of current_meter_offset is 0.1 mV, although Settings.md says “millivolts”. In practice it is easier to think in current: the offset removes offset / scale amps from the reading. The correction: new_offset = old_offset + I_INAV − I_ammeter × scale . The order: first scale from mAh a flight that uses more than 50 % of the capacity , then offset from the idle current, and a check flight. The current in flight is 20–40 times the idle current, so an offset error hardly affects the scale calculation. Failsafe in INAV Failsafe triggers if frames are lost on any of the roll, pitch, throttle or yaw channels, if a channel goes outside rx_min_usec … rx_max_usec 885…2115 or if the FAILSAFE mode is activated. It triggers 200 ms + failsafe_delay × 100 ms after valid frames stop: 0.7 s at the default failsafe_delay = 5 plus the receiver's own signal timeout: 100 ms for serial receivers, 200 ms for the MSP receiver , and then the procedure failsafe_procedure is executed: LAND default , DROP, RTH or NONE. For a GPS quadcopter choose RTH. Four things are important to know: - RTH requires GPS, a compass and a baro that is what docs/Failsafe.md 9.1 says; for heading without a compass see inav-intro . If one of the sensors is missing at the moment failsafe triggers, an emergency landing at nav_emerg_landing_speed 500 cm/s starts immediately. - failsafe_throttle_low_delay 0 = off : if the throttle has been low for a long time, the aircraft is considered to be on the ground and is simpl

text: summary GPS, the compass and the barometer from inav-gps cover outdoor flight. This module is about the other sensors of INAV 9.1.0: the rangefinder and the SURFACE mode, optical flow and position hold without GPS, the pitot tube and virtual airspeed, temperature sensors, and along the way the choice of the altitude source and flying without a barometer. From the source it works out which _hardware values exist, by what formula a sensor number turns into an altitude or a speed, and under which conditions the firmware discards a measurement. The lab needs no hardware: decide from a table of readings which rangefinder altitudes are accepted, compute airspeed from pressure and from GPS with wind, repeat the arithmetic of the flow calibration and find three errors in the settings of three aircraft. theory Common rules for all four sensors This module is about four optional INAV sensors — the rangefinder, optical flow, the pitot tube and temperature sensors — and about the choice of the altitude source. The reading order: first the common rules for enabling them this section , then the rangefinder: the list of sensors, the path from a reading to the AGL altitude and the SURFACE mode; after it optical flow and position hold without GPS; then the pitot and where the firmware uses airspeed; at the end temperature and the barometer. The sections are self-contained: if the aircraft has only a pitot, go straight to it after the common rules. GPS, the compass and the main barometer are in inav-gps , the fixed-wing landing with a rangefinder flare is in inav-geozones-landing . A sensor is enabled with a single _hardware setting the Configuration tab in Configurator 9, the lists Barometer, Pitot tube, Rangefinder, Optical flow and takes effect after a reboot. They have no separate feature flags. The rule that catches people most often sensors/diagnostics.c : a sensor that is selected but not found or silent is treated as a hardware failure. isHardwareHealthy returns false, and the arming-disabled flag HWFAIL appears in status . This applies to the barometer, the rangefinder, the pitot and optical flow alike. Hence: on a board without a barometer set baro_hardware = NONE , not AUTO ; if you removed the rangefinder, set rangefinder_hardware = NONE back. Serial sensors take a UART with a function from io/serial.h : RANGEFINDER — 65536 Rangefinder in Ports , OPTICAL_FLOW — 16384 Optic flow . MSP sensors have no function of their own: they need a port with the ordinary MSP function 1 . Rangefinder: the values of rangefinder_hardware Value Bus and protocol Limit in the driver, cm Cone, ° Max tilt, ° Period, ms --- --- --- --- --- --- NONE the default — — — — SRF10 I²C, ultrasonic; not part of the common build 2 targets 600 50 25 70 VL53L0X I²C 0x29, laser ToF 250 90 45 33 VL53L1X I²C, laser ToF 300 27 13.5 40 US42 I²C 0x70, ultrasonic 400 25 computed 30 15 100 TOF10120_I2C I²C 0x52, laser ToF 200 30 computed 45 22.5 100 TERARANGER_EVO I²C 0x31 its own “out of range” code 90 45 70 MSP a UART with the MSP function, the message MSP2_SENSOR_RANGEFINDER none 90 45 30 BENEWAKE UART RANGEFINDER , 115200, the TFmini protocol none 90 45 30 USD1_V0 UART RANGEFINDER , 115200 an NRA radar on the US-D1 protocol none 90 45 30 NRA UART RANGEFINDER , 115200 NanoRadar NRA15 / NRA24 none 90 45 30 FAKE simulator data X-Plane, RealFlight, HITL 250 90 45 30 The values are taken from drivers/rangefinder/ .c and rangefinder_virtual.h . The I²C drivers return “out of range” above their limit by themselves. The serial drivers have no limit: the maxRangeCm field is filled with the number 250 but is not read anywhere, and a radar faithfully reports its tens of meters. How much of that goes into the estimator is decided by one setting — inav_max_surface_altitude . The HC-SR04 and US-100 sensors are not supported docs/Rangefinder.md . The path of a reading: from the driver to the AGL altitude 1. The driver returns a distance in centimeters or a code: −1 “out of range”, −2 “failure”, −3 “no new data”. A reply of −1 counts as a live reply; health means “there was a reply within the last 500 ms”. 2. rangefinder_median_filter = ON enables a median over the last five readings quickMedianFilter5 , although the description of the setting speaks of three. 3. Tilt compensation rangefinderProcess : cos θ = cos roll × cos pitch . If cos θ is less than the cosine of half the cone — the reading is replaced with −1. Otherwise altitude = distance × cos θ, with the fractional part dropped. 4. The estimator navigation_pos_estimator_agl.c accepts a reading if 0 ≤ altitude ≤ inav_max_surface_altitude . An accepted reading gives a “1”, any other — a “0”, and from these ones and zeros a first-order filter computes the reliability : r ← r × 1 − α + reading × α, α = Δt / Δt + 0.478 s . A gap longer than 400 ms resets r to zero. 5. The AGL quality: HIGH at r ≥ 0.75, MID at 0.33 ≤ r < 0.75, otherwise LOW. The only way out of LOW is straight to HIGH. In HIGH the estimate of the altitude above the surface is pulled toward the rangefinder with the weights inav_w_z_surface_p and inav_w_z_surface_v ; in MID it is blended with the general altitude; in LOW it equals the general altitude minus a remembered offset. All of item 5 is executed only if the barometer is healthy : the condition in the code is EST_SURFACE_VALID and EST_BARO_VALID at the same time. Without a barometer the AGL quality is always LOW, no matter how much the rangefinder measures. The AGL altitude is a separate estimate. The rangefinder is not mixed into the Z altitude on which ALTHOLD, RTH and missions fly. text: summary In INAV the PID, rate and filter numbers look like those in Betaflight but are computed differently: roll_rate = 20 is 200 °/s, the RPM filter is fed by ESC telemetry over a UART and not by bidirectional DShot, and above stabilization there are four more navigation controllers with their own scales. This module works through all of that from the INAV 9.1.0 source: how an integer from diff turns into a gain, the stick curve formula, the filter chain in the order it is applied, every ez_ setting and the formulas by which EZ Tune rewrites the PIDs and filters, the multirotor navigation PIDs and the tuning order for a GPS copter with the Blackbox fields for each step. The practice needs no hardware and no simulator: compute the gains and the rate from a diff fragment, apply the EZ Tune formulas to three sets of sliders, choose a setting and a direction from altitude and position hold symptoms, and find three errors in a config. theory Where the settings live A control profile control_profile 1…3 holds 126 settings in three groups: 91 PID settings mc_ , fw_ , nav_mc_ , dterm_lpf_ , smith_predictor_ , 25 rate, expo and TPA settings, 10 EZ Tune settings. In older guides the command is called profile — 9.1 has no such command, type control_profile in the 8.0.1 source the rate group was called PG_CONTROL_RATE_PROFILES , in 9.x — PG_CONTROL_PROFILES ; the setting names did not change . The details of profiles and diff are in inav-cli-backup . Three things are not in the profile, and people trip over this: - the gyro filters gyro_ , dynamic_gyro_notch_ , setpoint_kalman_ , rpm_gyro_ and looptime — common to all profiles; - nav_mc_hover_thr — in the battery profile battery_profile ; - the navigation limits nav_mc_bank_angle , the speeds, nav_mc_braking_ — common. The rate loop: from an integer to a gain pid_type = AUTO the values are NONE , PID , PIFF , AUTO selects the PID controller with Control Derivative on a multirotor and PIFF on an airplane, rover and boat. The controller works in °/s and computes in float; the integers from the profile are divided by the constants of flight/pid.h : text kP = mc_p_ / 31 units / °/s P = kP · setpoint − gyro kI = mc_i_ / 4 units / °/s · s I += kI · error · dt kD = mc_d_ / 1905 units / °/s² D = −kD · d gyro /dt · dBoost kCD = mc_cd_ / 7270 units / °/s² CD = kCD · d setpoint /dt “Units” are axisPID units: the sum is limited to ±500 in roll and pitch and ±400 in yaw, and ±500 is the full travel of an axis in the mixer inav-mixer-vtol . CD is the counterpart of Betaflight feedforward: it responds to stick movement, not to the error; the setpoint signal before it is smoothed by the PT3 mc_cd_lpf_hz 30 Hz . D is computed from the gyro only. Axis P I D CD kP kI kD kCD --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- Roll, pitch mc_ _roll , mc_ _pitch 40 30 23 60 1.290 7.5 0.01207 0.00825 Yaw mc_ _yaw 85 45 0 60 2.742 11.25 0 0.00825 The range of each number is 0…255. An example: an error of 50 °/s with mc_p_roll = 40 gives P = 64.5 units, that is, 13 % of the travel. The scales are the same in 8.0.1. What else affects the rate loop: Setting Default range What it does --- --- --- mc_iterm_relax RP OFF , RP , RPY weakens the accumulation of I while the setpoint changes quickly: the factor is max 0, 1 − the HF part of the setpoint / 40 °/s mc_iterm_relax_cutoff 15 Hz 1…100 the cutoff of the filter that separates the “fast” part of the setpoint pid_iterm_limit_percent 33 % 0…200 the I ceiling: 33 % of the axis limit — ±165 units in roll and pitch, ±132 in yaw iterm_windup 50 % 0…90 the growth of I slows down when the spread of the motor commands takes more than this share of the range, and stops at 100 % d_boost_min , d_boost_max 0.5 0…1 , 1.25 1…3 the D multiplier: on a sharp stick movement it drops toward min, on a disturbance it grows toward max d_boost_max_at_acceleration 7500 °/s² 1000…16000 the gyro acceleration at which the multiplier reaches max antigravity_gain , antigravity_accelerator 1 and 1 1…20 I boost on a sharp throttle change; 1 — off antigravity_cutoff_lpf_hz 15 Hz 1…30 the filter that extracts the “sharpness” of the throttle tpa_rate 0 0…200; 0…100 in 8.0.1 attenuation of P, D and CD above tpa_breakpoint ; it does not touch I. On a multirotor — no more than 100: above that the factor at high throttle becomes negative, and P and D change sign tpa_breakpoint 1500 1000…2000 the throttle at which TPA starts tpa_on_yaw OFF extend TPA to yaw rate_accel_limit_roll_pitch , rate_accel_limit_yaw 0 and 10000 °/s² up to 500000 a limit on the rate of change of the setpoint; ≤ 50 — off yaw_lpf_hz 0 Hz 0…200 a PT1 on yaw P looptime 500 µs up to 9000 the period of the PID task: 2 kHz. The gyro is sampled by a separate 4 kHz task Multirotor TPA: factor = 100 − tpa_rate · throttle − breakpoint / 2000 − breakpoint / 100 at a throttle from the breakpoint to 1999; at exactly 2000 — 100 − min tpa_rate , 100 / 100. Warning: on a multirotor tpa_rate is no more than 100. The range up to 200 in 9.x exists for the airplane branch, where the factor is clamped to 0.3…2.0. The multirotor branch has no lower bound: the factor passes through zero at a throttle of breakpoint + 2000 − breakpoint · 100 / tpa_rate and is negative beyond that. An example for tpa_rate = 150 and breakpoint 1500: at throttle 1700 the factor is 100 − 150 · 200 / 500 / 100 = 0.40; around 1833 it is zero — P, D and CD are off; at 1900 — 100 − 150 · 400 / 500 / 100 = −0.20, at 1999 — −0.50. A negative factor flips the sign of P, D and CD: the controller amplifies the error instead of removing it, and at high throttle the aircraft shakes and flips itself; I meanwhile works as usual and does not save it. With tpa_rate = 200 the zero comes already at throttle 1750, and at 1999 the factor is almost −1. The CLI accepts such a value silently. And exactly 100 is not a safe maximum: at full throttle the factor is 0, and there is no P and D stabilization. The in-flight adjustment is limited to the same 0…200: function 54 in ad

The lab needs no hardware and no simulator: from a fragment of the diff all of an aircraft on 8.0.1 you mark up every line for 9.1, count what an ordinary diff would have lost, put the restore order together and decode a flag line from status . theory Entering the CLI and what it does to the aircraft The CLI is opened with the character on an MSP port the CLI tab in the Configurator does this itself . While the CLI is open, the arming-disabled flag CLI is set, logic conditions inav-ipf are not executed, and the MSP OSD is not updated. There are three ways out, and all three reboot the flight controller: save write and reboot , exit reboot without writing , defaults reset and reboot . save and exit have no noreboot argument in INAV — unlike Betaflight 2025.12 bf-cli . The CLI discards everything after in a line, so a backup file with comments can be pasted as is. An error always starts with ERROR: in Betaflight — ERROR IN : the client from bf-cli-automation is ported to INAV by replacing this string and the exit logic. text: summary One aircraft — a 1.2 m flying wing with a single pusher motor — goes all the way from a blank flight controller to a logged first flight with RTH and a loiter over home. The order is the 17 setup steps of the course. What is already covered in other modules is a one-line action and a link here. Covered in detail is what the course did not have for INAV: servos direction, center, endpoints, control throws , CG, the airplane motor/ESC, battery calibration, fixed-wing failsafe, autolaunch, the first throw, servo autotrim, fixed-wing autotune, RTH with a loiter and the diff all backup. The main path is INAV SITL; the steps that are possible only on hardware are collected in “Moving to real hardware”. The lab: a filled-in servo test table, the CG within the calculated range, a launch log, a recorded RTH loiter and a diff all . theory What the course already has and what this module adds Step Where in detail What is here --- --- --- 1–2 firmware, platform, mixer inav-intro, inav-wing the CLI smix rules for a flying wing and an airplane 3–5 ports, receiver, channels link-elrs, link-protocols the INAV actions: receiver_type , the range check 6–8 motor, ESC f-motors-esc motor_pwm_protocol , PWM ESC calibration, motorstop_on_low servos and control surfaces — direction, center, endpoints, throws in mm 9 accelerometer, CG aero-wing the CG calculation and a check on a balance stand 10 battery — vbat_scale , current_meter_scale with the proportion the right way round 11–12 modes, failsafe inav-intro, inav-wing fixed-wing failsafe and its test 13–14 OSD, GPS, RTH inav-gps, link-vtx fixed-wing RTH: a loiter instead of a landing 15–17 flight, tuning, backup inav-wing briefly the throw procedure with abort criteria, autotrim, autotune, diff all The parallel module inav-setup-scratch takes the same path for a GPS quadcopter; the receiver and the battery are the same there, but here the steps are given in full — a wing needs them with corrections. SITL for a wing: what it can do INAV SITL is the same firmware compiled for a PC; the Configurator has had the SITL tab since 6.1. The UARTs are replaced with TCP ports: UART1 — 5760, UART2 — 5761 and so on; the Configurator connects through “SITL” or TCP 127.0.0.1:5760 . Without a simulator SITL runs in “Configurator only” mode: you can go through the whole configuration platform, mixer, servos, modes, failsafe, navigation, diff all but not a flight — the sensors take their data from the simulator. For flying a wing the official documents name RealFlight 9.5S/Evolution suitable for autolaunch and mixers and X-Plane 11 the “AR Wing” aircraft from the INAV-X-Plane-HITL project . Both are paid. An X-Plane subtlety: its internal mixer cannot be deactivated, so the documentation says to always select “Aircraft with tail” in INAV, even for a flying wing. In RealFlight the mixers in the model are deleted, and INAV does the mixing. The standard Configurator profile “RealFlight Flying Wing” passes --chanmap=M01-01,S01-02,S02-03 : motor 1 → simulator channel 1, servos 1 and 2 → channels 2 and 3. The string is derived from the source tabs/sitl.js . What SITL cannot do: bind and the radio link, the direction and ESC of the real motor, servo mechanics slop, hard stops, throws in mm , CG, voltage and current calibration, a real throw. Those steps are done on hardware. Servos in INAV: smix → servo → output The chain: a rule smix <n <servo <input <weight <speed <lc takes an input 0 — stabilized roll, 1 — pitch, 2 — yaw and multiplies it by the weight −1000…1000 % ; rules with the same servo number are summed. Then servo <n <min <max <mid <rate : mid is the center 1500 µs by default , min / max limit the travel, rate is −125…125 % — a negative one reverses the whole servo. Hence the reversing rule: - the surface is wrong on both axes both roll and pitch — reverse the servo: rate with a minus sign; - it is wrong on one axis — change the sign of the weight of that axis in smix for this servo only. Reversing on the radio is forbidden: stabilization will go one way and the stick the other. The center is first set mechanically the servo arm perpendicular to the pushrod, the pushrod adjusted , and only the remainder with mid . Servo autotrim moves exactly mid ; the continuous feature FW_AUTOTRIM limits it to 1300–1700 µs, and the SERVO AUTOTRIM mode has no such limit servos.c . Servo signal and power — three rules settings.yaml 9.1.0 : - The outputs are enabled. While feature PWM_OUTPUT_ENABLE is off, neither the motor nor the servos get a signal, and a failed output assignment blocks arming with the PWMOUT flag status prints the line PWM output init error with the reason . Enable it after the output map on the Mixer tab matches the wiring. - Rate and filter. servo_pwm_rate = 50 Hz 50–498 is safe for any servo; 330 Hz is only for digital servos rated for it, otherwise an analog servo heats up and buzzes. servo_lpf_hz = 20 Hz 0–400, 0 — the filter is off smooths the command. The rule from the comment in servos.c : the cutoff below half of servo_pwm_rate — at 50 Hz everything above 25 Hz is distorted anyway; if you raise the servo rate, you can raise the cutoff too. The rate is one for all servos. - Power. A stalled servo draws amps, and the flight controller's BEC also feeds the receiver, the camera and the GPS; a 5 V sag reboots the MCU in the air. The current calculation and the choice of a separate BEC are in bf-servos-pwm the section on servo power is the same for any firmware . The bench check: both servos stalled at the diagonal stick extreme for 10 s — the flight controller does not reboot, the receiver does not lose the link, and the servo rail voltage in the OSD or on a voltmeter does not sag noticeably below the BEC rating. Battery calibration: the direction of the proportion In the source battery.c the voltage is proportional to vbat_scale , and the current is inversely proportional to current_meter_scale current = microvolts / scale . So: - vbat_scale_new = vbat_scal

text: summary The OSD in INAV is a grid of characters that the flight controller either overlays on the analog video itself with the MAX7456 chip or sends over a UART to a digital air unit, where the goggles draw it. This module covers both paths on INAV 9.1.0: which osd_video_system value and which port function to set for HDZero, Walksnail, DJI O3, DJI O4 and WTFOS, what grid each has, how the four layouts and their switching work, alarms with their units, the statistics screen, the custom elements osd_custom_elements , the CMS menu, the horizon and the correction of the home arrow for a pan servo. Power and wiring of the air units are in bf-hd-osd-video , the overview of the systems is in link-digital-video ; they are not repeated here. The lab needs no hardware: choose the port and the grid for four systems, parse ten osd_layout lines and find the elements that do not fit into a smaller grid, and convert alarm thresholds into firmware units. theory Who draws the OSD There are two paths, and they are mutually exclusive. - Analog. The board has a MAX7456 chip. The camera video passes through it, the chip, on commands from the processor SPI , overlays characters from the font stored in its own memory and passes the frame to the VTX. The grid is 30×16 PAL or 30×13 NTSC . - HD. The flight controller sends MSP DisplayPort commands to the air unit over a UART: “in row R, starting at column C, these characters”. The goggles draw them — with their own font. The flight controller does not know what is actually visible in the goggles. {{diagram:inav-osd-signal-path In analog the OSD is overlaid by the chip on the flight controller, in HD — by the goggles. If MSP DisplayPort is assigned in the ports, the MAX7456 is not initialized: both paths do not work at the same time.}} At startup fc_init.c INAV takes the first available output in this order: FrSky OSD → MSP DisplayPort if there is a port with this function → MAX7456. feature OSD must be enabled. The settings are read at boot, so after changing the port or osd_video_system you need save and a reboot. osd_video_system : value → grid → system In Betaflight HD goggles report the grid size themselves. In INAV you set the grid, with one setting. The nine values of 9.1.0 settings.yaml , the sizes — displayport_msp_osd.c : Value Grid columns×rows What for Font --- --- --- --- AUTO default analog: PAL or NTSC by the camera signal; over MSP — 30×16 an analog camera the MAX7456 memory PAL 30×16 analog PAL the MAX7456 memory NTSC 30×13 analog NTSC the MAX7456 memory HDZERO 50×18 HDZero the INAV font on the goggles side AVATAR 53×20 Walksnail Avatar the INAV font on the goggles side DJIWTF 60×22 old DJI Air Unit / Vista and DJI FPV goggles with WTFOS the INAV font, installed by WTFOS BF43COMPAT 30×16 DJI goggles with the Betaflight font, the SD grid the DJI font; what is missing — ? BFHDCOMPAT 53×20 DJI O3 and goggles without the INAV font the DJI font; what is missing — ? DJI_NATIVE 53×20 DJI O4 / O4 Pro and goggles on firmware that has the OSD type “INAV” the INAV font, built into the goggles What you need to know about DJI: - Compatibility modes BF43COMPAT , BFHDCOMPAT . The DJI font is single-page, 256 glyphs based on Betaflight; INAV has two pages, up to 512. The firmware remaps every INAV character to the nearest DJI glyph; if there is no match, it outputs ? osd_highlight_djis_missing_font_symbols = ON , default or a space OFF . In the document DJI compatible OSD.md these values are still called DJI43COMPAT and DJIHDCOMPAT — the 9.1.0 CLI does not accept such names. In the goggles the canvas has to be switched to HD by hand. - DJI_NATIVE appeared in 8.0.1. The release notes say: DJI released firmware for the O4 and the Goggles 2, 3, N3 and Integra that adds the INAV font and fixes arm detection on the O4; in the configurator select DJI_NATIVE, and in the goggles — the OSD type “INAV”; the value AVATAR gives the same grid and font. According to the 9.1.0 source DJI_NATIVE differs from AVATAR only in the index of the direction glyph osd.c , osd_hud.c . You cannot load your own font into such goggles OSD.md : “no custom fonts” . - Not verified: the version numbers of the goggles and air unit firmware from which the “INAV” OSD type works; whether the combination “O3 + updated Goggles 2 / Integra” shows the INAV font. If the goggles menu has no “INAV” item — use BFHDCOMPAT . - enable_broken_o4_workaround OFF : for an O4 on its first firmware, which did not see the arm state and stayed in low-power mode. The 8.0.1 notes promised to remove the setting in INAV 9, but it is there in 9.1.0. On an updated O4 it is not needed. WTFOS is a full DisplayPort implementation for the old DJI units: according to the INAV documentation it is better than the compatibility mode if you have the choice. The HDZero, Walksnail and WTFOS fonts are on the goggles side; the file names and folders on the SD card were not checked in this module — see the manual of your system. {{diagram:chart-inav-osd-canvas The grids differ by a factor of 2–3 in the number of cells. A layout built for 53×20 loses row 18 on 50×18, and six elements out of ten on 30×16: INAV does not move elements the way Betaflight does.}} The port: which function Port functions in INAV are bits of the mask in the serial command io/serial.h . The bit numbers do not match Betaflight, and serial lines are not moved between the firmwares. Function Mask When --- --- --- FUNCTION_MSP_OSD “MSP DisplayPort” on the Ports tab 33554432 1 << 25 all the HD systems from the table above; it is also VTX control over MSP FUNCTION_VTX_MSP is the same number FUNCTION_DJI_HD_OSD “DJI FPV VTX” 2097152 1 << 21 an old DJI Air Unit/Vista without WTFOS: a fixed set of DJI fields, not the INAV grid FUNCTION_FRSKY_OSD 1048576 1 << 20 FrSky PixelOSD The baud rate of the DisplayPort port is taken from the last field of the serial line the peripheral baud rate , 115200 by default. An example for UART4: serial 3 33554432 115200 115200 0 115200 . Th
