Look inside SITL Step 2. Trace the chain Step 3. Stop and start a module Step 4. Read a `.msg` What you should get and what to write down Lab
text: summary PX4 is not one program but a set of independent modules that exchange messages over the uORB bus using publish/subscribe. That explains almost everything about PX4: why you can restart a module in flight, why ROS 2 sees the autopilot's internals directly, and how data travels from a sensor to a motor. This module covers the flight stack and the middleware, .msg definitions, update rates and the tools for looking inside a running system. theory Two layers - Middleware : sensor drivers, communication with the outside world MAVLink, uXRCE-DDS , the uORB bus and the simulation layer. - Flight stack : the algorithms: state estimation estimator , controllers, navigator, commander, control allocation. From sensor to motor 1. IMU drivers read the sensor FIFO kilohertz rates, up to 8 kHz on modern IMUs ; after filtering, the gyro data is published to vehicle_angular_velocity at IMU_GYRO_RATEMAX 800 Hz on a multicopter: the airframe raises the parameter default of 400 through rc.mc_defaults , and integrated data goes to vehicle_imu at IMU_INTEG_RATE 200 Hz . 2. EKF2 fuses the IMU, GPS, barometer and magnetometer into an attitude, velocity and position estimate. 3. Navigator decides where to fly: mission, return, hold. 4. Position controller turns the desired position into a desired attitude and thrust. 5. Attitude controller → desired angular rates; rate controller → torques. 6. Control allocation turns torques and thrust into commands for specific motors and servos from the frame geometry CA_AIRFRAME , CA_ROTOR . 7. Output drivers: PWM/DShot. Commander is the arbiter: arming and disarming, mode changes, readiness checks, failsafes. uORB Each module publishes topics and subscribes to other modules' topics. A topic is defined by a .msg file CamelCase file name → snake_case topic: VehicleAttitude.msg → vehicle_attitude , and the uint64 timestamp field is mandatory. One .msg can define several topics TOPICS ... . The bus is asynchronous: a subscriber wakes up when new data arrives, so the publisher sets the module's rate. It is the same idea as ROS, which is why the uXRCE-DDS bridge feels so natural: it simply exposes part of the uORB topics to the outside. Execution Modules are separate tasks threads with priorities on NuttX; threads of one process on Linux/macOS in SITL . You start and stop them with <module start/stop , check the load with top on a flight controller; listener cpuload in SITL , topic rates with uorb top , and contents with listener <topic . Why it matters - When you debug odd behavior, you look for a module and a topic , not a "parameter": what was published, at what rate, and what the controller received. - Your own code in PX4 is a new module that subscribes to topics, not an edit of someone else's. - ULog logs are just recorded topics; when you analyze them you read the same messages. Modules by name where to look in the code src/modules/ : sensors sensor aggregation, sensor_combined , ekf2 state estimation , commander arming, modes, failsafes, preflight checks , navigator missions, RTL, geofence, position_setpoint_triplet , mc_pos_control position → attitude + thrust , mc_att_control attitude → angular rate , mc_rate_control rate → torques, vehicle_torque_setpoint / vehicle_thrust_setpoint , control_allocator torques → actuator_motors / actuator_servos , logger , mavlink , uxrce_dds_client , land_detector , battery_status , mc_autotune_attitude_control . Drivers are in src/drivers/ imu, gps, barometer, dshot, pwm_out . The IMU → motor path: sensors → ekf2 → mc_pos_control → mc_att_control → mc_rate_control → control_allocator → dshot / pwm_out . Execution: work queues and priorities On NuttX most modules are not separate threads but items on a work queue with a priority wq:rate_ctrl is higher; wq:nav_and_controllers , wq:hp_default , wq:lp_default are lower : fast tasks rate control wake up when gyro data arrives and run first; work_queue status lists them. Logger and mavlink are separate tasks; EKF2 also runs on a work queue ScheduledWorkItem . top in the console shows CPU load per task; overload shows up as growing latency and warnings. The firmware has one hard limit: with the load above COM_CPU_MAX 95 % for more than 2 s, arming is denied; the source defines no other load "norm", so judge the headroom for your build from top on the ground and from the log. Console: commands by architecture layer The console is nsh on a flight controller QGC → Analyze Tools → MAVLink Console and pxh in SITL. How to use it: start from the question "where in the chain sensor → module → topic → output did it get lost", run the layer's command from the table, and check the output against the last column. The full list, options and the nsh/pxh differences are in px4-console-params . Layer Question Command What counts as normal --- --- --- --- Firmware which board and build? ver all HW arch , PX4 version , PX4 git-hash ; write them down before any change Boot which drivers started? dmesg flight controller only the driver start line; Conflicting config means two drivers on one port Module is the module alive? <module status : sensors , ekf2 , commander , mavlink , logger , gps , dshot , pwm_out , uavcan , navigator not not running ; for ekf2 status , the estimate flags are 1 Topic is data flowing, and at what rate? listener <topic -n 5 , uorb top new messages, not Giving up ; the rate matches the publishing module Execution is there enough CPU? top flight controller , work_queue status ; listener cpuload in SITL load comfortably below COM_CPU_MAX = 95 % Module restart after a parameter change <module stop / start on the ground only, disarmed Commander why won't it arm? commander check , then dmesg Preflight Fail: … lines Parameters what value is actually set? param show <name x : the parameter is used; + : the value differs from the default; : changed and not saved yet Storage and configuration Parameters live in the file the board defines CONFIG_BOARD_PARAM_FILE : by default the FRAM/EEPRO

text: summary The PX4 console and parameter system, from the 1.17.0 source: how to get into nsh on a flight controller and pxh in SITL and what each one lacks, every param subcommand with its exact semantics, which layers make up a parameter value and which of them reach storage, how the four kinds of reset and the three kinds of backup differ, why a parameter "disappears" from QGC, which commands to use to inspect sensors, modules, CPU load and the log, and in what order rcS applies config.txt , extras.txt and rc.txt from the SD card. After this module you can look at a param show -c listing and say what will survive a reset and a reboot, pick the command for a question, and name the output line that confirms the hypothesis. The lab needs no hardware and no simulator: analyzing a training parameter list, four troubleshooting situations, a pair of files for the SD card, and finding the dangerous steps in a procedure; the answers are checked against the reference on the page. theory What is in the module and how to read it The module covers three topics, best read in this order. First the console: how to get into it and which commands exist on a flight controller and which only in the simulator. Then parameters: value layers, storage, the param command, resets, reboots and backups; this is where most of the non-obvious behavior lives. Last come the inspection commands, the startup scripts and the "which tool for which question" table. Port, output and failsafe assignment is not repeated here: that is in px4-hardware-peripherals, px4-outputs-servos and px4-safety-return. Getting into the console A flight controller runs the NuttX shell, nsh . SITL has no NuttX; it uses PX4's own shell, pxh . The PX4 modules are the same in both; the system commands differ. Entry How to open it What you see When to use it --- --- --- --- QGC MAVLink Console Analyze Tools → MAVLink Console, over USB or telemetry only the output of the command you ran by default: no soldering needed Tools/mavlink_shell.py ./Tools/mavlink_shell.py /dev/ttyACM0 , QGC closed the same, in a terminal scripts, recording a session to a file System console debug UART a 3.3 V USB–UART adapter on the debug port, terminal at 57600 8N1 all boot output and the output of every module the board does not boot, MAVLink did not come up nsh over USB SYS_USB_AUTO = 1, a terminal, press Enter three times a regular nsh no MAVLink client at hand pxh in SITL the terminal running make px4_sitl … all output of the process the simulator Rule of thumb: start with the MAVLink Console; you need the debug UART only where MAVLink is not running yet, that is, for hangs during boot and errors in the startup scripts. How it works. The MAVLink shell travels in SERIAL_CONTROL messages id 126 with the device SERIAL_CONTROL_DEV_SHELL = 10, 70 bytes per message; it is not a MAV_CMD . One shell per MAVLink instance. mavlink_shell.py takes a port device ,baud , IP:port for UDP, tcp:IP:port ; with no argument it looks for a serial port itself and --baudrate / -b , 57600 by default; it needs pymavlink and pyserial . SYS_USB_AUTO : 0 Disabled, 1 Auto-detect three carriage returns in a row start nshterm on /dev/ttyACM0 , the start of a u-blox packet gives GPS passthrough , 2 MAVLink only the default . The parameter needs a reboot. The fmu-v6x system console is USART3 at 57600 baud nuttx-config/nsh/defconfig . Messages from other modules do not reach the MAVLink shell. Read them with dmesg , a 4 KB ring buffer of console output: old lines get pushed out, so look at the boot output right after boot. dmesg -f & keeps the output running in the background. nsh and pxh: what is there and what is not The board build sets the command list, in boards/<vendor /<board /default.px4board . A command missing from the build answers command not found . Command px4/fmu-v6x SITL px4/sitl --- --- --- param , listener , uorb , work_queue , perf , ver yes yes actuator_test , tune_control , led_control , bsondump yes yes top , dmesg , reboot yes no i2cdetect , nshterm , hardfault_log , mtd yes no ls , cat , free , ps , df , cp , rm nsh built-ins yes no sd_bench no fmu-v6c has it yes failure no yes shutdown , list_tasks , list_files no yes This holds for all three releases 1.15–1.17 and for the v1.18.0 board files . Consequences: top does not work in SITL, so check the load there with listener cpuload and work_queue status ; the stock flight controller build has no failure px4-safety-return ; testing the card with sd_bench on a Pixhawk 6X needs a custom build. Where a parameter value comes from A parameter has three layers src/lib/parameters/parameters.cpp , and a module gets the value of the topmost non-empty one: 1. Firmware default : the number from PARAM_DEFINE_ or module.yaml , compiled in. 2. Startup default : what the board scripts rc.board_defaults , the airframe and config.txt wrote with param set-default . It lives in RAM and is rebuilt on every boot. 3. Saved value : everything written with param set , from QGC, by a calibration or by a driver itself. {{diagram:px4-console-param-layers The parameter value is the topmost non-empty of three layers; only what differs from the startup default goes to storage, so a value equal to the airframe default silently changes after a firmware update.}} Example: the firmware default of RTL_RETURN_ALT is 60 m, rc.mc_defaults sets 30 m for a multicopter, and the operator can write their own. The main storage rule: saving writes only third-layer values that are not equal to the startup default param_export_internal . If you set RTL_RETURN_ALT = 30 on a quadcopter, the file does not contain it. Hence the px4-intro rule: after a firmware update everything that matched a default gets the new default. Storage and autosave The storage format is BSON: a sequence of "type, name, value" records, integers as int32, floats as double. Where it goes depends on the board: Board Main storage Backup --- --- --- fmu-v6x, fmu-v6c FRAM /fs/mtd_params /fs/microsd/parameters_

text: summary Everything you connect to a PX4 flight controller apart from the motors and the receiver: GPS and compass, rangefinders, airspeed sensor, telemetry and MAVLink instances, DroneCAN, OSD, the status LED and the buzzer. They all follow one pattern: pick the port with a _CONFIG / _CFG parameter or enable the driver with a SENS_EN_ parameter, reboot, then check with status and listener . The module gives the PX4 1.18.0 parameter tables with defaults and the differences from 1.15–1.17, the fmu-v6x port numbers, the rule for computing a MAVLink stream in bytes per second, and what the LED colors and tunes mean. The lab needs no hardware and no simulator: assigning eight devices to Pixhawk 6X ports, a budget for a SiK link at 57600 baud, decoding the indications and finding errors in parameters; you check your answers against the reference on the page. theory The general pattern: parameter → reboot → check In PX4 a peripheral driver does not run "by itself". A script starts it at boot, and only if a parameter allows it. There are three ways. - UART. The driver has a port parameter: GPS_1_CONFIG , MAV_1_CONFIG , SENS_TFMINI_CFG , MSP_OSD_CONFIG . The value is a port number from the table below; 0 means the driver is off. The baud rate comes from SER_<port _BAUD . From these definitions the build generates the rc.serial script: for each driver it reads the port parameter and runs a command such as tfmini start -d /dev/ttyS1 . - I²C and SPI. There is no port to pick; the driver is enabled with SENS_EN_<sensor . The rc.sensors script checks the parameter and starts the driver on the external I²C bus the -X flag . - DroneCAN. The bus driver is enabled with UAVCAN_ENABLE , the data types it accepts with UAVCAN_SUB_ . Almost all of these parameters are marked reboot_required : nothing changes until you reboot. The check always has two steps, in the QGC MAVLink Console: 1. The driver is running: gps status , tfmini status , mavlink status , uavcan status , msp_osd status , airspeed_selector status , sensors status . 2. Data is flowing: listener <topic : sensor_gps , sensor_mag , distance_sensor , differential_pressure , airspeed_validated , telemetry_status . The second instance of a topic is the -i 1 flag. What a uORB topic and listener are is covered in px4-architecture. {{diagram:px4-periph-enable-flow The parameter only allows the start: the driver is started by a script at boot, so the order is always the same: parameter, reboot, status, listener.}} One port, one driver. If two parameters point at the same port, the script gives the port to the first one and prints Conflicting config for /dev/ttyS… for the second visible in dmesg and does not start it. Which one comes first depends on the order of drivers in the build, so do not rely on it. The driver may not be in the firmware. The set of drivers is defined by the boards/<vendor /<board /default.px4board file. If the parameter is not in the QGC list, the driver is not built; you add it with your own build make px4_fmu-v6x_default boardconfig . In the tables below the "v6x" column shows whether the driver is in the stock Pixhawk 6X firmware px4/fmu-v6x of version 1.18.0. fmu-v6x ports Port numbers are the same on every board Tools/serial/generate_config.py ; only the set of ports differs. Value Name in QGC Pixhawk 6X connector Device SER_ _BAUD , default Used by default --- --- --- --- --- --- 0 Disabled — — — — 101 TELEM 1 TELEM1 /dev/ttyS6 SER_TEL1_BAUD = 57600 MAV_0_CONFIG 102 TELEM 2 TELEM2 /dev/ttyS4 SER_TEL2_BAUD = 921600 — 103 TELEM 3 TELEM3 /dev/ttyS1 SER_TEL3_BAUD = 57600 — 201 GPS 1 GPS1 /dev/ttyS0 SER_GPS1_BAUD = 0 auto GPS_1_CONFIG 202 GPS 2 GPS2 /dev/ttyS7 SER_GPS2_BAUD = 0 auto — 300 Radio Controller PX4IO/RC line /dev/ttyS5 SER_RC_BAUD = 0 in the list since 1.17; on a board with an IO processor the line is taken by px4io 401 EXT2 UART4 & I2C /dev/ttyS3 SER_EXT2_BAUD = 57600 — 1000 Ethernet ETH network, UDP — MAV_2_CONFIG The value 1000 is available only to drivers with network support: MAVLink and uXRCE-DDS. SER_ _BAUD takes a fixed list of rates from 50 to 3 000 000; 0 means "auto" and only suits drivers that find the rate themselves GPS . {{diagram:px4-periph-ports-v6x fmu-v6x has six freely assignable UARTs: two GPS units, a companion, a telemetry radio, a rangefinder and an OSD take all of them, while airspeed and the ESCs go to I²C and CAN.}} GPS Parameter Default Values --- --- --- GPS_1_CONFIG / GPS_2_CONFIG 201 / 0 port of the main and the second receiver SER_GPS1_BAUD 0 auto: the driver tries the rates itself GPS_1_PROTOCOL / GPS_2_PROTOCOL 1 0 auto detect slower start , 1 u-blox, 2 MTK, 3 Ashtech / Trimble, 4 Emlid Reach, 5 Femtomes, 6 NMEA GPS_1_GNSS / GPS_2_GNSS 0 bitmask: bit 0 GPS with QZSS , 1 SBAS, 2 Galileo, 3 BeiDou, 4 GLONASS, 5 NAVIC; 0 means as the receiver is configured. u-blox only GPS_UBX_DYNMODEL 7 2 stationary, 4 automotive, 6 airborne < 1 g, 7 airborne < 2 g, 8 airborne < 4 g GPS_SAT_INFO 0 1 publishes satellite_info GPS_CFG_WIPE 0 1 wipes the flash configuration of the u-blox module at boot since 1.17 SENS_GPS_MASK 7 blending of two receivers: bit 0 uses speed accuracy, 1 horizontal position accuracy, 2 vertical position accuracy; 0 means no blending SENS_GPS_PRIME 0 primary instance without blending: 0, 1; −1 means equal priority SENS_GPS_TAU 10 s 1…100 s: time constant for smoothing the offsets between receivers GPS_UBX_DYNMODEL across versions. In 1.15 and 1.16 the multicopter airframe defaults rc.mc_defaults set 6, "airborne < 1 g". In 1.17 that line is gone, and a multicopter gets the parameter default, 7. A plane gets 8 in all three versions. If you fly 1.16 or older, set 7 by hand: the model tells the receiver's filter what dynamics to expect, and a multicopter easily exceeds 1 g. Two receivers. Gimbal servo pulse and the stick Step 2. Trigger distance and interval Step 3. Geotag error from delay Step 4. Three payloads and three errors Moving to real hardware
text: summary PX4 1.18.0 parameters and wiring for a gimbal and a survey camera: what MNT_MODE_IN and MNT_MODE_OUT select, how an angle becomes microseconds through MNT_MIN_PITCH / MNT_MAX_PITCH , MNT_RANGE_ROLL / MNT_RANGE_YAW and the output's MIN / CENT / MAX , which MAVLink Gimbal v2 messages the firmware accepts and sends, how TRIG_MODE , TRIG_INTERFACE , TRIG_DISTANCE , TRIG_MIN_INTERVA work, what the CAM_CAP_FBACK shutter feedback gives you, and which ULog topics carry the time and position of a frame. General gimbal theory is in payload-gimbal , GSD and overlap calculations are in per-mapping ; here is only the PX4 side. After the module you can pick the wiring by gimbal and camera type and compute the gimbal servo pulse, the trigger distance and interval, and the geotag error from shutter delay. The lab needs no hardware and no simulator: four calculations and a parameter fragment with three errors; you check the answers against the reference on the page. theory What the module covers and how to read it The module covers three PX4 subsystems: the gimbal module, the camera_trigger driver shutter release and the camera_capture driver hot shoe feedback , plus what they put in the log for georeferencing. The gimbal comes first: where the command comes from, where it goes, how the pulse is computed and how the firmware acts as the gimbal manager. Then the camera: trigger modes and interfaces, distance-based capture, feedback and geotags. At the end, two selection tables and the differences across 1.15–1.18. In 1.18 the gimbal module changed the most: pitch limits became asymmetric, the MNT_OFF_ offsets were removed, and a setpoint filter MNT_TAU appeared, which changes both the pulse arithmetic and how the stick behaves. The manager / device roles and the protocol messages themselves are covered in payload-gimbal and mav-services , GSD and overlap in per-mapping : here they are only referenced. Three modules and when they start All three modules are in the px4_fmu-v6x_default and px4_fmu-v6c_default builds CONFIG_MODULES_GIMBAL , CONFIG_DRIVERS_CAMERA_TRIGGER , CONFIG_DRIVERS_CAMERA_CAPTURE , CONFIG_MODULES_CAMERA_FEEDBACK in default.px4board , but the rcS startup script starts them based on parameters: Module Condition in rcS What it does --- --- --- gimbal MNT_MODE_IN −1 accepts commands, computes angles, sends them to the output camera_trigger and camera_feedback TRIG_MODE 0 releases the shutter; publishes camera_trigger and camera_capture camera_capture CAM_CAP_FBACK 0 catches the edge from the hot shoe, publishes camera_trigger with feedback = true By default MNT_MODE_IN = −1 and TRIG_MODE = 0: neither the gimbal nor the trigger runs, and gimbal status in the console px4-console-params answers "not running". MNT_MODE_IN , MNT_MODE_OUT and all TRIG_ and CAM_CAP_ are read at startup: change them and reboot the board. The module rereads the other MNT_ on the fly. camera_feedback starts only together with the trigger: feedback without TRIG_MODE 0 will not fill the camera_capture topic. Command source: MNT_MODE_IN Value Source When to choose it --- --- --- −1 disabled default no gimbal 0 Auto: RC and MAVLink Gimbal v2 together the pilot has the RC plus a ground station or a mission 1 RC only AUX channels a simple servo gimbal, no ground station or missions 2 ROI only protocol v1, to be deprecated do not choose for new projects 3 DO_MOUNT_CONTROL only v1, to be deprecated do not choose for new projects 4 MAVLink Gimbal v2 only control from a ground station, a mission or a companion; the RC does not steer the gimbal 5 since 1.18 fixed world-frame attitude, no commands accepted the gimbal holds pitch MNT_FIXED_PITCH −90…90°, default 0 , for example a camera that always looks at nadir The rule: you need the RC and something else, 0; the RC only, 1; software control only, 4. In mode 1 mission commands and ROI do not move the gimbal. In mode 0 whoever updated last is in control; to keep the RC from grabbing the gimbal by accident it needs a "large move": the channel must change by more than 0.25 on the −1…+1 scale one eighth of full travel, 12.5 % from the last accepted value, on any of the three axes. After such a move primary control goes to the autopilot, and the GIMBAL_MANAGER_SET_ATTITUDE stream from the ground station is ignored until the station takes control back with DO_GIMBAL_MANAGER_CONFIGURE . A detail from the code: the MAV_PROTOCOL_CAPABILITY_COMPONENT_IMPLEMENTS_GIMBAL_MANAGER flag in AUTOPILOT_VERSION is set only with MNT_MODE_IN = 4; with 0 it is absent. How a particular ground station reacts to that cannot be seen in the PX4 tree not verified . Where the command goes: MNT_MODE_OUT Value Output What PX4 computes --- --- --- 0 AUX: up to three PWM outputs with the Gimbal Roll / Pitch / Yaw functions angles, stabilization MNT_DO_STAB , limits, mapping to −1…+1 1 MAVLink v1: COMMAND_LONG DO_MOUNT_CONTROL to MNT_MAV_SYSID / MNT_MAV_COMPID angles in degrees after the limits before 1.18 MNT_OFF_ were added to them 2 MAVLink Gimbal v2: GIMBAL_DEVICE_SET_ATTITUDE nothing: the quaternion, rates and lock flags go to the device as they are The output functions are in output_functions.yaml : Gimbal Roll 420, Gimbal Pitch 421, Gimbal Yaw 422. You assign them on the Actuators screen like any servo; timer groups, 50 Hz and servo power are in px4-outputs-servos . text: summary Multicopter control in PX4 is a cascade of three loops position → attitude → angular rate plus control allocation, which distributes torques to the motors. This module shows which parameter belongs to which loop, how the rate controller form differs a K multiplier instead of a plain P , what manual tuning from the step response looks like, and why autotune is the right answer for most frames. If you come from Betaflight, there is a mapping table. theory The cascade 1. Position controller MPC_ : position error → desired velocity MPC_XY_P , MPC_Z_P , velocity error → desired acceleration/tilt MPC_XY_VEL_P_ACC and others . The hover throttle MPC_THR_HOVER and the velocity limits MPC_XY_VEL_MAX , MPC_Z_VEL_MAX_UP/DN live here too. 2. Attitude controller MC_ROLL_P , MC_PITCH_P , MC_YAW_P : attitude error → desired angular rate. P only. 3. Rate controller MC_ROLLRATE_P/I/D/K , the same for PITCH and YAW, plus MC_ RATE_FF : angular rate error → torque. The fastest loop; it defines how the vehicle "feels". 4. Control allocation : torques and thrust → motor commands from the geometry in CA_AIRFRAME , CA_ROTOR_COUNT , CA_ROTOR<n _PX/PY/KM . The rate controller form PX4 uses the parallel form with a common K gain: output = K × P·e + I·∫e + D·de/dt . MC_ROLLRATE_K scales all three at once, so the first step of coarse tuning is K, not P. Betaflight has no such multiplier; the Master Multiplier slider plays that role there. Mapping from Betaflight Betaflight PX4 --- --- P/I/D roll rate MC_ROLLRATE_P/I/D × MC_ROLLRATE_K Feedforward MC_ROLLRATE_FF Angle mode strength MC_ROLL_P Gyro filters IMU_GYRO_CUTOFF , IMU_DGYRO_CUTOFF , notch IMU_GYRO_NF _FRQ Throttle hover / air mode MPC_THR_HOVER , MC_AIRMODE Autotune For most frames the documentation recommends autotune outright: it is faster and usually gives a good result. It identifies a model from the responses in a hover and applies the rate gains and attitude P it finds; MC_AT_APPLY controls when they are applied in the air, after disarm, or not at all, logging only . Tune manually when autotune cannot cope: unusual frames, heavy vibration, large vehicles. Manual tuning from the step response Order: filters → rate K, then D, then I → attitude P → position. One step: Acro or Stabilized, sharp short stick inputs, a log, then vehicle_rates_setpoint vs. vehicle_angular_velocity in Flight Review. Overshoot: lower K or raise D; slow response: raise K; drift: raise I. Disable MC_AIRMODE while tuning; change gains by 20–30 % per iteration, 5–10 % for the final touch. Same method and same metrics as in the module on PID from data. Defaults and what they mean MC_ROLLRATE_P = 0.15, I = 0.2, D = 0.003, K = 1.0, FF = 0 the output is normalized torque per 1 rad/s of error ; MC_ROLL_P = 4.0 angular rate per radian of attitude error → 1/s; 6.5 before 1.17 , MC_YAW_P = 2.8; position: MPC_XY_P = 0.95 1/s , velocity → acceleration MPC_XY_VEL_P_ACC = 1.8, I_ACC = 0.4, D_ACC = 0.2; MPC_Z_P = 1.0. Hover throttle MPC_THR_HOVER = 0.5 normalized , refined by the hover thrust estimator HTE_ . Filters: IMU_GYRO_CUTOFF = 40 Hz, IMU_DGYRO_CUTOFF = 20 Hz 30 before 1.17 , loop rate IMU_GYRO_RATEMAX = 800 Hz on a multicopter the airframe raises the parameter default of 400 , static notch IMU_GYRO_NF0_FRQ / BW 0 = off, BW 20 Hz , dynamic notch from ESC RPM IMU_GYRO_DNF_EN bitmask: bit 0 ESC RPM, bit 1 onboard FFT IMU_GYRO_FFT_EN , IMU_GYRO_DNF_MIN = 25 Hz. Air mode MC_AIRMODE 0 Disabled, 1 Roll/Pitch, 2 Roll/Pitch/Yaw . All differences between the 1.15/1.16 and 1.17 defaults are in the upgrade table in px4-intro. Units matter: the error is in rad/s and the output is a fraction of the maximum torque. P = 0.15 means an error of 1 rad/s 57 deg/s gives 15% torque. Comparing with Betaflight dimensionless "45" only works qualitatively, through the "Control theory" module ζ, phase margin . Defaults for every axis v1.17.0; the same in v1.18.0 1.18 adds an optional feed-forward to the attitude loop from a second-order reference model: MC_REF_FF 0…1, default 0, the old behavior , natural frequency MC_REF_W_N 50 rad/s and the cap MC_REF_FF_MAX 100 deg/s mc_att_control_params.yaml , v1.18.0 . The table below is without it. How to read it: start from the axis and the cascade level; the table gives the number a generic airframe starts from 4001 Generic Quadcopter does not override the gains; ready-made airframes for specific frames can ; check that param show MC_ROLLRATE and MC_PITCHRATE , MC_YAWRATE ; is only allowed at the end of the filter in the console matches the table as long as you have changed nothing. Level Roll Pitch Yaw Unit --- --- --- --- --- rate P / I / D 0.15 / 0.2 / 0.003 0.15 / 0.2 / 0.003 0.2 / 0.1 / 0 torque fraction per rad/s rate K / FF 1.0 / 0 1.0 / 0 1.0 / 0 — integrator limit MC_RR_INT_LIM , MC_PR_INT_LIM , MC_YR_INT_LIM 0.30 0.30 0.30 torque fraction attitude P MC_ROLL_P , MC_PITCH_P , MC_YAW_P 4.0 6.5 before 1.17 4.0 6.5 before 1.17 2.8 1/s angular rate limit in attitude modes MC_ROLLRATE_MAX , MC_PITCHRATE_MAX , MC_YAWRATE_MAX 220 220 200 deg/s Yaw is different on purpose: D = 0, a higher P, a lower I, and MC_YAW_WEIGHT = 0.4 0…1 lowers the priority of yaw relative to roll and pitch in the attitude loop; it does not change the MC_YAW_P gain itself. The reason: a multicopter has much less control torque in yaw it comes from the difference in propeller reaction torques , and yaw is not critical for hovering. text: summary PX4 can expose uORB topics directly in ROS 2: the uXRCE-DDS client on the flight controller and the agent on the companion computer carry messages both ways. ROS nodes get attitude, position and commands without a MAVLink wrapper. This module shows how the bridge works inside where topic names with the _vN suffix come from, rates and QoS, how timestamps are translated , how to bring it up in SITL and on board, what px4_msgs is, how offboard control works OffboardControlMode + TrajectorySetpoint + VehicleCommand , and the exact rule by which PX4 drops you out of Offboard when you go quiet. Lab: a script reads dds_topics.yaml and the PX4 1.17.0 message definitions, prints the topic names, rate caps and UART load, and computes when Offboard is lost; then your own offboard node in SITL. theory The uXRCE-DDS bridge - The client uxrce_dds_client in PX4 publishes and subscribes to a limited set of uORB topics listed in dds_topics.yaml . - The agent MicroXRCEAgent on a companion computer or PC receives them over UDP or serial and exposes them in DDS, which means in ROS 2. - On the ROS 2 side the messages come from the px4_msgs package; the px4_msgs branch must match the PX4 version release/1.17 for 1.17 , or the definitions will not match. Since 1.16 messages are versioned: the topic of a message with a version above 0 gets a _vN suffix. In 1.17.0 these are the outgoing vehicle_status_v1 , vehicle_local_position_v1 , battery_status_v1 , home_position_v1 , airspeed_validated_v1 , arming_check_request_v1 and the incoming vehicle_attitude_setpoint_v1 , arming_check_reply_v1 ; in 1.16 only vehicle_status_v1 , and 1.15 has no suffixes. For mismatched versions there is the Message Translation Node experimental since 1.16 . Topics appear in ROS 2 as /fmu/out/ from PX4 and /fmu/in/ to PX4 . The client builds the name: the string from dds_topics.yaml plus _vN if the .msg sets MESSAGE_VERSION = N 0 generate_topic_name in src/modules/uxrce_dds_client/utilities.hpp . So VehicleLocalPosition.msg version 1 gives /fmu/out/vehicle_local_position_v1 , and TrajectorySetpoint.msg version 0 gives /fmu/in/trajectory_setpoint with no suffix. If a topic is not in dds_topics.yaml , it is not in ROS 2 either, however hard you look: 1.17.0 has 27 outgoing and 38 incoming topics, and vehicle_angular_velocity , for example, is commented out. To add a topic you edit dds_topics.yaml and rebuild the firmware; there is no parameter for it. {{diagram:px4-dds-topic-naming The _v1 suffix depends on the message version, not on the direction: the old name without the suffix goes silent after upgrading to 1.17.}} The version changes with an incompatible field change, and the next release may bump it. In PX4 1.18.0 released November 24, 2026, UTC VehicleStatus became version 4 and the topic is /fmu/out/vehicle_status_v4 ; vehicle_command_ack got the _v1 suffix, the vehicle_attitude cap dropped from 100 to 50 Hz, and arming_check_request_v1 lost its 5 Hz cap with no rate_limit it now runs at the default interval of 4 ms, up to 250 Hz ; new outgoing topics were added vtx , input_rc , config_overrides_confirm_v1 and others , and the step 1 output for v1.18.0 gives the full list checked with the lab below on the v1.17.0 and v1.18.0 tags . The lesson: do not type the topic name into a node by hand; build it from the message class's MESSAGE_VERSION constant, so updating px4_msgs together with the firmware changes the name by itself. Inside, the client works like this read from the uxrce_dds_client code, v1.17.0 . On start it creates a session with the agent key UXRCE_DDS_KEY , domain UXRCE_DDS_DOM_ID , then a DataWriter for each publications entry and a DataReader for each subscriptions entry. The client checks the link with pings: if the traffic in either direction is zero, it pings the agent once a second and after three missed replies ~3 s tears down the session and creates it again checkConnectivity . UXRCE_DDS_TX_TO 3 s drops the session if the client itself has sent nothing for that many seconds, UXRCE_DDS_RX_TO default −1, disabled if it has received nothing. So after an agent restart the client usually restores the session by itself, without rebooting the flight controller read from the code, not tested on a bench ; if /fmu/in/ topics do not get through after a restart, enable UXRCE_DDS_RX_TO . The client sends every topic in publications whether or not anyone in ROS 2 subscribes to it: the link load is set by the list in the firmware, not by your nodes. Rates, QoS and bandwidth The rate_limit field in dds_topics.yaml caps the rate of each outgoing topic: the client calls orb_set_interval with a period of 1000/ rate_limit ms, truncated to whole milliseconds, and 10 ms without rate_limit UXRCE_DEFAULT_POLL_INTERVAL_MS . So a topic without rate_limit goes out no faster than 100 Hz , even if uORB publishes it at 250 Hz, and the stock dds_topics.yaml of 1.17.0 has no values above 100, so every outgoing topic is capped at 100 Hz your own rate_limit: 200. in a custom build would raise the cap : vehicle_odometry and vehicle_attitude up to 100 Hz, vehicle_local_position_v1 up to 50, vehicle_status_v1 up to 5, battery_status_v1 up to 1 Hz. The real rate can be lower than the cap if the PX4 module publishes less often. In 1.18.0 the default interval is 4 ms 250 Hz , the period is rounded to the nearest millisecond, and rate_limit: 0 or unlimited removes the cap generate_dds_topics.py , dds_topics.h.em , v1.18.0 . QoS is hard-coded in the client: outgoing DataWriters are BEST_EFFORT, TRANSIENT_LOCAL, KEEP_LAST; incoming DataReaders are BEST_EFFORT, VOLATILE, KEEP_LAST. The DDS compatibility rules turn this into a simple rule: a ROS 2 subscriber to /fmu/out/ must be BEST_EFFORT a RELIABLE subscriber is incompatible with a best-effort writer: the topic shows in ros2 topic list , but no data arrives , while a publisher to /fmu/in/ can be either. text: summary The Jetson Orin Nano/NX is the standard vision companion for PX4: CUDA and TensorRT in 7–40 W. This module puts the whole setup together: roles and the boundary of responsibility, choosing JetPack and ROS 2 for the same Ubuntu as of November 2026, JetPack 7.2.2 on Ubuntu 24.04 supports the whole Orin family , power modes and Super Mode, power supply and heat, the physical connection to TELEM2, how to find the right UART on your JetPack version the device name differs between versions , the two links MAVLink and uXRCE-DDS with their PX4 parameters, bandwidth and checks, starting the agent with systemd, and the latency budget of the "camera → command" chain. The lab starts with a link and power budget a script that runs on any computer , then the connection and measurements on hardware. The first-generation Jetson Nano is out of support JetPack 4, Ubuntu 18.04 , so do not use it for new projects. theory Roles and the boundary The Pixhawk PX4 does stabilization, EKF, failsafes and missions; the Jetson does vision, planning, ROS 2 and networking. The boundary is the same as in the "Companion: role and boundaries" module: without the Jetson the vehicle must still fly and come back, and losing the companion in offboard is handled by the PX4 failsafe COM_OF_LOSS_T , COM_OBL_RC_ACT , not by hope. PX4 also watches the companion a second way: if the HEARTBEAT from a component of type "onboard controller" stops arriving over MAVLink, after 5 s COM_OBC_LOSS_T before 1.18, 5 s by default commander reports "Connection to mission computer lost". It is only a warning with no action Commander.cpp , v1.17.0 and v1.18.0 ; the offboard failsafe sets the reaction. In 1.18 the timeout is not a parameter: the 5 s are hard-coded and COM_OBC_LOSS_T is removed. Which Jetson and which system Board Power modes: original → Super nvpmodel INT8 sparse, TOPS: original → Super What it gives you --- --- --- --- Orin Nano 4 GB 7, 10 W → 7 or 10 , 25 W, MAXN SUPER 20 → 34 a minimal detector Orin Nano 8 GB 7, 15 W → 15, 25 W, MAXN SUPER 40 → 67 the main choice for detection and tracking Orin NX 8 GB 10, 15, 20 W, MAXN → +40 W, MAXN SUPER 70 → 117 the same module form factor, twice the compute Orin NX 16 GB 10, 15, 25 W, MAXN → +40 W, MAXN SUPER 100 → 157 several models at once Jetson Nano 2019 out of support, JetPack 4 — not for new projects The power modes and TOPS are from NVIDIA's Super Mode announcement JetPack 6.2, January 2025 . For the Orin Nano 4 GB the announcement contradicts itself 10 or 7 W in the lowest Super mode , so check nvpmodel -q on your board. TOPS are peak sparse INT8; the real speed of a model is in per-edge-ml and comp-jetson-nano . The JetPack version decides the Ubuntu version, and with it the ROS 2 distribution. As of November 2026 the current one is JetPack 7.2.2 Jetson Linux 39.2.2 : Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, CUDA 13.2.2, supporting Thor and the whole Orin family; it pairs with ROS 2 Jazzy and the Micro XRCE-DDS agent v2.4.3. The previous line is JetPack 6.2.x on Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble and agent v2.4.2. The PX4 1.17 documentation names Humble on 22.04 as the recommended platform, but it covers Jazzy too the agent version table . The rule: pick the "JetPack + ROS 2" pair for the same Ubuntu, and never install ROS 2 on an Ubuntu it was not built for; that road leads to source builds and endless dependency trouble. A new project on Orin: JetPack 7.2.x + Jazzy; an existing Humble stack is not worth moving for one Jetson. Two JetPack 7.2.x traps on the Orin Nano devkit. There is no SD card image any more: the system is installed from an ISO image or from an x86 host. The ISO does not switch to Super a board whose bootloader was flashed without the -super configuration an NVIDIA engineer's answer on the forum, June 2026 : such boards, including ones sold as the Super Developer Kit, list only the 7 and 15 W modes, and a mode set by hand with nvpmodel falls back to 15 W after a reboot. The sign: no -super suffix in /etc/nv_boot_control.conf . The fix is reflashing from an x86 host with the jetson-orin-nano-devkit-super configuration; check that sudo nvpmodel -q shows MAXN SUPER. Power and heat - Power the Jetson from a separate BEC or DC-DC converter on the main power bus with headroom, not from the flight controller; share ground with the Pixhawk. The battery-side current is I = P / η·U_min . The lab example: the module in the 25 W mode plus 5 W for the carrier board and camera, efficiency 0.9: on 4S at 13.2 V 3.3 V per cell 2.53 A, on 6S at 19.8 V 1.68 A; size the converter for 1.5 × 30 = 45 W a course guideline, as for the BEC in el-power-design . title: Vectors, matrices and rotations: the language of attitude
summary: Everything the autopilot says about attitude — the angles on the OSD, the quaternion in `ATT`/`AHRS`, the gravity vector in body axes, “where the camera is pointing” — comes down to a handful of linear algebra operations. This module gives you exactly those: a vector as an arrow and as a column of n
headings: A vector: an arrow and numbers Dot and cross products The rotation matrix Composition: order matters Euler angles and their singularity The quaternion Small rotations and the attitude derivative Coordinate frames to know by heart Step 1. The `rot.py` library Step 2. Gravity in body axes Step 3. Non-commutativity Step 4. Gyro integration
text: summary Everything the autopilot says about attitude — the angles on the OSD, the quaternion in ATT / AHRS , the gravity vector in body axes, “where the camera is pointing” — comes down to a handful of linear algebra operations. This module gives you exactly those: a vector as an arrow and as a column of numbers, the dot and cross products, a rotation matrix as “where the axes went”, composing rotations and why order matters, Euler angles and their singularity, the quaternion as a compact, singularity-free form of the same rotation, small rotations and the attitude derivative, and finally — the four coordinate frames people mix up most often NED/FRD in ArduPilot and PX4, ENU/FLU in ROS . Lab: a rot.py library of 14 functions, checked against scipy.spatial.transform . Not sure you need this elective? Take the 10-problem entry test ../pages/prerequisites.html . theory A vector: an arrow and numbers A vector is an arrow direction and length , and a column of numbers is its coordinates in a chosen basis . The same arrow “down toward the center of the Earth” is written as 0, 0, 9.81 in the NED basis, and as 0, 4.9, 8.5 in the axes of a vehicle rolled 30°. That's why every vector in code should be labeled with the axes it's expressed in: g_ned , a_body . Most attitude bugs are a vector in one basis used as if it were in another. Length: v = √ v·v . Unit vector: v/ v . A basis is three mutually perpendicular unit vectors; it's right-handed if x × y = z thumb x, index finger y, middle finger z of your right hand . Dot and cross products The dot product a·b = a b cos θ = aₓbₓ + a_yb_y + a_zb_z. It's “how much of a lies along b”. Uses: projecting thrust onto the vertical T·ẑ , the angle between vectors, checking perpendicularity = 0 . The vehicle's tilt from vertical: cos θ = g_body· 0,0,1 / g_body . The cross product a × b is a vector perpendicular to both, with length a b sin θ and direction by the right-hand rule. Components: a_yb_z − a_zb_y, a_zbₓ − aₓb_z, aₓb_y − a_yb_x . Uses: torque M = r × F lever arm times force — this is exactly how motor torques are computed in the mixer , the velocity of a point v = ω × r, the normal to a plane. It's anticommutative: b × a = − a × b . The rotation matrix A rotation is a linear transformation that preserves lengths and angles. Its matrix R 3×3 has these properties: Rᵀ R = I the columns are orthonormal , det R = +1. The set of such matrices is the group SO 3 . The most useful reading: the columns of R are the axes of the rotated basis, written in the original one . If R_nb takes you from body to NED v_ned = R_nb · v_body , then the first column of R_nb is where the vehicle's nose points in NED coordinates. The inverse rotation is the transpose: R⁻¹ = Rᵀ. So v_body = R_nbᵀ · v_ned, and there should be no matrix inversions in attitude code at all. Elementary rotations about the axes angle φ, right-hand rule — a positive rotation is counterclockwise when viewed from the tip of the axis : Rx φ = 1, 0, 0 , 0, cos φ, −sin φ , 0, sin φ, cos φ Ry θ = cos θ, 0, sin θ , 0, 1, 0 , −sin θ, 0, cos θ Rz ψ = cos ψ, −sin ψ, 0 , sin ψ, cos ψ, 0 , 0, 0, 1 Composition: order matters Rotations don't commute: Rx 90° ·Ry 90° ≠ Ry 90° ·Rx 90° — check it with a cube or in the lab. The rule for reading a product R = A·B·v: B is applied to the vector first, then A. The aerospace Euler angle sequence “yaw → pitch → roll” ZYX gives the matrix from body to NED: R_nb = Rz ψ · Ry θ · Rx φ Read it like this: a vector in body axes is first “unwound” in roll, then in pitch, then in yaw — and you get it in NED. In ArduPilot code this is Matrix3f::from_euler roll, pitch, yaw , in PX4 — matrix::Dcmf matrix::Eulerf ... . {{diagram:rot-order-noncommute Rx 90° ·Ry 90° and Ry 90° ·Rx 90° take 1, 0, 0 to different vectors — 0, 1, 0 and 0, 0, −1 : the right factor acts first.}} {{diagram:frames-rotations Coordinate frames: NED and FRD ArduPilot, PX4 versus ENU and FLU ROS . The same vehicle, different axis labels — and different signs for “up”.}} Euler angles and their singularity The angles roll φ, pitch θ, yaw ψ are convenient for humans and useless as an internal representation: at θ = ±90° the roll and yaw axes coincide gimbal lock , and you can't uniquely recover φ and ψ from the matrix — only their sum or difference. Ranges: φ ∈ −180°, 180° , θ ∈ −90°, 90° , ψ ∈ −180°, 180° the OSD usually shows heading as 0–360° . Extracting them from the matrix: θ = −asin R₃₁ , φ = atan2 R₃₂, R₃₃ , ψ = atan2 R₂₁, R₁₁ — atan2 , not atan , or you'll lose the quadrant. For aerobatics, a wing in vertical hover and any state estimation, Euler angles are not used inside the filter. The quaternion A quaternion q = w, x, y, z = cos α/2 , n ·sin α/2 encodes a rotation by angle α about the unit axis n . Four numbers instead of nine, one normalization instead of six orthogonality conditions, and no singularity. Operations: - The conjugate q = w, −x, −y, −z is the inverse rotation for a unit quaternion . - The product q₁ ⊗ q₂ is the composition of rotations q₂ first, then q₁, like with matrices, under the Hamilton convention : w = w₁w₂ − x₁x₂ − y₁y₂ − z₁z₂; x = w₁x₂ + x₁w₂ + y₁z₂ − z₁y₂; y = w₁y₂ − x₁z₂ + y₁w₂ + z₁x₂; z = w₁z₂ + x₁y₂ − y₁x₂ + z₁w₂. - Rotating a vector: v' = q ⊗ 0, v ⊗ q . In practice it's faster through the matrix: R q with elements R₁₁ = 1 − 2 y² + z² , R₁₂ = 2 xy − wz , R₁₃ = 2 xz + wy and so on. - q and −q are the same rotation double cover . That's why you look at the sign of the dot product when comparing and interpolating quaternions. - Normalize after every update, otherwise rounding errors accumulate and the “rotation” starts to scale. ArduPilot stores attitude in the EKF as a quaternion Quaternion in AP_Math , in the log — XKQ ; PX4 — vehicle_attitude.q in w, x, y, z order. ROS 2 geometry_msgs/Quaternion uses x, y, z, w order. A swapped order is a classic companion integration bug. Small rotations and the attitude derivative For a small angle δ: sin δ ≈ δ, cos δ ≈ 1, and a rotation by the ve

title: Differential equations and dynamics: from the motor to the loop
summary: PID tuning “by eye” ends where understanding *what exactly* you are tuning begins. This module gives you the minimal toolkit: the first-order equation and the time constant (motor, filter, delay mixed with inertia), the second-order equation and its three regimes (overdamped, critically damped, unde
headings: The first-order equation The second-order equation Poles: the address of behavior The transfer function Discretization: formulas for firmware Delay versus inertia Step 1. One axis with a PID in numpy Step 2. Motor τ from a log Step 3. Discretization
text: summary PID tuning “by eye” ends where understanding what exactly you are tuning begins. This module gives you the minimal toolkit: the first-order equation and the time constant motor, filter, delay mixed with inertia , the second-order equation and its three regimes overdamped, critically damped, underdamped , poles as the “address” of a system's behavior on the complex plane, the transfer function as a way to assemble blocks by multiplication, and — the thing without which no formula ever makes it into firmware — discretization: Euler, Tustin, what you lose at a 1/8000 s step and at 1/50 s. Lab: a numerical model of one quadcopter axis with a PID, which you will compare with the pid-sim widget and with a real motor response from a log. theory The first-order equation The most common model in a drone: τ·ẋ + x = K·u. This is how motor thrust responds to an ESC command, and how an RC filter output, temperature or a capacitor's charge behave. The solution for a step input u = 1 from zero: x t = K· 1 − e^ −t/τ . In time τ the output covers 63 % of the way, in 3τ — 95 %, in 5τ — 99 %. The time constant τ is the only dynamics parameter; it's also called “motor delay”, although it isn't a delay but inertia: the motor starts responding immediately, just smoothly. How to find τ from a log: on a command step, find the moment where the response reaches 63 % of the steady-state value. For a 5" motor with a prop τ ≈ 15–30 ms, for a 15" — 80–150 ms. It's τ that limits how “aggressive” you can make the D-term: D amplifies high frequencies, and the motor can't follow them anyway — it just heats up. The frequency side of the same equation: it's a low-pass filter with cutoff frequency f_c = 1/ 2πτ . A 100 Hz gyro filter means τ = 1.6 ms of “inertia” added to the loop. The second-order equation ẍ + 2ζω₀·ẋ + ω₀²·x = ω₀²·u. Two parameters: the natural frequency ω₀ rad/s and the damping ratio ζ. - ζ 1 — overdamped: creeps up slowly without overshoot. - ζ = 1 — critically damped: the fastest arrival without overshoot. - 0 < ζ < 1 — underdamped: overshoot and decaying oscillations at frequency ω₀√ 1 − ζ² ; overshoot in percent ≈ 100·e^ −πζ/√ 1 − ζ² ζ = 0.5 → 16 %, ζ = 0.7 → 5 % . - ζ = 0 — undamped oscillations; ζ < 0 — instability, the amplitude grows. A quadcopter axis with an angle PD controller is exactly this equation: inertia J·θ̈ = torque, torque = K_p· θ_target − θ − K_d·θ̇. Then ω₀ = √ K_p/J , ζ = K_d/ 2√ K_p·J . This gives the rule every tuner knows without knowing the formula: raise P — the oscillations get faster and the overshoot grows; raise D — the overshoot drops. The I-term, in turn, adds a third order and can turn ζ negative — low-frequency “I oscillations” with too much I. Poles: the address of behavior Any linear equation with constant coefficients has solutions of the form e^ st ; substituting gives the characteristic equation, and its roots s are the poles . A first-order system has one pole: s = −1/τ. A second-order one: s = −ζω₀ ± ω₀√ ζ² − 1 . Reading a pole map on the complex plane: - A negative real part — stable; the further left, the faster it decays settling time ≈ 4/ Re s . - The imaginary part is the oscillation frequency rad/s . - A pole in the right half-plane — instability: any error grows. - A pole on the imaginary axis — the boundary: undamped oscillations this is how a loop behaves with P raised until it self-oscillates . {{diagram:pole-response A pole map and the corresponding step responses: further left — faster, higher — more oscillatory, right of zero — growth.}} The transfer function For linear systems with zero initial conditions, differentiation in time turns into multiplication by s the Laplace transform . First order: G s = K/ τs + 1 . Second order: G s = ω₀²/ s² + 2ζω₀s + ω₀² . PID: C s = K_p + K_i/s + K_d·s. Blocks are combined by multiplication in series and by the closed-loop formula: T s = C·G/ 1 + C·G . The closed-loop poles are the roots of 1 + C s G s = 0: this is where the “right” PID values live. A pure delay packet transport, a filter is e^ −sL : it doesn't change the amplitude, but it shifts the phase by ω·L, and that's exactly what makes the loop unstable at high gains. Phase margin is how much more delay you can add before self-oscillation; on a well-tuned 5" combat quad it's 40–60°. Discretization: formulas for firmware The controller runs in ticks with period T_s Betaflight — PID loop 4–8 kHz, ArduPilot — 400 Hz, PX4 rate loop — 800 Hz by default, up to 2 kHz via IMU_GYRO_RATEMAX . Derivatives and integrals are replaced with differences: - Backward Euler : ẋ ≈ xₖ − xₖ₋₁ /T_s; ∫x ≈ Σ xₖ·T_s. Simple, but it adds a T_s/2 delay and distorts frequencies above f_s/10. - Tustin bilinear : s → 2/T_s · z − 1 / z + 1 . It preserves stability and the frequency response more accurately; all Betaflight filters biquad and PT1 are discretized exactly this way or through the exact RC filter formula. - A first-order PT1 in code: yₖ = yₖ₋₁ + k· xₖ − yₖ₋₁ , where k = T_s/ τ + T_s — this is the backward Euler transform, practically exact when f_c ≪ f_s. In Betaflight — pt1FilterGain . - What breaks with a large T_s: the Nyquist frequency f_s/2 — everything above it folds back aliases ; the derivative of noise grows as 1/T_s; with T_s comparable to τ, forward Euler can make a stable system unstable. Rule: the loop period should be no more than τ/10 of the fastest process the loop has to handle. {{diagram:chart-pt1-discrete-phase The larger the step, the further the phase of a discrete PT1 is from the continuous −26.6°; forward Euler departs first and is unstable at T_s 2τ ≈ 3.18 ms.}} Delay versus inertia People confuse them, but they're different: inertia τ is a smooth response that starts immediately; delay L is nothing happening, then an exact copy of the input. A loop with inertia can be “pushed” with gain almost without limit; a loop with delay can't: with gain K the phase margin gets eaten up, and at ω·L ≈ 1–1.5 rad the loop oscillates no matter what you do. title: Probability and estimation: noise, Gaussians, fusion
summary: The Kalman filter is not magic, it is two facts about Gaussian distributions applied a million times. This module gives you those facts and the language around them: a random variable, mean and variance, why sensor noise is treated as Gaussian, what independence and covariance are, what a covariance
headings: Random variable, mean, variance The Gaussian and why it is everywhere Two measurements of the same thing Vectors: covariance and the ellipse Noise over time: white, random walk, Allan deviation What of this is in the autopilot parameters Step 1. A gyro datasheet from a recording Step 2. Allan deviation Step 3. Fusion by hand Step 4. The ellipse
text: summary The Kalman filter is not magic, it is two facts about Gaussian distributions applied a million times. This module gives you those facts and the language around them: a random variable, mean and variance, why sensor noise is treated as Gaussian, what independence and covariance are, what a covariance matrix looks like as an ellipse and what “EKF variance” in a failsafe message means. The central result is the optimal fusion of two measurements, which is exactly one Kalman step. Then — how noise behaves over time: white noise, random walk, ARW/VRW and Allan deviation, which is how you read an IMU datasheet and pick EK3_GYRO_P_NSE . Lab: gyro noise and bias from a recording, Allan deviation, and a numeric problem on fusion. theory Random variable, mean, variance A sensor measurement is z = x + n: the true value plus noise. Noise is a random variable: we don't know the next value, but we know how the values are distributed. The mean μ = E n is the systematic part bias ; you can estimate it and subtract it. The variance σ² = E n − μ ² is the spread; σ the standard deviation is in the same units as the measurement. Sample estimates over N samples: μ̂ = 1/N Σzᵢ, σ̂² = 1/ N−1 Σ zᵢ − μ̂ ². For a gyro at rest μ̂ is the bias and σ̂ is the noise; both go into the sensor datasheet. The mean of N independent samples has variance σ²/N: averaging 100 samples reduces σ by a factor of 10. That is the limit of what “just filtering” gives you — and the reason slow sensors GPS at 5 Hz can't be made accurate by averaging over 0.2 s. The Gaussian and why it is everywhere The density of N μ, σ² : p x = 1/ σ√ 2π ·exp − x − μ ²/ 2σ² . Within ±1σ lie 68 % of the values, ±2σ — 95 %, ±3σ — 99.7 %. The innovation gates in the EKF EK3_ _I_GATE are exactly “reject everything farther than kσ”. The Gaussian arises from the central limit theorem: the sum of many small independent contributions thermal noise, vibration, quantization is distributed almost normally, whatever the individual contributions look like. The second argument is practical: a Gaussian is fully described by two numbers, and linear operations on Gaussians give Gaussians. For a filter that means the state can be stored as mean, covariance rather than as a histogram. Where the Gaussian model breaks: outliers GPS multipath, a magnetic anomaly — the tails are heavier than normal, hence the gates; quantization and saturation; noise that depends on the operating mode vibration under throttle . Two measurements of the same thing Measurements z₁ with variance σ₁² and z₂ with σ₂² of the same quantity x. The best minimum-variance, unbiased linear estimate weights them by inverse variances: x̂ = z₁/σ₁² + z₂/σ₂² / 1/σ₁² + 1/σ₂² , 1/σ̂² = 1/σ₁² + 1/σ₂². Rewritten with K = σ₁²/ σ₁² + σ₂² : x̂ = z₁ + K· z₂ − z₁ , σ̂² = 1 − K ·σ₁². Recognize it? z₁ is the prediction with uncertainty P, z₂ is the measurement with R, K is the Kalman gain, z₂ − z₁ is the innovation. One Kalman step is the fusion of two Gaussians. Everything else in the EKF is how to get the prediction and its P from the previous state model + process noise Q and how to do the same for a vector. {{diagram:gaussian-fusion Fusing two Gaussian estimates: the result is always narrower than either of them and shifted toward the more accurate one.}} Vectors: covariance and the ellipse For a state vector x for example, position N, E the covariance matrix is P = E x − μ x − μ ᵀ : the diagonal holds the variances of the components, the off-diagonal entries are covariances, that is, how strongly the errors are linked. The correlation ρ = P₁₂/ σ₁σ₂ ∈ −1, 1 . Geometrically P is an uncertainty ellipse: the axes lie along the eigenvectors of P, the semi-axes are √ eigenvalues . A GPS ellipse stretched along N says that north is known worse than east typical with poor satellite geometry . “EKF variance” in the ArduPilot failsafe is the normalized innovations the √test ratio of velocity, position, compass — the same numbers as in XKF4 exceeding FS_EKF_THRESH : the filter honestly admits it doesn't know where it is. A linear transform y = A·x carries the covariance as P_y = A·P·Aᵀ. This is the formula both for prediction A = F, the model matrix and for switching between coordinate frames A = R — the covariance rotates together with the ellipse . Independence: zero covariance, P is diagonal; that is exactly what you assume when you set EK3_ _NOISE with one number per source. {{diagram:cov-ellipse-rotation A 45° rotation turns the 2σ ellipse by the same 45°: the eigenvalues do not change, and the component variances become 0.725 and 5.525.}} Noise over time: white, random walk, Allan deviation White noise — the samples are independent; its integral is a random walk , whose σ grows as √t. For a gyro: the angular rate noise σ_g °/s per sample after integration gives an angle error σ_θ t = ARW·√t, where ARW = σ_g·√T_s angle random walk, in °/√h in datasheets . For an accelerometer it is VRW: the velocity error grows as √t, the position error as t^1.5. This explains why without GPS an IMU-only position drifts by meters in seconds, while the gyro angle holds for minutes. But the bias isn't constant either: it slowly wanders bias instability, flicker . Allan deviation σ τ — the standard deviation of the difference of averages over adjacent windows of length τ — separates these contributions on one plot: a slope of −½ white noise; ARW is read from it at τ = 1 s , a plateau bias instability — the best achievable bias stability , a slope of +½ rate random walk . This plot is what you use to pick the EKF process noise: EK3_GYRO_P_NSE is set in rad/s default 0.015 — with a large margin over the datasheet noise density, because it covers vibration and model errors , EK3_GBIAS_P_NSE — from the +½ slope. PX4: EKF2_GYR_NOISE , EKF2_GYR_B_NOISE . title: ROS 2 onboard: nodes, topics, QoS, tf2, bag
summary: ROS 2 isn't a “library for drones”, it's a way to build onboard software out of independent processes that talk over DDS. Its value for UAVs is ready-made nodes (cameras, lidars, SLAM, Nav2), common message types and debugging tools: recording and replaying all traffic, the node graph, visualization
headings: The graph: nodes, topics, services, actions QoS: why the subscription is silent Coordinate frames: REP-103 and REP-105 Time Launch and parameters ros2 bag Step 1. Environment Step 2. The graph by hand Step 3. Telemetry logger Step 4. Bag: record and replay Step 5. tf2
text: summary ROS 2 isn't a “library for drones”, it's a way to build onboard software out of independent processes that talk over DDS. Its value for UAVs is ready-made nodes cameras, lidars, SLAM, Nav2 , common message types and debugging tools: recording and replaying all traffic, the node graph, visualization. Its price is complexity: QoS, coordinate frames, time. This module gives you exactly the part of ROS 2 without which no offboard node will ever fly: the node graph, topics/services/actions, parameters and launch, QoS and why a subscription to PX4 “with defaults” stays silent, REP-103/105 and tf2 , simulation time and ros2 bag . Lab: a telemetry logger node, recording and replaying a bag, and working through a QoS incompatibility hands-on. The environment is examples/ros2-docker/ . theory The graph: nodes, topics, services, actions - A node is a process or part of a process with a name, parameters and interfaces. Design rule: one node — one responsibility bridge, perception, decision, safeguard . - A topic is a “one-to-many” stream of messages of one type; publishers and subscribers don't know about each other. Telemetry, setpoints, images. - A service is request-response ArmMotors , ModeSwitch . The semantics are synchronous, but inside a node you must call it asynchronously call_async , otherwise you can block your own executor. - An action is a long-running goal with feedback and cancellation NavigateToPose in Nav2 . It's topics + services assembled into a protocol. - Parameters are typed node settings ros2 param set /node alt 7.0 , with a validation callback on change. DDS finds participants on the network by itself discovery within a single ROS_DOMAIN_ID . On an aircraft with a companion and a laptop on the same Wi-Fi network, this means: without separate domains or filters, the laptop will “see” the vehicle's topics and be able to publish to them. For field flights — a separate domain, or better, ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE=LOCALHOST Jazzy; in Humble — ROS_LOCALHOST_ONLY=1 on board and a bridge to the outside only for the topics you need. {{diagram:ros2-graph The training system as a graph: the bridge to the autopilot, the logger, the state machine, perception and the watchdog are separate nodes.}} QoS: why the subscription is silent Every publisher and subscriber has a QoS profile: reliability RELIABLE/BEST_EFFORT , durability VOLATILE/TRANSIENT_LOCAL — whether a late subscriber gets the last message , history/depth how much to keep , deadline, lifespan, liveliness. A connection is established only with compatible profiles, and an incompatibility doesn't raise an error — the subscriber simply receives nothing an “incompatible QoS” warning may show up in the log . The main rule: BEST_EFFORT publisher + RELIABLE subscriber = no connection. PX4 publishes /fmu/out/ as BEST_EFFORT and TRANSIENT_LOCAL , while a ROS 2 subscriber is RELIABLE by default. That's why you subscribe to PX4 with the qos_profile_sensor_data profile BEST_EFFORT or an explicit QoSProfile . Why BEST_EFFORT for telemetry: when a packet is lost over Wi-Fi, resending an old position is useless, you need the next one — the same logic as UDP versus TCP in the mav-routing module. Check: ros2 topic info -v /fmu/out/vehicle_status_v1 shows the profiles of both sides. {{diagram:ros2-qos Reliability compatibility: a BEST_EFFORT publisher doesn't connect to a RELIABLE subscriber — silently.}} Coordinate frames: REP-103 and REP-105 ROS lives in ENU world and FLU body — REP-103; autopilots live in NED/FRD. This is the main source of integration bugs module math-linalg-rot : x/y swap places, z changes sign, yaw ψ_enu = 90° − ψ_ned, quaternions in ROS are stored as x, y, z, w . REP-105 defines the standard frames: map global, drift-free, can jump , odom continuous, drifts , base_link body . The bridges handle this differently: AP_DDS publishes directly in ENU/FLU poses with frame_id = base_link , cmd_vel accepted in map or base_link , PX4 uXRCE-DDS publishes in NED/FRD, as inside PX4, and the conversion is on your side. tf2 is a tree of transforms between frames over time: “where was the camera relative to map at the moment of the frame”. A node publishes TransformStamped to /tf dynamic and /tf_static sensor mounts , and a consumer asks lookup_transform target, source, time . A camera on a bracket is the static transform base_link → camera_link ; you set it once in the launch file. Time Every message with a header has a header.stamp . In simulation, time runs from /clock the parameter use_sim_time:=true , otherwise the nodes and the bag live in different times, and tf2 refuses to give transforms “from the future”. PX4 uses its own timestamps in microseconds timestamp and synchronizes them with the agent; ArduPilot publishes /ap/time and /ap/clock . Launch and parameters A launch file Python starts a set of nodes with parameters, namespaces and topic remapping remappings . This is what runs on board at startup: systemd service → ros2 launch . Parameters go in a YAML file, not in the code — so that the same package works on two different vehicles. ros2 bag ros2 bag record -o run1 /topic1 /topic2 writes the traffic to a file in Jazzy the default is MCAP, in Humble — SQLite3; the format is set with the -s flag ; ros2 bag play run1 replays it, and your nodes can't tell the replay from a flight. This is the main debugging tool: you recorded a flight with a bug — replay it and fix the node on the bench as many times as you like. Recording all topics with cameras on board quickly eats disk and CPU: record compressed images or at a reduced rate. practice Step 1. Environment bash cd examples/ros2-docker docker compose build ros docker compose run --rm ros bash ros2 doctor --report head -20 The image is built and tested in CI on ROS 2 Jazzy Ubuntu 24.04 inside the container, so the host can be on 22.04 as well . title: ROS 2 + PX4: uXRCE-DDS, an offboard node as a state machine
summary: The px4-ros2 module showed that PX4 “speaks” ROS 2 through the uXRCE-DDS bridge and that an offboard flight is three messages. Here you learn how to turn that into a node you can trust with a vehicle: `px4_msgs` message versions and the `_v<N>` suffixes, time synchronization, the Offboard rules (a “
headings: The uXRCE-DDS bridge Message versions Offboard rules Flight logic as a state machine Testing without a simulator Gazebo and SITL Step 1. Test the state machine Step 2. A square in Gazebo Step 3. Safeguards in the simulator Step 4. Replay from a bag
text: summary The px4-ros2 module showed that PX4 “speaks” ROS 2 through the uXRCE-DDS bridge and that an offboard flight is three messages. Here you learn how to turn that into a node you can trust with a vehicle: px4_msgs message versions and the _v<N suffixes, time synchronization, the Offboard rules a “proof of life” stream 2 Hz, setpoints before the mode switch , and most importantly, the flight logic as a state machine with no ROS inside, testable with plain pytest. The node becomes a thin wrapper: collect observations → step the state machine → execute the action. Lab: a square in Gazebo with safeguards position loss, stale status, pilot intervention , a test of the state machine against a toy vehicle model, and a flight replay from a bag. theory The uXRCE-DDS bridge Inside PX4 runs the client uxrce_dds_client : it publishes the selected uORB topics and subscribes to incoming ones according to the list in dds_topics.yaml in the PX4 sources . Outside runs the agent MicroXRCEAgent , which exposes these topics on the DDS network as ordinary ROS 2 topics /fmu/out/ from PX4 and /fmu/in/ to PX4 . The transport is UDP SITL: the agent on port 8888, the client starts automatically or a serial port UXRCE_DDS_CFG selects the port on a real flight controller . Unlike MAVLink, there are no “protocol messages” here — these are the PX4 uORB structures themselves, hence the requirement: px4_msgs on the ROS side must match the PX4 version . {{diagram:uxrce-scheme PX4 and ArduPilot connect to ROS 2 with the same scheme: “client in the firmware — agent on the companion.”}} Message versions Starting with PX4 v1.16, some messages have a version MESSAGE_VERSION in the definition , and their topics are published with a suffix: /fmu/out/vehicle_status_v1 . To keep old nodes compatible with new firmware and vice versa there is a translator node PX4 ROS 2 Message Translation Node . Practice for your own nodes: compute the topic name from the message class's MESSAGE_VERSION instead of typing it by hand — as done in px4_offboard_square.py : python def topic base, msg_cls : v = getattr msg_cls, "MESSAGE_VERSION", 0 return base if v == 0 else f"{base}_v{v}" Offboard rules 1. The external controller must continuously send OffboardControlMode which setpoints are active: position, velocity, acceleration, attitude, body_rate… well above 2 Hz the docs name 2 Hz; in the code PX4 loses the signal when the last message's timestamp is older than COM_OF_LOSS_T , see px4-ros2 — this is the “proof of life.” The actual setpoints go in TrajectorySetpoint position/velocity/acceleration/yaw, unused fields = NaN . 2. The stream must be running before the switch to Offboard and before arming in Offboard , otherwise PX4 refuses. 3. If the stream stops for longer than COM_OF_LOSS_T , PX4 leaves Offboard and switches to the mode set in COM_OBL_RC_ACT Position, Altitude, Manual, Return, Land . 4. Commands are VehicleCommand on /fmu/in/vehicle_command : arm with VEHICLE_CMD_COMPONENT_ARM_DISARM param1 = 1 , mode with VEHICLE_CMD_DO_SET_MODE param1 = 1 — custom, param2 = 6 — Offboard , land with VEHICLE_CMD_NAV_LAND . The acknowledgement comes on /fmu/out/vehicle_command_ack ; the state is in VehicleStatus.arming_state , nav_state . 5. Coordinates in TrajectorySetpoint are NED, local , with the origin at the EKF initialization point; altitude is negative. Flight logic as a state machine A typical mistake is logic in callbacks: “status arrived → if armed → send mode.” Such code can't be tested, can't be reproduced, and behaves unpredictably when messages are lost. The right way: a pure class OffboardFSM examples/ros2-docker/.../offboard_fsm.py with a single method step obs → action , no ROS and no time pulled “out of thin air”: - Observations Obs : time, age of the last status, position validity, armed, mode, NED position, whether landed. - Action Action : setpoint, arm/mode/land requests, a note. - States : WAIT_READY → STREAM_SETPOINTS ≥ 1 s of setpoints before the mode request → ARMING → OFFBOARD → TAKEOFF → SQUARE → LAND → DONE. - Safeguards checked in every active state : status stale 1 s → ABORT; position invalid → ABORT; step timeout → ABORT; pilot switched the mode themselves → DONE with no commands don't “fight” the human . The ROS node does only I/O: it builds Obs from the latest messages on a 20 Hz timer, calls step , publishes setpoints and rate-limited commands. The same state machine is used for ArduPilot the ros2-ardupilot module — only the wrapper changes. {{diagram:offboard-fsm Offboard node state machine: a linear scenario plus safeguards that lead to landing or hand control back to the pilot.}} Testing without a simulator test_offboard_fsm.py runs the state machine against a toy vehicle model arms on request, enters Offboard only if setpoints have been flowing for ≥ 0.5 s, flies to the setpoint at 2 m/s, lands : it checks the full scenario, the “setpoints before mode” order, and the reaction to position loss, stale status and pilot intervention. That's five tests in 50 ms — you can run them on every commit in this course, in CI , and only then go to Gazebo. Gazebo and SITL make px4_sitl gz_x500 — the x500 quadcopter in Gazebo Harmonic; the PX4 documentation main recommends ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04; on Ubuntu 22.04, Humble the same is stated in the v1.16/v1.17 release documentation . Agent: MicroXRCEAgent udp4 -p 8888 . For repeatable tests — headless HEADLESS=1 and a fixed world. QGroundControl connects over UDP 14550 in parallel — it's handy for watching modes and aborting the flight. practice Step 1. Test the state machine bash cd examples/ros2-docker/ws/src/uav_ros2_labs python -m pytest -q test/test_offboard_fsm.py Add your own test: battery a new field battery_low in Obs → ABORT. Test first, then code. Step 2. A square in Gazebo bash docker compose --profile px4 up or natively: MicroXRCEAgent + make px4_sitl gz_x500 ros2 launch uav_ros2_labs px4_square.launch.py The node log shows the state transitions; QGC shows
